column4: Disinflationary environments are when to look at sectors that were ‘left for dead’: Strategist
column10: [Great Hill Capital Chairman and Managing Member Thomas Hayes sits down with Yahoo Finance Live to discuss oil production, market outlooks amid Fed rate hikes, and Santa Claus rallies expected this year.Video TranscriptDAVE BRIGGS: Let's touch all those topics and go in reverse order and start with oil, which continues to move down despite the price cap and the EU sanctions, reflecting what?THOMAS HAYES: Well, I think one thing that no one's really talking about these days is the US rig count. And the US rig count is at 784 total rig count. Pre-pandemic, it was at 790. So while everyone's been focused on Russia, and they've been focused on production abroad from OPEC, they've kind of failed to focus on the production in the US has come back and has come back in spades. So I do think that supply is going to continue to come online, and we're seeing it reflected in prices.SEANA SMITH: And Tom, just more broadly speaking, where we stand right now in the equity markets with the final trading weeks of the year ahead of us, the fifth down day in a row for the S&P. How does this set us up not only for the next couple of weeks, but as we look ahead to next year?THOMAS HAYES: Well, there's a buyer strike. It's a low volume buyer strike right now, but there will be no Grinch. I think Santa Claus is going to come to town the last couple of weeks. But we're in a holding pattern waiting for the data. So we got the strong jobs report. Market didn't like that. We got the strong ISM services. The market didn't like that.But as we look forward to PPI on Friday and CPI on Tuesday, just before the Fed meeting, I think those numbers are going to come in better than expected, meaning lower than expected. And you need only look at the 10-year yield. I mean, it's telling us that there's a slowdown. It's telling us that the Fed is near the end of their job. I mean, today, the 10-year yield was down to 3.43. And that's just telling us that it's a disinflationary environment moving forward. And in disinflationary environments, you want to start to look at the things that people have left for dead-- communication services, tech, et cetera, and emerging markets, with the dollar starting to weaken.Story continuesDAVE BRIGGS: So you suspect that the sleigh that brings Santa will be the CPI data we get next week?THOMAS HAYES: Yeah, I think it's going to be the PPI, I think it's going to be the CPI. The key is going to be the dot plot, though. That's what I think is the biggest concern. The terminal rate at the last meeting in September was 4.6%. That's probably going to tick a little higher, hopefully 4.8, 4.9, nothing over 5-- that would spook the market. And in that case, Santa will have a sleigh full of presents for sure.SEANA SMITH: And Tom, speaking of spooking the market, lots of debate about whether or not we're going to be in a-- if we are already in a recession, if we're going to see a recession next year. Citi CEO Jane Fraser making some comments about that, expecting a recession next year. Where do you stand on this? Any difference from last time?THOMAS HAYES: Yeah, well, if you look at the last six cycles since 1957, there's a lot of pessimism in the market. Everyone's saying earnings are going to come down another 10% or 20% because we're going to have a recession. But in each instance, since 1957, the stock market bottomed 6 to 12 months before earnings bottomed.So if you buy all the pessimism that earnings are going to come down another 10%, you shouldn't be buying a new leg lower. You should be buying stocks because history shows us by the time earnings trough, the S&P 500 has made up most of the losses. Why is that? We know the market is a discounting mechanism. So this year, we discounted a lot of slowdown with a 33% peak to trough in the NASDAQ, 25% peak to trough in the S&P. This is not a time to buy wholesale to buy the S&P, but it is the time to buy selected opportunity. And there's a ton of it out there.DAVE BRIGGS: OK. What is it? What stocks? What sectors?THOMAS HAYES: Well, what do people want the least of right now, I would say tech. And if you look at the 10-year yield that's telling us a slowdown and what companies can actually generate earnings in a slowdown is historically tech. Amazon is trading at 2018 prices. The difference between now and 2018 is their ad business and their Amazon Web Service Cloud business have both tripled in those four years. The e-commerce business has doubled. Their Prime members have gone from 100 million to 163 million. And you can buy it at four year ago prices. So that's kind of interesting to us.The other thing, what's everyone been hot on this year has been energy. Well, if you look to next year's estimates for earnings, the worst performing sector in terms of earnings growth is going to be energy, with negative double digits, negative 10% or 11%. The best performing sector in terms of earnings, which no one wants to touch with a 10-foot pole, is communication services. And that's going to grow 35%. And consumer discretionary is going to grow, which also no one wants to touch with a 10-foot pole. They're growing off of low bases. And that's what we like.SEANA SMITH: So, Tom, when you're trying to identify some of those communication services names, also consumer discretionary, does it become more of a stock picker's type of market? Because there clearly are some winners or losers once you drill down into those two sectors.THOMAS HAYES: Unquestionably. You know, Warren Buffett says if you wait for the robins to sing, it's already spring. While everyone was sucking their thumbs, waiting for China to invade Taiwan, he was in buying $4 billion of Taiwan Semiconductor. So we like, whether it's Amazon down 55%, Disney's down 55%, that's an absolute no brainer when you look three years out. Taiwan Semiconductors down. KWEB, the China internet ETF, down 70%.There are only so many times in a lifetime or in a generation that you get an opportunity. The tech wreck was one when tech was down 80%. The KWEB was down peak to trough more than 80%. And then you go back to the Great Depression, buying the Dow Jones, down 80% in 1932. These are generational opportunities.The government has come out. They've pivoted on the COVID-zero policy. And they just came out in the last 24 hours and said, we're going to do forceful monetary and fiscal stimulus in 2023. No one believes them because we haven't seen it in the last 24 months. But when they say forceful historically, that's meaningful. And they don't have the inflation pressures that we have because they've been buying all the oil from Russia. They've got tons of storage of oil. They've got no inflationary pressure so that they can stimulate till the cows come home.DAVE BRIGGS: And no one is buying that China reopening because we've been sold this line a dozen times over the last couple of years. You are, though, this time. Why is it different?THOMAS HAYES: Well, I'll tell you what. I mean, you talked about Amazon. You can buy it at four year ago prices. You can buy Alibaba at its IPO prices from 2014. The only difference is, revenues are up 800% and earnings and cash flow are up 500%. This is a generational sale, and this is what the market does. It's a manic depressive. It's bipolar on the upside. It's bipolar on the downside. And it's overshot. It's back down to 58.DAVE BRIGGS: Are you talking about me?THOMAS HAYES: I'm talking about Mr. Market. As Ben Graham taught us and Warren Buffett has reiterated for many years, these are the opportunities that life serves up. And you have to seize them when they're there because if you look at the growth trajectory of Alibaba, their digitization, their Ali Cloud business is where AWS was in 2016. So this is going to be a monster opportunity. If you look at all the reports, they've got 38% share of the cloud business. It's going to triple by 2025. And we think that's a great opportunity.SEANA SMITH: And Tom, real quick, before we let you go here, what's your outlook when it comes to the jobs markets and the layoffs that we have seen? It started in tech. We started to see that kind of trickle out, kind of had a ripple effect throughout other industries. Something to be worried about, or more so, the correction that not so much that the Fed predicted, but I think many on the Street have been bracing for?THOMAS HAYES: Yeah, I think the contradiction in 2023, in our view, is that the stock market is going to get better. And the economy is going to get a little bit worse because we've discounted a lot of the pain. So I think the Fed will be successful in terms of they said they wanted unemployment to go up a little bit. I think we will see a four handle on that, maybe mid 4's max. It really depends how quickly they stop. We know we've got 50 in the bag in December.Question is February. There's a lot of data points between now and February. It could be 25 and done. I know that's not in the market. It's more like 50 and then maybe another 25. But we'll see. Two months of data points is an awful lot. And if that 10-year is right, I think we're going to see some disinflationary data, as we saw with the Manheim Used Car Index today.]

column4: Gas prices in summer 2023 ‘contingent on if refineries will meet demand’: Analyst
column10: [GasBuddy Head of Petroleum Analysis Patrick De Haan joins Yahoo Finance Live to examine forecasts for household gasoline spending in 2023, while also looking at the outlook for refinery capacities and regional pricing trends in the U.S.Video TranscriptJARED BLIKRE: Pain at the pump has been a major talking point throughout 2022, but as prices have been dropping this month, are they poised to jump back in the near future? Well, according to GasBuddy, prices in most US cities could reach $4 a gallon again come springtime. So for more on this, we welcome in Patrick De Haan, GasBuddy head of petroleum analysis. Patrick, thank you for joining us here today. So what should we expect with gas prices in the near future?PATRICK DE HAAN: Well, certainly a little bit of good news, a little bit of bad news. I think overall, the good news is that Americans in the household will spend less on gasoline in 2023 than they did in 2022. But it wouldn't be a normal year without the spikes that we see in spring and prices then going back down in fall. And eventually, while we're enjoying relatively low prices now, I'm afraid that with China reopening, this spring could see a nice spike. And that could bring the national average back above the $4 a gallon mark. But the good news is we're not expecting the record highs that we saw in 2022 of over the $5 a gallon level.SEANA SMITH: Yeah, Patrick, we just did-- Yahoo Finance Rick Newman was just on set talking about the predictions that our viewers wrote in. And that was one of the predictions that gas prices were going to be back above 4 bucks a gallon because of China lifting its restrictions. Let's talk, though, about the higher prices, how long it could potentially be above $4 a gallon. Are we talking about throughout next summer?PATRICK DE HAAN: I think that's certainly a strong possibility. It's really going to be contingent on if refineries are able to meet demand and what Americans do this summer, given the fact that prices may be lower. Do we see a big jump in demand? I think demand was struggling this summer under the weight of some of those high prices. So if a lot of Americans defer travel, they may want to get back out on the road, given the fact that gas prices this summer could be a little bit less.Story continuesBut I would say that probably between Memorial Day and Labor Day, you may see $4 a gallon for several weeks maybe beyond that. Of course, a lot mixed in to how China is looking and how much of their economy is reopening and what we see in terms of consumption from China.JARED BLIKRE: Patrick, we had a number of curveballs in 2022. You're opened up, and we have suddenly found ourselves in a war with-- embroiled in a war between Russia and Ukraine. Wondering what you're thinking about in terms of potential headwinds or stuff out of the blue in the new year.PATRICK DE HAAN: Well, I think refining will continue to be a headwind. It was a challenge in 2022. And I think we're going to get a little bit more breathing room in terms of refining capacity. Not so much in the US. We're going to add about 275,000 barrels a day of capacity, thanks to ExxonMobil's refining project that's been underway for three years in Texas. More so, we're going to get breathing room overseas. Africa opening refineries, additional capacity in Asia, as well as the Middle East. All likely helping to create some breathing room, but there still could be the seasonal challenges related to the switchover to summer gasoline, as refiners carry out that maintenance.And keep in mind the extreme cold weather that we saw across the US last week also caused a lot of refinery disruptions. So that's going to be the wild card this year, as well as I think China's economy. They appear to be embracing easing the restrictions. And so there could be a level of pent-up demand in China that we saw here in the US a couple of years ago. And that could be a wild card as well.SEANA SMITH: And Patrick, when it comes to higher prices in terms of areas of the country that are likely to see the highest prices, is that going to be consistent with what we saw last year when you take a look at California, obviously, being one of the outliers and experiencing much higher prices than what we saw in many other parts?PATRICK DE HAAN: Yeah, absolutely. The motto last year was certainly that the coasts felt a lot more of the pain, particularly the mid-Atlantic, the Northeast areas that are reliant on more imports, and the West Coast also somewhat segmented away from the rest of the country. So both the extremes, the Northeast and the West Coast, likely to see some of those refinery challenges persist. California certainly could see the return of $5, even $6, a gallon gasoline if refinery issues are significant this year. Much of the Northeast still also reliant on imports because of Russia's war in Ukraine. A lack of refining capacity in the Northeast also could point to prices that in New York, areas of New England could exceed $5 a gallon again this year.JARED BLIKRE: We're just recovering here in the Northeast from a bitter cold spell, a storm that passed through. Just wondering the implications that this might have had on the energy market overall, including heating, gas prices. Kind of give you the floor for the last question here.PATRICK DE HAAN: Well, we've seen a lot of volatility in natural gas. Things have really plummeted, but there's still the possibility that if natural gas surges due to cold spells, there could be switches back over to using oil, diesel and heating oil. So that's a huge wildcard, but the Northeast is going to be very susceptible to bouts of cold weather. Keep in mind much of the Northeast consumes heating oil. I think that's going to be a challenge this winter. Diesel and heating oil likely to remain rather expensive, comparing that to gasoline, for much of the winter.SEANA SMITH: All right, Patrick De Haan, always great to have you of GasBuddy. Thanks so much for joining us here this afternoon.]

column4: Oil: $70-$90 range is ‘somewhere we’re going to be’ for first two quarters of 2023, analyst says
column10: [Prosper Trading Academy CEO Scott Bauer joins Yahoo Finance Live to discuss predictions for oil prices in 2023, driving factors for energy stocks and commodities, and the outlook for demand.Video TranscriptJARED BLIKRE: Russia threatening to cut oil output by up to 7% or up to 700,000 barrels per day in response to sanctions and price caps placed on Russian oil in response to the country's invasion of Ukraine. Oil trading, we can see that's up about $2.70-- or 2.76% today, up about $2.00 and change. Just closing in on that $80 per barrel price level.Now we have Scott Bauer, CEO of Prosper Training Academy joining us. And, Scott, I was just reeling off the latest price of oil here. We bounced off $70. Now that's basis WTI here. We had-- and I think that was earlier in the month when we were first getting those actual sanctions by Russia pegged-- I guess plowed on, and now we really didn't see much of the way in negative price action from there. In fact, we're up about $8. Just wondering how you're viewing the oil market in response to this latest news.SCOTT BAUER: Yeah, I have been bullish oil ever since we've started dropping below $100 and buying it on every dip, selling it on any sort of rally here. I've had to get stopped out a couple of times, but $70, $71, Jared, that really, to me, is a short-term bottom. When I say short term, I'm saying at least six months.The floor is put in for a number of reasons. First off, that's where, you know, the administration has said we're going to replenish SPR if we get down there. So to me, that is somewhat of a floor.Also, I think there's just still a tremendous amount of tailwinds in the space here. Number one, as it has been for me all year is what's going on in Russia/Ukraine. Number two is what's going on in China, and I believe that we-- the oil market, anyway, has seen the worst-case scenario in terms of demand, in terms of lockdowns, even with the latest, you know, policy that they've talked about with kind of opening back up and people getting COVID. I think we've seen the worst in terms of demand. It's only going to get higher from here.Story continuesSo there are just a bunch of tailwinds, and that $70 number to me, because of the SPR, that absolutely is a floor.JARED BLIKRE: Yes, President Biden talked about buying oil at $70 per barrel for the SPR to replenish it from those-- from the lower levels that it's fallen to.Now you mentioned the double whammy this year, and we were talking about price bottoms. What about a ceiling? What would it take to see a ceiling in terms of the news flow, in terms of price action? What are you thinking about as you think about those upper targets here?SCOTT BAUER: It absolutely would not surprise me to see oil back in the $90s with a nine handle. To break $100, though, I think is going to be a real tough job. I just don't see any scenario other than-- other than some more major geopolitical conflict that we're going to see oil just get to those prices again. And listen, that's not out of the question-- out of the question, unfortunately. That can happen. But I think this range of the low $70s probably to the mid $90s is somewhere we're going to be for, you know, at least the first and second quarter of the year.JARED BLIKRE: All right, and what about natural gas and some of the other elements to the energy sector? We've seen natural gas prices drop off quite precipitously. That has its own supply-and-demand aspects, but maybe you can just comment on that market a little bit.SCOTT BAUER: It absolutely does. And, in fact, if you're looking at what's going on in Russia right now and the news that they announced that they might be pulling back production here, that is really just for crude and oil products. It is not for natural gas.So I know that, especially in Europe, there has been a shortage. But right now, I'm not going to say it's fine, but the natural-gas supply right now is not as dire, if you will, as what we're seeing on the crude side. And again, if we turn back to Russia, 40%-- almost 40% of all of their export revenues are from the oil space, not from natural gas.So natural gas is still flowing. I don't see that we're going to get a major, major spike again, certainly not to where we were. UMG, which I track very closely, is trading right around $15 and 1/2, $16 right now, which is a low we've seen in probably three, four months. That was as high as the mid $30s just a couple months ago. Maybe we see a 15%, 20% pop in natural gas from here just because of this massive selloff that we've had, but I don't think that we're going to get into the crunch like we might get with crude [AUDIO OUT].JARED BLIKRE: Well, we've been talking about the Russian-- I guess the Russian effect on crude-oil supplies. It seems to me when we-- this doesn't-- this hasn't had necessarily bearish price-action consequences when we talk about crude oil this year, and I think part of it comes from the fact that we have dark supplies so that you never see oil taken off the market considerably. You see a market-clearing price. So at some price, somebody is going to take Russian oil off the market.Just wondering, with all the sanctions in place, with all the eyeballs on this, what are the potentials for violations of that next year? What are some of the situations that could evolve that could actually be bearish for the price of energy that might not be factored in right now?SCOTT BAUER: So in all honesty, there's probably violations going on right now, and there will continue [AUDIO OUT] violations going on. Some of that's just going to be-- let's call it glanced over. But we're not going to see, in my opinion, the price get much below $60, which is that price cap there. Maybe we'll see it a little bit. But that is a number that the G-7 came up with to hopefully reduce Russian export revenue but a price high enough to keep it flowing to the market.So yes, there's always, always, you know, some underhanded deals out there. And when you're looking at, really, the four countries that are really still in the market buying Russian oil, you're looking at Bulgaria, China, India, and Turkey. You've got to think that there's [AUDIO OUT] be some violation there.JARED BLIKRE: Yeah, well, I love doing a deep dive on the oil market and the futures markets on the day before Christmas Eve here. Thank you for joining us, Scott Bauer.]

column4: Oil forecasts see prices at $80-96 per barrel next year
column10: [Yahoo Finance’s Ines Ferre joins the Live show to discuss how oil futures are performing in intraday trading as well as the expectations for oil going into 2023.Video TranscriptJULIE HYMAN: It's been a roller coaster ride for oil prices this year in the wake of Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Is this volatility set to bleed into next year? Yahoo Finance's Ines Ferre is here with a look ahead. Hi, Ines.INES FERRE: Hi, Julie. Hard to believe that earlier this year, we saw oil at just above $130 a barrel. Right now, we're looking at WTI around $80 and Brent crude at $83. But where will these oil prices be next year? Well, I asked several analysts, and let's put up a board so you can see some of the projections for 2023.You've got Ed Morse from Citi projecting that Brent crude will average around $80 per barrel, with WTI averaging $75 a barrel. JPMorgan says that Brent will average around $90 a barrel next year. And then you've got OPIS over at Dow Jones that are saying that Brent is going to be anywhere between $95 and $96, with WTI at around 90.Now several factors are assuming this, though. That supply grows with projects in Norway, in Brazil, Argentina, Mexico, US, Canada. Also the successful reopening of China, and also Western nations able to avoid a severe recession because there are many projections of a recession. But if that recession is severe, then, of course, that would impact demand, guys.BRIAN SOZZI: Ines, you're also tracking some supply news from Russia.INES FERRE: Yeah, that's right. Well, Russia now threatening to cut production of around anywhere between 500,000 and 700,000 barrels a day. And that's why you're seeing crude oil today jumping quite a bit. WTI up 3%-- part of the reason Brent crude up 3%. And that's in response to the G7 price cap of those $60 per barrel.And something interesting, though, some data from Bloomberg that was looking at tanker data in the first week that this measure took in effect, as well as the EU maritime ban of Russian imports-- that first week, you had imports total volumes shipped out of Russia down 54%. Now that's only one week. So you can't really go by one week's data. And there are some other factors that are involved here as well.But if this trend continues, then those measures may not be having the intended consequences that you'd want because what the consequences are of those measures is that Russia doesn't have as much money to fund the war.BRIAN SOZZI: Ines Ferre, thanks so much. Appreciate it.]

column4: Biden administration announces plan to replenish strategic petroleum reserve
column10: [Yahoo Finance Live's Jared Blikre details the Biden administration's goals to replenish strategic petroleum reserves and the Energy Department's latest barrel exchange.Video TranscriptJARED BLIKRE: Welcome back. The White House finally planning to replenish the SPR. That's the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Biden administration ordering 3 million barrels of crude oil to be delivered in February. However, they have a ways to go before they fully replace the 180 million barrels that were released so far.Energy Department also announcing a nearly 2 million barrel crude-oil exchange to relieve shortages at refineries after an oil spill last week shut down the Keystone crude pipeline.Oil futures closed today at $74.29, putting the price of crude well below the $96 a barrel the US sold the oil for originally.]

column4: Goldman Sachs says commodities are ‘underinvested’ with upside potential
column10: [Yahoo Finance anchors discuss a bullish note from Goldman Sachs on commodities.Video TranscriptRACHELLE AKUFFO: Commodities are key again. Goldman Sachs out with a new report calling commodities under-invested. Just as that market continues what the bank says is a supercycle, commodities are set to continue performing well because of supply constraints caused by things like the Russian invasion of Ukraine, even as CapEx or capital expenditure is down historically. So some interesting moves here, clearly taking this long view. Goldman saying that people really aren't thinking about the future right now. They're sort of looking at the present circumstances and not really thinking about investing for the long-term in this space.AKIKO FUJITA: Yeah, commodities the best performing asset class or on track to be the best performing asset class with just a few weeks left in the year. We're talking about a return of 20%. But I'm looking through these notes, Rachelle. I mean, Goldman is calling for a return of 43%, 43% in 2023. Specifically, they point to the economic growth that's set to rebound from China reopening.Of course, that's still a big question mark. It hasn't necessarily gone smoothly, although it's been just a few weeks here, but certainly that would boost demand. That would certainly help things in terms of the commodity side. And then that point that you just made, Rachelle, in terms of an underinvestment in CapEx, Goldman highlighting that specifically that there simply hasn't been that, even as we continue to see divestments from hydrocarbons.So those two key things, I mean, nobody's going to argue with the fact that this was the best performing asset class this year. But you have to wonder, I mean, how many of those factors all line up going into 2023? Obviously, what's happening between Russia and Ukraine still a big question mark. That has been a big reason behind the rally we've seen this year. But still, if you're talking about a 43% return, which is what Goldman is looking at, that's a pretty significant upside we're looking at next year.RACHELLE AKUFFO: And as you mentioned, a very big if when it comes to China's reopening. Every day, we're hearing about new cases and what the demand might look like. This still hasn't happened yet. The policy about changing zero-COVID only just kicked in. We still don't know what it's actually going to look like by this time next year and if China has the ability to get it under control. So I think a lot of countries are sort of looking at this China reopening story. A lot of hopes there, but we still actually don't have a clear picture of what that's going to look like at this point.AKIKO FUJITA: Yeah, I mean, if you're talking about, what, 3% growth this year, and yet, as we were saying earlier this week, potential projection of 5 and 1/2%-- at least, that's the aim going into 2023-- certainly, that would support the case for what Goldman is saying, but as you point out, still a lot of questions about how quickly things ease up and demand picks up over there.]

column4: Energy: ‘There’s a lot of longs’ ahead of China’s re-opening plans, analyst says
column10: [Blue Line Futures President Bill Baruch joins Yahoo Finance Live to weigh in on U.S. gas prices, what to expect from the energy sector in 2023, and the effects of China reopening on oil markets.Video Transcript[AUDIO LOGO]JARED BLIKRE: Gasoline prices continue to decline across the nation, falling for a fifth consecutive week. The national gas price average currently stands at $3.26 a gallon. And for more on the energy sector, let's bring in Bill Baruch, Blue Line Futures President. And, Bill, always good to see you here. We can get into the nitty gritty weeds of the futures market in a little bit. But first, your comment on these declining gas prices, which we kind of saw up until now, and also coming off the election. But they're here, and they are resonating in the public's mind.BILL BARUCH: You're right. I mean, there's been a bit more tepid demand than the market was really prepared for. We've seen really this price action come down in the $2 gasoline futures and retest that level when it was Omicron breaking in November, Thanksgiving of last year. So this is a pretty big-- pretty big level. I think there's a lot of support down here, and we're actually getting excited at this.But if you look at jet fuel inventory levels, sort of in line with historical averages. That's something relative to all the travel. You're seeing the numbers there. It's showing-- more alludes to tepid demand. Crack spreads have come in. And then also, I think overall, there's a lot of sentiment taking this further as some liquidation comes into the market when it hit some levels.SEANA SMITH: So, Bill, I guess it sounds like this is presenting a pretty good buying opportunity, at least from your perspective.BILL BARUCH: Yeah. Yeah, we've looked at it as a buying opportunity. I was joking around in interviews I've done in recent weeks and months that I've probably done as little in the energy space as I have done the last-- probably my whole career. I have sort of just been patient, and patience was really going to bring opportunity. And now we're seeing crude oil WTI contract get to $70. There's a lot of support down there on a technical basis, but also on a psychological basis. You don't want to see it break and close below 70.Story continuesBut-- so futures portfolios that were trading very actively, I'm getting long in some call spreads in the February contract, 77 and a half, $81 call spreads. They're under $1. I think there's some pretty good upside there on a good rebound. We're also buying OXY in securities portfolios. I think there's really tremendous value. It's a great trading vehicle we've used for much of the year.JARED BLIKRE: I wanted to ask you that there had been a bit of a discrepancy between XLE-- that's the S&P 500 energy sector-- the way that was trading and the way crude oil was trading. And not that they're always supposed to be in lockstep, but energy final-- energy stocks finally came down a bit to meet crude oil prices, which has declined. And then taking your thesis that energy prices, at least WTI above $70, is constructively bullish, anything besides OXY? Are you liking the sector as a whole? What other energy stocks would you be thinking about buying here?BILL BARUCH: Yeah, we're very bullish in the sector as a whole. We've had between 15% and 20% exposure in the energy stocks, in those portfolios this year. We dialed back in a couple of recent weeks, kind of fearful in the crack spreads. So Phillips 66 is one that we had stepped out of. Kind of rolling back, I think, a little more of a high beta play in OXY here.But historical averages, if you look at the relative-- XLE relative to crude oil, I mean, it was beaten down over the past, really, 18 months. And this is a rebound back towards the more historical mean. So I think this is something to keep in mind. You know, overall, broadly, crude oil is an area-- $50 to $70 I'd like to just broadly think as, you know, vicious volatility can happen in between it. But there's good bull markets well out above 70, 80 area that can anchor, but vicious volatility between that. And then bear markets below that $50 benchmark.So I think right now, if we hold 70, I remain very upbeat. But again, it's a very underinvested space. And these companies, they have tremendous free cash flow. Free cash flow yields like OXY, 12%, 13%. I mean, Exxon, 10%. Pioneer right around, I think, 10%. And, I mean, a lot of these companies, I mean, the cash flow is terrific. They've got themselves and their balance sheets into a really great spot here for the foreseeable future, given especially an underinvested industry. I remain very bullish.SEANA SMITH: Bill, what about the biggest drivers of the price action that we've seen recently? Because I think a lot of traders heading into the month of December thought it was going to be a tough month when it comes to oil because of the Russian sanctions on-- the sanctions on Russian oil, excuse me, that were going into effect this month. But it simply looks like demand seems to be the number one driving factor. Is that true?BILL BARUCH: Yeah, I think the demand is, like I said, a little weaker than one would expect. And you're seeing that with some of the crack spread movement, a bunch of different indicators that are out there. But I think broadly speaking, the headwind has been the SPR release. And I think that's going to become a more bullish factor as you look into next year.The other factor, too, I think, again, this is a market-- the underlying crude oil prices, these global growth fears that really became very relevant last week. And they've been relevant for weeks prior as well. But I think last week really kind of started to get that-- people scared in just kind of a lot of the headlines. So I think a lot of liquidation really took place.But the other side of that is the China reopening. And it's not something that's going to happen all at once. It's something that's going to happen sort of slowly, marginally through the first quarter of next year. And I think a lot of-- there's a lot of longs in the space that were sort of leaning on this China reopening. And the fact that we couldn't get out above $83 technical resistance, I think, just led to a lot of liquidations through last week. And then if you were patient enough and you weren't caught up in that windfall of price action, then the opportunity is here for you.JARED BLIKRE: All right, real quick here, SPR refueling the Strategic Petroleum Reserve at $70 per barrel. Is that a floor? Is that something big? At least in my mind, I haven't heard of a floor in terms of US crude prices in some time. What does this mean to you?BILL BARUCH: We haven't heard a lot of jawboning in recent sessions. But you go back a couple of weeks, OPEC Plus was clearly looking at $70 in WTI as an area of-- to lean against and jawbone, $80 in brent, roughly speaking, as an area that we would hear some jargon coming from. And if we don't see an uptick in global growth, we're likely to see potentially more production withheld in the coming meetings. And that's going to be a bullish factor.There was a bit of keepaway, I think, that was being played because the White House said they were looking for $70 or below $70 to start replenishing that SPR. So I think a good response off the $70 level here today. There's definitely, I think, a great trade. But the incoming news, I mean, CPI tomorrow is going to be a big one.And the Fed and the narrative that we get from the Fed and the rate hikes to come here in what would be a rate hike on Wednesday as well as coming in February, I think that's going to just be a good pulse on the risk-- the risk environment. You need to keep a pulse of the risk environment in order to really kind of trade this market and navigate. But for now, that's a really good response off $70. I think there's room to run. But again, it's going to be a very volatile week.JARED BLIKRE: All right, got to leave it there. Bill Baruch, thank you, as always.]

column4: China ‘is self-insuring’ energy supply with Russian oil, strategist says
column10: [Path Trading Partners Co-Founder Bob Iaccino joins Yahoo Finance Live to discuss global oil demand amid the COVID resurgence in China and the outlook for commodity markets.Video Transcript[AUDIO LOGO]RACHELLE AKUFFO: We're also keeping an eye on crude oil, just one part of the commodity market that will be impacted by China's reopening. Let's not forget, expansionary economic policies in Beijing have been the main driver of everything from silver to copper and iron ore for over two decades now, the latter hitting its highest level in four months today on expectations of a revival of the crucial property sector.Well, for a broad look at the commodity space now we're joined by Path Training Partners co-founder and Chief Market Strategist Bobby Iaccino. Thank you for joining us today, Bob. So first I want to start with the oil picture. We're seeing that oil is down for the week, a lot of that perhaps tied to the reopening, some of it jitters wondering with the Fed, as well. But what are you watching in terms of the oil picture and what we can expect in terms of demand with China?BOB IACCINO: Well, good morning, and thanks for having me again. Oil, to me, has a characteristic to it. It almost has a personality in terms of price action, and that personality is basically it trades at a wide sideways band of price until there's some sort of disruption to either supply or demand. Recently, we've had disruption to demand expectations based on slowing economies. The China story has been priced in multiple times in crude oil and it hasn't really stuck.Now that doesn't mean it's going to change things now that there is a version of reopening, but you know, there's a devil in the details to the reopening. China hasn't been buying as much crude as they had, but they were still buying quite a bit of it from Russia. There's evidence right now from some of the people we speak to that they're buying despite the price cap and Russia is self insuring to get around those rules, so they have a source of energy that isn't necessarily going to be crude oil that is taken off the global market because it's Russian crude oil, which theoretically, is already off the global market.Story continuesSo while I agree that if they come back like they did in 2011 we're going to see higher energy prices. There's a caveat to that. When you reopen and you don't have widespread vaccinations or very good health care that is COVID based, you could lock down sectors again, you could see people voluntarily not traveling at the rate that they maybe would have. That's probably down the road. We saw in the protests that the Chinese populace really wants to get out of these lockdowns. But once those numbers start crawling up and the death rates start crawling up again, they may change their minds and you could see a little bit of a slowdown. That's crude oil specific.AKIKO FUJITA: So Bob, I mean, if we bring it back to those comments that Rick got from S&P Global saying that China's COVID policy is the most important fundamental factor, I mean, it sound like you're saying that's not exactly the case because the virus case counts could really sort of dampen this push for additional demand coming out of one of the largest markets.BOB IACCINO: Well, Akiko, I'm not saying it's not the case, I'm just saying there's two sides to that story. It isn't a guarantee that simply because China is reopening they're going to go gangbusters buying energy like they were in 2011. And to be fair, I don't think that's what Rick was saying either. I just think he was bringing up the upside case since we've been so far to the downside. And I do think we've put in a short to medium term bottom in crude oil here. A while back, I was on, I believe, it was your show where I said 65 before 105.I still believe that. That's a little easier to say now that we're in the low 70s, but then I really don't see us getting to 100 at least until the US summer driving season arrives again, simply because, number one, you have to worry about the health of the global economy. And whether you believe there's going to be a recession or not, there's a slowdown in place.You see it everywhere except for the non-farm payrolls data. Everywhere else they're slow down, at least in the US economy. And also, we're likely to see the ECB and the Bank of England be aggressive next week in the face of double-digit inflation, so you're likely to see slowdowns continue there. But from that perspective, China can make up for their own consumption and get prices up maybe $15 to $20 from where they are now.RACHELLE AKUFFO: And how reliant should they be on what they're seeing in terms of domestic demand, especially when you think of things like metals, as well?BOB IACCINO: Well, copper, obviously, a key one. China has been, for quite a long time, the biggest consumer and smelter of copper. We've seen copper go up in the last 12 sessions almost 9%. Since the end of September, since those lows when the talk of the COVID Zero Policy being pulled back by China started, copper is up 18.25%, so there's been quite a move, but we're still only back to February 2021 levels.And I think this reflects, Rachelle, the balance between global slowdown and China reopening. China will absolutely spend, they will build, so that's why I think crude oil and industrial metals are almost two separate stories on the backs of the China reopening. If China is reopening aggressively and putting that stimulus into play without sort of policy lockdowns, people can decide on their own, sick or not, to use less fuel, especially as we get into warmer temperatures in the spring, but the government can still build and they're likely still to drive copper higher.Plus, longer term, I believe copper is a play long anyway. And why I say that is because I don't think electrification is slowing down and the amount of copper and other industrial metals involved in the electrification of the globe, the decarbonization of the globe, those numbers are large.AKIKO FUJITA: Bob Iaccino, always good to get your insight. Path Training Partners co-founder and Chief Market Strategist.]

column4: Oil market ‘wrestling with’ China reopening, Europe recession fears into 2023: Analyst
column10: [Lipow Oil Associates President Andrew Lipow joins Yahoo Finance Live to discuss geopolitical pressures in foreign markets, trends in energy prices, and U.S. oil refining capacities amid cold winter months.Video TranscriptJARED BLIKRE: Welcome back. US oil prices are on track for another year of gains, small gains. And that's despite tight supplies caused by Russia's war with Ukraine and weakening demand from the world's top crude importer. That would be China due to lockdowns.Joining us now for more is Lipow Oil Associates founder and president Andrew Lipow. Andy, great to have you here as always. I'm looking at your price target and where you think WTI and Brent are going to go. You're saying WTI could go to $90. That's about $10 above the current price, and Brent also a similar amount, to 95. Just wondering what factors into your analysis here.ANDY LIPOW: Well, we have a lot of things that are happening in the oil market. First, if we were to look at the demand side of the equation, the two things that the oil market is wrestling with is, number one, is the reopening of the Chinese economy as the lockdowns are eased. But I don't think that we're going to see a real big impact of that reopening until the middle of next year. But it could be worth about 500,000 to 700,000 barrels a day of additional demand.But on the other side of that demand picture is the fears of a recession, especially in Europe, as they're coping with high energy prices from natural gas, as well as high oil prices as they seek oil products to replace that natural gas supply from Russia. Meanwhile, on the supply side, in 2022, the world has really been making its way through with Strategic Petroleum Reserve releases in the United States, as well as elsewhere around the world. And if we look across the year, that has really added about 3/4 of a million barrels a day of supply.As we go forward, these lower oil prices that we've seen recently are going to impact the supply growth we're expecting in the United States, where the Energy Information Administration has been continually revising downward their growth forecasts of increased supplies here in the US now to about 500,000 barrels a day, whereas one time, several months ago, it was as high as 900,000 barrels a day increase.Story continuesSEANA SMITH: Andy, when you take a look at where prices are today, we have WTI crude just around 80 bucks a barrel. We certainly have seen this movement to the upside over the last several days. The winter storm over the holiday, I guess, how big of a factor has that been for supply?ANDY LIPOW: Well, this has been a pretty big impact, especially on refined products. At its peak, nearly 2 million barrels a day of Texas Gulf Coast refining capacity was offline. That's about 35% of the Texas refining capacity. So of course, if the refineries aren't running, they're not making gasoline and diesel.When we think about on the production of oil, the blizzards in North Dakota took off about 300,000 barrels a day of production, which will slowly recover, but more seriously, on the natural gas side, we lost about 10% to 15% of our natural gas production throughout the country, as the cold weather impacted those fields in Texas and Oklahoma, all the way up through Appalachia.JARED BLIKRE: Andy, I want to ask you about those sanctions that we were talking about a little bit. Just touch on them against Russian oil. Those seem to be largely symbolic. And the net effect is that we do have oil, low priced oil being piped into Europe from the Urals. But what do you see in the new year? If things escalate with respect to Russia, Ukraine again, could we get another situation where we see crude, at least momentarily, spike up well above your price targets for the end of the year?ANDY LIPOW: Well, it certainly could happen because in 2022, we saw oil prices for WTI get to $130 a barrel. So there can be a significant amount of volatility in the oil market. We had the European Union impose their sanctions on Russian crude oil purchases starting December 5. Now what I'm looking ahead to is February 5th when the sanctions begin on Russian refined products, and more specifically, on diesel supply, where Europe has been buying about 700,000 barrels a day of diesel from Russia.So there is going to be a scramble for new supplies to backfill those lost supplies that are available-- have been available out of Russia. And we're going to be looking towards new refining expansions and capacity coming online in the Middle East, as well as China, in order to make up the difference.SEANA SMITH: Andy, when you look over at what's happening in China, of course, we've had the surge in cases, lots of questions about how extensively, or I guess, how much that could really hold back the reopening there. When it comes to the impact that you see that having on crude, could we potentially maybe not hit your target and actually end up below 90 bucks a barrel at the end of 2023?ANDY LIPOW: We certainly could, especially if the return of Chinese demand becomes a disappointment, and the economic factors around the rest of the world cause a deeper recession than people are calling for. And you could actually see oil prices plummet. And we saw that happen in 2008 and 2009, as well as in 2014 and 2015, where we saw oil prices back in the $30 a barrel range and $45 a barrel range respectively.SEANA SMITH: All right, Andy, always great to have you. Andy Lipow, Lipow Oil Associates founder and president.]

column4: Energy stocks outperformed as crude oil gave back gains in 2022

We're about eight minutes into today's trading session. Let's get on over to Jared Blikre at the YFi Interactive for a deeper dive into today's tape this morning.JARED BLIKRE: Yes. column4: Gas prices in summer 2023 ‘contingent on if refineries will meet demand’: Analyst
column10: [GasBuddy Head of Petroleum Analysis Patrick De Haan joins Yahoo Finance Live to examine forecasts for household gasoline spending in 2023, while also looking at the outlook for refinery capacities and regional pricing trends in the U.S.Video TranscriptJARED BLIKRE: Pain at the pump has been a major talking point throughout 2022, but as prices have been dropping this month, are they poised to jump back in the near future? Well, according to GasBuddy, prices in most US cities could reach $4 a gallon again come springtime. So for more on this, we welcome in Patrick De Haan, GasBuddy head of petroleum analysis. Patrick, thank you for joining us here today. So what should we expect with gas prices in the near future?PATRICK DE HAAN: Well, certainly a little bit of good news, a little bit of bad news. I think overall, the good news is that Americans in the household will spend less on gasoline in 2023 than they did in 2022. But it wouldn't be a normal year without the spikes that we see in spring and prices then going back down in fall. And eventually, while we're enjoying relatively low prices now, I'm afraid that with China reopening, this spring could see a nice spike. And that could bring the national average back above the $4 a gallon mark. But the good news is we're not expecting the record highs that we saw in 2022 of over the $5 a gallon level.SEANA SMITH: Yeah, Patrick, we just did-- Yahoo Finance Rick Newman was just on set talking about the predictions that our viewers wrote in. And that was one of the predictions that gas prices were going to be back above 4 bucks a gallon because of China lifting its restrictions. Let's talk, though, about the higher prices, how long it could potentially be above $4 a gallon. Are we talking about throughout next summer?PATRICK DE HAAN: I think that's certainly a strong possibility. It's really going to be contingent on if refineries are able to meet demand and what Americans do this summer, given the fact that prices may be lower. Do we see a big jump in demand? I think demand was struggling this summer under the weight of some of those high prices. So if a lot of Americans defer travel, they may want to get back out on the road, given the fact that gas prices this summer could be a little bit less.Story continuesBut I would say that probably between Memorial Day and Labor Day, you may see $4 a gallon for several weeks maybe beyond that. Of course, a lot mixed in to how China is looking and how much of their economy is reopening and what we see in terms of consumption from China.JARED BLIKRE: Patrick, we had a number of curveballs in 2022. You're opened up, and we have suddenly found ourselves in a war with-- embroiled in a war between Russia and Ukraine. Wondering what you're thinking about in terms of potential headwinds or stuff out of the blue in the new year.PATRICK DE HAAN: Well, I think refining will continue to be a headwind. It was a challenge in 2022. And I think we're going to get a little bit more breathing room in terms of refining capacity. Not so much in the US. We're going to add about 275,000 barrels a day of capacity, thanks to ExxonMobil's refining project that's been underway for three years in Texas. More so, we're going to get breathing room overseas. Africa opening refineries, additional capacity in Asia, as well as the Middle East. All likely helping to create some breathing room, but there still could be the seasonal challenges related to the switchover to summer gasoline, as refiners carry out that maintenance.And keep in mind the extreme cold weather that we saw across the US last week also caused a lot of refinery disruptions. So that's going to be the wild card this year, as well as I think China's economy. They appear to be embracing easing the restrictions. And so there could be a level of pent-up demand in China that we saw here in the US a couple of years ago. And that could be a wild card as well.SEANA SMITH: And Patrick, when it comes to higher prices in terms of areas of the country that are likely to see the highest prices, is that going to be consistent with what we saw last year when you take a look at California, obviously, being one of the outliers and experiencing much higher prices than what we saw in many other parts?PATRICK DE HAAN: Yeah, absolutely. The motto last year was certainly that the coasts felt a lot more of the pain, particularly the mid-Atlantic, the Northeast areas that are reliant on more imports, and the West Coast also somewhat segmented away from the rest of the country. So both the extremes, the Northeast and the West Coast, likely to see some of those refinery challenges persist. California certainly could see the return of $5, even $6, a gallon gasoline if refinery issues are significant this year. Much of the Northeast still also reliant on imports because of Russia's war in Ukraine. A lack of refining capacity in the Northeast also could point to prices that in New York, areas of New England could exceed $5 a gallon again this year.JARED BLIKRE: We're just recovering here in the Northeast from a bitter cold spell, a storm that passed through. Just wondering the implications that this might have had on the energy market overall, including heating, gas prices. Kind of give you the floor for the last question here.PATRICK DE HAAN: Well, we've seen a lot of volatility in natural gas. Things have really plummeted, but there's still the possibility that if natural gas surges due to cold spells, there could be switches back over to using oil, diesel and heating oil. So that's a huge wildcard, but the Northeast is going to be very susceptible to bouts of cold weather. Keep in mind much of the Northeast consumes heating oil. I think that's going to be a challenge this winter. Diesel and heating oil likely to remain rather expensive, comparing that to gasoline, for much of the winter.SEANA SMITH: All right, Patrick De Haan, always great to have you of GasBuddy. Thanks so much for joining us here this afternoon.]

column4: Oil: $70-$90 range is ‘somewhere we’re going to be’ for first two quarters of 2023, analyst says
column10: [Prosper Trading Academy CEO Scott Bauer joins Yahoo Finance Live to discuss predictions for oil prices in 2023, driving factors for energy stocks and commodities, and the outlook for demand.Video TranscriptJARED BLIKRE: Russia threatening to cut oil output by up to 7% or up to 700,000 barrels per day in response to sanctions and price caps placed on Russian oil in response to the country's invasion of Ukraine. Oil trading, we can see that's up about $2.70-- or 2.76% today, up about $2.00 and change. Just closing in on that $80 per barrel price level.Now we have Scott Bauer, CEO of Prosper Training Academy joining us. And, Scott, I was just reeling off the latest price of oil here. We bounced off $70. Now that's basis WTI here. We had-- and I think that was earlier in the month when we were first getting those actual sanctions by Russia pegged-- I guess plowed on, and now we really didn't see much of the way in negative price action from there. In fact, we're up about $8. Just wondering how you're viewing the oil market in response to this latest news.SCOTT BAUER: Yeah, I have been bullish oil ever since we've started dropping below $100 and buying it on every dip, selling it on any sort of rally here. I've had to get stopped out a couple of times, but $70, $71, Jared, that really, to me, is a short-term bottom. When I say short term, I'm saying at least six months.The floor is put in for a number of reasons. First off, that's where, you know, the administration has said we're going to replenish SPR if we get down there. So to me, that is somewhat of a floor.Also, I think there's just still a tremendous amount of tailwinds in the space here. Number one, as it has been for me all year is what's going on in Russia/Ukraine. Number two is what's going on in China, and I believe that we-- the oil market, anyway, has seen the worst-case scenario in terms of demand, in terms of lockdowns, even with the latest, you know, policy that they've talked about with kind of opening back up and people getting COVID. I think we've seen the worst in terms of demand. It's only going to get higher from here.Story continuesSo there are just a bunch of tailwinds, and that $70 number to me, because of the SPR, that absolutely is a floor.JARED BLIKRE: Yes, President Biden talked about buying oil at $70 per barrel for the SPR to replenish it from those-- from the lower levels that it's fallen to.Now you mentioned the double whammy this year, and we were talking about price bottoms. What about a ceiling? What would it take to see a ceiling in terms of the news flow, in terms of price action? What are you thinking about as you think about those upper targets here?SCOTT BAUER: It absolutely would not surprise me to see oil back in the $90s with a nine handle. To break $100, though, I think is going to be a real tough job. I just don't see any scenario other than-- other than some more major geopolitical conflict that we're going to see oil just get to those prices again. And listen, that's not out of the question-- out of the question, unfortunately. That can happen. But I think this range of the low $70s probably to the mid $90s is somewhere we're going to be for, you know, at least the first and second quarter of the year.JARED BLIKRE: All right, and what about natural gas and some of the other elements to the energy sector? We've seen natural gas prices drop off quite precipitously. That has its own supply-and-demand aspects, but maybe you can just comment on that market a little bit.SCOTT BAUER: It absolutely does. And, in fact, if you're looking at what's going on in Russia right now and the news that they announced that they might be pulling back production here, that is really just for crude and oil products. It is not for natural gas.So I know that, especially in Europe, there has been a shortage. But right now, I'm not going to say it's fine, but the natural-gas supply right now is not as dire, if you will, as what we're seeing on the crude side. And again, if we turn back to Russia, 40%-- almost 40% of all of their export revenues are from the oil space, not from natural gas.So natural gas is still flowing. I don't see that we're going to get a major, major spike again, certainly not to where we were. UMG, which I track very closely, is trading right around $15 and 1/2, $16 right now, which is a low we've seen in probably three, four months. That was as high as the mid $30s just a couple months ago. Maybe we see a 15%, 20% pop in natural gas from here just because of this massive selloff that we've had, but I don't think that we're going to get into the crunch like we might get with crude [AUDIO OUT].JARED BLIKRE: Well, we've been talking about the Russian-- I guess the Russian effect on crude-oil supplies. It seems to me when we-- this doesn't-- this hasn't had necessarily bearish price-action consequences when we talk about crude oil this year, and I think part of it comes from the fact that we have dark supplies so that you never see oil taken off the market considerably. You see a market-clearing price. So at some price, somebody is going to take Russian oil off the market.Just wondering, with all the sanctions in place, with all the eyeballs on this, what are the potentials for violations of that next year? What are some of the situations that could evolve that could actually be bearish for the price of energy that might not be factored in right now?SCOTT BAUER: So in all honesty, there's probably violations going on right now, and there will continue [AUDIO OUT] violations going on. Some of that's just going to be-- let's call it glanced over. But we're not going to see, in my opinion, the price get much below $60, which is that price cap there. Maybe we'll see it a little bit. But that is a number that the G-7 came up with to hopefully reduce Russian export revenue but a price high enough to keep it flowing to the market.So yes, there's always, always, you know, some underhanded deals out there. And when you're looking at, really, the four countries that are really still in the market buying Russian oil, you're looking at Bulgaria, China, India, and Turkey. You've got to think that there's [AUDIO OUT] be some violation there.JARED BLIKRE: Yeah, well, I love doing a deep dive on the oil market and the futures markets on the day before Christmas Eve here. Thank you for joining us, Scott Bauer.]

column4: Oil forecasts see prices at $80-96 per barrel next year
column10: [Yahoo Finance’s Ines Ferre joins the Live show to discuss how oil futures are performing in intraday trading as well as the expectations for oil going into 2023.Video TranscriptJULIE HYMAN: It's been a roller coaster ride for oil prices this year in the wake of Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Is this volatility set to bleed into next year? Yahoo Finance's Ines Ferre is here with a look ahead. Hi, Ines.INES FERRE: Hi, Julie. Hard to believe that earlier this year, we saw oil at just above $130 a barrel. Right now, we're looking at WTI around $80 and Brent crude at $83. But where will these oil prices be next year? Well, I asked several analysts, and let's put up a board so you can see some of the projections for 2023.You've got Ed Morse from Citi projecting that Brent crude will average around $80 per barrel, with WTI averaging $75 a barrel. JPMorgan says that Brent will average around $90 a barrel next year. And then you've got OPIS over at Dow Jones that are saying that Brent is going to be anywhere between $95 and $96, with WTI at around 90.Now several factors are assuming this, though. That supply grows with projects in Norway, in Brazil, Argentina, Mexico, US, Canada. Also the successful reopening of China, and also Western nations able to avoid a severe recession because there are many projections of a recession. But if that recession is severe, then, of course, that would impact demand, guys.BRIAN SOZZI: Ines, you're also tracking some supply news from Russia.INES FERRE: Yeah, that's right. Well, Russia now threatening to cut production of around anywhere between 500,000 and 700,000 barrels a day. And that's why you're seeing crude oil today jumping quite a bit. WTI up 3%-- part of the reason Brent crude up 3%. And that's in response to the G7 price cap of those $60 per barrel.And something interesting, though, some data from Bloomberg that was looking at tanker data in the first week that this measure took in effect, as well as the EU maritime ban of Russian imports-- that first week, you had imports total volumes shipped out of Russia down 54%. Now that's only one week. So you can't really go by one week's data. And there are some other factors that are involved here as well.But if this trend continues, then those measures may not be having the intended consequences that you'd want because what the consequences are of those measures is that Russia doesn't have as much money to fund the war.BRIAN SOZZI: Ines Ferre, thanks so much. Appreciate it.]

column10: [Yahoo Finance Live's Jared Blikre details the Biden administration's goals to replenish strategic petroleum reserves and the Energy Department's latest barrel exchange.Video TranscriptJARED BLIKRE: Welcome back.
