And if we look across the year, that has really added about 3/4 of a million barrels a day of supply.As we go forward, these lower oil prices that we've seen recently are going to impact the supply growth we're expecting in the United States, where the Energy Information Administration has been continually revising downward their growth forecasts of increased supplies here in the US now to about 500,000 barrels a day, whereas one time, several months ago, it was as high as 900,000 barrels a day increase.Story continuesSEANA SMITH: Andy, when you take a look at where prices are today, we have WTI crude just around 80 bucks a barrel. We certainly have seen this movement to the upside over the last several days. The winter storm over the holiday, I guess, how big of a factor has that been for supply?ANDY LIPOW: Well, this has been a pretty big impact, especially on refined products. At its peak, nearly 2 million barrels a day of Texas Gulf Coast refining capacity was offline. That's about 35% of the Texas refining capacity. So of course, if the refineries aren't running, they're not making gasoline and diesel.When we think about on the production of oil, the blizzards in North Dakota took off about 300,000 barrels a day of production, which will slowly recover, but more seriously, on the natural gas side, we lost about 10% to 15% of our natural gas production throughout the country, as the cold weather impacted those fields in Texas and Oklahoma, all the way up through Appalachia.JARED BLIKRE: Andy, I want to ask you about those sanctions that we were talking about a little bit. Just touch on them against Russian oil. Those seem to be largely symbolic. And the net effect is that we do have oil, low priced oil being piped into Europe from the Urals. But what do you see in the new year? If things escalate with respect to Russia, Ukraine again, could we get another situation where we see crude, at least momentarily, spike up well above your price targets for the end of the year?ANDY LIPOW: Well, it certainly could happen because in 2022, we saw oil prices for WTI get to $130 a barrel. So there can be a significant amount of volatility in the oil market. We had the European Union impose their sanctions on Russian crude oil purchases starting December 5. Now what I'm looking ahead to is February 5th when the sanctions begin on Russian refined products, and more specifically, on diesel supply, where Europe has been buying about 700,000 barrels a day of diesel from Russia.So there is going to be a scramble for new supplies to backfill those lost supplies that are available-- have been available out of Russia. And we're going to be looking towards new refining expansions and capacity coming online in the Middle East, as well as China, in order to make up the difference.SEANA SMITH: Andy, when you look over at what's happening in China, of course, we've had the surge in cases, lots of questions about how extensively, or I guess, how much that could really hold back the reopening there. When it comes to the impact that you see that having on crude, could we potentially maybe not hit your target and actually end up below 90 bucks a barrel at the end of 2023?ANDY LIPOW: We certainly could, especially if the return of Chinese demand becomes a disappointment, and the economic factors around the rest of the world cause a deeper recession than people are calling for. And you could actually see oil prices plummet. And we saw that happen in 2008 and 2009, as well as in 2014 and 2015, where we saw oil prices back in the $30 a barrel range and $45 a barrel range respectively.SEANA SMITH: All right, Andy, always great to have you. Andy Lipow, Lipow Oil Associates founder and president.]

column4: Gas prices in summer 2023 ‘contingent on if refineries will meet demand’: Analyst
column10: [GasBuddy Head of Petroleum Analysis Patrick De Haan joins Yahoo Finance Live to examine forecasts for household gasoline spending in 2023, while also looking at the outlook for refinery capacities and regional pricing trends in the U.S.Video TranscriptJARED BLIKRE: Pain at the pump has been a major talking point throughout 2022, but as prices have been dropping this month, are they poised to jump back in the near future? Well, according to GasBuddy, prices in most US cities could reach $4 a gallon again come springtime. So for more on this, we welcome in Patrick De Haan, GasBuddy head of petroleum analysis. Patrick, thank you for joining us here today. So what should we expect with gas prices in the near future?PATRICK DE HAAN: Well, certainly a little bit of good news, a little bit of bad news. I think overall, the good news is that Americans in the household will spend less on gasoline in 2023 than they did in 2022. But it wouldn't be a normal year without the spikes that we see in spring and prices then going back down in fall. And eventually, while we're enjoying relatively low prices now, I'm afraid that with China reopening, this spring could see a nice spike. And that could bring the national average back above the $4 a gallon mark. But the good news is we're not expecting the record highs that we saw in 2022 of over the $5 a gallon level.SEANA SMITH: Yeah, Patrick, we just did-- Yahoo Finance Rick Newman was just on set talking about the predictions that our viewers wrote in. And that was one of the predictions that gas prices were going to be back above 4 bucks a gallon because of China lifting its restrictions. Let's talk, though, about the higher prices, how long it could potentially be above $4 a gallon. Are we talking about throughout next summer?PATRICK DE HAAN: I think that's certainly a strong possibility. It's really going to be contingent on if refineries are able to meet demand and what Americans do this summer, given the fact that prices may be lower. Do we see a big jump in demand? I think demand was struggling this summer under the weight of some of those high prices. So if a lot of Americans defer travel, they may want to get back out on the road, given the fact that gas prices this summer could be a little bit less.Story continuesBut I would say that probably between Memorial Day and Labor Day, you may see $4 a gallon for several weeks maybe beyond that. Of course, a lot mixed in to how China is looking and how much of their economy is reopening and what we see in terms of consumption from China.JARED BLIKRE: Patrick, we had a number of curveballs in 2022. You're opened up, and we have suddenly found ourselves in a war with-- embroiled in a war between Russia and Ukraine. Wondering what you're thinking about in terms of potential headwinds or stuff out of the blue in the new year.PATRICK DE HAAN: Well, I think refining will continue to be a headwind. It was a challenge in 2022. And I think we're going to get a little bit more breathing room in terms of refining capacity. Not so much in the US. We're going to add about 275,000 barrels a day of capacity, thanks to ExxonMobil's refining project that's been underway for three years in Texas. More so, we're going to get breathing room overseas. Africa opening refineries, additional capacity in Asia, as well as the Middle East. All likely helping to create some breathing room, but there still could be the seasonal challenges related to the switchover to summer gasoline, as refiners carry out that maintenance.And keep in mind the extreme cold weather that we saw across the US last week also caused a lot of refinery disruptions. So that's going to be the wild card this year, as well as I think China's economy. They appear to be embracing easing the restrictions. And so there could be a level of pent-up demand in China that we saw here in the US a couple of years ago. And that could be a wild card as well.SEANA SMITH: And Patrick, when it comes to higher prices in terms of areas of the country that are likely to see the highest prices, is that going to be consistent with what we saw last year when you take a look at California, obviously, being one of the outliers and experiencing much higher prices than what we saw in many other parts?PATRICK DE HAAN: Yeah, absolutely. The motto last year was certainly that the coasts felt a lot more of the pain, particularly the mid-Atlantic, the Northeast areas that are reliant on more imports, and the West Coast also somewhat segmented away from the rest of the country. So both the extremes, the Northeast and the West Coast, likely to see some of those refinery challenges persist. California certainly could see the return of $5, even $6, a gallon gasoline if refinery issues are significant this year. Just wondering the implications that this might have had on the energy market overall, including heating, gas prices. Kind of give you the floor for the last question here.PATRICK DE HAAN: Well, we've seen a lot of volatility in natural gas. column4: Oil: $70-$90 range is ‘somewhere we’re going to be’ for first two quarters of 2023, analyst says
column10: [Prosper Trading Academy CEO Scott Bauer joins Yahoo Finance Live to discuss predictions for oil prices in 2023, driving factors for energy stocks and commodities, and the outlook for demand.Video TranscriptJARED BLIKRE: Russia threatening to cut oil output by up to 7% or up to 700,000 barrels per day in response to sanctions and price caps placed on Russian oil in response to the country's invasion of Ukraine. Oil trading, we can see that's up about $2.70-- or 2.76% today, up about $2.00 and change. When I say short term, I'm saying at least six months.The floor is put in for a number of reasons. Number one, as it has been for me all year is what's going on in Russia/Ukraine. Number two is what's going on in China, and I believe that we-- the oil market, anyway, has seen the worst-case scenario in terms of demand, in terms of lockdowns, even with the latest, you know, policy that they've talked about with kind of opening back up and people getting COVID. I think we've seen the worst in terms of demand. It's only going to get higher from here.Story continuesSo there are just a bunch of tailwinds, and that $70 number to me, because of the SPR, that absolutely is a floor.JARED BLIKRE: Yes, President Biden talked about buying oil at $70 per barrel for the SPR to replenish it from those-- from the lower levels that it's fallen to.Now you mentioned the double whammy this year, and we were talking about price bottoms. What about a ceiling? What would it take to see a ceiling in terms of the news flow, in terms of price action? What are you thinking about as you think about those upper targets here?SCOTT BAUER: It absolutely would not surprise me to see oil back in the $90s with a nine handle. To break $100, though, I think is going to be a real tough job. And listen, that's not out of the question-- out of the question, unfortunately. That can happen. But I think this range of the low $70s probably to the mid $90s is somewhere we're going to be for, you know, at least the first and second quarter of the year.JARED BLIKRE: All right, and what about natural gas and some of the other elements to the energy sector? I don't see that we're going to get a major, major spike again, certainly not to where we were. That was as high as the mid $30s just a couple months ago. Maybe we see a 15%, 20% pop in natural gas from here just because of this massive selloff that we've had, but I don't think that we're going to get into the crunch like we might get with crude [AUDIO OUT].JARED BLIKRE: Well, we've been talking about the Russian-- I guess the Russian effect on crude-oil supplies. It seems to me when we-- this doesn't-- this hasn't had necessarily bearish price-action consequences when we talk about crude oil this year, and I think part of it comes from the fact that we have dark supplies so that you never see oil taken off the market considerably. You see a market-clearing price. So at some price, somebody is going to take Russian oil off the market.Just wondering, with all the sanctions in place, with all the eyeballs on this, what are the potentials for violations of that next year? What are some of the situations that could evolve that could actually be bearish for the price of energy that might not be factored in right now?SCOTT BAUER: So in all honesty, there's probably violations going on right now, and there will continue [AUDIO OUT] violations going on. Some of that's just going to be-- let's call it glanced over. But we're not going to see, in my opinion, the price get much below $60, which is that price cap there. Maybe we'll see it a little bit. But that is a number that the G-7 came up with to hopefully reduce Russian export revenue but a price high enough to keep it flowing to the market.So yes, there's always, always, you know, some underhanded deals out there. And when you're looking at, really, the four countries that are really still in the market buying Russian oil, you're looking at Bulgaria, China, India, and Turkey. You've got to think that there's [AUDIO OUT] be some violation there.JARED BLIKRE: Yeah, well, I love doing a deep dive on the oil market and the futures markets on the day before Christmas Eve here. Thank you for joining us, Scott Bauer.]

column4: Gas prices in summer 2023 ‘contingent on if refineries will meet demand’: Analyst
column10: [GasBuddy Head of Petroleum Analysis Patrick De Haan joins Yahoo Finance Live to examine forecasts for household gasoline spending in 2023, while also looking at the outlook for refinery capacities and regional pricing trends in the U.S.Video TranscriptJARED BLIKRE: Pain at the pump has been a major talking point throughout 2022, but as prices have been dropping this month, are they poised to jump back in the near future? Well, according to GasBuddy, prices in most US cities could reach $4 a gallon again come springtime. So for more on this, we welcome in Patrick De Haan, GasBuddy head of petroleum analysis. Patrick, thank you for joining us here today. So what should we expect with gas prices in the near future?PATRICK DE HAAN: Well, certainly a little bit of good news, a little bit of bad news. I think overall, the good news is that Americans in the household will spend less on gasoline in 2023 than they did in 2022. But it wouldn't be a normal year without the spikes that we see in spring and prices then going back down in fall. And eventually, while we're enjoying relatively low prices now, I'm afraid that with China reopening, this spring could see a nice spike. And that could bring the national average back above the $4 a gallon mark. But the good news is we're not expecting the record highs that we saw in 2022 of over the $5 a gallon level.SEANA SMITH: Yeah, Patrick, we just did-- Yahoo Finance Rick Newman was just on set talking about the predictions that our viewers wrote in. And that was one of the predictions that gas prices were going to be back above 4 bucks a gallon because of China lifting its restrictions. Let's talk, though, about the higher prices, how long it could potentially be above $4 a gallon. Are we talking about throughout next summer?PATRICK DE HAAN: I think that's certainly a strong possibility. It's really going to be contingent on if refineries are able to meet demand and what Americans do this summer, given the fact that prices may be lower. Do we see a big jump in demand? I think demand was struggling this summer under the weight of some of those high prices. So if a lot of Americans defer travel, they may want to get back out on the road, given the fact that gas prices this summer could be a little bit less.Story continuesBut I would say that probably between Memorial Day and Labor Day, you may see $4 a gallon for several weeks maybe beyond that. Of course, a lot mixed in to how China is looking and how much of their economy is reopening and what we see in terms of consumption from China.JARED BLIKRE: Patrick, we had a number of curveballs in 2022. You're opened up, and we have suddenly found ourselves in a war with-- embroiled in a war between Russia and Ukraine. Wondering what you're thinking about in terms of potential headwinds or stuff out of the blue in the new year.PATRICK DE HAAN: Well, I think refining will continue to be a headwind. It was a challenge in 2022. And I think we're going to get a little bit more breathing room in terms of refining capacity. Not so much in the US. We're going to add about 275,000 barrels a day of capacity, thanks to ExxonMobil's refining project that's been underway for three years in Texas. More so, we're going to get breathing room overseas. Africa opening refineries, additional capacity in Asia, as well as the Middle East. All likely helping to create some breathing room, but there still could be the seasonal challenges related to the switchover to summer gasoline, as refiners carry out that maintenance.And keep in mind the extreme cold weather that we saw across the US last week also caused a lot of refinery disruptions. So that's going to be the wild card this year, as well as I think China's economy. They appear to be embracing easing the restrictions. And so there could be a level of pent-up demand in China that we saw here in the US a couple of years ago. And that could be a wild card as well.SEANA SMITH: And Patrick, when it comes to higher prices in terms of areas of the country that are likely to see the highest prices, is that going to be consistent with what we saw last year when you take a look at California, obviously, being one of the outliers and experiencing much higher prices than what we saw in many other parts?PATRICK DE HAAN: Yeah, absolutely. The motto last year was certainly that the coasts felt a lot more of the pain, particularly the mid-Atlantic, the Northeast areas that are reliant on more imports, and the West Coast also somewhat segmented away from the rest of the country. So both the extremes, the Northeast and the West Coast, likely to see some of those refinery challenges persist. California certainly could see the return of $5, even $6, a gallon gasoline if refinery issues are significant this year. Much of the Northeast still also reliant on imports because of Russia's war in Ukraine. A lack of refining capacity in the Northeast also could point to prices that in New York, areas of New England could exceed $5 a gallon again this year.JARED BLIKRE: We're just recovering here in the Northeast from a bitter cold spell, a storm that passed through. Just wondering the implications that this might have had on the energy market overall, including heating, gas prices. Kind of give you the floor for the last question here.PATRICK DE HAAN: Well, we've seen a lot of volatility in natural gas. Things have really plummeted, but there's still the possibility that if natural gas surges due to cold spells, there could be switches back over to using oil, diesel and heating oil. So that's a huge wildcard, but the Northeast is going to be very susceptible to bouts of cold weather. Keep in mind much of the Northeast consumes heating oil. I think that's going to be a challenge this winter. Diesel and heating oil likely to remain rather expensive, comparing that to gasoline, for much of the winter.SEANA SMITH: All right, Patrick De Haan, always great to have you of GasBuddy. Thanks so much for joining us here this afternoon.]

column4: Oil: $70-$90 range is ‘somewhere we’re going to be’ for first two quarters of 2023, analyst says
column10: [Prosper Trading Academy CEO Scott Bauer joins Yahoo Finance Live to discuss predictions for oil prices in 2023, driving factors for energy stocks and commodities, and the outlook for demand.Video TranscriptJARED BLIKRE: Russia threatening to cut oil output by up to 7% or up to 700,000 barrels per day in response to sanctions and price caps placed on Russian oil in response to the country's invasion of Ukraine. Oil trading, we can see that's up about $2.70-- or 2.76% today, up about $2.00 and change. Just closing in on that $80 per barrel price level.Now we have Scott Bauer, CEO of Prosper Training Academy joining us. And, Scott, I was just reeling off the latest price of oil here. We bounced off $70. Now that's basis WTI here. We had-- and I think that was earlier in the month when we were first getting those actual sanctions by Russia pegged-- I guess plowed on, and now we really didn't see much of the way in negative price action from there. In fact, we're up about $8. Just wondering how you're viewing the oil market in response to this latest news.SCOTT BAUER: Yeah, I have been bullish oil ever since we've started dropping below $100 and buying it on every dip, selling it on any sort of rally here. I've had to get stopped out a couple of times, but $70, $71, Jared, that really, to me, is a short-term bottom. When I say short term, I'm saying at least six months.The floor is put in for a number of reasons. First off, that's where, you know, the administration has said we're going to replenish SPR if we get down there. So to me, that is somewhat of a floor.Also, I think there's just still a tremendous amount of tailwinds in the space here. Number one, as it has been for me all year is what's going on in Russia/Ukraine. Number two is what's going on in China, and I believe that we-- the oil market, anyway, has seen the worst-case scenario in terms of demand, in terms of lockdowns, even with the latest, you know, policy that they've talked about with kind of opening back up and people getting COVID. I think we've seen the worst in terms of demand. It's only going to get higher from here.Story continuesSo there are just a bunch of tailwinds, and that $70 number to me, because of the SPR, that absolutely is a floor.JARED BLIKRE: Yes, President Biden talked about buying oil at $70 per barrel for the SPR to replenish it from those-- from the lower levels that it's fallen to.Now you mentioned the double whammy this year, and we were talking about price bottoms. What about a ceiling? What would it take to see a ceiling in terms of the news flow, in terms of price action? What are you thinking about as you think about those upper targets here?SCOTT BAUER: It absolutely would not surprise me to see oil back in the $90s with a nine handle. To break $100, though, I think is going to be a real tough job. I just don't see any scenario other than-- other than some more major geopolitical conflict that we're going to see oil just get to those prices again. And listen, that's not out of the question-- out of the question, unfortunately. That can happen. But I think this range of the low $70s probably to the mid $90s is somewhere we're going to be for, you know, at least the first and second quarter of the year.JARED BLIKRE: All right, and what about natural gas and some of the other elements to the energy sector? We've seen natural gas prices drop off quite precipitously. That has its own supply-and-demand aspects, but maybe you can just comment on that market a little bit.SCOTT BAUER: It absolutely does. And, in fact, if you're looking at what's going on in Russia right now and the news that they announced that they might be pulling back production here, that is really just for crude and oil products. It is not for natural gas.So I know that, especially in Europe, there has been a shortage. But right now, I'm not going to say it's fine, but the natural-gas supply right now is not as dire, if you will, as what we're seeing on the crude side. And again, if we turn back to Russia, 40%-- almost 40% of all of their export revenues are from the oil space, not from natural gas.So natural gas is still flowing. I don't see that we're going to get a major, major spike again, certainly not to where we were. UMG, which I track very closely, is trading right around $15 and 1/2, $16 right now, which is a low we've seen in probably three, four months. That was as high as the mid $30s just a couple months ago. Maybe we see a 15%, 20% pop in natural gas from here just because of this massive selloff that we've had, but I don't think that we're going to get into the crunch like we might get with crude [AUDIO OUT].JARED BLIKRE: Well, we've been talking about the Russian-- I guess the Russian effect on crude-oil supplies. It seems to me when we-- this doesn't-- this hasn't had necessarily bearish price-action consequences when we talk about crude oil this year, and I think part of it comes from the fact that we have dark supplies so that you never see oil taken off the market considerably. You see a market-clearing price. So at some price, somebody is going to take Russian oil off the market.Just wondering, with all the sanctions in place, with all the eyeballs on this, what are the potentials for violations of that next year? What are some of the situations that could evolve that could actually be bearish for the price of energy that might not be factored in right now?SCOTT BAUER: So in all honesty, there's probably violations going on right now, and there will continue [AUDIO OUT] violations going on. Some of that's just going to be-- let's call it glanced over. But we're not going to see, in my opinion, the price get much below $60, which is that price cap there. Maybe we'll see it a little bit. But that is a number that the G-7 came up with to hopefully reduce Russian export revenue but a price high enough to keep it flowing to the market.So yes, there's always, always, you know, some underhanded deals out there. And when you're looking at, really, the four countries that are really still in the market buying Russian oil, you're looking at Bulgaria, China, India, and Turkey. You've got to think that there's [AUDIO OUT] be some violation there.JARED BLIKRE: Yeah, well, I love doing a deep dive on the oil market and the futures markets on the day before Christmas Eve here. Thank you for joining us, Scott Bauer.]

column4: Oil market ‘wrestling with’ China reopening, Europe recession fears into 2023: Analyst
column10: [Lipow Oil Associates President Andrew Lipow joins Yahoo Finance Live to discuss geopolitical pressures in foreign markets, trends in energy prices, and U.S. oil refining capacities amid cold winter months.Video TranscriptJARED BLIKRE: Welcome back. US oil prices are on track for another year of gains, small gains. And that's despite tight supplies caused by Russia's war with Ukraine and weakening demand from the world's top crude importer. That would be China due to lockdowns.Joining us now for more is Lipow Oil Associates founder and president Andrew Lipow. Andy, great to have you here as always. I'm looking at your price target and where you think WTI and Brent are going to go. You're saying WTI could go to $90. That's about $10 above the current price, and Brent also a similar amount, to 95. Just wondering what factors into your analysis here.ANDY LIPOW: Well, we have a lot of things that are happening in the oil market. First, if we were to look at the demand side of the equation, the two things that the oil market is wrestling with is, number one, is the reopening of the Chinese economy as the lockdowns are eased. But I don't think that we're going to see a real big impact of that reopening until the middle of next year. But it could be worth about 500,000 to 700,000 barrels a day of additional demand.But on the other side of that demand picture is the fears of a recession, especially in Europe, as they're coping with high energy prices from natural gas, as well as high oil prices as they seek oil products to replace that natural gas supply from Russia. Meanwhile, on the supply side, in 2022, the world has really been making its way through with Strategic Petroleum Reserve releases in the United States, as well as elsewhere around the world. And if we look across the year, that has really added about 3/4 of a million barrels a day of supply.As we go forward, these lower oil prices that we've seen recently are going to impact the supply growth we're expecting in the United States, where the Energy Information Administration has been continually revising downward their growth forecasts of increased supplies here in the US now to about 500,000 barrels a day, whereas one time, several months ago, it was as high as 900,000 barrels a day increase.Story continuesSEANA SMITH: Andy, when you take a look at where prices are today, we have WTI crude just around 80 bucks a barrel. We certainly have seen this movement to the upside over the last several days. The winter storm over the holiday, I guess, how big of a factor has that been for supply?ANDY LIPOW: Well, this has been a pretty big impact, especially on refined products. At its peak, nearly 2 million barrels a day of Texas Gulf Coast refining capacity was offline. That's about 35% of the Texas refining capacity. So of course, if the refineries aren't running, they're not making gasoline and diesel.When we think about on the production of oil, the blizzards in North Dakota took off about 300,000 barrels a day of production, which will slowly recover, but more seriously, on the natural gas side, we lost about 10% to 15% of our natural gas production throughout the country, as the cold weather impacted those fields in Texas and Oklahoma, all the way up through Appalachia.JARED BLIKRE: Andy, I want to ask you about those sanctions that we were talking about a little bit. Just touch on them against Russian oil. Those seem to be largely symbolic. And the net effect is that we do have oil, low priced oil being piped into Europe from the Urals. But what do you see in the new year? If things escalate with respect to Russia, Ukraine again, could we get another situation where we see crude, at least momentarily, spike up well above your price targets for the end of the year?ANDY LIPOW: Well, it certainly could happen because in 2022, we saw oil prices for WTI get to $130 a barrel. So there can be a significant amount of volatility in the oil market. We had the European Union impose their sanctions on Russian crude oil purchases starting December 5. Now what I'm looking ahead to is February 5th when the sanctions begin on Russian refined products, and more specifically, on diesel supply, where Europe has been buying about 700,000 barrels a day of diesel from Russia.So there is going to be a scramble for new supplies to backfill those lost supplies that are available-- have been available out of Russia. And we're going to be looking towards new refining expansions and capacity coming online in the Middle East, as well as China, in order to make up the difference.SEANA SMITH: Andy, when you look over at what's happening in China, of course, we've had the surge in cases, lots of questions about how extensively, or I guess, how much that could really hold back the reopening there. When it comes to the impact that you see that having on crude, could we potentially maybe not hit your target and actually end up below 90 bucks a barrel at the end of 2023?ANDY LIPOW: We certainly could, especially if the return of Chinese demand becomes a disappointment, and the economic factors around the rest of the world cause a deeper recession than people are calling for. And you could actually see oil prices plummet. And we saw that happen in 2008 and 2009, as well as in 2014 and 2015, where we saw oil prices back in the $30 a barrel range and $45 a barrel range respectively.SEANA SMITH: All right, Andy, always great to have you. Andy Lipow, Lipow Oil Associates founder and president.]

Wondering what you're thinking about in terms of potential headwinds or stuff out of the blue in the new year.PATRICK DE HAAN: Well, I think refining will continue to be a headwind. It was a challenge in 2022. And I think we're going to get a little bit more breathing room in terms of refining capacity. Not so much in the US. We're going to add about 275,000 barrels a day of capacity, thanks to ExxonMobil's refining project that's been underway for three years in Texas. More so, we're going to get breathing room overseas. Africa opening refineries, additional capacity in Asia, as well as the Middle East. All likely helping to create some breathing room, but there still could be the seasonal challenges related to the switchover to summer gasoline, as refiners carry out that maintenance.And keep in mind the extreme cold weather that we saw across the US last week also caused a lot of refinery disruptions. So that's going to be the wild card this year, as well as I think China's economy. They appear to be embracing easing the restrictions. And so there could be a level of pent-up demand in China that we saw here in the US a couple of years ago. And that could be a wild card as well.SEANA SMITH: And Patrick, when it comes to higher prices in terms of areas of the country that are likely to see the highest prices, is that going to be consistent with what we saw last year when you take a look at California, obviously, being one of the outliers and experiencing much higher prices than what we saw in many other parts?PATRICK DE HAAN: Yeah, absolutely. The motto last year was certainly that the coasts felt a lot more of the pain, particularly the mid-Atlantic, the Northeast areas that are reliant on more imports, and the West Coast also somewhat segmented away from the rest of the country. So both the extremes, the Northeast and the West Coast, likely to see some of those refinery challenges persist. California certainly could see the return of $5, even $6, a gallon gasoline if refinery issues are significant this year. Much of the Northeast still also reliant on imports because of Russia's war in Ukraine. A lack of refining capacity in the Northeast also could point to prices that in New York, areas of New England could exceed $5 a gallon again this year.JARED BLIKRE: We're just recovering here in the Northeast from a bitter cold spell, a storm that passed through. Just wondering the implications that this might have had on the energy market overall, including heating, gas prices. Kind of give you the floor for the last question here.PATRICK DE HAAN: Well, we've seen a lot of volatility in natural gas. Things have really plummeted, but there's still the possibility that if natural gas surges due to cold spells, there could be switches back over to using oil, diesel and heating oil. So that's a huge wildcard, but the Northeast is going to be very susceptible to bouts of cold weather. Keep in mind much of the Northeast consumes heating oil. I think that's going to be a challenge this winter. Diesel and heating oil likely to remain rather expensive, comparing that to gasoline, for much of the winter.SEANA SMITH: All right, Patrick De Haan, always great to have you of GasBuddy. Thanks so much for joining us here this afternoon.]

column4: Oil: $70-$90 range is ‘somewhere we’re going to be’ for first two quarters of 2023, analyst says
column10: [Prosper Trading Academy CEO Scott Bauer joins Yahoo Finance Live to discuss predictions for oil prices in 2023, driving factors for energy stocks and commodities, and the outlook for demand.Video TranscriptJARED BLIKRE: Russia threatening to cut oil output by up to 7% or up to 700,000 barrels per day in response to sanctions and price caps placed on Russian oil in response to the country's invasion of Ukraine. Oil trading, we can see that's up about $2.70-- or 2.76% today, up about $2.00 and change. Just closing in on that $80 per barrel price level.Now we have Scott Bauer, CEO of Prosper Training Academy joining us. And, Scott, I was just reeling off the latest price of oil here. We bounced off $70. Now that's basis WTI here. We had-- and I think that was earlier in the month when we were first getting those actual sanctions by Russia pegged-- I guess plowed on, and now we really didn't see much of the way in negative price action from there. In fact, we're up about $8. Just wondering how you're viewing the oil market in response to this latest news.SCOTT BAUER: Yeah, I have been bullish oil ever since we've started dropping below $100 and buying it on every dip, selling it on any sort of rally here. I've had to get stopped out a couple of times, but $70, $71, Jared, that really, to me, is a short-term bottom. When I say short term, I'm saying at least six months.The floor is put in for a number of reasons. First off, that's where, you know, the administration has said we're going to replenish SPR if we get down there. So to me, that is somewhat of a floor.Also, I think there's just still a tremendous amount of tailwinds in the space here. Number one, as it has been for me all year is what's going on in Russia/Ukraine. Number two is what's going on in China, and I believe that we-- the oil market, anyway, has seen the worst-case scenario in terms of demand, in terms of lockdowns, even with the latest, you know, policy that they've talked about with kind of opening back up and people getting COVID. I think we've seen the worst in terms of demand. It's only going to get higher from here.Story continuesSo there are just a bunch of tailwinds, and that $70 number to me, because of the SPR, that absolutely is a floor.JARED BLIKRE: Yes, President Biden talked about buying oil at $70 per barrel for the SPR to replenish it from those-- from the lower levels that it's fallen to.Now you mentioned the double whammy this year, and we were talking about price bottoms. What about a ceiling? What would it take to see a ceiling in terms of the news flow, in terms of price action? What are you thinking about as you think about those upper targets here?SCOTT BAUER: It absolutely would not surprise me to see oil back in the $90s with a nine handle. To break $100, though, I think is going to be a real tough job. I just don't see any scenario other than-- other than some more major geopolitical conflict that we're going to see oil just get to those prices again. And listen, that's not out of the question-- out of the question, unfortunately. That can happen. But I think this range of the low $70s probably to the mid $90s is somewhere we're going to be for, you know, at least the first and second quarter of the year.JARED BLIKRE: All right, and what about natural gas and some of the other elements to the energy sector? We've seen natural gas prices drop off quite precipitously. That has its own supply-and-demand aspects, but maybe you can just comment on that market a little bit.SCOTT BAUER: It absolutely does. And, in fact, if you're looking at what's going on in Russia right now and the news that they announced that they might be pulling back production here, that is really just for crude and oil products. It is not for natural gas.So I know that, especially in Europe, there has been a shortage. But right now, I'm not going to say it's fine, but the natural-gas supply right now is not as dire, if you will, as what we're seeing on the crude side. And again, if we turn back to Russia, 40%-- almost 40% of all of their export revenues are from the oil space, not from natural gas.So natural gas is still flowing. I don't see that we're going to get a major, major spike again, certainly not to where we were. UMG, which I track very closely, is trading right around $15 and 1/2, $16 right now, which is a low we've seen in probably three, four months. That was as high as the mid $30s just a couple months ago. Maybe we see a 15%, 20% pop in natural gas from here just because of this massive selloff that we've had, but I don't think that we're going to get into the crunch like we might get with crude [AUDIO OUT].JARED BLIKRE: Well, we've been talking about the Russian-- I guess the Russian effect on crude-oil supplies. It seems to me when we-- this doesn't-- this hasn't had necessarily bearish price-action consequences when we talk about crude oil this year, and I think part of it comes from the fact that we have dark supplies so that you never see oil taken off the market considerably. You see a market-clearing price. So at some price, somebody is going to take Russian oil off the market.Just wondering, with all the sanctions in place, with all the eyeballs on this, what are the potentials for violations of that next year? What are some of the situations that could evolve that could actually be bearish for the price of energy that might not be factored in right now?SCOTT BAUER: So in all honesty, there's probably violations going on right now, and there will continue [AUDIO OUT] violations going on. Some of that's just going to be-- let's call it glanced over. But we're not going to see, in my opinion, the price get much below $60, which is that price cap there. Maybe we'll see it a little bit. But that is a number that the G-7 came up with to hopefully reduce Russian export revenue but a price high enough to keep it flowing to the market.So yes, there's always, always, you know, some underhanded deals out there. And when you're looking at, really, the four countries that are really still in the market buying Russian oil, you're looking at Bulgaria, China, India, and Turkey. You've got to think that there's [AUDIO OUT] be some violation there.JARED BLIKRE: Yeah, well, I love doing a deep dive on the oil market and the futures markets on the day before Christmas Eve here. Thank you for joining us, Scott Bauer.]

column4: Oil forecasts see prices at $80-96 per barrel next year
column10: [Yahoo Finance’s Ines Ferre joins the Live show to discuss how oil futures are performing in intraday trading as well as the expectations for oil going into 2023.Video TranscriptJULIE HYMAN: It's been a roller coaster ride for oil prices this year in the wake of Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Is this volatility set to bleed into next year? Yahoo Finance's Ines Ferre is here with a look ahead. Hi, Ines.INES FERRE: Hi, Julie. Hard to believe that earlier this year, we saw oil at just above $130 a barrel. Right now, we're looking at WTI around $80 and Brent crude at $83. But where will these oil prices be next year? Well, I asked several analysts, and let's put up a board so you can see some of the projections for 2023.You've got Ed Morse from Citi projecting that Brent crude will average around $80 per barrel, with WTI averaging $75 a barrel. JPMorgan says that Brent will average around $90 a barrel next year. And then you've got OPIS over at Dow Jones that are saying that Brent is going to be anywhere between $95 and $96, with WTI at around 90.Now several factors are assuming this, though. That supply grows with projects in Norway, in Brazil, Argentina, Mexico, US, Canada. Also the successful reopening of China, and also Western nations able to avoid a severe recession because there are many projections of a recession. But if that recession is severe, then, of course, that would impact demand, guys.BRIAN SOZZI: Ines, you're also tracking some supply news from Russia.INES FERRE: Yeah, that's right. Well, Russia now threatening to cut production of around anywhere between 500,000 and 700,000 barrels a day. And that's why you're seeing crude oil today jumping quite a bit. WTI up 3%-- part of the reason Brent crude up 3%. And that's in response to the G7 price cap of those $60 per barrel.And something interesting, though, some data from Bloomberg that was looking at tanker data in the first week that this measure took in effect, as well as the EU maritime ban of Russian imports-- that first week, you had imports total volumes shipped out of Russia down 54%. Now that's only one week. So you can't really go by one week's data. And there are some other factors that are involved here as well.But if this trend continues, then those measures may not be having the intended consequences that you'd want because what the consequences are of those measures is that Russia doesn't have as much money to fund the war.BRIAN SOZZI: Ines Ferre, thanks so much. Appreciate it.]

column4: Oil market ‘wrestling with’ China reopening, Europe recession fears into 2023: Analyst
column10: [Lipow Oil Associates President Andrew Lipow joins Yahoo Finance Live to discuss geopolitical pressures in foreign markets, trends in energy prices, and U.S. oil refining capacities amid cold winter months.Video TranscriptJARED BLIKRE: Welcome back. US oil prices are on track for another year of gains, small gains. And that's despite tight supplies caused by Russia's war with Ukraine and weakening demand from the world's top crude importer. That would be China due to lockdowns.Joining us now for more is Lipow Oil Associates founder and president Andrew Lipow. Andy, great to have you here as always. I'm looking at your price target and where you think WTI and Brent are going to go. You're saying WTI could go to $90. That's about $10 above the current price, and Brent also a similar amount, to 95. Just wondering what factors into your analysis here.ANDY LIPOW: Well, we have a lot of things that are happening in the oil market. First, if we were to look at the demand side of the equation, the two things that the oil market is wrestling with is, number one, is the reopening of the Chinese economy as the lockdowns are eased. But I don't think that we're going to see a real big impact of that reopening until the middle of next year. But it could be worth about 500,000 to 700,000 barrels a day of additional demand.But on the other side of that demand picture is the fears of a recession, especially in Europe, as they're coping with high energy prices from natural gas, as well as high oil prices as they seek oil products to replace that natural gas supply from Russia. Meanwhile, on the supply side, in 2022, the world has really been making its way through with Strategic Petroleum Reserve releases in the United States, as well as elsewhere around the world. And if we look across the year, that has really added about 3/4 of a million barrels a day of supply.As we go forward, these lower oil prices that we've seen recently are going to impact the supply growth we're expecting in the United States, where the Energy Information Administration has been continually revising downward their growth forecasts of increased supplies here in the US now to about 500,000 barrels a day, whereas one time, several months ago, it was as high as 900,000 barrels a day increase.Story continuesSEANA SMITH: Andy, when you take a look at where prices are today, we have WTI crude just around 80 bucks a barrel. We certainly have seen this movement to the upside over the last several days. The winter storm over the holiday, I guess, how big of a factor has that been for supply?ANDY LIPOW: Well, this has been a pretty big impact, especially on refined products. At its peak, nearly 2 million barrels a day of Texas Gulf Coast refining capacity was offline. That's about 35% of the Texas refining capacity. So of course, if the refineries aren't running, they're not making gasoline and diesel.When we think about on the production of oil, the blizzards in North Dakota took off about 300,000 barrels a day of production, which will slowly recover, but more seriously, on the natural gas side, we lost about 10% to 15% of our natural gas production throughout the country, as the cold weather impacted those fields in Texas and Oklahoma, all the way up through Appalachia.JARED BLIKRE: Andy, I want to ask you about those sanctions that we were talking about a little bit. Just touch on them against Russian oil. Those seem to be largely symbolic. And the net effect is that we do have oil, low priced oil being piped into Europe from the Urals. But what do you see in the new year? If things escalate with respect to Russia, Ukraine again, could we get another situation where we see crude, at least momentarily, spike up well above your price targets for the end of the year?ANDY LIPOW: Well, it certainly could happen because in 2022, we saw oil prices for WTI get to $130 a barrel. So there can be a significant amount of volatility in the oil market. We had the European Union impose their sanctions on Russian crude oil purchases starting December 5. Now what I'm looking ahead to is February 5th when the sanctions begin on Russian refined products, and more specifically, on diesel supply, where Europe has been buying about 700,000 barrels a day of diesel from Russia.So there is going to be a scramble for new supplies to backfill those lost supplies that are available-- have been available out of Russia. And we're going to be looking towards new refining expansions and capacity coming online in the Middle East, as well as China, in order to make up the difference.SEANA SMITH: Andy, when you look over at what's happening in China, of course, we've had the surge in cases, lots of questions about how extensively, or I guess, how much that could really hold back the reopening there. When it comes to the impact that you see that having on crude, could we potentially maybe not hit your target and actually end up below 90 bucks a barrel at the end of 2023?ANDY LIPOW: We certainly could, especially if the return of Chinese demand becomes a disappointment, and the economic factors around the rest of the world cause a deeper recession than people are calling for. And you could actually see oil prices plummet. And we saw that happen in 2008 and 2009, as well as in 2014 and 2015, where we saw oil prices back in the $30 a barrel range and $45 a barrel range respectively.SEANA SMITH: All right, Andy, always great to have you. Andy Lipow, Lipow Oil Associates founder and president.]

column4: Gas prices in summer 2023 ‘contingent on if refineries will meet demand’: Analyst

I think overall, the good news is that Americans in the household will spend less on gasoline in 2023 than they did in 2022. But it wouldn't be a normal year without the spikes that we see in spring and prices then going back down in fall. And eventually, while we're enjoying relatively low prices now, I'm afraid that with China reopening, this spring could see a nice spike. And that could bring the national average back above the $4 a gallon mark. And so there could be a level of pent-up demand in China that we saw here in the US a couple of years ago. And that could be a wild card as well.SEANA SMITH: And Patrick, when it comes to higher prices in terms of areas of the country that are likely to see the highest prices, is that going to be consistent with what we saw last year when you take a look at California, obviously, being one of the outliers and experiencing much higher prices than what we saw in many other parts?PATRICK DE HAAN: Yeah, absolutely. The motto last year was certainly that the coasts felt a lot more of the pain, particularly the mid-Atlantic, the Northeast areas that are reliant on more imports, and the West Coast also somewhat segmented away from the rest of the country. So both the extremes, the Northeast and the West Coast, likely to see some of those refinery challenges persist. California certainly could see the return of $5, even $6, a gallon gasoline if refinery issues are significant this year. Much of the Northeast still also reliant on imports because of Russia's war in Ukraine. A lack of refining capacity in the Northeast also could point to prices that in New York, areas of New England could exceed $5 a gallon again this year.JARED BLIKRE: We're just recovering here in the Northeast from a bitter cold spell, a storm that passed through. Thanks so much for joining us here this afternoon.]

I've had to get stopped out a couple of times, but $70, $71, Jared, that really, to me, is a short-term bottom. When I say short term, I'm saying at least six months.The floor is put in for a number of reasons. First off, that's where, you know, the administration has said we're going to replenish SPR if we get down there. So to me, that is somewhat of a floor.Also, I think there's just still a tremendous amount of tailwinds in the space here. Number one, as it has been for me all year is what's going on in Russia/Ukraine. Number two is what's going on in China, and I believe that we-- the oil market, anyway, has seen the worst-case scenario in terms of demand, in terms of lockdowns, even with the latest, you know, policy that they've talked about with kind of opening back up and people getting COVID. I think we've seen the worst in terms of demand. It's only going to get higher from here.Story continuesSo there are just a bunch of tailwinds, and that $70 number to me, because of the SPR, that absolutely is a floor.JARED BLIKRE: Yes, President Biden talked about buying oil at $70 per barrel for the SPR to replenish it from those-- from the lower levels that it's fallen to.Now you mentioned the double whammy this year, and we were talking about price bottoms. What about a ceiling? What would it take to see a ceiling in terms of the news flow, in terms of price action? What are you thinking about as you think about those upper targets here?SCOTT BAUER: It absolutely would not surprise me to see oil back in the $90s with a nine handle. To break $100, though, I think is going to be a real tough job. I just don't see any scenario other than-- other than some more major geopolitical conflict that we're going to see oil just get to those prices again. And listen, that's not out of the question-- out of the question, unfortunately. That can happen. But I think this range of the low $70s probably to the mid $90s is somewhere we're going to be for, you know, at least the first and second quarter of the year.JARED BLIKRE: All right, and what about natural gas and some of the other elements to the energy sector? We've seen natural gas prices drop off quite precipitously. That has its own supply-and-demand aspects, but maybe you can just comment on that market a little bit.SCOTT BAUER: It absolutely does. And, in fact, if you're looking at what's going on in Russia right now and the news that they announced that they might be pulling back production here, that is really just for crude and oil products. It is not for natural gas.So I know that, especially in Europe, there has been a shortage. But right now, I'm not going to say it's fine, but the natural-gas supply right now is not as dire, if you will, as what we're seeing on the crude side. And again, if we turn back to Russia, 40%-- almost 40% of all of their export revenues are from the oil space, not from natural gas.So natural gas is still flowing. I don't see that we're going to get a major, major spike again, certainly not to where we were. UMG, which I track very closely, is trading right around $15 and 1/2, $16 right now, which is a low we've seen in probably three, four months. That was as high as the mid $30s just a couple months ago. Maybe we see a 15%, 20% pop in natural gas from here just because of this massive selloff that we've had, but I don't think that we're going to get into the crunch like we might get with crude [AUDIO OUT].JARED BLIKRE: Well, we've been talking about the Russian-- I guess the Russian effect on crude-oil supplies. It seems to me when we-- this doesn't-- this hasn't had necessarily bearish price-action consequences when we talk about crude oil this year, and I think part of it comes from the fact that we have dark supplies so that you never see oil taken off the market considerably. You see a market-clearing price. So at some price, somebody is going to take Russian oil off the market.Just wondering, with all the sanctions in place, with all the eyeballs on this, what are the potentials for violations of that next year? What are some of the situations that could evolve that could actually be bearish for the price of energy that might not be factored in right now?SCOTT BAUER: So in all honesty, there's probably violations going on right now, and there will continue [AUDIO OUT] violations going on. Some of that's just going to be-- let's call it glanced over. But we're not going to see, in my opinion, the price get much below $60, which is that price cap there. Maybe we'll see it a little bit. But that is a number that the G-7 came up with to hopefully reduce Russian export revenue but a price high enough to keep it flowing to the market.So yes, there's always, always, you know, some underhanded deals out there. And when you're looking at, really, the four countries that are really still in the market buying Russian oil, you're looking at Bulgaria, China, India, and Turkey. You've got to think that there's [AUDIO OUT] be some violation there.JARED BLIKRE: Yeah, well, I love doing a deep dive on the oil market and the futures markets on the day before Christmas Eve here. Thank you for joining us, Scott Bauer.]

column4: Oil forecasts see prices at $80-96 per barrel next year
column10: [Yahoo Finance’s Ines Ferre joins the Live show to discuss how oil futures are performing in intraday trading as well as the expectations for oil going into 2023.Video TranscriptJULIE HYMAN: It's been a roller coaster ride for oil prices this year in the wake of Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Is this volatility set to bleed into next year? Yahoo Finance's Ines Ferre is here with a look ahead. Hi, Ines.INES FERRE: Hi, Julie. Hard to believe that earlier this year, we saw oil at just above $130 a barrel. Right now, we're looking at WTI around $80 and Brent crude at $83. But where will these oil prices be next year? Well, I asked several analysts, and let's put up a board so you can see some of the projections for 2023.You've got Ed Morse from Citi projecting that Brent crude will average around $80 per barrel, with WTI averaging $75 a barrel. JPMorgan says that Brent will average around $90 a barrel next year. And then you've got OPIS over at Dow Jones that are saying that Brent is going to be anywhere between $95 and $96, with WTI at around 90.Now several factors are assuming this, though. That supply grows with projects in Norway, in Brazil, Argentina, Mexico, US, Canada. Also the successful reopening of China, and also Western nations able to avoid a severe recession because there are many projections of a recession. But if that recession is severe, then, of course, that would impact demand, guys.BRIAN SOZZI: Ines, you're also tracking some supply news from Russia.INES FERRE: Yeah, that's right. Well, Russia now threatening to cut production of around anywhere between 500,000 and 700,000 barrels a day. And that's why you're seeing crude oil today jumping quite a bit. WTI up 3%-- part of the reason Brent crude up 3%. And that's in response to the G7 price cap of those $60 per barrel.And something interesting, though, some data from Bloomberg that was looking at tanker data in the first week that this measure took in effect, as well as the EU maritime ban of Russian imports-- that first week, you had imports total volumes shipped out of Russia down 54%. Now that's only one week. So you can't really go by one week's data. And there are some other factors that are involved here as well.But if this trend continues, then those measures may not be having the intended consequences that you'd want because what the consequences are of those measures is that Russia doesn't have as much money to fund the war.BRIAN SOZZI: Ines Ferre, thanks so much. Appreciate it.]

column4: Oil market ‘wrestling with’ China reopening, Europe recession fears into 2023: Analyst
column10: [Lipow Oil Associates President Andrew Lipow joins Yahoo Finance Live to discuss geopolitical pressures in foreign markets, trends in energy prices, and U.S. oil refining capacities amid cold winter months.Video TranscriptJARED BLIKRE: Welcome back. US oil prices are on track for another year of gains, small gains. And that's despite tight supplies caused by Russia's war with Ukraine and weakening demand from the world's top crude importer. That would be China due to lockdowns.Joining us now for more is Lipow Oil Associates founder and president Andrew Lipow. Andy, great to have you here as always. I'm looking at your price target and where you think WTI and Brent are going to go. You're saying WTI could go to $90. That's about $10 above the current price, and Brent also a similar amount, to 95. Just wondering what factors into your analysis here.ANDY LIPOW: Well, we have a lot of things that are happening in the oil market. First, if we were to look at the demand side of the equation, the two things that the oil market is wrestling with is, number one, is the reopening of the Chinese economy as the lockdowns are eased. But I don't think that we're going to see a real big impact of that reopening until the middle of next year. But it could be worth about 500,000 to 700,000 barrels a day of additional demand.But on the other side of that demand picture is the fears of a recession, especially in Europe, as they're coping with high energy prices from natural gas, as well as high oil prices as they seek oil products to replace that natural gas supply from Russia. Meanwhile, on the supply side, in 2022, the world has really been making its way through with Strategic Petroleum Reserve releases in the United States, as well as elsewhere around the world. And if we look across the year, that has really added about 3/4 of a million barrels a day of supply.As we go forward, these lower oil prices that we've seen recently are going to impact the supply growth we're expecting in the United States, where the Energy Information Administration has been continually revising downward their growth forecasts of increased supplies here in the US now to about 500,000 barrels a day, whereas one time, several months ago, it was as high as 900,000 barrels a day increase.Story continuesSEANA SMITH: Andy, when you take a look at where prices are today, we have WTI crude just around 80 bucks a barrel. We certainly have seen this movement to the upside over the last several days. The winter storm over the holiday, I guess, how big of a factor has that been for supply?ANDY LIPOW: Well, this has been a pretty big impact, especially on refined products. At its peak, nearly 2 million barrels a day of Texas Gulf Coast refining capacity was offline. That's about 35% of the Texas refining capacity. So of course, if the refineries aren't running, they're not making gasoline and diesel.When we think about on the production of oil, the blizzards in North Dakota took off about 300,000 barrels a day of production, which will slowly recover, but more seriously, on the natural gas side, we lost about 10% to 15% of our natural gas production throughout the country, as the cold weather impacted those fields in Texas and Oklahoma, all the way up through Appalachia.JARED BLIKRE: Andy, I want to ask you about those sanctions that we were talking about a little bit. Just touch on them against Russian oil. Those seem to be largely symbolic. And the net effect is that we do have oil, low priced oil being piped into Europe from the Urals. But what do you see in the new year? If things escalate with respect to Russia, Ukraine again, could we get another situation where we see crude, at least momentarily, spike up well above your price targets for the end of the year?ANDY LIPOW: Well, it certainly could happen because in 2022, we saw oil prices for WTI get to $130 a barrel. So there can be a significant amount of volatility in the oil market. We had the European Union impose their sanctions on Russian crude oil purchases starting December 5. Now what I'm looking ahead to is February 5th when the sanctions begin on Russian refined products, and more specifically, on diesel supply, where Europe has been buying about 700,000 barrels a day of diesel from Russia.So there is going to be a scramble for new supplies to backfill those lost supplies that are available-- have been available out of Russia. And we're going to be looking towards new refining expansions and capacity coming online in the Middle East, as well as China, in order to make up the difference.SEANA SMITH: Andy, when you look over at what's happening in China, of course, we've had the surge in cases, lots of questions about how extensively, or I guess, how much that could really hold back the reopening there. When it comes to the impact that you see that having on crude, could we potentially maybe not hit your target and actually end up below 90 bucks a barrel at the end of 2023?ANDY LIPOW: We certainly could, especially if the return of Chinese demand becomes a disappointment, and the economic factors around the rest of the world cause a deeper recession than people are calling for. And you could actually see oil prices plummet. And we saw that happen in 2008 and 2009, as well as in 2014 and 2015, where we saw oil prices back in the $30 a barrel range and $45 a barrel range respectively.SEANA SMITH: All right, Andy, always great to have you. Andy Lipow, Lipow Oil Associates founder and president.]

column4: Gas prices in summer 2023 ‘contingent on if refineries will meet demand’: Analyst
column10: [GasBuddy Head of Petroleum Analysis Patrick De Haan joins Yahoo Finance Live to examine forecasts for household gasoline spending in 2023, while also looking at the outlook for refinery capacities and regional pricing trends in the U.S.Video TranscriptJARED BLIKRE: Pain at the pump has been a major talking point throughout 2022, but as prices have been dropping this month, are they poised to jump back in the near future? Well, according to GasBuddy, prices in most US cities could reach $4 a gallon again come springtime. So for more on this, we welcome in Patrick De Haan, GasBuddy head of petroleum analysis. Patrick, thank you for joining us here today. So what should we expect with gas prices in the near future?PATRICK DE HAAN: Well, certainly a little bit of good news, a little bit of bad news. I think overall, the good news is that Americans in the household will spend less on gasoline in 2023 than they did in 2022. But it wouldn't be a normal year without the spikes that we see in spring and prices then going back down in fall. And eventually, while we're enjoying relatively low prices now, I'm afraid that with China reopening, this spring could see a nice spike. And that could bring the national average back above the $4 a gallon mark. But the good news is we're not expecting the record highs that we saw in 2022 of over the $5 a gallon level.SEANA SMITH: Yeah, Patrick, we just did-- Yahoo Finance Rick Newman was just on set talking about the predictions that our viewers wrote in. And that was one of the predictions that gas prices were going to be back above 4 bucks a gallon because of China lifting its restrictions. Let's talk, though, about the higher prices, how long it could potentially be above $4 a gallon. Are we talking about throughout next summer?PATRICK DE HAAN: I think that's certainly a strong possibility. It's really going to be contingent on if refineries are able to meet demand and what Americans do this summer, given the fact that prices may be lower. Do we see a big jump in demand? I think demand was struggling this summer under the weight of some of those high prices. So if a lot of Americans defer travel, they may want to get back out on the road, given the fact that gas prices this summer could be a little bit less.Story continuesBut I would say that probably between Memorial Day and Labor Day, you may see $4 a gallon for several weeks maybe beyond that. Of course, a lot mixed in to how China is looking and how much of their economy is reopening and what we see in terms of consumption from China.JARED BLIKRE: Patrick, we had a number of curveballs in 2022. You're opened up, and we have suddenly found ourselves in a war with-- embroiled in a war between Russia and Ukraine. Wondering what you're thinking about in terms of potential headwinds or stuff out of the blue in the new year.PATRICK DE HAAN: Well, I think refining will continue to be a headwind. It was a challenge in 2022. And I think we're going to get a little bit more breathing room in terms of refining capacity. Not so much in the US. We're going to add about 275,000 barrels a day of capacity, thanks to ExxonMobil's refining project that's been underway for three years in Texas. More so, we're going to get breathing room overseas. Africa opening refineries, additional capacity in Asia, as well as the Middle East. All likely helping to create some breathing room, but there still could be the seasonal challenges related to the switchover to summer gasoline, as refiners carry out that maintenance.And keep in mind the extreme cold weather that we saw across the US last week also caused a lot of refinery disruptions. So that's going to be the wild card this year, as well as I think China's economy. They appear to be embracing easing the restrictions. And so there could be a level of pent-up demand in China that we saw here in the US a couple of years ago. And that could be a wild card as well.SEANA SMITH: And Patrick, when it comes to higher prices in terms of areas of the country that are likely to see the highest prices, is that going to be consistent with what we saw last year when you take a look at California, obviously, being one of the outliers and experiencing much higher prices than what we saw in many other parts?PATRICK DE HAAN: Yeah, absolutely. The motto last year was certainly that the coasts felt a lot more of the pain, particularly the mid-Atlantic, the Northeast areas that are reliant on more imports, and the West Coast also somewhat segmented away from the rest of the country. So both the extremes, the Northeast and the West Coast, likely to see some of those refinery challenges persist. California certainly could see the return of $5, even $6, a gallon gasoline if refinery issues are significant this year. Much of the Northeast still also reliant on imports because of Russia's war in Ukraine. A lack of refining capacity in the Northeast also could point to prices that in New York, areas of New England could exceed $5 a gallon again this year.JARED BLIKRE: We're just recovering here in the Northeast from a bitter cold spell, a storm that passed through. Just wondering the implications that this might have had on the energy market overall, including heating, gas prices. Kind of give you the floor for the last question here.PATRICK DE HAAN: Well, we've seen a lot of volatility in natural gas. Things have really plummeted, but there's still the possibility that if natural gas surges due to cold spells, there could be switches back over to using oil, diesel and heating oil. So that's a huge wildcard, but the Northeast is going to be very susceptible to bouts of cold weather. Keep in mind much of the Northeast consumes heating oil. I think that's going to be a challenge this winter. Diesel and heating oil likely to remain rather expensive, comparing that to gasoline, for much of the winter.SEANA SMITH: All right, Patrick De Haan, always great to have you of GasBuddy. Thanks so much for joining us here this afternoon.]

column4: Oil: $70-$90 range is ‘somewhere we’re going to be’ for first two quarters of 2023, analyst says
column10: [Prosper Trading Academy CEO Scott Bauer joins Yahoo Finance Live to discuss predictions for oil prices in 2023, driving factors for energy stocks and commodities, and the outlook for demand.Video TranscriptJARED BLIKRE: Russia threatening to cut oil output by up to 7% or up to 700,000 barrels per day in response to sanctions and price caps placed on Russian oil in response to the country's invasion of Ukraine. Oil trading, we can see that's up about $2.70-- or 2.76% today, up about $2.00 and change. Just closing in on that $80 per barrel price level.Now we have Scott Bauer, CEO of Prosper Training Academy joining us. And, Scott, I was just reeling off the latest price of oil here. We bounced off $70. Now that's basis WTI here. We had-- and I think that was earlier in the month when we were first getting those actual sanctions by Russia pegged-- I guess plowed on, and now we really didn't see much of the way in negative price action from there. In fact, we're up about $8. Just wondering how you're viewing the oil market in response to this latest news.SCOTT BAUER: Yeah, I have been bullish oil ever since we've started dropping below $100 and buying it on every dip, selling it on any sort of rally here. I've had to get stopped out a couple of times, but $70, $71, Jared, that really, to me, is a short-term bottom. When I say short term, I'm saying at least six months.The floor is put in for a number of reasons. First off, that's where, you know, the administration has said we're going to replenish SPR if we get down there. So to me, that is somewhat of a floor.Also, I think there's just still a tremendous amount of tailwinds in the space here. Number one, as it has been for me all year is what's going on in Russia/Ukraine. Number two is what's going on in China, and I believe that we-- the oil market, anyway, has seen the worst-case scenario in terms of demand, in terms of lockdowns, even with the latest, you know, policy that they've talked about with kind of opening back up and people getting COVID. I think we've seen the worst in terms of demand. It's only going to get higher from here.Story continuesSo there are just a bunch of tailwinds, and that $70 number to me, because of the SPR, that absolutely is a floor.JARED BLIKRE: Yes, President Biden talked about buying oil at $70 per barrel for the SPR to replenish it from those-- from the lower levels that it's fallen to.Now you mentioned the double whammy this year, and we were talking about price bottoms. What about a ceiling? What would it take to see a ceiling in terms of the news flow, in terms of price action? What are you thinking about as you think about those upper targets here?SCOTT BAUER: It absolutely would not surprise me to see oil back in the $90s with a nine handle. To break $100, though, I think is going to be a real tough job. I just don't see any scenario other than-- other than some more major geopolitical conflict that we're going to see oil just get to those prices again. And listen, that's not out of the question-- out of the question, unfortunately. That can happen. But I think this range of the low $70s probably to the mid $90s is somewhere we're going to be for, you know, at least the first and second quarter of the year.JARED BLIKRE: All right, and what about natural gas and some of the other elements to the energy sector? We've seen natural gas prices drop off quite precipitously. That has its own supply-and-demand aspects, but maybe you can just comment on that market a little bit.SCOTT BAUER: It absolutely does. And, in fact, if you're looking at what's going on in Russia right now and the news that they announced that they might be pulling back production here, that is really just for crude and oil products. It is not for natural gas.So I know that, especially in Europe, there has been a shortage. But right now, I'm not going to say it's fine, but the natural-gas supply right now is not as dire, if you will, as what we're seeing on the crude side. And again, if we turn back to Russia, 40%-- almost 40% of all of their export revenues are from the oil space, not from natural gas.So natural gas is still flowing. I don't see that we're going to get a major, major spike again, certainly not to where we were. UMG, which I track very closely, is trading right around $15 and 1/2, $16 right now, which is a low we've seen in probably three, four months. That was as high as the mid $30s just a couple months ago. Maybe we see a 15%, 20% pop in natural gas from here just because of this massive selloff that we've had, but I don't think that we're going to get into the crunch like we might get with crude [AUDIO OUT].JARED BLIKRE: Well, we've been talking about the Russian-- I guess the Russian effect on crude-oil supplies. It seems to me when we-- this doesn't-- this hasn't had necessarily bearish price-action consequences when we talk about crude oil this year, and I think part of it comes from the fact that we have dark supplies so that you never see oil taken off the market considerably. You see a market-clearing price. So at some price, somebody is going to take Russian oil off the market.Just wondering, with all the sanctions in place, with all the eyeballs on this, what are the potentials for violations of that next year? What are some of the situations that could evolve that could actually be bearish for the price of energy that might not be factored in right now?SCOTT BAUER: So in all honesty, there's probably violations going on right now, and there will continue [AUDIO OUT] violations going on. Some of that's just going to be-- let's call it glanced over. But we're not going to see, in my opinion, the price get much below $60, which is that price cap there. Maybe we'll see it a little bit. You've got to think that there's [AUDIO OUT] be some violation there.JARED BLIKRE: Yeah, well, I love doing a deep dive on the oil market and the futures markets on the day before Christmas Eve here. Thank you for joining us, Scott Bauer.]

column4: Oil forecasts see prices at $80-96 per barrel next year

Hard to believe that earlier this year, we saw oil at just above $130 a barrel. Right now, we're looking at WTI around $80 and Brent crude at $83. But where will these oil prices be next year? Well, I asked several analysts, and let's put up a board so you can see some of the projections for 2023.You've got Ed Morse from Citi projecting that Brent crude will average around $80 per barrel, with WTI averaging $75 a barrel. JPMorgan says that Brent will average around $90 a barrel next year.
