column4: Energy: ‘No trigger was pulled’ on U.S. crude oil pricing opportunities, analyst explains
column10: [Bob Iaccino, Path Trading Partners Co-Founder and Chief Market Strategist and The Stock Think Tank Co-Portfolio Manager, talks about oil prices and the U.S. petroleum reserve.Video TranscriptSEANA SMITH: Oil prices under pressure today, closing off just over 1%, below $80 a barrel. Now, the move lower coming after the Biden administration said that it is selling more crude from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. This time, 26 million barrels of oil will be delivered to the market starting in April, fulfilling the budget directives mandated by Congress.Here with more on this, we want to bring in Bob Iaccino, Path Training Partners Co-Founder and Chief Market Strategist. Bob, it's great to see you here. So let's talk about what this means for the energy market, for the crude market in the longer term. Yes, we're seeing the pressure on prices today. How much more pressure, maybe, could we expect because of this?BOB IACCINO: Well, hey, Seana, it's good to see you again. It's likely a temporary bit of pressure. Most of the pressure has come to the upside lately. It's interesting, because we actually had crude oil down about 1.3% on the open. It was a gap lower. There was weakness, definitely, depending on that story about more SPR releases coming up.But then as it kind of fed through the market that this was a pre-scheduled sale, of which there's more to come-- there were only some temporarily suspended by Congress-- the concern now becomes the level of the SPR. We've got about 372 million barrels in the SPR now. You take this 26 away, and you're only about 93.6 million barrels away from where the law halts sales for the SPR.And there's a lot of dominoes to fall when that happens, not the least of which being that Congress has mandated many different levels and the timing of sales to fill other budget holes, which kind of always happens when Congress starts mixing their messages here and mixing their assets and their liabilities. This is another case like that.Story continuesPresident Biden asked for these to be suspended. In this particular political climate after the midterms, not likely to happen. So it's going to put the President and the SPR specifically in the country in a pretty bad spot going forward.DAVE BRIGGS: Aren't there actual physical concerns when we start to get this low at the Strategic Petroleum Reserve? And what's the plan to refill it?BOB IACCINO: So the plan was to buy oil at $70 a barrel. We got there. We got below $69 a barrel-- I'm sorry, $70 a barrel, in that $69 range, last October. But no trigger was pulled. Part of that might be because filling the SPR has very little to do with West Texas Intermediate crude. It's more of a heavy base crude oil.Remember, all crude is not made the same. So they need a heavier base crude, which is the type that our refineries are processing. Brent crude never got down there, as well as some of the necessary types of oil that we could have refilled with.There's physical issues as well. You fill those tanks with brine and then you pump that brine out to refill it with oil. And there's only so much time they can be empty. There's only so much time crude oil can stay in those storage tanks, which has a lot to do with the circular motion of the sales, and the filling, and the sales, and the filling. The issue becomes as you look forward, both Saudi Arabia and the UAE have talked about potential shortages of supply in 2024.We do have a record coming from the Permian Basin in March-- another 75,000 barrels a day is going to put us at a record for shale drilling. But again, that's not the type of oil that goes into the SPR. And that's why looking ahead, it causes more of a lift to prices than it does pressure on prices that we're seeing a little bit yesterday and also this morning.SEANA SMITH: So, Bob, then, what does that mean in terms of when we could expect to see those higher prices? And then when it comes to gas prices, certainly there's a lot of fear that we're heading back above $4 a gallon-- do you think we will break above that level?BOB IACCINO: Well, I do think that's why the stake is going to be bought by the economist as opposed to the other way around. I think energy prices are going to be one of the areas that is not going to back off as easily as had previously been hoped. When you look at what's going on with the SPR now, they need to start filling it regardless of price.And I suspect they're going to start doing that quickly and soon-- maybe before, even, the summer driving season begins again. And we're only in February. But that's the time when speculators and people start planning for that seasonal bump-up of gasoline prices.It's coming in the next six weeks or so. So I suspect there'll be announcements of the filling of the SPR sometime in the next two to three weeks.DAVE BRIGGS: All right, gas prices, up, what $0.17 from a month ago. Bob Iaccino, good to see you, sir. Thank you.BOB IACCINO: Good to see you as well.]

column4: The oil market looks drastically different today than it did when Russia invaded Ukraine
column10: [The oil market looks drastically different today than it did a year ago, when Russia invaded Ukraine.“It is the most significant set of market dislocations and distortions in energy markets generally speaking that I ever recall,” Ed Morse, global head of commodity research at Citi, told Yahoo Finance.Prior to the invasion on February 24, 2022, Russia was exporting much of its crude and petroleum products to Europe, with a much smaller portion going to China, India, and other Asian nations.By the end of 2022, that ratio had completely flipped.“It has, from a markets’ perspective, created two markets, a transparent [oil] market, and a non-transparent market,” said Morse.This content is not available due to your privacy preferences.Update your settings here to see it.“Russian crude oil was simply reshuffled from old customers in Europe to new customers in Asia,” Andy Lipow of Lipow Oil Associates recently wrote in a client note. “Europe’s energy divorce from Russia is nearly complete.”The latest in a series of sanctions on Moscow by Western nations in response to the war was imposed earlier this month: Those include an E.U. ban on Russian oil product exports. Prior to that, a G7 price cap on Russian oil was implemented in order to weaken the country's coffers.“In a roundabout way, the December 5, 2022, price caps that were imposed on Russian crude oil exports are working. The E.U. and USA and others are not buying from Russia, that leaves Russia with a limited number of customers. Those customers are demanding lower prices,” said Lipow.It's not every year that energy prices skyrocket like they did over the past year. Days after Russia's invasion, West Texas Intermediate (WTI) reached a closing peak of $123.70 per barrel and Brent futures settled at $127.98.The Biden administration authorized releases from the U.S. strategic petroleum reserve in order to bring down gasoline prices, which reached record highs by mid-June of last year.Eventually prices fell, and today, WTI is trading around the $75 per barrel level while Brent is hovering around $82 per barrel.Story continuesThis content is not available due to your privacy preferences.Update your settings here to see it.The reopening of China following strict COVID lockdowns is seen as bullish for energy prices going forward, but so far oil has been mostly been trading in a tight range.“Crude has gone sideways as the China expansion story battles with the ‘recession around the corner’ story. So far it’s a stalemate,” Stewart Glickman, energy equity analyst at CFRA Research, told Yahoo Finance.Natural gas prices both in Europe and the U.S. have also come down considerably from their peaks. The energy sector, which had a blockbuster 2022, is seeing a lackluster 2023."Energy prices have been relatively weak this year as we have a very warm winter in both North America and Europe. The weather has caused natural gas prices to plummet and oil prices to weaken, which weighs on energy stocks,” Jay Hatfield, CEO at Infrastructure Capital Advisors.'Energy transition seeing an acceleration'Both the U.S. and Europe have increased their efforts to go green with renewable energy efforts, as companies invest in solar, wind, and biofuels.Renewable electricity capacity in the E.U. is projected to double between 2022 and 2027, according to the International Energy Association. “The energy transition is absolutely seeing an acceleration as a result of Russia/Ukraine,” says Citi’s Morse. “It was on the path, but it got accelerated.”Ines is a senior business reporter for Yahoo Finance. column4: Energy: ‘No trigger was pulled’ on U.S. crude oil pricing opportunities, analyst explains
column10: [Bob Iaccino, Path Trading Partners Co-Founder and Chief Market Strategist and The Stock Think Tank Co-Portfolio Manager, talks about oil prices and the U.S. petroleum reserve.Video TranscriptSEANA SMITH: Oil prices under pressure today, closing off just over 1%, below $80 a barrel. Now, the move lower coming after the Biden administration said that it is selling more crude from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. This time, 26 million barrels of oil will be delivered to the market starting in April, fulfilling the budget directives mandated by Congress.Here with more on this, we want to bring in Bob Iaccino, Path Training Partners Co-Founder and Chief Market Strategist. Bob, it's great to see you here. So let's talk about what this means for the energy market, for the crude market in the longer term. Yes, we're seeing the pressure on prices today. How much more pressure, maybe, could we expect because of this?BOB IACCINO: Well, hey, Seana, it's good to see you again. It's likely a temporary bit of pressure. Most of the pressure has come to the upside lately. It's interesting, because we actually had crude oil down about 1.3% on the open. It was a gap lower. There was weakness, definitely, depending on that story about more SPR releases coming up.But then as it kind of fed through the market that this was a pre-scheduled sale, of which there's more to come-- there were only some temporarily suspended by Congress-- the concern now becomes the level of the SPR. We've got about 372 million barrels in the SPR now. You take this 26 away, and you're only about 93.6 million barrels away from where the law halts sales for the SPR.And there's a lot of dominoes to fall when that happens, not the least of which being that Congress has mandated many different levels and the timing of sales to fill other budget holes, which kind of always happens when Congress starts mixing their messages here and mixing their assets and their liabilities. This is another case like that.Story continuesPresident Biden asked for these to be suspended. In this particular political climate after the midterms, not likely to happen. So it's going to put the President and the SPR specifically in the country in a pretty bad spot going forward.DAVE BRIGGS: Aren't there actual physical concerns when we start to get this low at the Strategic Petroleum Reserve? And what's the plan to refill it?BOB IACCINO: So the plan was to buy oil at $70 a barrel. We got there. We got below $69 a barrel-- I'm sorry, $70 a barrel, in that $69 range, last October. But no trigger was pulled. Part of that might be because filling the SPR has very little to do with West Texas Intermediate crude. It's more of a heavy base crude oil.Remember, all crude is not made the same. So they need a heavier base crude, which is the type that our refineries are processing. Brent crude never got down there, as well as some of the necessary types of oil that we could have refilled with.There's physical issues as well. You fill those tanks with brine and then you pump that brine out to refill it with oil. And there's only so much time they can be empty. There's only so much time crude oil can stay in those storage tanks, which has a lot to do with the circular motion of the sales, and the filling, and the sales, and the filling. The issue becomes as you look forward, both Saudi Arabia and the UAE have talked about potential shortages of supply in 2024.We do have a record coming from the Permian Basin in March-- another 75,000 barrels a day is going to put us at a record for shale drilling. But again, that's not the type of oil that goes into the SPR. And that's why looking ahead, it causes more of a lift to prices than it does pressure on prices that we're seeing a little bit yesterday and also this morning.SEANA SMITH: So, Bob, then, what does that mean in terms of when we could expect to see those higher prices? And then when it comes to gas prices, certainly there's a lot of fear that we're heading back above $4 a gallon-- do you think we will break above that level?BOB IACCINO: Well, I do think that's why the stake is going to be bought by the economist as opposed to the other way around. I think energy prices are going to be one of the areas that is not going to back off as easily as had previously been hoped. When you look at what's going on with the SPR now, they need to start filling it regardless of price.And I suspect they're going to start doing that quickly and soon-- maybe before, even, the summer driving season begins again. And we're only in February. But that's the time when speculators and people start planning for that seasonal bump-up of gasoline prices.It's coming in the next six weeks or so. So I suspect there'll be announcements of the filling of the SPR sometime in the next two to three weeks.DAVE BRIGGS: All right, gas prices, up, what $0.17 from a month ago. Bob Iaccino, good to see you, sir. Thank you.BOB IACCINO: Good to see you as well.]

column4: The oil market looks drastically different today than it did when Russia invaded Ukraine
column10: [The oil market looks drastically different today than it did a year ago, when Russia invaded Ukraine.“It is the most significant set of market dislocations and distortions in energy markets generally speaking that I ever recall,” Ed Morse, global head of commodity research at Citi, told Yahoo Finance.Prior to the invasion on February 24, 2022, Russia was exporting much of its crude and petroleum products to Europe, with a much smaller portion going to China, India, and other Asian nations.By the end of 2022, that ratio had completely flipped.“It has, from a markets’ perspective, created two markets, a transparent [oil] market, and a non-transparent market,” said Morse.This content is not available due to your privacy preferences.Update your settings here to see it.“Russian crude oil was simply reshuffled from old customers in Europe to new customers in Asia,” Andy Lipow of Lipow Oil Associates recently wrote in a client note. “Europe’s energy divorce from Russia is nearly complete.”The latest in a series of sanctions on Moscow by Western nations in response to the war was imposed earlier this month: Those include an E.U. ban on Russian oil product exports. Prior to that, a G7 price cap on Russian oil was implemented in order to weaken the country's coffers.“In a roundabout way, the December 5, 2022, price caps that were imposed on Russian crude oil exports are working. The E.U. and USA and others are not buying from Russia, that leaves Russia with a limited number of customers. Those customers are demanding lower prices,” said Lipow.It's not every year that energy prices skyrocket like they did over the past year. Days after Russia's invasion, West Texas Intermediate (WTI) reached a closing peak of $123.70 per barrel and Brent futures settled at $127.98.The Biden administration authorized releases from the U.S. strategic petroleum reserve in order to bring down gasoline prices, which reached record highs by mid-June of last year.Eventually prices fell, and today, WTI is trading around the $75 per barrel level while Brent is hovering around $82 per barrel.Story continuesThis content is not available due to your privacy preferences.Update your settings here to see it.The reopening of China following strict COVID lockdowns is seen as bullish for energy prices going forward, but so far oil has been mostly been trading in a tight range.“Crude has gone sideways as the China expansion story battles with the ‘recession around the corner’ story. So far it’s a stalemate,” Stewart Glickman, energy equity analyst at CFRA Research, told Yahoo Finance.Natural gas prices both in Europe and the U.S. have also come down considerably from their peaks. The energy sector, which had a blockbuster 2022, is seeing a lackluster 2023."Energy prices have been relatively weak this year as we have a very warm winter in both North America and Europe. The weather has caused natural gas prices to plummet and oil prices to weaken, which weighs on energy stocks,” Jay Hatfield, CEO at Infrastructure Capital Advisors.'Energy transition seeing an acceleration'Both the U.S. and Europe have increased their efforts to go green with renewable energy efforts, as companies invest in solar, wind, and biofuels.Renewable electricity capacity in the E.U. is projected to double between 2022 and 2027, according to the International Energy Association. “The energy transition is absolutely seeing an acceleration as a result of Russia/Ukraine,” says Citi’s Morse. “It was on the path, but it got accelerated.”Ines is a senior business reporter for Yahoo Finance. column4: How impacts from the Russia-Ukraine war rippled across the energy market

Julie.JULIE HYMAN: Thanks so much, Jared. I appreciate it.]

column4: Decline in gasoline demand a 'noticeable' and 'permanent change,' says analyst
column10: [A decline in gasoline consumption in the U.S. could be a trend that's here to stay, according to one analyst.“There has been a noticeable, and I believe permanent, change toward lower gasoline demand,” Andy Lipow of Lipow Oil Associates told Yahoo Finance.The analyst noted that demand peaked between 2017 and 2019 at just over 9.3 million barrels per day, according to data from the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA).The lockdowns during the pandemic impacted demand in 2020 and 2021. However 2022’s level was down 0.5% from the prior year. Indications of gasoline demand in 2023 are thus far running behind 2022.“It is the case, in part, because of early retirements," Ed Morse, head of global commodity research at Citi told Yahoo Finance. "It's [also] the case in part because of changing work habits on how many days people go to work."Many workers who used to commute five days a week now drive less. The meteoric rise in energy costs in 2022 also impacted demand as gasoline prices temporarily surged past $5 per gallon last year.“Not only has working remotely impacted Americans' driving habits, but the higher cost of gasoline has caused the consumer to drive a bit less. Combined with increasing availability and sales of electric vehicles at the expense of gasoline-powered cars, I expect that gasoline demand will continue to decline about 1% annually over the next few years,” said Lipow.Gas prices advertised at a Mobil Station in Santa Monica, California, U.S., May 23, 2022. REUTERS/David SwansonDiesel demand is also lower. That may be attributed to trucks going greener. coupled with less deliveries and a decline in trade port volumes.Gasoline usage is seasonal, and it's expected that come spring and summer, drivers will see prices rise above the current national average of $3.36 per gallon.China is in recovery mode from its Covid lockdowns, and some analysts see the cost for oil and refined products increasing as that economy ramps up its consumption of energy.Lipow forecasts a price of $3.65 per gallon going into the summer driving season: “According to my Tarot cards, I do not see the national average of gasoline hitting $4.00 per gallon.”Story continuesOn Wednesday, Brent futures (BZ=F) hovered above $84 per barrel while U.S. West Texas Intermediate (CL=F) crude traded above $77 per barrel.Ines Ferre is a senior business reporter for Yahoo Finance. column4: The oil market looks drastically different today than it did when Russia invaded Ukraine
column10: [The oil market looks drastically different today than it did a year ago, when Russia invaded Ukraine.“It is the most significant set of market dislocations and distortions in energy markets generally speaking that I ever recall,” Ed Morse, global head of commodity research at Citi, told Yahoo Finance.Prior to the invasion on February 24, 2022, Russia was exporting much of its crude and petroleum products to Europe, with a much smaller portion going to China, India, and other Asian nations.By the end of 2022, that ratio had completely flipped.“It has, from a markets’ perspective, created two markets, a transparent [oil] market, and a non-transparent market,” said Morse.This content is not available due to your privacy preferences.Update your settings here to see it.“Russian crude oil was simply reshuffled from old customers in Europe to new customers in Asia,” Andy Lipow of Lipow Oil Associates recently wrote in a client note. “Europe’s energy divorce from Russia is nearly complete.”The latest in a series of sanctions on Moscow by Western nations in response to the war was imposed earlier this month: Those include an E.U. ban on Russian oil product exports. Prior to that, a G7 price cap on Russian oil was implemented in order to weaken the country's coffers.“In a roundabout way, the December 5, 2022, price caps that were imposed on Russian crude oil exports are working. The E.U. and USA and others are not buying from Russia, that leaves Russia with a limited number of customers. Those customers are demanding lower prices,” said Lipow.It's not every year that energy prices skyrocket like they did over the past year. Days after Russia's invasion, West Texas Intermediate (WTI) reached a closing peak of $123.70 per barrel and Brent futures settled at $127.98.The Biden administration authorized releases from the U.S. strategic petroleum reserve in order to bring down gasoline prices, which reached record highs by mid-June of last year.Eventually prices fell, and today, WTI is trading around the $75 per barrel level while Brent is hovering around $82 per barrel.Story continuesThis content is not available due to your privacy preferences.Update your settings here to see it.The reopening of China following strict COVID lockdowns is seen as bullish for energy prices going forward, but so far oil has been mostly been trading in a tight range.“Crude has gone sideways as the China expansion story battles with the ‘recession around the corner’ story. So far it’s a stalemate,” Stewart Glickman, energy equity analyst at CFRA Research, told Yahoo Finance.Natural gas prices both in Europe and the U.S. have also come down considerably from their peaks. The energy sector, which had a blockbuster 2022, is seeing a lackluster 2023."Energy prices have been relatively weak this year as we have a very warm winter in both North America and Europe. The weather has caused natural gas prices to plummet and oil prices to weaken, which weighs on energy stocks,” Jay Hatfield, CEO at Infrastructure Capital Advisors.'Energy transition seeing an acceleration'Both the U.S. and Europe have increased their efforts to go green with renewable energy efforts, as companies invest in solar, wind, and biofuels.Renewable electricity capacity in the E.U. is projected to double between 2022 and 2027, according to the International Energy Association. “The energy transition is absolutely seeing an acceleration as a result of Russia/Ukraine,” says Citi’s Morse. “It was on the path, but it got accelerated.”Ines is a senior business reporter for Yahoo Finance. column4: Russia-Ukraine war: Looking back at a volatile year for energy markets

And yet Russia's economy has not suffered as much as some analysts had estimated. Over the last year, relatively holding its ground, trading sideways--Here's Scotts Miracle-Gro, maybe more levered to home improvement. But we can see this is just breaking out of a long-term trend line here. But you go back a year ago, prices were definitely higher.Story continuesJULIE HYMAN: Yeah, I suspect. If you look at something more traditional like a CF, for example maybe, or Intrepid Potash, there--JARED BLIKRE: Yes.JULIE HYMAN: --you would see it a little more clearly. These are the large fertilizer makers. Nitrogen right is their main output. So that's--JARED BLIKRE: And one more look here at the futures market. Just stick with me on the YFi Interactive. We're going to take a one-year look. We're talking about some of those moves that we saw in energy. More red than green here overall, we're not going to expect to see long-lasting effects in the orange juice market, for instance.But let me find crude oil because a year ago, there was a buildup. There was a spike in crude oil prices, I believe up to about $130. They've subsided since then. A lot of that coincided with China. China was a huge story, which is now ripping. column4: How impacts from the Russia-Ukraine war rippled across the energy market
column10: [Yahoo Finance Live’s Jared Blikre discusses the major swings in oil prices and energy stocks in the wake of Russia's invasion of Ukraine a year ago and how it stacks up to previous oil price changes in response to world events.Video TranscriptJULIE HYMAN: One year ago today, Russia launched its invasion of Ukraine, sending energy prices on a volatile run, and where is the energy market now a year into the war? Here to break it all down in this installment of What Just Happened, Yahoo Finance's Jared Blikre. Jared.JARED BLIKRE: Yes, well, we saw a number of events fold out not only in the energy markets, but also in the futures and equities as well. I have a timeline of oil price changes in response to world events that goes back 50 years. Let me just show you real quick on our energy heat map what has happened to energy stocks over the last year. And we can see Exxon up 45%, Occidental Petroleum up 50%. It's not only within the last year that this happened. A lot of these trends started before. And the war over in Ukraine was just kind of icing on the cake.Here's a three-year chart, and you can see leading into that, this would be about the timeline of that initial invasion. The trend had definitely been up. It was only a couple of years before that crude oil went negative. WTI traded at negative $40 per barrel. I will still remember that. And now let's take a little journey in this timeline because we've seen the price of oil react positively, that is, with higher prices, to geopolitical events in the past.And you can look right here. Here is the Iranian revolution in 1978, the Iran-Iraq War in 1980. Iraq invades Kuwait in 1990. The September 11, the 9/11 attacks. Over here, we had the global financial crisis. So that was not-- critically not a geopolitical event. But nevertheless, over here on the right-hand edge, we are seeing that as well with the Russian invasion of the Ukraine.And one thing I want to point out here is that the price of oil is extremely volatile. And this makes it very difficult for producers to forecast in their own models. And both prices to the upside and swinging down to the downside give as much consternation to a lot of these producers. So it's not just higher prices equals better. It's volatility in the oil and energy markets is not necessarily a good thing for a lot of these energy majors.Story continuesNow let me show you what's happened in the futures markets. This is commodities over the last year. Right here, in the middle or thereabouts is crude oil. And let me put a three-year chart on there. So you can see, here's that run-up from those lows in 2020 in April of that year into the invasion time period. And then we saw a general fall off from that initial move higher. And put that in a little bit more granularity by looking at a one-year chart.Now a big part of this, too, there's other things going on in the world, of course. We had the slowdown in China because of their zero-COVID policy. We've recently seen the reversal of that, but we're not really seeing liftoff in terms of the price of crude oil just yet. Now OPEC+ is a huge factor. We did receive news that Russia has been cutting their supply of crude oil to the world markets I believe that announcement was made about a month ago. But overall, OPEC+ has pledged to keep its policy in place over or throughout the rest of this year. It's a policy that they put in place last year. And they don't want to disrupt that.Now you got to think if crude oil prices plunged to $60, $50 per barrel, they might get up in arms a little bit, might start restricting some of their own production volumes, but no sign of that yet. And of course, we also have political considerations within the US. That gets to the Biden administration. And you have, on the one hand, the transition to a carbon-free environment by a certain year, by certain deadlines, 2030, '35, '40. And on the other hand, you have the pressing needs of a public that is dealing with high inflation. And so prices at the pump have definitely been front and center as well.I want to point out natural gas. We showed the crude oil prices. Natural gas, they call it the widowmaker for a reason. Very volatile price action over the last year. You can see down about 46% from that level, but down quite a bit more from these highs that we saw in August, September of last year. Julie.JULIE HYMAN: Thanks so much, Jared. I appreciate it.]

column4: How Russia’s invasion of Ukraine dislocated energy markets
column10: [Yahoo Finance’s Ines Ferre joins the Live show to discuss the state of energy markets one year after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.Video Transcript[MUSIC PLAYING]- Welcome back. Russia's invasion of Ukraine one year ago created a major shift in the global energy landscape, the disruption sending oil prices higher around the world and amplifying calls for an accelerated energy transition. Now, for more on the state of energy markets on the anniversary of Russia's invasion, let's get to Yahoo Finance's Ines Ferre. Ines?INES FERRE: And, Jared, how the landscape has changed for the energy markets. Put aside the volatility that we saw last year. One of the most significant changes from the Russian invasion of Ukraine has been the massive dislocations that you've seen in the energy markets. Europe pretty much has tried to divorce itself from its dependency on Russia.And just to give you an idea of what I'm talking about, just prior to the invasion, Russia, a top exporter of petroleum and petroleum products, 80% of its exports were going mostly to Europe, 20% to China, India and other Asian countries. With the Western sanctions that were put on, the Nord Stream pipeline that was sabotaged, by the end of 2022, that ratio had flipped and basically creating two markets. You've got a transparent market and a nontransparent market because Russia is now sending most of its exports to China and India. And it's really dislocated the markets.Now, getting back to the price volatility that we saw over the last year, I want to show you where WTI, for instance, was at the day before the Russian invasion. That price was at $92 a barrel. This week, WTI has been between $75 and $76 a barrel. It settled at $122 back in June of last year.And then the gasoline national average prior to the invasion, it was at $3.53 per gallon. We saw that high of over $5 per gallon back in June of last year. Today it's $3.39 a gallon. The question is now where are oil prices going to be going? Where is energy going to be going?Story continuesWell, the oil forecasts have been coming down. US demand is down for both diesel and gasoline. I got off the phone earlier this morning with Ed Morse, Citi's head of global commodities. He says that part of this may have to do with hybrid work, people going to the office less also, the transition to a green energy as well.Citi has one of the more bearish forecasts when it comes to crude oil prices. They predict low 70s for Brent by the end of the year, high 60s for WTI by the end of the year. But you've got other analysts also, they have been bringing down their forecasts for oil, guys.- Yeah, well, we'll see what ends up happening, Ines. Thank you so much. Appreciate it.]

column10: [GasBuddy Head of Petroleum Analysis Patrick De Haan joins Yahoo Finance Live to discusses the state of gas and oil prices.Video Transcript- This coming Friday marks one year since the Russian invasion of Ukraine. And while the devastating humanitarian and economic impacts have spread far and wide, one peculiar result can be seen at the pump. The average price of a gallon of gas is now down $0.13 from a year ago, according to AAA, averaging $3.40 per gallon today. Let's discuss why and where we are headed with Patrick De Haan, GasBuddy head of petroleum analysis. Good to see you, sir. How do you account for that number down $0.13 since the war began?PATRICK DE HAAN: Well, I think there's a lot of certainty now, even though amidst uncertainty over how the war could continue to unfold, we are now 12 months into Russia's war in Ukraine. And a lot of the initial fears have not been realized that as the flow of oil from Russia does continue though, of course, there have been some challenges, a lot of sanctions, Russian promises to cut production, and overall as well, some help from the Fed, which is trying to restrain interest rates, or excuse me, trying to restrain inflation by raising interest rates, thus acting to cool off consumption. And we are in the time of year that consumption is much weaker. So we've seen gas prices now cooling back off after jumping in late December and early January as it was related to that cold weather that we had that really inundated refineries with shutdowns and cold weather related issues.- So, Patrick, here we are today at $3.40, the National average for regular gas today. What do you think that number is going to look like as we head into the summer months?PATRICK DE HAAN: Well, I think that it will creep lower here over the next couple of weeks as we still are in the time of year that demand is rather anemic, but in March and lasting through Memorial Day, I would expect some more fireworks to emerge. Now, all of this really not considering China and the reopening of their economy, which has really been slow as COVID cases have surged. So there's a lot of wild cards here, but the average increase between March and Memorial Day is in the neighborhood of $0.35 to $0.85 a gallon, so I do expect that will move higher. Much of the nation now is going to be starting the transition to more expensive summer gasoline in March, and with refineries also starting a big maintenance turnaround season, I think that will eventually lead to rising prices.Story continues- Do you have any thoughts on the plummet of natural gas, how long it will continue?PATRICK DE HAAN: Boy, for natural gas, certainly being helped by lower than expected consumption in the U.S. We've had some cold weather blasts here and there, but overall, mother nature has been very favorable. And of course, a lot of the skirmish ahead of the winter last fall was to fill inventories. U.S. Inventories have been adequate, and part of the reason is, of course, Freeport LNG down time, but now with their facilities back online, now with the closing innings of winter here, things are looking much better than we had initially feared. And I think there may have been an overreaction in natural gas, but be that as it may, natural gas, the question is when could we see a one handle on natural gas.- Yeah, that chart is shocking. Real quickly, before we go, I've always wondered this about you, because you know more about gas than anybody I know. Do you drive an EV?PATRICK DE HAAN: I don't drive an EV. I drive an internal combustion engine. You got to still drive internal combustion if I'm going to be a petroleum analyst.[LAUGHING]- OK, I always wondered that about you. When you pivot we will know. You tell us, right? Patrick De Haan, good to see you, man.PATRICK DE HAAN: That's right, I will do that. Thanks.- Check out GasBuddy. Appreciate it.]

column4: Energy stocks ‘in the crosshairs’ of Fed policy, analyst says
column10: [The Energy Word Founder Daniel Dicker joins Yahoo Finance Live to discuss the rise in oil prices as traders weigh the optimism of increased demand from China, tightening monetary policy, and the outlook for oil.Video Transcript[AUDIO LOGO]JULIE HYMAN: And now, let's get to the eternal push-pull. Oil traders are weighing the optimism for increased demand coming from China, while at the same time grappling with concerns over tighter US monetary policy. And not just in the US, of course. So where does this leave prices?Here to discuss is Daniel Dicker, founder of the Energy Word. Dan, it's good to see you. So we have these kind-- this kind of push-and-pull, right? On the one hand, increased China demand, good for oil. On the other hand, tightening monetary policy is not traditionally great for oil. How does it all shake out?DANIEL DICKER: Hi. Julie, we don't want to do another monetary policy segment. You've got 40 of those set up for the rest of the day. And you know, let's talk oil. Oil, fundamentally, is about as strong as I've ever seen it. And sure, we've got prices that are lower than what they probably fundamentally should be. And it's all because of all those 40 other segments you're going to do for the rest of the day.But you know, I look at something like ExxonMobil, and it's trading $110, $111, $112, $113 a share. And the last time that oil was bouncing around the $70 mark, you know, right before the beginning of the year, Exxon was actually trying very hard to breach $70 a share itself. Now, one of these two is wrong.Either oil is too cheap or Exxon is too expensive. And you know, my feeling has always been that the stocks are really representing the profitability of oil and the long-term possibilities of oil.We know very-- how deeply involved Russia remains in Ukraine and how this problem, this systemic supply problem coming from the largest natural gas producer in the world and the third-largest oil producer in the world is going to be going forward. That is going to go on for a long, long time.Story continuesThere are hold backs going on from the Saudis. In the United States, there's all sorts of-- all of the great plays have been drilled. And now, you see shops like, for example, Pioneer supposedly bidding on range resources because there's no new production to be found or really golden new production to be found in the United States. Everybody's looking to buy it at this point.So I'm looking at a long term-- for your investors, I'm looking at a very long-term picture of reducing supply and not much of a demand destruction going on from anywhere. In fact, I see a lot of places where I think that because of the global dustups going on in Europe and elsewhere, that demand picture for fossil fuels, despite all the renewable pressures, is going to increase going forward, at least for the next five years.BRAD SMITH: Yeah, I want to actually get to more on that renewable pressure there. Because when you layer on everything that you were talking about from a longer term perspective with some of the ambitious goals that we've seen rolled out by many companies in energy included, about how to get to more clean energy and sustainable energy, what is the investor's mindset and how they should be kind of pricing their time horizon?DANIEL DICKER: Right, Brad. And I think this stuff is very much on hold right now, unfortunately. I mean, I read article after article about the Indians-- in India, they're absolutely-- they're absolutely thrilled about going back to coal because it's cheap, it's fungible, they have the infrastructure set up for it. And even in Europe, the best stocks of 2022 were coal stocks.I mean, it's terrible to say, but when there's a shortage of energy, people are gonna reach to what's cheapest and what's most easily used. And to heck with the environment. And that's what's really going on right now. And for that, I see a lot of the oil companies, BP for example, who has spent the last 10 years trying to refashion themselves as a sort of sustainable energy company, pivot back to oil and other fossil fuels at least for the foreseeable future.And particularly because of what's going on in Europe and with Ukraine, I think those pressures are far less serious than they were perceived to be even a couple of years ago. I saw Larry Fink, you know, several months ago, very much abandon his push in ESG.I mean, these are the signs that you look at where it's not allowed-- nobody wants to loudly say, oh, I'm going back to burning oil, as opposed to trying to, you know, make solar work for me. But it is something that economically, you see happening over and over again, basically because of what's going on in Europe.JULIE HYMAN: And so what does all of this mean for investors, Dan? To go back to your first point here. I mean, we've talked to a lot of people this year who have said, we still like energy stocks. Energy stocks have not done so great so far this year, at least here in the US. So is that gonna change? Or is it just people are not picking the right, specific ones?DANIEL DICKER: Yeah, you know, what I've been telling my subscribers for a long time is that you really have to play defense. The Fed has control of this market. They're targeting inflation on commodities, and that means oil, number one. And that means, you know, that energy is in the crosshairs.But at times, you find these tremendous values. And you know, I've been, you know, pointing out to my subscribers for example, EQT, last week, was under $30. Just a tremendous value to buy some and put it away. And something like Core, Core Labs, which is a services company that's directly in Europe. It has a very strong presence in Europe.And these services companies because of what's going on in Europe, when they reach values, when they reach levels are worth a long-term play. And all of this right now is long term. I would not be looking, you know, to find a bottom. I would not expect some of these stocks to go down further. I do expect them to go down further. It's gonna be a tough year. But there are spots where tremendous, tremendous long-term values in energy stocks can be found.JULIE HYMAN: All right, well, we'll see what ends up happening with them over the long term. Thanks so much, Dan Dicker of the Energy Word. Appreciate it.]

column4: How impacts from the Russia-Ukraine war rippled across the energy market
column10: [Yahoo Finance Live’s Jared Blikre discusses the major swings in oil prices and energy stocks in the wake of Russia's invasion of Ukraine a year ago and how it stacks up to previous oil price changes in response to world events.Video TranscriptJULIE HYMAN: One year ago today, Russia launched its invasion of Ukraine, sending energy prices on a volatile run, and where is the energy market now a year into the war? Here to break it all down in this installment of What Just Happened, Yahoo Finance's Jared Blikre. Jared.JARED BLIKRE: Yes, well, we saw a number of events fold out not only in the energy markets, but also in the futures and equities as well. I have a timeline of oil price changes in response to world events that goes back 50 years. Let me just show you real quick on our energy heat map what has happened to energy stocks over the last year. And we can see Exxon up 45%, Occidental Petroleum up 50%. It's not only within the last year that this happened. A lot of these trends started before. And the war over in Ukraine was just kind of icing on the cake.Here's a three-year chart, and you can see leading into that, this would be about the timeline of that initial invasion. The trend had definitely been up. It was only a couple of years before that crude oil went negative. WTI traded at negative $40 per barrel. I will still remember that. And now let's take a little journey in this timeline because we've seen the price of oil react positively, that is, with higher prices, to geopolitical events in the past.And you can look right here. Here is the Iranian revolution in 1978, the Iran-Iraq War in 1980. Iraq invades Kuwait in 1990. The September 11, the 9/11 attacks. Over here, we had the global financial crisis. So that was not-- critically not a geopolitical event. column4: How Russia’s invasion of Ukraine dislocated energy markets
column10: [Yahoo Finance’s Ines Ferre joins the Live show to discuss the state of energy markets one year after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.Video Transcript[MUSIC PLAYING]- Welcome back. Russia's invasion of Ukraine one year ago created a major shift in the global energy landscape, the disruption sending oil prices higher around the world and amplifying calls for an accelerated energy transition. Now, for more on the state of energy markets on the anniversary of Russia's invasion, let's get to Yahoo Finance's Ines Ferre. Ines?INES FERRE: And, Jared, how the landscape has changed for the energy markets. Put aside the volatility that we saw last year. One of the most significant changes from the Russian invasion of Ukraine has been the massive dislocations that you've seen in the energy markets. Europe pretty much has tried to divorce itself from its dependency on Russia.And just to give you an idea of what I'm talking about, just prior to the invasion, Russia, a top exporter of petroleum and petroleum products, 80% of its exports were going mostly to Europe, 20% to China, India and other Asian countries. With the Western sanctions that were put on, the Nord Stream pipeline that was sabotaged, by the end of 2022, that ratio had flipped and basically creating two markets. You've got a transparent market and a nontransparent market because Russia is now sending most of its exports to China and India. And it's really dislocated the markets.Now, getting back to the price volatility that we saw over the last year, I want to show you where WTI, for instance, was at the day before the Russian invasion. That price was at $92 a barrel. This week, WTI has been between $75 and $76 a barrel. It settled at $122 back in June of last year.And then the gasoline national average prior to the invasion, it was at $3.53 per gallon. column4: Energy stocks ‘in the crosshairs’ of Fed policy, analyst says
column10: [The Energy Word Founder Daniel Dicker joins Yahoo Finance Live to discuss the rise in oil prices as traders weigh the optimism of increased demand from China, tightening monetary policy, and the outlook for oil.Video Transcript[AUDIO LOGO]JULIE HYMAN: And now, let's get to the eternal push-pull. So where does this leave prices?Here to discuss is Daniel Dicker, founder of the Energy Word. Dan, it's good to see you. So we have these kind-- this kind of push-and-pull, right? On the one hand, increased China demand, good for oil. On the other hand, tightening monetary policy is not traditionally great for oil. How does it all shake out?DANIEL DICKER: Hi. Julie, we don't want to do another monetary policy segment. You've got 40 of those set up for the rest of the day. And you know, let's talk oil. Oil, fundamentally, is about as strong as I've ever seen it. And sure, we've got prices that are lower than what they probably fundamentally should be. And it's all because of all those 40 other segments you're going to do for the rest of the day.But you know, I look at something like ExxonMobil, and it's trading $110, $111, $112, $113 a share. And the last time that oil was bouncing around the $70 mark, you know, right before the beginning of the year, Exxon was actually trying very hard to breach $70 a share itself. Now, one of these two is wrong.Either oil is too cheap or Exxon is too expensive. And you know, my feeling has always been that the stocks are really representing the profitability of oil and the long-term possibilities of oil.We know very-- how deeply involved Russia remains in Ukraine and how this problem, this systemic supply problem coming from the largest natural gas producer in the world and the third-largest oil producer in the world is going to be going forward. That is going to go on for a long, long time.Story continuesThere are hold backs going on from the Saudis. In the United States, there's all sorts of-- all of the great plays have been drilled. And now, you see shops like, for example, Pioneer supposedly bidding on range resources because there's no new production to be found or really golden new production to be found in the United States. Everybody's looking to buy it at this point.So I'm looking at a long term-- for your investors, I'm looking at a very long-term picture of reducing supply and not much of a demand destruction going on from anywhere. Because when you layer on everything that you were talking about from a longer term perspective with some of the ambitious goals that we've seen rolled out by many companies in energy included, about how to get to more clean energy and sustainable energy, what is the investor's mindset and how they should be kind of pricing their time horizon?DANIEL DICKER: Right, Brad. And I think this stuff is very much on hold right now, unfortunately. I mean, I read article after article about the Indians-- in India, they're absolutely-- they're absolutely thrilled about going back to coal because it's cheap, it's fungible, they have the infrastructure set up for it. And even in Europe, the best stocks of 2022 were coal stocks.I mean, it's terrible to say, but when there's a shortage of energy, people are gonna reach to what's cheapest and what's most easily used. And to heck with the environment. And that's what's really going on right now. And for that, I see a lot of the oil companies, BP for example, who has spent the last 10 years trying to refashion themselves as a sort of sustainable energy company, pivot back to oil and other fossil fuels at least for the foreseeable future.And particularly because of what's going on in Europe and with Ukraine, I think those pressures are far less serious than they were perceived to be even a couple of years ago. I saw Larry Fink, you know, several months ago, very much abandon his push in ESG.I mean, these are the signs that you look at where it's not allowed-- nobody wants to loudly say, oh, I'm going back to burning oil, as opposed to trying to, you know, make solar work for me. But it is something that economically, you see happening over and over again, basically because of what's going on in Europe.JULIE HYMAN: And so what does all of this mean for investors, Dan? To go back to your first point here. I mean, we've talked to a lot of people this year who have said, we still like energy stocks. Energy stocks have not done so great so far this year, at least here in the US. So is that gonna change? Or is it just people are not picking the right, specific ones?DANIEL DICKER: Yeah, you know, what I've been telling my subscribers for a long time is that you really have to play defense. The Fed has control of this market. They're targeting inflation on commodities, and that means oil, number one. And that means, you know, that energy is in the crosshairs.But at times, you find these tremendous values. And you know, I've been, you know, pointing out to my subscribers for example, EQT, last week, was under $30. Just a tremendous value to buy some and put it away. And something like Core, Core Labs, which is a services company that's directly in Europe. It has a very strong presence in Europe.And these services companies because of what's going on in Europe, when they reach values, when they reach levels are worth a long-term play. And all of this right now is long term. I would not be looking, you know, to find a bottom. I would not expect some of these stocks to go down further. I do expect them to go down further. It's gonna be a tough year. But there are spots where tremendous, tremendous long-term values in energy stocks can be found.JULIE HYMAN: All right, well, we'll see what ends up happening with them over the long term. Thanks so much, Dan Dicker of the Energy Word. Appreciate it.]

column4: Decline in gasoline demand a 'noticeable' and 'permanent change,' says analyst
column10: [A decline in gasoline consumption in the U.S. could be a trend that's here to stay, according to one analyst.“There has been a noticeable, and I believe permanent, change toward lower gasoline demand,” Andy Lipow of Lipow Oil Associates told Yahoo Finance.The analyst noted that demand peaked between 2017 and 2019 at just over 9.3 million barrels per day, according to data from the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA).The lockdowns during the pandemic impacted demand in 2020 and 2021. However 2022’s level was down 0.5% from the prior year. Indications of gasoline demand in 2023 are thus far running behind 2022.“It is the case, in part, because of early retirements," Ed Morse, head of global commodity research at Citi told Yahoo Finance. "It's [also] the case in part because of changing work habits on how many days people go to work."Many workers who used to commute five days a week now drive less. The meteoric rise in energy costs in 2022 also impacted demand as gasoline prices temporarily surged past $5 per gallon last year.“Not only has working remotely impacted Americans' driving habits, but the higher cost of gasoline has caused the consumer to drive a bit less. Combined with increasing availability and sales of electric vehicles at the expense of gasoline-powered cars, I expect that gasoline demand will continue to decline about 1% annually over the next few years,” said Lipow.Gas prices advertised at a Mobil Station in Santa Monica, California, U.S., May 23, 2022. That may be attributed to trucks going greener. coupled with less deliveries and a decline in trade port volumes.Gasoline usage is seasonal, and it's expected that come spring and summer, drivers will see prices rise above the current national average of $3.36 per gallon.China is in recovery mode from its Covid lockdowns, and some analysts see the cost for oil and refined products increasing as that economy ramps up its consumption of energy.Lipow forecasts a price of $3.65 per gallon going into the summer driving season: “According to my Tarot cards, I do not see the national average of gasoline hitting $4.00 per gallon.”Story continuesOn Wednesday, Brent futures (BZ=F) hovered above $84 per barrel while U.S. West Texas Intermediate (CL=F) crude traded above $77 per barrel.Ines Ferre is a senior business reporter for Yahoo Finance. How do you account for that number down $0.13 since the war began?PATRICK DE HAAN: Well, I think there's a lot of certainty now, even though amidst uncertainty over how the war could continue to unfold, we are now 12 months into Russia's war in Ukraine. And a lot of the initial fears have not been realized that as the flow of oil from Russia does continue though, of course, there have been some challenges, a lot of sanctions, Russian promises to cut production, and overall as well, some help from the Fed, which is trying to restrain interest rates, or excuse me, trying to restrain inflation by raising interest rates, thus acting to cool off consumption. column4: Energy stocks ‘in the crosshairs’ of Fed policy, analyst says
column10: [The Energy Word Founder Daniel Dicker joins Yahoo Finance Live to discuss the rise in oil prices as traders weigh the optimism of increased demand from China, tightening monetary policy, and the outlook for oil.Video Transcript[AUDIO LOGO]JULIE HYMAN: And now, let's get to the eternal push-pull. Oil traders are weighing the optimism for increased demand coming from China, while at the same time grappling with concerns over tighter US monetary policy. And not just in the US, of course. On the one hand, increased China demand, good for oil. On the other hand, tightening monetary policy is not traditionally great for oil. How does it all shake out?DANIEL DICKER: Hi. Julie, we don't want to do another monetary policy segment. You've got 40 of those set up for the rest of the day. And you know, let's talk oil. Oil, fundamentally, is about as strong as I've ever seen it. And sure, we've got prices that are lower than what they probably fundamentally should be. And it's all because of all those 40 other segments you're going to do for the rest of the day.But you know, I look at something like ExxonMobil, and it's trading $110, $111, $112, $113 a share. And the last time that oil was bouncing around the $70 mark, you know, right before the beginning of the year, Exxon was actually trying very hard to breach $70 a share itself. Now, one of these two is wrong.Either oil is too cheap or Exxon is too expensive. And you know, my feeling has always been that the stocks are really representing the profitability of oil and the long-term possibilities of oil.We know very-- how deeply involved Russia remains in Ukraine and how this problem, this systemic supply problem coming from the largest natural gas producer in the world and the third-largest oil producer in the world is going to be going forward. Because when you layer on everything that you were talking about from a longer term perspective with some of the ambitious goals that we've seen rolled out by many companies in energy included, about how to get to more clean energy and sustainable energy, what is the investor's mindset and how they should be kind of pricing their time horizon?DANIEL DICKER: Right, Brad. And I think this stuff is very much on hold right now, unfortunately. I mean, I read article after article about the Indians-- in India, they're absolutely-- they're absolutely thrilled about going back to coal because it's cheap, it's fungible, they have the infrastructure set up for it. And even in Europe, the best stocks of 2022 were coal stocks.I mean, it's terrible to say, but when there's a shortage of energy, people are gonna reach to what's cheapest and what's most easily used. And you know, I've been, you know, pointing out to my subscribers for example, EQT, last week, was under $30. Just a tremendous value to buy some and put it away. It's gonna be a tough year. But there are spots where tremendous, tremendous long-term values in energy stocks can be found.JULIE HYMAN: All right, well, we'll see what ends up happening with them over the long term. Thanks so much, Dan Dicker of the Energy Word. Appreciate it.]

column4: Decline in gasoline demand a 'noticeable' and 'permanent change,' says analyst
column10: [A decline in gasoline consumption in the U.S. could be a trend that's here to stay, according to one analyst.“There has been a noticeable, and I believe permanent, change toward lower gasoline demand,” Andy Lipow of Lipow Oil Associates told Yahoo Finance.The analyst noted that demand peaked between 2017 and 2019 at just over 9.3 million barrels per day, according to data from the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA).The lockdowns during the pandemic impacted demand in 2020 and 2021. However 2022’s level was down 0.5% from the prior year. Indications of gasoline demand in 2023 are thus far running behind 2022.“It is the case, in part, because of early retirements," Ed Morse, head of global commodity research at Citi told Yahoo Finance. "It's [also] the case in part because of changing work habits on how many days people go to work."Many workers who used to commute five days a week now drive less. The meteoric rise in energy costs in 2022 also impacted demand as gasoline prices temporarily surged past $5 per gallon last year.“Not only has working remotely impacted Americans' driving habits, but the higher cost of gasoline has caused the consumer to drive a bit less. Combined with increasing availability and sales of electric vehicles at the expense of gasoline-powered cars, I expect that gasoline demand will continue to decline about 1% annually over the next few years,” said Lipow.Gas prices advertised at a Mobil Station in Santa Monica, California, U.S., May 23, 2022. REUTERS/David SwansonDiesel demand is also lower. That may be attributed to trucks going greener. coupled with less deliveries and a decline in trade port volumes.Gasoline usage is seasonal, and it's expected that come spring and summer, drivers will see prices rise above the current national average of $3.36 per gallon.China is in recovery mode from its Covid lockdowns, and some analysts see the cost for oil and refined products increasing as that economy ramps up its consumption of energy.Lipow forecasts a price of $3.65 per gallon going into the summer driving season: “According to my Tarot cards, I do not see the national average of gasoline hitting $4.00 per gallon.”Story continuesOn Wednesday, Brent futures (BZ=F) hovered above $84 per barrel while U.S. West Texas Intermediate (CL=F) crude traded above $77 per barrel.Ines Ferre is a senior business reporter for Yahoo Finance. column4: The oil market looks drastically different today than it did when Russia invaded Ukraine
column10: [The oil market looks drastically different today than it did a year ago, when Russia invaded Ukraine.“It is the most significant set of market dislocations and distortions in energy markets generally speaking that I ever recall,” Ed Morse, global head of commodity research at Citi, told Yahoo Finance.Prior to the invasion on February 24, 2022, Russia was exporting much of its crude and petroleum products to Europe, with a much smaller portion going to China, India, and other Asian nations.By the end of 2022, that ratio had completely flipped.“It has, from a markets’ perspective, created two markets, a transparent [oil] market, and a non-transparent market,” said Morse.This content is not available due to your privacy preferences.Update your settings here to see it.“Russian crude oil was simply reshuffled from old customers in Europe to new customers in Asia,” Andy Lipow of Lipow Oil Associates recently wrote in a client note. “Europe’s energy divorce from Russia is nearly complete.”The latest in a series of sanctions on Moscow by Western nations in response to the war was imposed earlier this month: Those include an E.U. ban on Russian oil product exports. Prior to that, a G7 price cap on Russian oil was implemented in order to weaken the country's coffers.“In a roundabout way, the December 5, 2022, price caps that were imposed on Russian crude oil exports are working. The E.U. and USA and others are not buying from Russia, that leaves Russia with a limited number of customers. Those customers are demanding lower prices,” said Lipow.It's not every year that energy prices skyrocket like they did over the past year. Days after Russia's invasion, West Texas Intermediate (WTI) reached a closing peak of $123.70 per barrel and Brent futures settled at $127.98.The Biden administration authorized releases from the U.S. strategic petroleum reserve in order to bring down gasoline prices, which reached record highs by mid-June of last year.Eventually prices fell, and today, WTI is trading around the $75 per barrel level while Brent is hovering around $82 per barrel.Story continuesThis content is not available due to your privacy preferences.Update your settings here to see it.The reopening of China following strict COVID lockdowns is seen as bullish for energy prices going forward, but so far oil has been mostly been trading in a tight range.“Crude has gone sideways as the China expansion story battles with the ‘recession around the corner’ story. So far it’s a stalemate,” Stewart Glickman, energy equity analyst at CFRA Research, told Yahoo Finance.Natural gas prices both in Europe and the U.S. have also come down considerably from their peaks. The energy sector, which had a blockbuster 2022, is seeing a lackluster 2023."Energy prices have been relatively weak this year as we have a very warm winter in both North America and Europe. The weather has caused natural gas prices to plummet and oil prices to weaken, which weighs on energy stocks,” Jay Hatfield, CEO at Infrastructure Capital Advisors.'Energy transition seeing an acceleration'Both the U.S. and Europe have increased their efforts to go green with renewable energy efforts, as companies invest in solar, wind, and biofuels.Renewable electricity capacity in the E.U. is projected to double between 2022 and 2027, according to the International Energy Association. “The energy transition is absolutely seeing an acceleration as a result of Russia/Ukraine,” says Citi’s Morse. “It was on the path, but it got accelerated.”Ines is a senior business reporter for Yahoo Finance. column4: Oil prices: Many ‘initial fears have not been realized’ since Russian invasion in 2022, analyst says
column10: [GasBuddy Head of Petroleum Analysis Patrick De Haan joins Yahoo Finance Live to discusses the state of gas and oil prices.Video Transcript- This coming Friday marks one year since the Russian invasion of Ukraine. And while the devastating humanitarian and economic impacts have spread far and wide, one peculiar result can be seen at the pump. The average price of a gallon of gas is now down $0.13 from a year ago, according to AAA, averaging $3.40 per gallon today. How do you account for that number down $0.13 since the war began?PATRICK DE HAAN: Well, I think there's a lot of certainty now, even though amidst uncertainty over how the war could continue to unfold, we are now 12 months into Russia's war in Ukraine. What do you think that number is going to look like as we head into the summer months?PATRICK DE HAAN: Well, I think that it will creep lower here over the next couple of weeks as we still are in the time of year that demand is rather anemic, but in March and lasting through Memorial Day, I would expect some more fireworks to emerge. Now, all of this really not considering China and the reopening of their economy, which has really been slow as COVID cases have surged. So there's a lot of wild cards here, but the average increase between March and Memorial Day is in the neighborhood of $0.35 to $0.85 a gallon, so I do expect that will move higher. column4: Energy stocks ‘in the crosshairs’ of Fed policy, analyst says
column10: [The Energy Word Founder Daniel Dicker joins Yahoo Finance Live to discuss the rise in oil prices as traders weigh the optimism of increased demand from China, tightening monetary policy, and the outlook for oil.Video Transcript[AUDIO LOGO]JULIE HYMAN: And now, let's get to the eternal push-pull. Oil traders are weighing the optimism for increased demand coming from China, while at the same time grappling with concerns over tighter US monetary policy. And not just in the US, of course. So where does this leave prices?Here to discuss is Daniel Dicker, founder of the Energy Word. Dan, it's good to see you. So we have these kind-- this kind of push-and-pull, right? On the one hand, increased China demand, good for oil. On the other hand, tightening monetary policy is not traditionally great for oil. How does it all shake out?DANIEL DICKER: Hi. Julie, we don't want to do another monetary policy segment. You've got 40 of those set up for the rest of the day. And you know, let's talk oil. Oil, fundamentally, is about as strong as I've ever seen it. And sure, we've got prices that are lower than what they probably fundamentally should be. And it's all because of all those 40 other segments you're going to do for the rest of the day.But you know, I look at something like ExxonMobil, and it's trading $110, $111, $112, $113 a share. And the last time that oil was bouncing around the $70 mark, you know, right before the beginning of the year, Exxon was actually trying very hard to breach $70 a share itself. Now, one of these two is wrong.Either oil is too cheap or Exxon is too expensive. And you know, my feeling has always been that the stocks are really representing the profitability of oil and the long-term possibilities of oil.We know very-- how deeply involved Russia remains in Ukraine and how this problem, this systemic supply problem coming from the largest natural gas producer in the world and the third-largest oil producer in the world is going to be going forward. That is going to go on for a long, long time.Story continuesThere are hold backs going on from the Saudis. In the United States, there's all sorts of-- all of the great plays have been drilled. And now, you see shops like, for example, Pioneer supposedly bidding on range resources because there's no new production to be found or really golden new production to be found in the United States. Everybody's looking to buy it at this point.So I'm looking at a long term-- for your investors, I'm looking at a very long-term picture of reducing supply and not much of a demand destruction going on from anywhere. In fact, I see a lot of places where I think that because of the global dustups going on in Europe and elsewhere, that demand picture for fossil fuels, despite all the renewable pressures, is going to increase going forward, at least for the next five years.BRAD SMITH: Yeah, I want to actually get to more on that renewable pressure there. Because when you layer on everything that you were talking about from a longer term perspective with some of the ambitious goals that we've seen rolled out by many companies in energy included, about how to get to more clean energy and sustainable energy, what is the investor's mindset and how they should be kind of pricing their time horizon?DANIEL DICKER: Right, Brad. And I think this stuff is very much on hold right now, unfortunately. I mean, I read article after article about the Indians-- in India, they're absolutely-- they're absolutely thrilled about going back to coal because it's cheap, it's fungible, they have the infrastructure set up for it. And even in Europe, the best stocks of 2022 were coal stocks.I mean, it's terrible to say, but when there's a shortage of energy, people are gonna reach to what's cheapest and what's most easily used. And to heck with the environment. And that's what's really going on right now. And for that, I see a lot of the oil companies, BP for example, who has spent the last 10 years trying to refashion themselves as a sort of sustainable energy company, pivot back to oil and other fossil fuels at least for the foreseeable future.And particularly because of what's going on in Europe and with Ukraine, I think those pressures are far less serious than they were perceived to be even a couple of years ago. I saw Larry Fink, you know, several months ago, very much abandon his push in ESG.I mean, these are the signs that you look at where it's not allowed-- nobody wants to loudly say, oh, I'm going back to burning oil, as opposed to trying to, you know, make solar work for me. But it is something that economically, you see happening over and over again, basically because of what's going on in Europe.JULIE HYMAN: And so what does all of this mean for investors, Dan? To go back to your first point here. I mean, we've talked to a lot of people this year who have said, we still like energy stocks. Energy stocks have not done so great so far this year, at least here in the US. So is that gonna change? Or is it just people are not picking the right, specific ones?DANIEL DICKER: Yeah, you know, what I've been telling my subscribers for a long time is that you really have to play defense. The Fed has control of this market. They're targeting inflation on commodities, and that means oil, number one. And that means, you know, that energy is in the crosshairs.But at times, you find these tremendous values. And you know, I've been, you know, pointing out to my subscribers for example, EQT, last week, was under $30. Just a tremendous value to buy some and put it away. And something like Core, Core Labs, which is a services company that's directly in Europe. It has a very strong presence in Europe.And these services companies because of what's going on in Europe, when they reach values, when they reach levels are worth a long-term play. And all of this right now is long term. I would not be looking, you know, to find a bottom. I would not expect some of these stocks to go down further. I do expect them to go down further. It's gonna be a tough year. But there are spots where tremendous, tremendous long-term values in energy stocks can be found.JULIE HYMAN: All right, well, we'll see what ends up happening with them over the long term. Thanks so much, Dan Dicker of the Energy Word. Appreciate it.]

column4: Decline in gasoline demand a 'noticeable' and 'permanent change,' says analyst
column10: [A decline in gasoline consumption in the U.S. could be a trend that's here to stay, according to one analyst.“There has been a noticeable, and I believe permanent, change toward lower gasoline demand,” Andy Lipow of Lipow Oil Associates told Yahoo Finance.The analyst noted that demand peaked between 2017 and 2019 at just over 9.3 million barrels per day, according to data from the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA).The lockdowns during the pandemic impacted demand in 2020 and 2021. However 2022’s level was down 0.5% from the prior year. Indications of gasoline demand in 2023 are thus far running behind 2022.“It is the case, in part, because of early retirements," Ed Morse, head of global commodity research at Citi told Yahoo Finance. "It's [also] the case in part because of changing work habits on how many days people go to work."Many workers who used to commute five days a week now drive less. The meteoric rise in energy costs in 2022 also impacted demand as gasoline prices temporarily surged past $5 per gallon last year.“Not only has working remotely impacted Americans' driving habits, but the higher cost of gasoline has caused the consumer to drive a bit less. Combined with increasing availability and sales of electric vehicles at the expense of gasoline-powered cars, I expect that gasoline demand will continue to decline about 1% annually over the next few years,” said Lipow.Gas prices advertised at a Mobil Station in Santa Monica, California, U.S., May 23, 2022. REUTERS/David SwansonDiesel demand is also lower. That may be attributed to trucks going greener. coupled with less deliveries and a decline in trade port volumes.Gasoline usage is seasonal, and it's expected that come spring and summer, drivers will see prices rise above the current national average of $3.36 per gallon.China is in recovery mode from its Covid lockdowns, and some analysts see the cost for oil and refined products increasing as that economy ramps up its consumption of energy.Lipow forecasts a price of $3.65 per gallon going into the summer driving season: “According to my Tarot cards, I do not see the national average of gasoline hitting $4.00 per gallon.”Story continuesOn Wednesday, Brent futures (BZ=F) hovered above $84 per barrel while U.S. West Texas Intermediate (CL=F) crude traded above $77 per barrel.Ines Ferre is a senior business reporter for Yahoo Finance. column4: The oil market looks drastically different today than it did when Russia invaded Ukraine
column10: [The oil market looks drastically different today than it did a year ago, when Russia invaded Ukraine.“It is the most significant set of market dislocations and distortions in energy markets generally speaking that I ever recall,” Ed Morse, global head of commodity research at Citi, told Yahoo Finance.Prior to the invasion on February 24, 2022, Russia was exporting much of its crude and petroleum products to Europe, with a much smaller portion going to China, India, and other Asian nations.By the end of 2022, that ratio had completely flipped.“It has, from a markets’ perspective, created two markets, a transparent [oil] market, and a non-transparent market,” said Morse.This content is not available due to your privacy preferences.Update your settings here to see it.“Russian crude oil was simply reshuffled from old customers in Europe to new customers in Asia,” Andy Lipow of Lipow Oil Associates recently wrote in a client note. “Europe’s energy divorce from Russia is nearly complete.”The latest in a series of sanctions on Moscow by Western nations in response to the war was imposed earlier this month: Those include an E.U. ban on Russian oil product exports. Prior to that, a G7 price cap on Russian oil was implemented in order to weaken the country's coffers.“In a roundabout way, the December 5, 2022, price caps that were imposed on Russian crude oil exports are working. The E.U. and USA and others are not buying from Russia, that leaves Russia with a limited number of customers. Those customers are demanding lower prices,” said Lipow.It's not every year that energy prices skyrocket like they did over the past year. Days after Russia's invasion, West Texas Intermediate (WTI) reached a closing peak of $123.70 per barrel and Brent futures settled at $127.98.The Biden administration authorized releases from the U.S. strategic petroleum reserve in order to bring down gasoline prices, which reached record highs by mid-June of last year.Eventually prices fell, and today, WTI is trading around the $75 per barrel level while Brent is hovering around $82 per barrel.Story continuesThis content is not available due to your privacy preferences.Update your settings here to see it.The reopening of China following strict COVID lockdowns is seen as bullish for energy prices going forward, but so far oil has been mostly been trading in a tight range.“Crude has gone sideways as the China expansion story battles with the ‘recession around the corner’ story. So far it’s a stalemate,” Stewart Glickman, energy equity analyst at CFRA Research, told Yahoo Finance.Natural gas prices both in Europe and the U.S. have also come down considerably from their peaks. The energy sector, which had a blockbuster 2022, is seeing a lackluster 2023."Energy prices have been relatively weak this year as we have a very warm winter in both North America and Europe. The weather has caused natural gas prices to plummet and oil prices to weaken, which weighs on energy stocks,” Jay Hatfield, CEO at Infrastructure Capital Advisors.'Energy transition seeing an acceleration'Both the U.S. and Europe have increased their efforts to go green with renewable energy efforts, as companies invest in solar, wind, and biofuels.Renewable electricity capacity in the E.U. is projected to double between 2022 and 2027, according to the International Energy Association. “The energy transition is absolutely seeing an acceleration as a result of Russia/Ukraine,” says Citi’s Morse. “It was on the path, but it got accelerated.”Ines is a senior business reporter for Yahoo Finance.
