column4: Are oil bears missing supply risks ahead?
column10: [Geopolitical pressures loom over oil supply and pricing heading into the second half of 2023. Claudio Galimberti, Rystad Energy SVP and Head of Americas Research, joins Yahoo Finance Live to examine crude oil inventory outlooks and how EVs and electrification trends could weigh on energy markets.Video TranscriptBRAD SMITH: Welcome back. Oil prices are on the move this morning. And moving higher as we near the end of the first half of 2023. And Brent crude has had a rocky start. On track for its worst run of quarterly losses on record, as elevated supply and concerns over demand hit prices.Let's bring in Claudio Lamberti, who is the Rystad Energy SVP and Head of Americas Research for more on this. All right. So just broad strokes here, what most notably should we take away from or extrapolate from the first half of 2023?CLAUDIO LAMBERTI: Thank you for inviting me back. Well, it's been indeed a rocky ride for the past six months. Because you will recall that we started the year at a much higher level. And then, there has been for the past, I would say, two quarters a negative risk premium in the market. There has been a lot of uncertainty about one key demand area, which is China.Now, we need to be aware that the first quarter of China, when I look at the actual data, was actually strong. And the real-time data that we have also shows that the situation in China is still under control. There also is a question about the OPEC plus, what OPEC plus is doing. One thing are the pledges. Another thing is the total oil, which is produced.But what I would say is that we are probably going into his second half of the year when we will see tightening balances. So it means that our focus for oil prices is upwards. But indeed, as you pointed out, a lot of contrasting factors in the first half. And that's the reason why we have been seeing the oil price going up and down. Currently, 75.So it does look though, that there is some a floor to the oil price. And that's due to the determination of Saudi Arabia and the OPEC Plus to keep the oil prices above that level.Story continuesJULIE HYMAN: And Claudio, what do you think will change that? Because to your point, we already have seen some discipline on the part of OPEC Plus, and, particularly, in Saudi Arabia. But all that's done is place a floor. It hasn't certainly caused oil prices to take off. So where do you see more supply coming out of the market that might cause that?CLAUDIO LAMBERTI: Well, first of all, Saudi Arabia made it very clear that between now and the end of the year, they can voluntarily and unilaterally take off the market, every month, a million barrels. So that's what I would call a very strong put option. I wouldn't bet against it. Because one million barrels a day is a lot of volume that comes off. So I do not expect oil prices to fall below $70 per barrel. Unless, we are going to see very negative data from China or from other parts of the world.So that is the point number one. I would say that we also need to take into consideration what's happening in other producing part of the world. For instance, in the United States, we haven't seen a whole lot of growth. And that is very important, if you ask me. And the reason for that is that it gives the OPEC Plus the confidence that they can cut volume, they can reduce volume without the fear, without the risk of losing market share to taxes to the United States.So these two gives me confidence that we will see prices going upwards. But the most important thing in the trading community is the inventory. So we are yet to see inventories, significant inventory draws globally. We saw some significant inventory drop this week in the United States. And that resulted in the Brent and WTI bouncing back up by 3%, 4%.The moment we see the global crude inventories to drop and to draw significantly and consistently, this is the point in time when I expect really strong backwardation, which, at the end of the day, means higher oil prices.RACHELLE AKUFFO: And so what about countries like, Iraq and Nigeria trying to offset, especially some of the Saudi cuts? What's that going to do to demand when you factor in things like electrification and, perhaps, reduce demand overall as people start to pivot to some of these other vehicles?CLAUDIO LAMBERTI: Well, this is an excellent question. Thank you for asking that. The way I put it is as follows. We have seen a lot of electrification in the past five years. So as a matter of fact, the pace of electrification globally has been exponential. We're sending 1% of electric vehicle in terms of global sales in 2018 and 16% last year.So it means that every year, it basically doubled. The problem is that we are already seeing a plateauing of those sales. So year-to-date, the total global sales of electric vehicle is below 16. It's actually 14%. So there is some problem there. It can be fixed, of course. But the pace of electrification is slowing down, at least, so far this year.The second is I would say, what is the total effect on our demand? So far, it's very limited. So we're talking about the zero point percentage effect on our demand. So you can already see. But you really need to use the microscope because imagine global demand is still enormous. More than a million barrels per day and the effect of electrification is in the order of a few 100,000 barrels per day.But there is another effect, which I think is more important. So if people and investors think that the electrification is displacing a lot of demand, and it is not, at least, in the short, medium term might not be willing to invest in oil production. So you may have a counter effect. As a matter of fact, a counterintuitive effect, which is-- the electrification, yes, will have an effect. But the effect is probably be seen five years from now.And if you stop investing, then, because you fear that there is already very strong electrification, then you might end up with under-investment in the next few years, so in the short to medium term.But, overall, what I would say as far as the electrification is concerned is that it is going on for sure. But the effect is still relatively limited so that we are seeing oil demand continue to grow for the next two, three, five years for sure.JULIE HYMAN: Claudio, thank you for joining us. Good to see you. Claudio Lamberti is Rystad Energy SVP and Head of Americas Research. Thanks.]

column4: 4th of July gas prices more than a dollar cheaper than last year: Analyst
column10: [Average U.S. gas prices are $1.35 cheaper than they were this time last year, but how have the travel trends changed this holiday weekend? GasBuddy Head of Petroleum Analysis Patrick De Haan joins Yahoo Finance Live to discuss the international consumption factors that could loom over summer gas prices, while commenting on California's new price gouging law.Video Transcript- Well, gas prices have been steadily declining, with the national average now at $3.55 a gallon. That is welcome news, with nearly 40% of drivers planning a road trip over the July 4th weekend. That's at least according to GasBuddy's new summer travel survey that marks a 9% jump from last year.For more, let's bring-- let's welcome in Patrick de Haan, GasBuddy head of petroleum analysis. Patrick, what does this all mean in terms of the demand picture?PATRICK DE HAAN: Well, you know, a lot of Americans have started to make the transition in light of last year's record setting prices. Some Americans have made the transition over EVs. It probably won't be a record setting holiday weekend for gasoline consumption. There are still some slowdowns that we're seeing when it comes to gasoline consumption.And so I would look for gasoline demand to be about 9.4 million barrels. That's still one of the higher numbers that we've seen so far this year. But that's going to be down from about 10 million barrels that we saw back in 2019. So still a lot of Americans hitting the road. Gas prices now $1.35 on average, below what they were a year ago. That's going to save Americans about $20 every time they fill their tank up.Most welcome is 47 of the nation's 50 states seeing average prices over $1 a gallon less than what we saw a year ago.- Patrick, you just mentioned the average price there, $3.55. There was talk going into the summer that we could retest $4 a gallon. Is that still on the table, do you think?PATRICK DE HAAN: Well, it's still a low level possibility. Especially in August, we've already seen some tropical disturbances. That can affect refinery operations. Half of the nation's refining capacity is on the coast in Texas and Louisiana. So Mother Nature, if we don't see her play nice, there still could be an impact.Story continuesThough I think the odds are rather low. It's something to watch for, especially in August, once we get into the peak of hurricane season.- Yeah, it's certainly a good time to kind of look ahead to the rest of the year, Patrick. The second half of the year, at least. You look at where oil prices have been trading. You know, we're still seeing a lot of supply coming online from Russia despite the cuts that we've heard from OPEC plus or at least Saudi Arabia. As we look to the second half of the year, I mean, where do you expect some of these prices to trend?PATRICK DE HAAN: Well, I think we could go a little bit lower. I think really a lot of the disappointment that has offset OPEC's production cuts has been China. Chinese demand has been very soft, very lackluster, even as their economy has reopened after COVID-19. And the thinking earlier this year was that China could have a tremendous reopening that could spark global consumption. But it really hasn't panned out yet.And I think the second half of the summer, especially as we get into the fall, we could eventually see the national average falling below $3 a gallon with the typical caveats. Again, hurricane season and refinery disruptions are the wild card. But once you get into October and November, we could see the national average making a run at that sub $3 a gallon level.- Patrick, even though we are seeing prices declining we are seeing states, some states taking action, trying to limit some of the very high prices that we saw. Just about a year ago, California has a new law that they just passed aimed at stopping oil companies from what they say inflating gas prices. I was taking a look at your Twitter account, and you were saying that this could potentially backfire. Why?PATRICK DE HAAN: Well, you know, a lot of politicians have demonized the oil sector as being the lone wolf as the reason for higher prices. But what a lot of californians don't realize is the cost of regulations is extremely high. That's why California has almost always led the nation with the highest gas prices, because they have their own blend of fuel. They essentially tell refiners how to do it. In addition to having clap and trade and wildly high gasoline taxes.So it's going to shed light on how the industry works. But it also could shed light onto how those regulations impact the price of gasoline.- Yeah. I mean, looking at just how this would work in California, I mean, it specifically calls for oil companies to hand over additional information. It's not sort of just jumping on and saying, well, you know, we will decide who's actually price gouging. So ultimately, isn't that additional information a good thing?PATRICK DE HAAN: Yeah, the price transparency is certainly good. Especially if people sit down and try to understand how it all works. Especially if the government makes it clear how taxes and regulation impact those refinery operations. So absolutely shining a light on it is not a bad thing. But again, will the government disclose that a lot of the burden from high prices are from regulations in California?- Finally, Patrick, we're noticing this banner here. Norton Shores, Michigan. What's going on behind you? Is that just close to home?PATRICK DE HAAN: We've got a station-- yeah, it's, you know, I've hit the road myself already, making a jump start. The station behind me here today earlier today was at $3.59. And since, then the station is now charging basically the national average. So the perfect example right behind me of a station that's about $1.50 below a year ago to kick off the July 4 weekend.- OK, certainly a good example there. Patrick de Haan, GasBuddy head of petroleum analysis. Great to have you on today. Enjoy the long holiday weekend.PATRICK DE HAAN: Thanks for having me.]

column4: China needs to prep for 'some draconian activity' from Biden admin. in AI chip battle: Strategist
column10: [Chinese chip stocks are facing pressure as reports suggest the Biden administration is re-examining its position on semiconductor export restrictions. U.S. officials continue to consider the future of trade relations with China ahead of Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen's trip to China. Phil Orlando, Federated Hermes Chief Equity Strategist, lays out how geopolitical pressures could slow the rapid growth of AI-tied stocks.Video TranscriptSEANA SMITH: Let's get a little bit more on the movement that we're seeing in chips. Nvidia among the names taking a hit on reports that the Biden administration is considering new restrictions on chip exports to China. We want to bring in Phil Orlando, Chief Equity Strategist at Federated Hermes.Phil, it's good to see you here. From your perspective, this crackdown here that maybe could be coming-- or further crackdown, I should say-- on some of the exports from US companies to China when it comes to chips, how big of a headwind, a challenge, do you see this being for the industry at large?PHIL ORLANDO: Well, understand that what the Biden administration is trying to do, I think, is look forward and consider national security as an issue. Do you want your chief competitors, like China, like Russia, et cetera, to have these very high-powered AI chips? Now, as we take that back and look at from a market perspective, Nvidia, just as an example, the stock's done phenomenally well as a result of this artificial intelligence FOMO that's been going on over the last eight months or so.The stock has literally quadrupled from a little over $100 a share to about $440 a share over the last eight months. From a valuation perspective, stocks now selling at, you know, north of about 30 times revenues and about 130 times earnings. So you've got some frothy valuation levels. So if sentiment suddenly gets hit, because there's concern about whether the Biden administration is going to put any restrictions on the ability of these companies to export their goods, then those valuation levels could come in. There's plenty of profits to take off the table.Story continuesSo it might in their pocket be coming if that's the direction the Biden administration wants to go. Certainly, that's something you can't rule out.JARED BLIKRE: Phil, sticking with chips here, how much of a headwind is all of this all of these restrictions is it for the Chinese government there? And also, when we think about AI, it's the next big thing, requires tons of resources and computing power. If the US amps the arms race against China, at what point do they throw in the towel or do something a little bit more drastic than just tit-for-tat retaliations?PHIL ORLANDO: Well, you can't rule out the fact that you've got the two greatest economies of the world. And if China doesn't like the direction that we're taking this discussion, who's to say that they don't counter with something that's even more draconian. Now, speculation is that Treasury Secretary Yellen is heading over to China to meet with President Xi for a summit to try to smooth things over next month. So it's expected that the Biden administration won't put forth their formal plans until after Secretary Yellen's trip. They don't want to muddy the waters even more.But I mean, you can certainly see how the tea leaves are shaping up here. I think China has got to be prepared for some draconian activity out of the Biden administration. And who's to say that they don't counter with something that's even worse? And what's the impact going to be on, you know, technology companies generally here in the United States that have done really, really well over the last 18-- the last eight months with this huge rally in growth stocks?SEANA SMITH: And Phil, going on with that massive rally that we've seen in growth stocks, you mentioned the valuation of Nvidia, the massive run-up that we've seen in that stock since the start of the year. We've started to see some of the participation widen out just a bit. There was so much focus on that narrow market breadth up until about a couple of weeks or so. I mean, we're still talking about it. But when we talk about the next leg higher the leadership, where do you see that coming from?PHIL ORLANDO: Well, you know, you made a great point, Seana. And as we look at the market, you know, over the course of the last eight months, even just so far this year, you know, the S&P 500 as a whole has had a pretty good run, all right? You're up about 15% or so.The big eight technology names, you know, Nvidia, Microsoft, Apple, you know, the obvious names, there are more than 50%. If you strip those eight names out of the rest of the S&P 500, the other 492 names are up like 2% or 3%. So what we would expect to see over, you know, the next couple of quarters is, as you said, sort of a reversion to the mean. The technology stocks may give up some of those gains. They're frothy to be sure.You've got a lot of value-oriented areas, like energy, for example. Tech stocks in general are up 40% first part of the year. Energy stocks are down 10%. You've got a 50% spread in valuation. The energy stocks are selling at, you know, 10 times earnings. They've got dividend yields that are, you know, 3%, 4%, or 5%, you know, double or more versus the S&P 500.So we would expect to see sort of a reversion to the mean. The bad stocks doing better. The really good performing stocks sort of giving up some of those gains.JARED BLIKRE: I want to ask you about the Fed, because we had Jerome Powell saying earlier this morning that two consecutive rate hikes are not off the table. And that's after pausing at the last meeting. So what happens if we get another rate hike, another two rate hikes? At what point does this become-- does this require a repricing in the bond market of investor expectations? Because we've seen rate cuts now get pushed out to 2025 from a number-- by a number of analysts.PHIL ORLANDO: Well, I think that's exactly right. And the bond market in all of you has had it right throughout. You look at some of the key inversion metrics that we look at in Federated Hermes-- the relationship of the Fed funds rate and benchmark tends, two-year treasuries and 10-year treasuries, three-month treasuries and 10-year treasuries. All of those metrics are significantly inverted and are telling us that we should be expecting a recession in the United States, not today or tomorrow, but perhaps a year from now.And then you've got some of the economic metrics. The leading economic indicators have been negative 14 months in a row. The ISM manufacturing index has been below the critical 50 contraction level seven months in a row. All of these things have been excellent leading indicators to tell you that the economy is slowing, and perhaps slowing in a recession when you go back and study the last 50, 75 years worth of data.So when the chairman of the Federal Reserve comes out and tells you, we are fully recognized that nominal headline inflation has come down sharply over the last year, but-- but core inflation, which is the metric that we're really paying attention to, has been very, very sticky, and it may take another two or three years before it gets to our target level. And therefore, you can fully expect that we're going to tighten policy a few more times in the second half of this year.You've got to recognize that when you look at something like a Phillips curve analysis, for example, when you're trying to bring inflation down, you're raising interest rates to do that, the rate of unemployment is likely to move up. The pace of economic growth is likely to slow. And I think the equity market, you know, to a significant degree, has been whistling past the graveyard the last six months. And I think there needs to be a reversion to the mean with stocks as well.SEANA SMITH: Well, Phil, what do you think the reaction will be in the equity market more specifically if we do see a recession? Because we've been talking about the threat of recession now for quite some time. And to your point, investors haven't seemed to care too much. They're not too worried about it.PHIL ORLANDO: Well, again, because it's far off. I mean, we're calling for a slowdown in the economy, maybe it's recession. But it's not going to be tomorrow. It's probably going to be something next year. So equity markets right now are sort of thinking, well, maybe we dodged a bullet. Maybe, you know, it's going to be a rocky landing or a soft landing or maybe no landing at all. Maybe the economy just reaccelerates, and we, you know, we dodged that bullet completely.We're a little more cautious at Federated Hermes. We're still considering the possibility that we go into recession, perhaps six months from now or a year from now. And as a result, we're still keeping the defense on the field. You know, we've got some growth, some technology, but we're underweight those areas. We're more overweight the more defensive, cheaper, higher-- lower-beta, higher dividend-yielding areas, anticipating that, you know, maybe we hit an air pocket over the next couple of quarters, because the realization of an impending recession, maybe that risk becomes, you know, clearer to investors later this year.JARED BLIKRE: And Phil, all of this is happening not in a vacuum in the US, but we have a number of central banks all over the world doing different things. Some are raising, some are raising interest rates. Some are lowering different strategies, different goals. And it's been a long time since we've seen all the central banks kind of acting in unison. What are the dynamics here? And do you see the central banks getting back to a place where finally everyone seems to be on board marching in the same direction?PHIL ORLANDO: So I might take a slightly different tone there that certainly Europe is tightening because of the inflation problem. Even though the United States, our central bank, paused at the June 14 meeting, I still think the bias is hawkish and higher here. You know, as Bernanke-- Bernanke. As Powell said this morning, we may very well see two more, you know, quarter-point rate hikes in the second half of this year because of this divergence between headline and core inflation.The only central bank that has taken a different tack is China, PBOC. And the reason for that is the economic growth that they've seen coming out of eliminating their self-imposed COVID lockdowns, you know, late last year, beginning of this year, I think they expected much more robust economic growth. And that hasn't happened. They're starting to get nervous now.So I think you're going to see more aggressive fiscal and monetary policy coming out of China to try to boost their economic growth prospects and get GDP back to, you know, maybe a 5% run rate by the end of this year, maybe something in the 6% to 8% neighborhood by the end of next year. I think the rest of the world, the eurozone, the UK, Japan, the United States, we're still significantly concerned about how sticky, how persistent core inflation is. And as a result, that suggests tighter monetary policy out of those central banks, which is likely to slow economic growth and increase the rate of unemployment, you know, as they're continuing this policy.SEANA SMITH: Phil, let's talk about how to play all this. You mentioned the fact that you're seeing some opportunity in some of the names that haven't exactly participated in the rally that we've seen in the first half of the year. Energy is of the sectors that certainly has not participated in a lot of this enthusiasm. Is there a buying opportunity there?PHIL ORLANDO: Yeah. I really think so, both from a crude oil standpoint and from a market standpoint. We touched upon the market a moment ago. In the first half of the year, the technology stocks, growth stocks, have done phenomenally well. They're up 40%. Energy stocks are down 10%. So you've kind of 50% valuation in balance just in the last six months between how these groups will perform.And as I mentioned from a valuation standpoint, you've got single digit PEs in energy. And you've got dividend yields that are double the broad market. From a crude oil standpoint, you're in sort of a mid-60 to mid-80 kind of a trading range on WTI. We're only a couple of dollars off the bottom end of that range.And let's see how the fundamentals play out over, you know, the next six to 12 months. OPEC has cut production by about 4 and 1/2 million barrels a day. We've still got to refill 370 million or so barrels of oil into the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. We've just passed, we've gotten into the summer now, summer driving season, heat, air conditioning season. We've got an El Nino effect. What does that do to the risk of the hurricane season? Might there be any damage to refining capacity in the Gulf of Mexico?There's any number of things that could reduce the supply, increase the demand, force price is higher over the course of the next six months or so. And prices are coming off a very low base. So given our contrarian nature here, you know, I think energy doesn't look like a bad bet. It's cheap and the risk in crude prices, in our view, appears to be higher.JARED BLIKRE: Yeah. Let me ask you about OPEC, because we had the Saudis unilaterally cut, I believe, it was a million barrels per day. And that was to shore up the price of oil. That was about a month ago. And now, we see Russia, there is an attempted coup, maybe call it what you will. Maybe the power structure there is in danger. The Russians haven't really been playing that much ball. They haven't been cutting their production in line with the rest of OPEC Plus, which maybe it's only the Saudis anyway. Just wondering how those dynamics shape your view of the oil market.PHIL ORLANDO: Well, it's potentially significant, because the three major energy producers in the world are Russia, Saudi Arabia, and the United States. OPEC Plus has cut production by 4.66 million barrels a day. And they plan on keeping those cuts in place through the end of next year. The Saudis step forward and announce they're going to part of that 4.66 million barrels. They have a million barrels of it. The Russians have cut a half a million barrels.But to your point, given the political instability that's going on in Washington right now, potential coup, whatever, is that represents an instability in the energy production industry within Russia. That's a very important industry for them. So if their problems result in them at least temporarily reducing their production, given incremental demand, you know, summer driving season, heat, need for more air conditioning, disruption with production capacity due to hurricane season, anything of that nature, that could create a temporary imbalance which would push the prices of energy. And theoretically, the prices of energy stocks higher as well.So I mean, the sort of wild cards that we're talking about, I mean, we don't have any knowledge of whether or not it's going to be a bad hurricane season, or whether or not we're going to have an extraordinarily hot summer, or whether or not Russia is going to have, you know, some sort of a political coup. But the risk of those things suggest that given the price of crude oil being as low as it is, we could see crude oil move higher. And that could certainly boost the prospects of energy stocks at least in the near term.JARED BLIKRE: Lots of moving parts here. I'd forgotten we have potentially a Southern Oscillation to deal with in the form of El Nino. We have to leave it there. Really appreciate all of your insights. Phil Orlando, Chief Equity Strategist at Federated Hermes, thank you.]

column4: Russia turmoil: With oil supply safe, investors are shaking off attempted coup, strategist says
column10: [Markets managed to dodge any geopolitical pressures tied to the attempted coup by the Wagner Group in Russia. One key factor was maintaining the flow of Russian oil supplies in overseas markets. NewEdge Advisors CIO Cameron Dawson joins Yahoo Finance Live to discuss Russia's latest conflict and the market outlook as the Fed leans more hawkish.Video TranscriptSEANA SMITH: Investors largely shrugging off a failed revolt inside Russia, that is leading to questions about Putin's grip on power. Stocks are mixed. With an hour to go until the closing bell, the Dow barely holding onto gains. We want to bring in Cameron Dawson, NewEdge Advisors Chief Investment Officer. Cameron, it's good to see you again.Let's start with the latest developments out of Russia, how investors are looking at that. We did see some reaction in some commodities. Crude didn't move on the news as well as wheat. But more broadly speaking, we take a look at the equity market, we haven't seen a heck of a lot of reaction. Why is the market, at least for now looking at this as a non-event?CAMERON DAWSON: Yeah, I think you had it exactly correct, which is that it is just a shrug. And I think that the risk would have been if this event would have caused Russia to be unable to continue to flood the markets with heavily discounted oil. This has been one of the reasons why we have seen weaker oil prices, which really has helped and benefited the inflation story in the US, meaning that we have seen it filter in through lower goods prices.And so if we were to be in a scenario where Russia's ability to continue to pump oil into global markets was disrupted and that would have caused an inflationary episode, that really would have been the key risk off signal. But because this was resolved for now, it doesn't seem to be an event that the market is taking as a key negative yet.AKIKO FUJITA: But, Cameron, in many ways, this points to just how much more the concerns are in the market about the slowdown in the broader economy. The fact that this event that was significant within the Russia-Ukraine war wasn't necessarily the driving factor in the oil prices, at least in the trade that we saw today.Story continuesWe're looking at prices that are still below that $8 level that OPEC would like it to be. To what extent does that put pressure on the cartel in terms of this next meeting? And are we likely to see further pressure to the upside?CAMERON DAWSON: Well, it's really interesting that all of these supply cuts that have come out from OPEC Plus really have been falling on deaf ears from an oil market perspective, meaning that oil prices have continued to slide since they started cutting production, which really speaks to that we're still living in a world where demand concerns seem to be the bigger issue. And it's really demand all around the world.Fears that maybe the US economy could stumble, those have not been verified by data yet, meaning the US economy still remains rather robust. But then, of course, we had increased fear coming out of Europe last week with those weak PMIs. And then it's China. And China really has been disappointing as far as an oil demand has been from their reopening.And there is concern that reopening even as lackluster as it has been is continuing to flag, which just means that the overall demand picture remains uncertain, which is why we continue to see these oil prices struggling to get above the $80 level.SEANA SMITH: Cameron, one of the key things obviously that investors are watching here in the US is what's going to come from the Fed next. Lots of questions just about what policy is going to look like going forward, whether or not another rate hike should be and will be likely here going forward, and more specifically, at the next meeting in July. What do you think is necessary at this point, given the fact that we're still so far from the 2% inflation target?CAMERON DAWSON: Yeah, exactly. We still think that this is a Fed that's in inflation-fighting mode. And we do think that they will hike in July, that the data continues to support that. The bond market agrees. There's now about a 71% chance that the Fed does hike in July, which just means that inflation remains far too sticky and far too elevated on a core basis for their liking. We're not close to that 2% level.And things like wages are not consistent of getting down to 2%. Atlanta Fed wage tracker is still running at about 6%. It's starting to roll over, but that is not consistent with a rapid return to the pre-pandemic level of inflation. So when you put it all in together, it means that the Fed is likely still to lean hawkish from here with one more hike in July.And September is still a very live meeting. And, of course, we'll be listening to the Fed's comments in August at Jackson Hole, to really see how they're looking at this balance between inflation, which is moderating, but still a very tight labor market, which could just keep them in this higher for longer camp.AKIKO FUJITA: So, Cameron, you're in the camp that you think the Fed is actually going to raise come July. To what extent did that shift your expectations or your outlook for the market?CAMERON DAWSON: Well, the Fed really hasn't mattered for the market this year. And this is one of the things that has surprised us the most, is that we expected the economy to remain more resilient, inflation to remain hotter, which would keep the Fed tighter and that to keep a downward pressure and kind of a lid on where valuations could go within equity markets.But equity markets haven't cared at all. We've seen huge valuation expansion in equities and mostly in growth stocks, which have typically been those that are most sensitive to the path of Fed policy. So it's a good question if the Fed continues to ratchet up its hawkishness. Will equities eventually listen?We've seen a big divergence between interest rates and growth valuations. And it's a good question of, is that sustainable if the Fed doesn't deliver on the hoped for easing that the bond market has been so eagerly pricing in really all year long.SEANA SMITH: Is it sustainable, do you think?CAMERON DAWSON: I think that eventually, gravity applies. Eventually, yields will matter. The problem or the challenge is that valuations are really a terrible timing tool, meaning that if you look at the correlation of valuations and forward returns, there really isn't much predictive power. You really have to look out past two, three years to get a sense of if high valuations are today that it correlates to lower forward returns.So for us as long-term investors, what we see is a world where valuations are very high and that likely requires us to lower our expectations for returns really over the next two to three years. But that doesn't mean that markets can't continue in the short run. Valuations can go high and stay high. Markets can have great momentum. And so as we continue to see markets with momentum press higher, valuations diverge from yields, that's where the risk-reward begins to look less and less attractive.AKIKO FUJITA: So am I hearing that you're still in the risk trade or you're taking risk off the table now in anticipation of some of the chopping up?CAMERON DAWSON: So one of the things for us as long-term investors is that we do remain fully invested. And we have had a higher weighting to cash over the last couple of months and really the last year. But a lot of that's coming from the fixed income side, meaning that we are neutral equities. What we've been doing is staying in the high-quality part of the equity market, meaning that we haven't been chasing low-quality.We haven't been chasing the beta and the speculative trade, which has led us to lag in certain rallies that have really led this market in those parts of the market this year. But as we look over the long run, we think it's very important for us to have that steady exposure to quality, mostly if we go into a period of weaker economic growth.And so overall, we remain invested, but we express some of our valuation discipline by focusing on cheaper parts of the market and those quality factors.SEANA SMITH: Cameron, what are some of those cheaper parts of the market, more specifically when we're diving down into sectors, which do you prefer at this point, given the fact that there's so much uncertainty?CAMERON DAWSON: Yeah. It's one of the things that really is interesting is that if we're looking for new capital, we prefer and we're looking at an index portion of capital, meaning we want to index something. We'll favor the equal weight index instead of the value index because value is so very overweight to financials. And financials continue to have really weak trends within the market. Banks are starting to break down on a relative and absolute basis.So instead of looking at the value sector, we'll look at that equal weight, which allows us to de-emphasize some of the really expensive parts of the market, like the tech and communication stocks, which really are the key source of why this market is very expensive.Overall, we still have an overweight to technology, just because the momentum, the trends are so very strong. But then we counter that with a slight overweight to energy as a geopolitical and inflation hedge and then an overweight to health care as a defensive play. That's one of the cheaper ways to get defensiveness within this market.SEANA SMITH: It sounds like you've got to be balanced. All right. Well, Cameron Dawson, great to have you. NewEdge Advisors Chief Investment Officer. Thanks for taking the time.]

column4: Russia: How will Wagner Group's failed coup impact markets?
column10: [Russian President Vladimir Putin had a potential challenge to his regime led by Wagner Group leader Yevgeny Prigozhin. Yahoo Finance discussed the impact on markets, including commodities, energy, and oil, with various experts, analysts, and strategists.Allison Fedirka, Geopolitical Futures Director of Analysis, broke down the biggest takeaways and impact on global markets. Fedirka said, "The fact that the coup did not work, it's not entirely clear that the Wagner Group will come back and fight with Russia ... until people can be certain that Putin is the man in charge ... the idea of a negotiated settlement with Russia is now just off the table."Tony Dwyer, Canaccord Genuity Chief Market Strategist, also discussed the potential market reaction. Dwyer said, "What I do know is companies and lenders will not lend money to lose money ... that ultimately should have some kind of impact on economic growth, and therefore the markets."Yahoo Finance senior columnist Rick Newman expressed his surprise to the rebellion. Newman said, "Just a mind-blowing series of developments in Russia, and many analysts think it's not close to being over yet."Yahoo Finance markets reporter Jared Blikre broke down oil prices with regard to the news of the failed coup. Blikre said, "The price action since the open yesterday and Sunday evening, really not that volatile."Yahoo Finance markets reporter Ines Ferre also discussed oil prices and commodities outlook. Ferre said, "I was able to reach out to Andy Lipow of Lipow Oil Associates ... if this does lead to a civil war, if this is the beginning of the end for Vladimir Putin, you could see a disruption when it comes to the oil coming out of Russia."Mike McGlone, Bloomberg Intelligence Senior Macro Strategist, discussed his outlook for oil and energy markets with a global recession looming. McGlone said, "To me, it's tilting the whole world toward recession ... I see crude oil as more likely to head toward 50, maybe even 40, based on what's already happened."Story continuesVideo highlights:00:00:03 - Geopolitical Futures Director of Analysis Allison Fedirka00:00:32 - Canaccord Genuity Chief Market Strategist Tony Dwyer00:00:46 - Yahoo Finance senior columnist Rick Newman00:00:56 - Yahoo Finance markets reporter Jared Blikre00:01:12 - Yahoo Finance markets reporter Ines Ferre00:01:39 - Bloomberg Intelligence Senior Macro Strategist Mike McGloneVideo Transcript[AUDIO LOGO]ALLISON FEDIRKA: Prior to the weekend events, the Kremlin and Wagner Group worked collaboratively. The fact that the coup did not work, it's not entirely clear if Wagner will come back and fight with Russia. And then, once you have something like this happen, people are questioning the staying power of Putin. So until people can be certain that Putin is the man in charge and is the person that they can talk to, the idea of a negotiated settlement with Russia is now just off the table.TONY DWYER: I didn't see it coming. I have no idea what it means. What I do know is companies and lenders will not lend money to lose money. And with all the yield curves inverted, that ultimately should have some kind of impact on economic growth. And therefore, the markets.RICK NEWMAN: Is Vladimir Putin's leadership falling apart? It's just a mind-blowing series of developments in Russia. And many analysts think it's not close to being over yet.JARED BLIKRE: I think the real interesting news that's really peaking, catching trader's attention is what's happening in Russia. And that's with the potential coup on Vladimir Putin. Now I'm taking a look at the YFi Interactive. The price action since the open yesterday and Sunday evening, really not that volatile.INES FERRE: I was able to reach out to Andy Lipow of Lipow Oil Associates. If this does lead to a Civil War, if this is the beginning of the end for Vladimir Putin, you could see a disruption when it comes to the oil coming out of Russia. Although there is a contrarian view, which is that if Vladimir Putin continues with his strategy, you could see more supply of oil coming into the market and this would be bearish for the oil markets.MIKE MCGLONE: China's leader made a major mistake of his unlimited friendship with Mr Putin. And what's that doing overall? To me, it's tilting the whole world towards recession. China is having a problem. With all that data it's disappointing. That's the body in motion. You have to ask yourself, what stops this? So I say, crude oil is more likely to head towards 50, maybe even 40, priced on what happened.]

column4: Russia turmoil: Putin has to recognize there is 'unhappiness' here, expert says
column10: [Wagner leader Yevgeny Prigozhin says he was not aiming for a regime change when he led a mutiny against the Russian government. Michael O’Hanlon, Brookings Senior Fellow & Director of Research in Foreign Policy, tells Yahoo Finance Live that though, in the short-term it appears Russian President Vladimir Putin has prevailed, he will have to acknowledge there is some "unhappiness" in his country about his actions in Ukraine.Video TranscriptAKIKO FUJITA: We are beginning this hour with those latest developments you just alluded to in this ongoing war between Russia and Ukraine. The head of the mercenary group that led a rebellion against Vladimir Putin over the weekend breaking his silence, saying he was not attempting to oust the Russian president but simply demonstrating his protest over the Russian military.Now, the actions led by Yevgeny Prigozhin raising questions on Putin's control and the stability of one of the world's largest producers of oil now. Here to discuss the rippling ramifications of it all, we've got Michael O'Hanlon, Brookings Senior Fellow and Director of Research in Foreign Policy. Michael, great to talk to you today. Give me your assessment on the effect you think this rebellion or not rebellion will have on the ongoing war effort.MICHAEL O'HANLON: Greetings. I think the effect will likely be modest, but we can't really be sure. I think in the short term, it looks like Putin has prevailed even though Prigozhin is, as you say, pushing back a little and now trying to defend himself a little bit more fully, maybe make this seem like less of an out and out showdown with Putin and maybe even establish a little bit of a base in Belarus.But the fact that he's talking about that latter idea for the Wagner Group underscores that he really has to retreat here, because, of course, Belarus is essentially a Russian puppet. So you're not going to get any kind of protection or sanctuary just because you're operating there either at his individual level or in terms of the Wagner Group.Story continuesAnd as you know, Russia's been trying to bring the Wagner Group back into the fold, so to speak, in recent months. I think that effort will continue, maybe even more so. And at the same time, I think that we probably won't see a dramatic effect on Russian fighting positions inside of Ukraine because chances are that Putin is going to go slow here and not, sort of, dismantle the Wagner Group too quickly.So he's going to try to make sure the Wagner people on whom he depends for some of that fraction of the front line still feel like they are better off fighting for Russia than fleeing or fighting against Russia. And my guess is if they're being asked to defend trench lines, they will have enough morale to do that even in light of what's happened. So my best guess is no dramatic change within Russia itself or on the Ukrainian battlefield. But, of course, we'll have to see, and things could change over a period of months partly as a result of this.SEANA SMITH: Michael, what message, though, do you think this sends to the rest of the world, not only inside Russia, but more specifically what it means for China, which we know clearly has close ties with Russia?MICHAEL O'HANLON: I think China is just going to keep hedging and doing what's best for China. In this regard, they don't send weapons to Russia as best we can tell. I don't think they'll change that policy. They give Putin a certain amount of rhetorical support in the sense of blaming NATO expansion for this conflict, but they don't go so far as to actually help him in any material way besides just buying stuff they want to buy from Russia anyway.And frankly, buying stuff that we want them to buy from Russia because as you know, we've been part of this oil cap concept which actually is a way to keep Russian oil and gas on the global market even if we in the West choose not to want to buy it ourselves. So China's going to stay in this middle zone. They're pro Putin at some level, but they're not going to go so far as to become an active participant or to send him any appreciable amount of weaponry. And I don't think they're going to change their view.They'll be a little more nervous, but they'll also recognize that he's probably survived this challenge from the number one potential rival he had in the entire country. And therefore, it's hard to see somebody else rivaling Putin, challenging Putin, mounting a mutiny or a coup attempt anytime soon. At least that's my best assessment, and that's what I believe the Chinese will conclude as well.AKIKO FUJITA: So Michael, it doesn't sound like you think there's a dramatic shift in the war, but you did have the likes of Secretary of State Antony Blinken, at least over the weekend, sort of, pointing to how this could signal some Russian fragility here. And I wonder from a policy standpoint, how do you think this shifts the discussion for the US and NATO allies?MICHAEL O'HANLON: Well, it only shifts it a little. Secretary Blinken, I certainly think correct, but the weakening may be modest, and Putin won't want to acknowledge it. And therefore, it will play out over a period of weeks and months, not hours and days.And so what think you could imagine, let's say we get to the fall and the Ukrainians have taken back some of their territory, my guess is they won't get back more than, I don't know, a quarter of it, the 17% of their country that Russia still occupies. And then Putin's got a decision and does Zelenskyy and so do all of us. Are we going to, sort of, help get ready for another round of similar fighting in 2024 with no end in sight to this conflict? Or are we going to think of ways to compromise?And at that point, in the fall, I'm suggesting, Putin may say, you know, I've got internal problems. The economy is not in good shape. The Wagner Group remnants are still upset about what happened. Maybe I'm better off not fighting this war for three or four more years. Maybe I'm better off looking like the peacemaker trying to wind it down.I could imagine that kind of shifting a bit at least partially as a result of what's just happened. But again, I think months, and this is just speculation. It's also possible that by the fall, Putin will have completely stamped this whole incident down and out of our memories, so at least out of active policy making and he won't be affected in the least.SEANA SMITH: Michael, what about the image that Russia is still trying to portray? At least up until this point, they seem to be trying to send this message that it's business as usual. You mentioned the fact that you don't see this having any real material impact, at least for right now in Russia's advancement in Ukraine. At what point, when you're talking about the fact that maybe this conversation could change by the fall, what would be the trigger of that?MICHAEL O'HANLON: I think that Putin will internalize the extent to which he's seen a serious domestic uprising against him. Now, he managed to rein it in, and now the guy who instigated it is saying it wasn't really against Putin anyway. And I don't know that there's anybody else who could do this besides Prigozhin.Still, Putin's got to recognize there's some unhappiness here. There's some unhappiness in the sense that Wagner Group's been more popular than his own military. They're a year and a half into a war they're not winning even if they're also not really losing at the moment.He has to think hard about does he want World War I? Does he want four more years of carnage with uncertain prospects? Or does he want to say whatever fraction of Russia-- or of Ukraine he still holds by the fall, let's see if he can solidify his control of that in some kind of an armistice and get back to some quasi normalcy.It won't be like it was before, but maybe he could end the fighting and end the economic decline of his own country. That's possible. But this would just be one of the factors that would go into that thinking and maybe not even the most important.AKIKO FUJITA: Yeah, I mean, that sounds like a better case scenario, I wouldn't say the best case scenario. But from a market's perspective, clearly, investors watching the commodities market to see how in fact Vladimir Putin could potentially weaponize the energy markets. I mean, that's been dangled before. Is there any likelihood because of what played out now of that risk increasing?MICHAEL O'HANLON: Well, yeah, I think that I just get nervous about any kind of big war in the middle of Europe going on indefinitely, because I see no reason to just assume that things will be extrapolated out and, sort of, follow the same trajectory they've been on. So the fact that the war, sort of, stalemated, the energy and grain markets are, sort of, semi-stable that we haven't heard a lot of nuclear threats in the last few months, I don't take any of that for granted as a prediction of what may ensue this summer or fall.And at some point, somebody could have a big incentive to try to really destabilize or disrupt the whole situation. So I'm a pretty big proponent of trying to find a way to wind down the violence relatively soon, even if Ukraine doesn't get everything back that it wants, and maybe play the longer game diplomatically to try to get back the full extent of its territory rather than think it can do so on the battlefield.There's no reason-- wars don't tend to go in straight lines. If you look at a period of a few months, whether historically or in real time, it might seem like you have a period of a few months where you have more or less a steady state, but then there usually is some kind of a divergence off of that, and it's an inherently unpredictable business that we're in right now.AKIKO FUJITA: It certainly is. Michael, it's good to get your perspective today. Michael O'Hanlon, Brookings Senior Fellow and Director of Research in Foreign Policy.MICHAEL O'HANLON: Thanks.]

column4: With 59% institutional ownership, Loews Corporation (NYSE:L) is a favorite amongst the big guns
column10: [Key InsightsGiven the large stake in the stock by institutions, Loews' stock price might be vulnerable to their trading decisionsA total of 10 investors have a majority stake in the company with 51% ownership Insiders have bought recently If you want to know who really controls Loews Corporation (NYSE:L), then you'll have to look at the makeup of its share registry. The group holding the most number of shares in the company, around 59% to be precise, is institutions. That is, the group stands to benefit the most if the stock rises (or lose the most if there is a downturn).Because institutional owners have a huge pool of resources and liquidity, their investing decisions tend to carry a great deal of weight, especially with individual investors. Hence, having a considerable amount of institutional money invested in a company is often regarded as a desirable trait.Let's take a closer look to see what the different types of shareholders can tell us about Loews. See our latest analysis for Loews ownership-breakdownWhat Does The Institutional Ownership Tell Us About Loews?Many institutions measure their performance against an index that approximates the local market. So they usually pay more attention to companies that are included in major indices.Loews already has institutions on the share registry. Indeed, they own a respectable stake in the company. This implies the analysts working for those institutions have looked at the stock and they like it. But just like anyone else, they could be wrong. When multiple institutions own a stock, there's always a risk that they are in a 'crowded trade'. When such a trade goes wrong, multiple parties may compete to sell stock fast. This risk is higher in a company without a history of growth. You can see Loews' historic earnings and revenue below, but keep in mind there's always more to the story.earnings-and-revenue-growthInvestors should note that institutions actually own more than half the company, so they can collectively wield significant power. Hedge funds don't have many shares in Loews. The Vanguard Group, Inc. is currently the largest shareholder, with 10% of shares outstanding. James Tisch is the second largest shareholder owning 7.4% of common stock, and BlackRock, Inc. holds about 6.4% of the company stock. James Tisch, who is the second-largest shareholder, also happens to hold the title of Chief Executive Officer.Story continuesWe did some more digging and found that 10 of the top shareholders account for roughly 51% of the register, implying that along with larger shareholders, there are a few smaller shareholders, thereby balancing out each others interests somewhat.Researching institutional ownership is a good way to gauge and filter a stock's expected performance. The same can be achieved by studying analyst sentiments. We're not picking up on any analyst coverage of the stock at the moment, so the company is unlikely to be widely held.Insider Ownership Of LoewsWhile the precise definition of an insider can be subjective, almost everyone considers board members to be insiders. The company management answer to the board and the latter should represent the interests of shareholders. Notably, sometimes top-level managers are on the board themselves.Insider ownership is positive when it signals leadership are thinking like the true owners of the company. However, high insider ownership can also give immense power to a small group within the company. This can be negative in some circumstances.It seems insiders own a significant proportion of Loews Corporation. It is very interesting to see that insiders have a meaningful US$2.5b stake in this US$14b business. Most would say this shows a good degree of alignment with shareholders, especially in a company of this size. You can  click here to see if those insiders have been buying or selling. General Public OwnershipThe general public, who are usually individual investors, hold a 22% stake in Loews. While this size of ownership may not be enough to sway a policy decision in their favour, they can still make a collective impact on company policies.Next Steps:It's always worth thinking about the different groups who own shares in a company. But to understand Loews better, we need to consider many other factors. Consider for instance, the ever-present spectre of investment risk.   We've identified 1 warning sign  with Loews , and understanding them should be part of your investment process.Of course this may not be the best stock to buy.
