column4: Gas prices close to a peak, hot weather helping prop up oil prices: Analyst
column10: [Oil prices are up about 16 percent in July, putting it on track to be the largest monthly gain in crude prices in over a year. OPIS Global Head of Energy Analysis Tom Kloza tells Yahoo Finance Live there are a couple of supply factors causing oil prices to rise. Kloza cites OPEC+ production cuts and the extreme heat in the U.S., saying "you have refineries that are coughing and wheezing instead of running at close to 100 percent rates as they would typically do in July." When it comes to gas prices, Kloza says, barring a hurricane impacting production, prices "should be very, very close to a peak right now." Kloza says a change in what can be added to gasoline and demand falling off after Labor Day as reasons why gasoline prices is closing to peaking.Video TranscriptDIANE KING HALL: Oil prices soaring this month up about 16%. That's the largest one-month gain in over the year. Our next guest says, this is all a supply story. Joining us now is Tom Kloza, OPIS Global Head of Energy Analysis.Thank you so much for joining us, Tom. So let's talk about where these oil prices stand. And pardon the pun. What is fueling this, especially when you consider where they were earlier in the year?TOM KLOZA: Well, it's not too bad. It's really supply. And you have two things that are working against comfortable supply. Number one is the OPEC+ cartel, principally the Saudis and the Russians, cutting crude oil. And we'll probably see demand outstrip supply by about 2 million barrels a day in the summertime.The other thing that's really manifesting itself here in the United States is the intense heat. And in places like Texas, Louisiana, Tennessee, even in some of the Rocky Mountain places, you've got refineries that are coughing and wheezing instead of running at close to 100% rates as they would typically do in July. And, you know, you mentioned crude oil prices up 17%.But inflation has really reared its head in the energy patch with other liquids this month. We're looking at diesel and jet fuel prices up anywhere from 25% to 30%. And that's going to rear itself in the producer price numbers that come out next month.Story continuesSEANA SMITH: So, Tom, then where do we go from here? When we talk about the fact that we've seen such large increases over the last several weeks, what does it look like headed out to the fall?TOM KLOZA: I think crude oil is going to stay, you know, somewhere between $80 and $89 a barrel, whether it's Brent or WTI. The chacha might be done a little bit by refined products. Now, normally, in August, gasoline prices ease a little bit because you start to disperse some ingredients in the gasoline formula that are much cheaper as you get into August.But this August, you know, with the Gulf of Mexico water temperatures in the 90s, you really have to be aware of what could happen maybe not even with a hurricane landfall, but a hurricane threat. And, you know, I would use kind of a little metric that if you have a category 3 storm in the Gulf of Mexico, you might cube that number and it might have a $0.27 sort of upwelling in prices should it actually target Texas or Louisiana. Let's hope that doesn't happen.Most of the time, hurricanes destroy demand without destroying supply. But this year is really special in the climate that's for sure.DIANE KING HALL: And, Tom, so you say this is a supply-based case for why oil is where it is, but there was a note from Goldman about oil demand reaching a record high in July. What do you make of that?TOM KLOZA: Well, I think they're accurate. I mean, global oil demand is up. In the United States, it's not necessarily up. As a matter of fact, gasoline demand is probably running about 500,000 barrels a day lower than it was from 2016 through 2019 in the summertime. And, you know, the electric vehicle is starting to have a little bit of an impact on the market, a little bit of disintermediation of liquid fuels.And the other thing that has a big impact since COVID is commuting. I mean, it looks as congested as ever on the weekend. I'm here at the Jersey Shore, and I can tell you, it's, like, gridlocked on the weekend. But during the week, I think the commuter traffic is down. And that's never going to go back to where it was.The other thing is, you know, the cars get so much better mileage these days. I think the new cars are probably 33 miles per gallon. And then you have the EVs interspersed with that.So we've seen peak demand in the United States. We haven't seen peak demand in the world. And places like India and even the European Union are creeping up a little bit because so far, they haven't seen that recession rear its head.SEANA SMITH: Tom, going back to what you just said a moment ago when it comes to EVs and EV adoption and how that's playing into the demand story, I guess how material is that impact versus what we maybe would have been expecting at this point, given the fact that adoption isn't as quick as many forecasters had initially anticipated?TOM KLOZA: It's not as quick as anticipated, and I think it will be a slow bleed to the EVs. But it's having an impact in some markets. You know, California, for example, we were well above $6 last year.In California, I think EVs are probably accounting for as great of a share of new car sales in California than anything. And they've made it clear that they want to get rid of the sale of fossil fuel cars by 2035. You know, we're going to have to start to use the calculus. For every million EVs, you know, you diminish this much in terms of fossil fuel usage here in the United States.And I would dare say that in China, you're seeing that as well. The Chinese economy may be very, very close to sort of its maximum gasoline usage, even though there's a lot of people there who are moving into the middle class. And with the move into the middle class comes mobility and the need to travel.DIANE KING HALL: Tom, let's talk quickly about gas prices here domestically. So according to AAA, they're at $3.75 a gallon. That is up, obviously, from a month ago but far cry from a year ago when we had a four-handle. So what are you expecting through the balance of this summer? Could we expect to see a four-handle again? And then through the balance of the year, Tom?TOM KLOZA: I think you only see a four-handle if you have one of those cyclonic formations in the Gulf of Mexico threatening the coasts with a hurricane. Without that, gasoline prices should be very, very close to a peak right now. You can use a lot more ingredients to manufacture gasoline in the middle of August, and then demand drops right after Labor Day.So under most circumstances, I would say we're very, very close to a top. And I would say this much. By November or December, you may be $0.35 to $0.55 lower than what you see in August.DIANE KING HALL: All right, looking forward to that relief at the pump because I don't have an EV yet. Tom Kloza, we appreciate you. Thank you. [LAUGHS]]

column4: Oil rallies in July as traders give up 'growth pessimism': Goldman Sachs
column10: [Crude oil just finished its biggest monthly gain since January 2022, with the price of West Texas Intermediate (CL=F) and Brent (BZ=F) futures rising more than 15% and 14%, respectively in July.And according to analysts at Goldman Sachs, this rally has been spurred by traders growing more constructive on their outlook for the global economy."The market has abandoned its growth pessimism," Goldman Sachs senior energy economist Daan Struyven and his team wrote in a note to clients."Oil prices have rallied by 18% since mid-June on the return to deficits and on the oil market abandoning its negative growth views, which we saw as too pessimistic."Goldman estimates global oil demand rose to an all-time high in July and revised up its 2023 demand forecast to about 500,000 barrels per day.Goldman Sachs is maintaining its 12-month-ahead forecast of $93 per barrel for Brent crude and $86 in December 2023. Brent crude settled near $85.50 on Monday.Expectations the Federal Reserve is near the end of its tightening cycle have also bolstered crude prices amid greater optimism the economy may achieve a "soft landing" that sees inflation come down while a recession is avoided.In a press conference last week, Fed Chair Jay Powell said he still sees this as a likely outcome for the US economy. Data out Friday showed the Fed's preferred inflation measure in June rose at the slowest pace since September 2021. Meanwhile, second quarter GDP showed the economy grew faster than expected in the second quarter of this year.Production cuts have also bolstered the oil market with demand turning the corner.Since October of last year, OPEC+ has announced production cuts which total over 5 million barrels per day into August 2023, notes Andy Lipow of Lipow Oil Associates."While [OPEC+] have not taken that much oil off the market, the amount that they are cutting in August is substantial — probably closer to 3.3 million barrels per day. It's a lot," said Lipow.Story continuesThe world's largest oil producers are expected to extend voluntary production cuts into September. Goldman notes the global oil market fell into a supply deficit in July after having been, on average, in a surplus of about 600,000 barrels per day over the prior year.A view shows an oil pump jack outside Almetyevsk in the Republic of Tatarstan, Russia. (Alexander Manzyuk/REUTERS)"I think [the oil rally] is market participants taking a more risk-on attitude and belief that China is actually going to grow its economy in a robust fashion this year," Stewart Glickman, energy equity analyst at CFRA Research, told Yahoo Finance on Monday."This has always been the key issue for 2023 — how quickly will China's GDP improve. I think the jury is still out."On Monday, WTI settled at $81.80 per barrel and Brent closed at $85.56 per barrel.Ines Ferre is a senior business reporter for Yahoo Finance. Follow her on Twitter at @ines_ferre.Click here for the latest stock market news and in-depth analysis, including events that move stocksRead the latest financial and business news from Yahoo Finance]

column4: Loews profit more than doubles as market rebound boosts investment returns
column10: [(Reuters) - Loews Corp said on Monday its second-quarter profit more than doubled as a jump in investment income cushioned a hit from higher catastrophe losses in its insurance unit, CNA Financial.Markets have staged a comeback this year on rising bets that the Federal Reserve was done with the bulk of its tightening cycle that had taken the economy on the edge of a recession.Loews reported a higher return on investments, helped by a broader market rally.Investment income for New York-based Loews jumped to $592 million in the second quarter ended June 30 from $366 million a year earlier.The company earns most of its revenue from CNA, in which it holds about 90% stake. It also operates a natural gas transportation pipeline business and a chain of hotels.Catastrophe losses in CNA's property and casualty operations rose to $68 million from $37 million.The U.S. Midwest and South were hit by violent storms in the quarter that knocked over houses and led to loss of life, adding to a series of weather-related events that have hurt insurers' profitability.CNA's peer Travelers Companies, earlier this month, reported about a 98% rise in catastrophe losses due to extreme weather.Meanwhile, CNA reported an underlying combined ratio of 91.1%, compared with 90.8% a year earlier. A ratio below 100% means the insurer earned more in premiums than it paid out in claims."CNA reported stellar results, despite high industry catastrophe losses," President and CEO James Tisch said in a statement.The income attributable to Loews for the second quarter was $360 million, or $1.58 per share, compared with $167 million, or 68 cents a year earlier.(Reporting by Pritam Biswas in Bengaluru; Editing by Shinjini Ganguli)]

column4: Oil prices rise after Saudi Arabia, Russia extend supply cuts
column10: [Saudi Arabia has extended its one million barrel-per-day production cuts into September, while Russia announce it will cut oil exports, sending oil prices higher. Lipow Oil Associates President Andrew Lipow tells Yahoo Finance Live the move is "very significant." Lipow say the cuts "really emphasize the point that they are looking for higher prices, because the domestic budgets of these OPEC+ countries simply could not last when oil was under $70 a barrel."Video TranscriptAKIKO FUJITA: Oil prices rising for a sixth straight week. And today's gains driven by Saudi Arabia and Russia's decision to extend production cuts. Remaining OPEC plus members though deciding to keep output unchanged in a meeting today causing prices to rally further. It comes as extreme weather poses threats to US production.Let's bring in Andy Lipow, president of Lipow Oil Associates. Andy, good to talk to you today. I'm looking at where oil prices are trading today-- oil futures, I should say, above that $80 a barrel mark. How supportive do you think these cuts announced by Saudi Arabia, as well as Russia will be in terms of price action?ANDREW LIPOW: Well, thanks for having me. I think these cuts are very significant. If we look back to October of last year, OPEC plus has cut over 5 million barrels a day from their production quotas. And these last voluntary cuts by Russia and Saudi Arabia really emphasized the point that they're looking for higher prices because the domestic budgets of these OPEC plus countries simply could not last when oil was under $70 a barrel.- So Andy, do we expect to see oil hit $90 a barrel before the year is out?ANDREW LIPOW: I think there's a very good possibility, especially as we've seen Saudi Arabia take these proactive steps to get the price of oil higher. I think they'd be quite comfortable to see Brent crude oil prices at around $90 a barrel and WTI at about $85. But the market could move higher because OPEC plus tends to be reactive. And of course, as prices rise, they're certainly going to think it's in their benefit to keep those higher prices higher for a longer period of time without triggering a recession around the world.Story continuesAKIKO FUJITA: Andy, what are the supply-demand dynamics looking like right now? You know, on the one hand, we've got the prices above $80 a barrel, you've got the Russian cuts taking shape more. And yet you look at the demand picture at least in China where the biggest market is, we just haven't seen the kind of pickup in economic activity.ANDREW LIPOW: Well, I think that their economic activity is lagging, but we do see in the physical oil market China is buying record amounts of crude oil and processing record amounts of that oil in their new refineries and existing refineries. So the oil market is seeing the demand. The latest cut of 500,000 barrels a day by Russia was actually impacting China at the most because China, India, Turkey, and Bulgaria have become the four main customers of that Russian oil. So it does look to me like inventories around the world are declining and supplies are getting tighter- Andy, I want to ask you about just the impact of heat. It's not something over the years-- I've covered crude oil and it's not something that's been often in the conversation when you're talking about oil prices, oil inventories. What is the impact of extreme weather on that market?ANDREW LIPOW: Well, there's a number of impacts. The first is that in the Middle East, we see them burning more crude oil for power generation to run their air conditioners during the summer. As far as refinery operations go, refineries, like people, do not like it when the heat index is 110 to 115. They simply can't have the equipment work as efficiently. And as a result, they're cutting their operating rates not only here in the Southern us, but in places like Greece and Italy where temperatures are even higher than what we see here in Texas.AKIKO FUJITA: So when you think about refineries having a breakdown, I mean this is already coming at a time when US inventory is low. To what extent is this-- as in the factor with the heat-- driving prices higher?ANDREW LIPOW: Well, it certainly exacerbates the problem along with these refinery unscheduled outages that we've seen around the coast, as well as in the Midwest. So as-- gasoline demand is increased about 3% over the last four weeks compared to last year and inventories are declining and makes for a mix of higher gasoline prices for the consumer- Andy, I want to ask you about this. I've seen the Biden administration delaying some plans to restock the emergency oil reserves. Given where prices are, they've canceled this planned purchase. The energy department canceling this, this week.So what does that say to you? Is that a good move? I mean, considering, especially given that you see WTI heading towards $85 a barrel, what's your thought on that?ANDREW LIPOW: I think that the Biden administration is very focused on gasoline prices because it's such a pocketbook issue. I think the fact that the administration canceled the Strategic Petroleum Reserve purchases of 3 million barrels a month, they're really very small in the scheme of the oil market. It's less than 100,000 barrels a day when world oil demand is over 100 million barrels a day.AKIKO FUJITA: Looking at gas prices right now, Andy, I'm looking at $3.80 right now a gallon. We have seen that number continue to tick up over the last few weeks. Are we going to see it push even higher going into year end or is this just something that we're seeing given the inventory picture right now?ANDREW LIPOW: Well, I think over the next couple of weeks, we could see gasoline prices tick a little bit higher. We've got the bulk of the hurricane season ahead of us in the Gulf of Mexico. But as we get into the winter months being October for the oil market, we see that refiners are able to make the cheaper grade of winter gasoline. And that would mitigate further price rises.- All right, Andy Lipow, president of Lipow Oil Associates. Thank you so much, and have a great weekend, and try to stay cool in Texas.ANDREW LIPOW: Thanks very much. Appreciate it.]

column4: Oil, commodities, small-caps in focus amid inflation woes
column10: [Economic prints show inflation to be cooling, but could there be another round of inflation ahead for consumers? Marketgauge.com Chief Strategist Michele Schneider remains defensive in case of an inflation spiking, citing increased oil demand in commodity markets, the Fed's rate hike outlook, and how the Russell 2000 and regional banks are performing in 2023.Video TranscriptJARED BLIKRE: Another round of inflation around the corner. That doesn't sound like something a lot of people are expecting.MICHELE SCHNEIDER: Well, we're really looking at the energy and oil market because a lot of the numbers that have come to date really have shown a decline that we saw in energy and oil. And of course, that was a very celebratory reason to think that inflation had cooled and would stay cooled.But what we're seeing now is just the reverse. The CRB has gone up, and the oil market has inclined about 15%. We're trading at around $81 a barrel right now, and that $80 a barrel was a really key area. And of course, we have many, many stories, not just because of OPEC Plus. But even here at home with the reserves being extremely low and demand being greater than what they thought.So I'd say that before I would go in full hog into this prediction. We have to continue really to watch what's happening there with oil. Because regardless of the yields going up today, or the dollar going up, we know that there are factors in commodities that ignore all of that when we come into a real supply-demand situation. So that's kind of what we have our eyes on right here.JARED BLIKRE: All right. What I have on the interactive right now, this is WTI crude oil. We're just looking at that. I want to show everybody the S&P-- the S&P Goldman Sachs commodity index. This has been for a while, and you can see here just breaking through its negative trend line.I think it's above the 200-day moving average as well. There you go. What's the importance? What's the significance of this for markets in general? Because a lot of times this just spells more inflation, something we've been talking about.Story continuesMICHELE SCHNEIDER: Well, it's kind of-- I think we're at a really interesting spot here, in terms of the consumer, and we can certainly talk about that sector in a moment. But we have a situation now where the yields have gone up, obviously, right now. People were looking based on what Powell said, and I've certainly heard many, many people talk about the potential pause or possibly pivot in 2024.But essentially, what you've got right now is folks feeling it from two areas. They're feeling it not only from an inflation standpoint, and prices have not really come down very much, at least that I can see when we go out, just basically to a supermarket or for anything for that matter.And we have a lot of commodity prices still high, cotton being one. Food prices still being high on many levels. And two, is now with the higher interest rates, you're pinching people two ways. They're going to pay more in both ends-- what they borrow, their credit card debt, and even what they pay even if they're paying with cash in terms of inflation.So that, to me, is somewhat dangerous. Because that means that the Fed before they start cheering, soft landing, have to worry what's going to happen over the next six months, if these things we're talking about actually continue to go up. And I'd say energy is probably the biggest area because that impacts everyone.As much as we like to think we're in a total EV world, we're not.JARED BLIKRE: Sure.MICHELE SCHNEIDER: But-- and so people still rely on oil and gas, and seasonally right now, we've had a lot of grid problems because of the extreme heat. So all of this is in my mind constantly.And I think that's really what we have to watch now; is if this CRB continues to go up, what all these numbers that we've seen soften over the last few months will start to rise. And how aggressive the Fed gets when they're already pinching and knowing the economy is growing basically, because of a lot of government spending and consumers right now still cheerful. Go ahead. I'm sorry.JARED BLIKRE: I just want to get to some tickers here. So we can put your charting skills to work.MICHELE SCHNEIDER: [LAUGHING] OK.JARED BLIKRE: I've got all the tickers we talked-- I can go transportation, regional banks. You just go, and I will outline here, and I'll be your graphics operator.MICHELE SCHNEIDER: OK. Well, yeah. I mean, let's-- and I'm sorry to go on a rant, Jared.JARED BLIKRE: No, it's OK.MICHELE SCHNEIDER: It's just that I feel very passionate about people being careful right-- now getting too complacent.JARED BLIKRE: Very good.MICHELE SCHNEIDER: Right. OK, so there we go. All right. So let's go with my economic modern family, right? Because that has always been my guide technically. So we can start with the Russell 2000, because I think that's key. A lot of people anticipated that we might see a little bit of softening in the tech and growth stocks in the NASDAQ and see some of that rotation to value.And, of course, that would be a better sign for the economy. And right now, that's not so terrible to think because IWM is actually doing pretty good. It is somewhat outperforming the spy. That's always a good thing. 193 was a key breakout on a two-year business cycle.The only thing right now is the momentum is declining, but there's no real divergence between what we're seeing in price and momentum. So right now, we could just say, yay, that's a good sign that we can notch up today's readiness as just a normal amount of correction that one would expect after so many green days.JARED BLIKRE: All right. A key part constituent of the Russell 2000 small caps is a financial sector. Regional banks, been under huge pressure this year. But we've seen them surge recently. I'm going to put up a chart of KRE, that's the SPDR S&P regional banking ETF. And what are what are we seeing here? We haven't quite made it back to that breakdown level from earlier in the year. In fact, we got quite a bit of space in there.MICHELE SCHNEIDER: Right. Actually, 52 would be a really good area to clear, to prove that we can actually get above all of that resistance that we had before. But right now-- again, this is actually also outperforming the S&P 500 right now. That's kind of an interesting sign that the banking is doing better.But on the momentum, once again, with this being read, we're seeing a slight possibility of a mean reversion here. So I'd say some kind of correction would not be crazy. It wouldn't necessarily mean tremendous weakness. But we're watching around that 44 level to really hold our 44-45. And if we can get through 52, that should be a nice rally, and a lot of these banks that were basically written off as dead.]

column4: Is Now The Time To Put Loews (NYSE:L) On Your Watchlist?
column10: [Investors are often guided by the idea of discovering 'the next big thing', even if that means buying 'story stocks' without any revenue, let alone profit. Sometimes these stories can cloud the minds of investors, leading them to invest with their emotions rather than on the merit of good company fundamentals. Loss-making companies are always racing against time to reach financial sustainability, so investors in these companies may be taking on more risk than they should.So if this idea of high risk and high reward doesn't suit, you might be more interested in profitable, growing companies, like Loews (NYSE:L). While profit isn't the sole metric that should be considered when investing, it's worth recognising businesses that can consistently produce it. View our latest analysis for Loews How Fast Is Loews Growing Its Earnings Per Share?In the last three years Loews' earnings per share took off; so much so that it's a bit disingenuous to use these figures to try and deduce long term estimates. As a result, we'll zoom in on growth over the last year, instead. Loews' EPS skyrocketed from US$4.25 to US$5.52, in just one year; a result that's bound to bring a smile to shareholders. That's a commendable gain of 30%.Careful consideration of revenue growth and earnings before interest and taxation (EBIT) margins can help inform a view on the sustainability of the recent profit growth. Our analysis has highlighted that Loews' revenue from operations did not account for all of their revenue in the previous 12 months, so our analysis of its margins might not accurately reflect the underlying business. EBIT margins for Loews remained fairly unchanged over the last year, however the company should be pleased to report its revenue growth for the period of 8.3% to US$15b. That's encouraging news for the company!In the chart below, you can see how the company has grown earnings and revenue, over time. For finer detail, click on the image.Story continuesearnings-and-revenue-historyWhile it's always good to see growing profits, you should always remember that a weak balance sheet could come back to bite. So check Loews' balance sheet strength, before getting too excited.Are Loews Insiders Aligned With All Shareholders?It's said that there's no smoke without fire. For investors, insider buying is often the smoke that indicates which stocks could set the market alight. That's because insider buying often indicates that those closest to the company have confidence that the share price will perform well. However, insiders are sometimes wrong, and we don't know the exact thinking behind their acquisitions.The good news for Loews is that one insider has illustrated their belief in the company's future with a huge purchase of shares in the last 12 months. In other words, the Senior VP of Corporate Development & Strategy, Benjamin Tisch, acquired US$19m worth of shares over the previous 12 months at an average price of around US$56.91. Big insider buys like that are a rarity and should prompt discussion on the merits of the business.On top of the insider buying, it's good to see that Loews insiders have a valuable investment in the business. Notably, they have an enviable stake in the company, worth US$2.6b. That equates to 18% of the company, making insiders powerful and aligned with other shareholders. Looking very optimistic for investors.While insiders are apparently happy to hold and accumulate shares, that is just part of the big picture. That's because Loews' CEO, James Tisch, is paid at a relatively modest level when compared to other CEOs for companies of this size. The median total compensation for CEOs of companies similar in size to Loews, with market caps over US$8.0b, is around US$12m.Loews' CEO took home a total compensation package worth US$6.4m in the year leading up to December 2022. That seems pretty reasonable, especially given it's below the median for similar sized companies. CEO remuneration levels are not the most important metric for investors, but when the pay is modest, that does support enhanced alignment between the CEO and the ordinary shareholders. It can also be a sign of a culture of integrity, in a broader sense.Does Loews Deserve A Spot On Your Watchlist?You can't deny that Loews has grown its earnings per share at a very impressive rate. That's attractive. Better still, insiders own a large chunk of the company and one has even been buying more shares. So it's fair to say that this stock may well deserve a spot on your watchlist. While we've looked at the quality of the earnings, we haven't yet done any work to value the stock. So if you like to buy cheap, you may want to check if Loews is trading on a high P/E or a low P/E, relative to its industry.The good news is that Loews is not the only growth stock with insider buying. column4: Gas prices close to a peak, hot weather helping prop up oil prices: Analyst
column10: [Oil prices are up about 16 percent in July, putting it on track to be the largest monthly gain in crude prices in over a year. OPIS Global Head of Energy Analysis Tom Kloza tells Yahoo Finance Live there are a couple of supply factors causing oil prices to rise. Kloza cites OPEC+ production cuts and the extreme heat in the U.S., saying "you have refineries that are coughing and wheezing instead of running at close to 100 percent rates as they would typically do in July." When it comes to gas prices, Kloza says, barring a hurricane impacting production, prices "should be very, very close to a peak right now." Kloza says a change in what can be added to gasoline and demand falling off after Labor Day as reasons why gasoline prices is closing to peaking.Video TranscriptDIANE KING HALL: Oil prices soaring this month up about 16%. That's the largest one-month gain in over the year. Our next guest says, this is all a supply story. Joining us now is Tom Kloza, OPIS Global Head of Energy Analysis.Thank you so much for joining us, Tom. So let's talk about where these oil prices stand. And pardon the pun. What is fueling this, especially when you consider where they were earlier in the year?TOM KLOZA: Well, it's not too bad. It's really supply. And you have two things that are working against comfortable supply. Number one is the OPEC+ cartel, principally the Saudis and the Russians, cutting crude oil. And we'll probably see demand outstrip supply by about 2 million barrels a day in the summertime.The other thing that's really manifesting itself here in the United States is the intense heat. And in places like Texas, Louisiana, Tennessee, even in some of the Rocky Mountain places, you've got refineries that are coughing and wheezing instead of running at close to 100% rates as they would typically do in July. And, you know, you mentioned crude oil prices up 17%.But inflation has really reared its head in the energy patch with other liquids this month. We're looking at diesel and jet fuel prices up anywhere from 25% to 30%. And that's going to rear itself in the producer price numbers that come out next month.Story continuesSEANA SMITH: So, Tom, then where do we go from here? When we talk about the fact that we've seen such large increases over the last several weeks, what does it look like headed out to the fall?TOM KLOZA: I think crude oil is going to stay, you know, somewhere between $80 and $89 a barrel, whether it's Brent or WTI. The chacha might be done a little bit by refined products. Now, normally, in August, gasoline prices ease a little bit because you start to disperse some ingredients in the gasoline formula that are much cheaper as you get into August.But this August, you know, with the Gulf of Mexico water temperatures in the 90s, you really have to be aware of what could happen maybe not even with a hurricane landfall, but a hurricane threat. And, you know, I would use kind of a little metric that if you have a category 3 storm in the Gulf of Mexico, you might cube that number and it might have a $0.27 sort of upwelling in prices should it actually target Texas or Louisiana. Let's hope that doesn't happen.Most of the time, hurricanes destroy demand without destroying supply. But this year is really special in the climate that's for sure.DIANE KING HALL: And, Tom, so you say this is a supply-based case for why oil is where it is, but there was a note from Goldman about oil demand reaching a record high in July. What do you make of that?TOM KLOZA: Well, I think they're accurate. I mean, global oil demand is up. In the United States, it's not necessarily up. As a matter of fact, gasoline demand is probably running about 500,000 barrels a day lower than it was from 2016 through 2019 in the summertime. And, you know, the electric vehicle is starting to have a little bit of an impact on the market, a little bit of disintermediation of liquid fuels.And the other thing that has a big impact since COVID is commuting. I mean, it looks as congested as ever on the weekend. I'm here at the Jersey Shore, and I can tell you, it's, like, gridlocked on the weekend. But during the week, I think the commuter traffic is down. And that's never going to go back to where it was.The other thing is, you know, the cars get so much better mileage these days. I think the new cars are probably 33 miles per gallon. And then you have the EVs interspersed with that.So we've seen peak demand in the United States. We haven't seen peak demand in the world. And places like India and even the European Union are creeping up a little bit because so far, they haven't seen that recession rear its head.SEANA SMITH: Tom, going back to what you just said a moment ago when it comes to EVs and EV adoption and how that's playing into the demand story, I guess how material is that impact versus what we maybe would have been expecting at this point, given the fact that adoption isn't as quick as many forecasters had initially anticipated?TOM KLOZA: It's not as quick as anticipated, and I think it will be a slow bleed to the EVs. But it's having an impact in some markets. You know, California, for example, we were well above $6 last year.In California, I think EVs are probably accounting for as great of a share of new car sales in California than anything. And they've made it clear that they want to get rid of the sale of fossil fuel cars by 2035. You know, we're going to have to start to use the calculus. For every million EVs, you know, you diminish this much in terms of fossil fuel usage here in the United States.And I would dare say that in China, you're seeing that as well. The Chinese economy may be very, very close to sort of its maximum gasoline usage, even though there's a lot of people there who are moving into the middle class. And with the move into the middle class comes mobility and the need to travel.DIANE KING HALL: Tom, let's talk quickly about gas prices here domestically. So according to AAA, they're at $3.75 a gallon. That is up, obviously, from a month ago but far cry from a year ago when we had a four-handle. So what are you expecting through the balance of this summer? Could we expect to see a four-handle again? And then through the balance of the year, Tom?TOM KLOZA: I think you only see a four-handle if you have one of those cyclonic formations in the Gulf of Mexico threatening the coasts with a hurricane. Without that, gasoline prices should be very, very close to a peak right now. You can use a lot more ingredients to manufacture gasoline in the middle of August, and then demand drops right after Labor Day.So under most circumstances, I would say we're very, very close to a top. And I would say this much. By November or December, you may be $0.35 to $0.55 lower than what you see in August.DIANE KING HALL: All right, looking forward to that relief at the pump because I don't have an EV yet. Tom Kloza, we appreciate you. Thank you. [LAUGHS]]

column4: Oil rallies in July as traders give up 'growth pessimism': Goldman Sachs
column10: [Crude oil just finished its biggest monthly gain since January 2022, with the price of West Texas Intermediate (CL=F) and Brent (BZ=F) futures rising more than 15% and 14%, respectively in July.And according to analysts at Goldman Sachs, this rally has been spurred by traders growing more constructive on their outlook for the global economy."The market has abandoned its growth pessimism," Goldman Sachs senior energy economist Daan Struyven and his team wrote in a note to clients."Oil prices have rallied by 18% since mid-June on the return to deficits and on the oil market abandoning its negative growth views, which we saw as too pessimistic."Goldman estimates global oil demand rose to an all-time high in July and revised up its 2023 demand forecast to about 500,000 barrels per day.Goldman Sachs is maintaining its 12-month-ahead forecast of $93 per barrel for Brent crude and $86 in December 2023. Brent crude settled near $85.50 on Monday.Expectations the Federal Reserve is near the end of its tightening cycle have also bolstered crude prices amid greater optimism the economy may achieve a "soft landing" that sees inflation come down while a recession is avoided.In a press conference last week, Fed Chair Jay Powell said he still sees this as a likely outcome for the US economy. Data out Friday showed the Fed's preferred inflation measure in June rose at the slowest pace since September 2021. Meanwhile, second quarter GDP showed the economy grew faster than expected in the second quarter of this year.Production cuts have also bolstered the oil market with demand turning the corner.Since October of last year, OPEC+ has announced production cuts which total over 5 million barrels per day into August 2023, notes Andy Lipow of Lipow Oil Associates."While [OPEC+] have not taken that much oil off the market, the amount that they are cutting in August is substantial — probably closer to 3.3 million barrels per day. It's a lot," said Lipow.Story continuesThe world's largest oil producers are expected to extend voluntary production cuts into September. Goldman notes the global oil market fell into a supply deficit in July after having been, on average, in a surplus of about 600,000 barrels per day over the prior year.A view shows an oil pump jack outside Almetyevsk in the Republic of Tatarstan, Russia. (Alexander Manzyuk/REUTERS)"I think [the oil rally] is market participants taking a more risk-on attitude and belief that China is actually going to grow its economy in a robust fashion this year," Stewart Glickman, energy equity analyst at CFRA Research, told Yahoo Finance on Monday."This has always been the key issue for 2023 — how quickly will China's GDP improve. I think the jury is still out."On Monday, WTI settled at $81.80 per barrel and Brent closed at $85.56 per barrel.Ines Ferre is a senior business reporter for Yahoo Finance. Follow her on Twitter at @ines_ferre.Click here for the latest stock market news and in-depth analysis, including events that move stocksRead the latest financial and business news from Yahoo Finance]

column4: Loews profit more than doubles as market rebound boosts investment returns
column10: [(Reuters) - Loews Corp said on Monday its second-quarter profit more than doubled as a jump in investment income cushioned a hit from higher catastrophe losses in its insurance unit, CNA Financial.Markets have staged a comeback this year on rising bets that the Federal Reserve was done with the bulk of its tightening cycle that had taken the economy on the edge of a recession.Loews reported a higher return on investments, helped by a broader market rally.Investment income for New York-based Loews jumped to $592 million in the second quarter ended June 30 from $366 million a year earlier.The company earns most of its revenue from CNA, in which it holds about 90% stake. It also operates a natural gas transportation pipeline business and a chain of hotels.Catastrophe losses in CNA's property and casualty operations rose to $68 million from $37 million.The U.S. Midwest and South were hit by violent storms in the quarter that knocked over houses and led to loss of life, adding to a series of weather-related events that have hurt insurers' profitability.CNA's peer Travelers Companies, earlier this month, reported about a 98% rise in catastrophe losses due to extreme weather.Meanwhile, CNA reported an underlying combined ratio of 91.1%, compared with 90.8% a year earlier. A ratio below 100% means the insurer earned more in premiums than it paid out in claims."CNA reported stellar results, despite high industry catastrophe losses," President and CEO James Tisch said in a statement.The income attributable to Loews for the second quarter was $360 million, or $1.58 per share, compared with $167 million, or 68 cents a year earlier.(Reporting by Pritam Biswas in Bengaluru; Editing by Shinjini Ganguli)]

column4: China: 'Pessimism is enormous' on country's economic slowdown, strategist says
column10: [President Biden characterized China's economic situation as a "ticking time bomb" this week as the nation experiences a growth slowdown accompanied by deflation."It is the world's second-largest economy, and, on top of that, they've got some demographic headwinds: they have to grow rich before they grow old and they're growing old very quickly," Martin Schulz, Federated Hermes Head of International Equity Group, tells Yahoo Finance Live on the pressure Chinese officials are feeling to re-stimulate the economy.Schulz discusses how investors with exposure to China and Chinese stocks should feel about the country's economic outlook, while also eyeing emerging markets like Brazil, geopolitical headwinds surrounding energy prices, and U.S. recession risks.Video Transcript[MUSIC PLAYING]SEANA SMITH: Well, President Biden taking aim at China this week, warning that its economy is a ticking time bomb. The President pointed to recent challenges, including weak growth as evidence that the Chinese economy is in trouble.For more on what this means for investors, we want to bring in Martin Schulz, the Federated Hermes Head of International Equity Group. Martin, it's great to see you here.So it's no secret that China's recovery has been struggling to say the least. What does this mean, though, for investors? Is it way too early for investors to write off any investment opportunity within China?MARTIN SCHULZ: Well, Seana, thanks for having us. So at Federated Hermes here, we've actually been visiting China a lot the last few months. And you're absolutely correct that it's been a really tough road. In fact, I think the one takeaway that we had in our recent visits is that the pessimism is just enormous, whether it's the consumer, investors on the ground, private investors.Obviously, the market has been in a tough slide. Economically you've got property market, you have, again, lack of confidence, again, both on the consumption side, as well as on the investment side. And so it's been tough.Story continuesBut we think that as of about two or three weeks ago, the government started to really notice some of the issues that have been out there for us investors for quite some while, that indicate that they may actually be taking some steps right now to change their policy. And that's very, very important because at the end of the day, policy prescriptions in China have been very, very important to the property markets, which then in turn have led to a fairly strong economic situation.And for us, I think this contrarian view of being now thinking that China will actually outperform is probably one that we're behind.AKIKO FUJITA: Yep, Martin, with that said, I mean, how significant do you think some of these reforms are likely to be? Certainly a lot of focus on the real estate market right now, given where it's been. To what extent can any of these policies help stimulate the economy? And how big are they likely to be?MARTIN SCHULZ: Well, in the past, they've actually been very big. And I think for the last 10 years, the government has tried to kind of step back. And, Akiko, I think that's a very good question because at the end of the day, China is not growing nearly as fast as it once was as we all know. It is the world's second largest economy. And on top of that, they've got some demographic headwinds. They have to grow rich before they grow old. And they're growing old very quickly.So the government has a bunch of levers, a little less than what they used to. But on the monetary policy front, they've started to kind of just jiggle a little bit, but they've got the ability there to cut rates, much like some of the other emerging market banks such as Brazil and other places around the world. They've got that policy flexibility. And then on the property market, they really can they just moved some of the goalposts. They, for example, during COVID, you had to have an 80% cash down payment to get a mortgage. That's now down to 30% to 40%. So they do have levers to continue to knock that down.But, again, they are dealing with these demographic headwinds, but still remember that China is an economy and a nation that is still urbanizing. There are a lot of people still moving to the cities. And so you still have this job creation and this household formation situation that will continue to drive this economy forward.SEANA SMITH: Martin, what do you think is a realistic timeline from an investor's perspective when you're trying to identify investment opportunities over there, what looks most attractive? How do you view that recovery timeline and what this recovery phase is going to look like?MARTIN SCHULZ: Well, as you know, Seana, it's been very frustrating. We actually started to go even away to China last summer with the expectation that COVID restrictions would be lifted earlier. We also thought that some of the regulatory overhang would go away quicker. That's now starting to happen. But I think in the meantime obviously, we lost some confidence or investors have lost confidence, if you will.So we believe for the next two to three years and even from a technical perspective, China looks very, very interesting because it has been in such a funk for such a long time. So we think the next 6 to 12 months and therein lies, from our perspective, really a focus on internet commerce, consumption names that we like, the Alibabas of the world, if you will, the Tencents of the world-- companies that we think that will generate some really strong earnings going forward. And because the valuations are so low, the expectations are so low that we think they'll be able to outperform longer term.AKIKO FUJITA: Martin, outside of China, you've talked about other opportunities in emerging markets, particularly looking around central bank policy. I think you're the second or third guest this week to talk about Brazil as a potential opportunity when you consider monetary policy there. But talk about how you're viewing other central banks in this context and where the good investments are.MARTIN SCHULZ: Sure. So the emerging markets fronts, you're absolutely right, Brazil is one of the places that we've been overweight for quite some time. Our top down country allocation process, which we utilize is basically gets us to focus on those markets that are undervalued and have the least amount of risk. And Brazil fits in that category.And as they've been very-- using very conventional monetary policy. So they've been ahead of the game, ahead of the Fed, ahead of the ECB. And so they've been really a central bank and, you know, obviously political politics aside, a market that we think will continue to do well. And those companies that have the ability to leverage obviously declining rates are going to win the most.And so-- but on the other hand, there's been one central bank out there in Japan that is really trying to navigate the yield control, curve control situation. And so we think Japan is also a place, not obviously in the emerging markets, but one that we think will generate some decent upside returns for investors in the next few months and years.SEANA SMITH: Martin let's talk about what's going on with oil, with crude and not only here in the US, but really on a global scale because the International Energy Agency, the IEA out earlier today saying that OPEC plus supply cuts that they could potentially drive oil prices even higher. They went on to say that June was a record month here in terms of world oil demand.We've seen this steady rise in the price of crude, up now seven weeks in a row. How are you looking at this just in terms of a potential headwind to the economic recovery not only here in the US, but also when we talk about China and other areas of the world, the international picture as well?MARTIN SCHULZ: Yeah, Seana, that's a really great question. Because oil, at the end of the day, for both consumers as well as producers, there's obviously a tax if it goes up relative to it going down. So we do expect oil to stay stable and potentially rise. Part of that is because we think the global economy is bottoming and starting to grow.And in fact, China, thus far, has not been a big buyer of oil. I think the biggest issue is that, here in the US, we've been selling oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. And so there is this, if you will, a game being played between the oil producers and the US as it relates to oil price.But again, I think if we see the US not entering a recession, if the recession in Europe is fairly shallow as we expect, then we do expect that demand will increase. And as this ESG or environmental kind of focus on the green world continues, obviously, this transition period is going to be very long.Carbon, unfortunately, energy are going to continue to be a big part and a source of energy for the world's economy. And so we think that energy prices will be higher than expected. And what that's going to lead to is particularly, in the case of the Fed, that's going to lead to higher inflation rates.And we saw this in the PPI numbers today. We think that it will continue. And so I think investors, on the one hand, they're seeing inflation rates come down pretty quickly. And that's the good sign. But I think it's going to be a little stickier than people expect.And that's probably the one, if you will risk, that we see out there. And again, as oil prices remain high or at least these levels or higher, obviously, that, as I mentioned earlier, is a tax on the average consumer or producer. And so that's something we need to watch out for. And it may mean that rates around the world will remain higher than expected, because of that situation.AKIKO FUJITA: Yeah, that certainly adds to concerns about inflation reaccelerating. So when you're talking about where prices are likely to remain, I mean, the IEA says it could be-- it could go even higher in terms of demand this month. Is your base case here that they do remain elevated into year end?MARTIN SCHULZ: We do believe that they will remain elevated. Again, part of that has to do with the geopolitics and what happens with Saudi Arabia and Russia and some of the other swing producers right now. The problem is the US, for many years, was that swing producer.But right now, for several reasons, we are not that swing producer to the degree that we were once before in the last several 10-- some 10 years ago. And so for the near-term, we do expect that we will see elevated prices if these levels are higher.SEANA SMITH: Martin, when it comes to the US and the readings that we got on inflation this week, we got PPI, the producer price index, this morning coming in hotter than expected. And that contrasts to what we saw yesterday from CPI when, once again, we saw inflation pressures at least easing more than the Street had been looking for. What's your read on these two conflicting reports and what that tells us just about the Fed's long fight against inflation and the path forward?MARTIN SCHULZ: Yeah, you're basically highlighting a very interesting phenomena which is that interest rates are generally coming down much quicker than expected. But it's not a one-way direction, one-way street, so to speak. Obviously, post-COVID and the supply chain issues that we've had and some of the other machinations within the economy, we do think that inflation is coming down, but it will remain stickier than expected.And so in that vein, again, I think that the central banks-- I mean, you look at what's happening in the UK, the Bank of England either in Canada and in Australia, they're being much more careful about where they take interest rates based on some of these inflation numbers.So obviously, the risk is that higher rates will drive the global economy, or in this case, the US economy into a potential recession. But in the near-term, I think fighting inflation is going to be the number one task, and that's what they're focused on.AKIKO FUJITA: So in that debate, Martin, which camp are you in? Are you in the camp that expects a mild recession at least given how elevated rates are likely to remain?You know, at Federated Hermes, we were expecting a recession earlier in the year. And I think we've decided that because of where we are in the economic cycle and the monetary policy cycle and what we're seeing elsewhere, we do think that if we have a recession, it will be not-- it will be delayed until much later, probably late 2024. We'll see if that comes to fruition.But right now, the markets are telling us-- again, obviously at the end of the day, we are seeing some economic data that is very weak. But on the other hand, we're also seeing some other data, both economic as well as market-oriented, where we're seeing the market broadening out. And we're seeing a situation which we're getting so far away from this. And we could be in a very different situation.If you think about monetary policy in the past usually between 9 and 18 months, you saw some type of effect on the economy. It may be less pronounced now because of disintermediation. And it may be because the economy is just a post-COVID economy that is one that is growing, that is in a catch-up phase that will continue to move forward, unlike past cycles. And so we do expect that we'll see some slowdown next year, but probably not a recession at this point.SEANA SMITH: All right, optimistic tone here to end the conversation. Martin Schulz, always great to get your perspective, Federated Hermes, Head of International Equity Group, thanksMARTIN SCHULZ: Thank you.]

column4: China's economic slowdown: 'The rules can change moment to moment,' strategist says
column10: [China has been in focus this week after consumer prices ticked lower for the country for the first time in two years. President Biden is calling China's growth concerns a "ticking time bomb."Kace Capital Advisors, LLC Managing Partner Kenny Polcari remains skeptical of some of the numbers he's seeing out of China. "You have to be very careful when you go into China because the rules can change from moment to moment," he tells Yahoo Finance.Polcari also discusses the weight of oil prices on China's economy, and how investors should be looking at international markets, including Europe.Video Transcript- Well, China's been a big focus for investors this week after the country saw consumer prices tick lower for the first time in two years. President Biden, calling China's growth concerns a ticking time bomb at a political fundraiser. Our next guest remains skeptical of some of the numbers we are getting out of that nation. Kenny Polcari, Kace Capital Advisors Managing Partner, is with us now.Kenny, it's great to see you. So what do we make of all of the China data, and the China rhetoric, and what it means for investors here in the US?KENNY POLCARI: Listen, I think you have to be very careful when you go into China because the rules can change from moment to moment, right? So you never really know what you're getting. They're telling us one day, that the China country is expanding.They tell you the next day, China economy is declining. Then, they tell you China is buying oil, then, they tell you China is not buying oil. And so, they create all this chaos.So, I actually do not invest directly into China just because I don't want to-- I don't want to add that chaos to what else I'm doing. I have exposure to China through things like Apple, but therefore it's controlled by Apple, right? Not so much by what the Chinese want to do. So I tend to stay away, but that's me personally.There are people certainly that find opportunity in China. But I think you have to understand going in that it can be a very volatile investment part of your portfolio.Story continues- But even your Apple holdings would still be impacted by whether or not China decided to put more liquidity into the economy and into consumers' hands, and their spending propensity as well, yeah?KENNY POLCARI: Agreed. So, therefore, I do have some exposure to China. But I like to think because I own Apple, it's really a US company. While it maybe-- it may respond to what's going on in China, that's different than China being able to go in there and change the rules on Apple, or change the way they can in Chinese listed companies, right? Where they can suddenly just decide, you know this isn't going to happen anymore, we're changing the rules.They can't really do that to Apple. And by the way, even though Apple depends on China for a lot, they are starting to and we've seen it ever since COVID, they are starting to broaden out their supplier base, whether it's Vietnam, whether it's India, other parts of Asia, so that they're becoming less dependent on what happens in China.- Kenny, I want to pivot if we could-- you mentioned oil in passing with reference to China. We just heard our Jared Bleakley talking about it. You also have been writing about it in your morning notes, oil's been creeping up. How much of an issue is that going? It hasn't seemed to be much of a problem for stocks, but will it be?KENNY POLCARI: Well, oil stocks certainly have done well, right? With oil creeping up, it's up 25% just from two and 1/2 weeks ago when it was trading down at 65. It's now trading at $84.And likely, probably going higher. We see that the production cuts by. The Saudis and Russia are starting to take hold. We see global demand increasing.In fact, I put it in my note today that "Bloomberg" ran with an article about how global demand is robust. And actually, China-- China's buying plenty of oil. So this whole idea, once again, about China was, kind of, conflicting.But one way or the other, at some point, yes. If oil becomes way too expensive, is it going to hurt our economy? And then, therefore, hurt the market potentially? Yes. So I think you have to be careful going in.But that doesn't mean you should panic and start selling everything. It just means you need to take advantage of the opportunity that's going to create and other sectors of the market.- Is there any different way that investors should be playing, kind of, the international equation going into 2024? Now that we've essentially got a quarter and a half left in 2023, a lot of people are going to start paying attention to what is 2024, and that is a general election year here in the US.KENNY POLCARI: Yeah, yeah. It's going to be-- there's going to be a lot going on. I tend to, like, in terms of international markets, I tend to favor European markets versus the other markets, versus the Asian markets-- China, Hong Kong, any of that, I tend to-- my exposure is in international, is in Europe.Now, I do think, and I like Europe. The UK has been underperforming this year. If you look at the list, the UK's only up 1% on the year while all the other markets in that region are up double digits, right? From the euro stocks Italy, Spain, Germany, they're all-- France, they're all up 14, 13, and 14%.The UK is lagging way behind. Now, part of that is the economy in the UK. I get it inflation is sticky, the Boe remains hawkish, the same way the Fed is going to remain over here. But I think you have to be selective like anything.I don't think you can just passively go in and buy the market. I think have to really look and find the sectors that you think, like, here, are going to do better in a rising rate environment. Those would be names, like, consumer staple names, for me, banks and health care. Whether it's here or whether it's in Europe.- And what about the market overall here? Because as you've been writing recently, maybe the market's a little tired. We've seen evidence of that over the past couple of weeks. We've already seen stocks drop a bit. Are we going to see more of that?KENNY POLCARI: I think we are. Look, you know as well as I do that this tends to be a seasonally, kind of, volatile weak time of year, August into September, maybe even so much into October. I don't think the market's going to crash at all, but I would love to see the market back off 7 or 8 or even 9% because remember, anything within a 10% range is well within the normal range of trading.The issue that I think we're going to find is, as the market starts to back off, I don't think it's going to back off enough because there's a lot of portfolio managers that went to cash, expecting the Morgan Stanley S&P 3,000 call, that never came. And so, they're sitting there with plenty of cash that they have to now put to work. We're in the second half of the year. Markets are already up double digits, and these guys are lagging.So therefore, I think any dip is going to be bought, unless, of course, the economic data should suddenly change so drastically that it would change the narrative, which I don't think it's going to do. So, yes, I think the market is going to back off, but I don't think it's-- I'm not looking for a crash. If we move 6% or 7%, I'd love to see that, and we're already down. The S&P is already down 4% from the highs two weeks ago.- Yes, exactly. We've seen kind of a rapid deceleration here. As always, I like to end with talking about your daily recipe today. It's another pasta. One pasta, zucchini, and guanciale.KENNY POLCARI: Guanciale.- Guanciale.KENNY POLCARI: Yes, it's like the fat from the pig's cheek, right? But if you don't have that, if you can't get it, you can always use bacon. But one way or the other, it's a simple recipe, and I put it in my note, right?You want to saute the guanciale first-- make it nice and crispy. Take it out. Leave the fat that it that's left behind in the saute pan, take your zucchini.I would use green and yellow because it's colorful, right? Cut them in half lengthwise, and then cut them this way so you get like these half moon shapes-- put that right in the saute pan, sauteed up. The zucchini will make its own water, right?Boil the pasta, make it Al dente. I would use penne regate with this one, like, kind of, the short pasta. Then, when the pasta is done, put it in with the zucchini, then add back the guanciale, toss it a couple of handfuls of Pecorino Romano cheese, toss it up, and serve it immediately. It is delicious.- It sounds delicious, I got to say, Kenny.KENNY POLCARI: It takes-- the whole thing takes you 20 minutes start to finish. It's also easy to prepare.- And I appreciate the last time you took a little bit of recipe advice from me, which was an honor, I have to say. And then, you put out a recipe.KENNY POLCARI: Yes. I did it. Yes, I did. And I actually gave you credit for letting me think about that because it was perfect, right? It was your idea.- Thank you so much. I appreciate it. I don't have any-- I don't have any inspiration for you today. I'm sorry to say. But I will next time.I'll know the pressure's on. Kenny Polcari, Kace Capital Advisors, Managing Partner, great to see you as always.]

column4: Oil prices on the rise as energy stocks lead sector gains
column10: [Oil prices are trading above $84 per barrel ahead of Wednesday's closing bell. Yahoo Finance Markets Reporter Jared Blikre breaks down crude oil's pricing behavior year-to-date in 2023, while taking a look at the sector action surrounding energy stocks.Video TranscriptAKIKO FUJITA: Jared Blikre is on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange with his eye on the energy patch. Jared?JARED BLIKRE: Hi, Akiko. Let's take a look at the YFi interactive. And we can see indeed WTI Crude Oil has risen today. Got past a little stumbling block there. And in the context of the longer term-- this is a 2-year chart-- you can see it's been trading in a range here that is just trying to break out all year long, and in fact, going back to about the fourth quarter of last year.A definitive breakout from here would be a really big deal for not only crude oil but commodities in general and also the energy stock patch. Commodity ?] Index.Now, here's a year-to-date chart, and we can see that has really picked up since July. It has broken to the upside today, but it in fact is still in a trading range as well. But when you go to a [? year-to-date, ?] you're going to find it's barely positive. And that's because XLE has been taken for quite the wild ride this year. column4: Oil prices rise after Saudi Arabia, Russia extend supply cuts
column10: [Saudi Arabia has extended its one million barrel-per-day production cuts into September, while Russia announce it will cut oil exports, sending oil prices higher. Lipow Oil Associates President Andrew Lipow tells Yahoo Finance Live the move is "very significant." Lipow say the cuts "really emphasize the point that they are looking for higher prices, because the domestic budgets of these OPEC+ countries simply could not last when oil was under $70 a barrel."Video TranscriptAKIKO FUJITA: Oil prices rising for a sixth straight week. And today's gains driven by Saudi Arabia and Russia's decision to extend production cuts. Remaining OPEC plus members though deciding to keep output unchanged in a meeting today causing prices to rally further. It comes as extreme weather poses threats to US production.Let's bring in Andy Lipow, president of Lipow Oil Associates. Andy, good to talk to you today. I'm looking at where oil prices are trading today-- oil futures, I should say, above that $80 a barrel mark. How supportive do you think these cuts announced by Saudi Arabia, as well as Russia will be in terms of price action?ANDREW LIPOW: Well, thanks for having me. I think these cuts are very significant. If we look back to October of last year, OPEC plus has cut over 5 million barrels a day from their production quotas. And these last voluntary cuts by Russia and Saudi Arabia really emphasized the point that they're looking for higher prices because the domestic budgets of these OPEC plus countries simply could not last when oil was under $70 a barrel.- So Andy, do we expect to see oil hit $90 a barrel before the year is out?ANDREW LIPOW: I think there's a very good possibility, especially as we've seen Saudi Arabia take these proactive steps to get the price of oil higher. I think they'd be quite comfortable to see Brent crude oil prices at around $90 a barrel and WTI at about $85. But the market could move higher because OPEC plus tends to be reactive. And of course, as prices rise, they're certainly going to think it's in their benefit to keep those higher prices higher for a longer period of time without triggering a recession around the world.Story continuesAKIKO FUJITA: Andy, what are the supply-demand dynamics looking like right now? You know, on the one hand, we've got the prices above $80 a barrel, you've got the Russian cuts taking shape more. And yet you look at the demand picture at least in China where the biggest market is, we just haven't seen the kind of pickup in economic activity.ANDREW LIPOW: Well, I think that their economic activity is lagging, but we do see in the physical oil market China is buying record amounts of crude oil and processing record amounts of that oil in their new refineries and existing refineries. So the oil market is seeing the demand. The latest cut of 500,000 barrels a day by Russia was actually impacting China at the most because China, India, Turkey, and Bulgaria have become the four main customers of that Russian oil. So it does look to me like inventories around the world are declining and supplies are getting tighter- Andy, I want to ask you about just the impact of heat. It's not something over the years-- I've covered crude oil and it's not something that's been often in the conversation when you're talking about oil prices, oil inventories. What is the impact of extreme weather on that market?ANDREW LIPOW: Well, there's a number of impacts. The first is that in the Middle East, we see them burning more crude oil for power generation to run their air conditioners during the summer. As far as refinery operations go, refineries, like people, do not like it when the heat index is 110 to 115. They simply can't have the equipment work as efficiently. And as a result, they're cutting their operating rates not only here in the Southern us, but in places like Greece and Italy where temperatures are even higher than what we see here in Texas.AKIKO FUJITA: So when you think about refineries having a breakdown, I mean this is already coming at a time when US inventory is low. To what extent is this-- as in the factor with the heat-- driving prices higher?ANDREW LIPOW: Well, it certainly exacerbates the problem along with these refinery unscheduled outages that we've seen around the coast, as well as in the Midwest. So as-- gasoline demand is increased about 3% over the last four weeks compared to last year and inventories are declining and makes for a mix of higher gasoline prices for the consumer- Andy, I want to ask you about this. I've seen the Biden administration delaying some plans to restock the emergency oil reserves. Given where prices are, they've canceled this planned purchase. The energy department canceling this, this week.So what does that say to you? Is that a good move? I mean, considering, especially given that you see WTI heading towards $85 a barrel, what's your thought on that?ANDREW LIPOW: I think that the Biden administration is very focused on gasoline prices because it's such a pocketbook issue. I think the fact that the administration canceled the Strategic Petroleum Reserve purchases of 3 million barrels a month, they're really very small in the scheme of the oil market. It's less than 100,000 barrels a day when world oil demand is over 100 million barrels a day.AKIKO FUJITA: Looking at gas prices right now, Andy, I'm looking at $3.80 right now a gallon. We have seen that number continue to tick up over the last few weeks. Are we going to see it push even higher going into year end or is this just something that we're seeing given the inventory picture right now?ANDREW LIPOW: Well, I think over the next couple of weeks, we could see gasoline prices tick a little bit higher. We've got the bulk of the hurricane season ahead of us in the Gulf of Mexico. But as we get into the winter months being October for the oil market, we see that refiners are able to make the cheaper grade of winter gasoline. And that would mitigate further price rises.- All right, Andy Lipow, president of Lipow Oil Associates. Thank you so much, and have a great weekend, and try to stay cool in Texas.ANDREW LIPOW: Thanks very much. Appreciate it.]

column4: Oil, commodities, small-caps in focus amid inflation woes
column10: [Economic prints show inflation to be cooling, but could there be another round of inflation ahead for consumers? Marketgauge.com Chief Strategist Michele Schneider remains defensive in case of an inflation spiking, citing increased oil demand in commodity markets, the Fed's rate hike outlook, and how the Russell 2000 and regional banks are performing in 2023.Video TranscriptJARED BLIKRE: Another round of inflation around the corner. That doesn't sound like something a lot of people are expecting.MICHELE SCHNEIDER: Well, we're really looking at the energy and oil market because a lot of the numbers that have come to date really have shown a decline that we saw in energy and oil. And of course, that was a very celebratory reason to think that inflation had cooled and would stay cooled.But what we're seeing now is just the reverse. The CRB has gone up, and the oil market has inclined about 15%. We're trading at around $81 a barrel right now, and that $80 a barrel was a really key area. And of course, we have many, many stories, not just because of OPEC Plus. But even here at home with the reserves being extremely low and demand being greater than what they thought.So I'd say that before I would go in full hog into this prediction. We have to continue really to watch what's happening there with oil. Because regardless of the yields going up today, or the dollar going up, we know that there are factors in commodities that ignore all of that when we come into a real supply-demand situation. So that's kind of what we have our eyes on right here.JARED BLIKRE: All right. What I have on the interactive right now, this is WTI crude oil. We're just looking at that. I want to show everybody the S&P-- the S&P Goldman Sachs commodity index. This has been for a while, and you can see here just breaking through its negative trend line.I think it's above the 200-day moving average as well. There you go. What's the importance? What's the significance of this for markets in general? Because a lot of times this just spells more inflation, something we've been talking about.Story continuesMICHELE SCHNEIDER: Well, it's kind of-- I think we're at a really interesting spot here, in terms of the consumer, and we can certainly talk about that sector in a moment. But we have a situation now where the yields have gone up, obviously, right now. People were looking based on what Powell said, and I've certainly heard many, many people talk about the potential pause or possibly pivot in 2024.But essentially, what you've got right now is folks feeling it from two areas. They're feeling it not only from an inflation standpoint, and prices have not really come down very much, at least that I can see when we go out, just basically to a supermarket or for anything for that matter.And we have a lot of commodity prices still high, cotton being one. Food prices still being high on many levels. And two, is now with the higher interest rates, you're pinching people two ways. They're going to pay more in both ends-- what they borrow, their credit card debt, and even what they pay even if they're paying with cash in terms of inflation.So that, to me, is somewhat dangerous. Because that means that the Fed before they start cheering, soft landing, have to worry what's going to happen over the next six months, if these things we're talking about actually continue to go up. And I'd say energy is probably the biggest area because that impacts everyone.As much as we like to think we're in a total EV world, we're not.JARED BLIKRE: Sure.MICHELE SCHNEIDER: But-- and so people still rely on oil and gas, and seasonally right now, we've had a lot of grid problems because of the extreme heat. So all of this is in my mind constantly.And I think that's really what we have to watch now; is if this CRB continues to go up, what all these numbers that we've seen soften over the last few months will start to rise. And how aggressive the Fed gets when they're already pinching and knowing the economy is growing basically, because of a lot of government spending and consumers right now still cheerful. Go ahead. I'm sorry.JARED BLIKRE: I just want to get to some tickers here. So we can put your charting skills to work.MICHELE SCHNEIDER: [LAUGHING] OK.JARED BLIKRE: I've got all the tickers we talked-- I can go transportation, regional banks. You just go, and I will outline here, and I'll be your graphics operator.MICHELE SCHNEIDER: OK. Well, yeah. I mean, let's-- and I'm sorry to go on a rant, Jared.JARED BLIKRE: No, it's OK.MICHELE SCHNEIDER: It's just that I feel very passionate about people being careful right-- now getting too complacent.JARED BLIKRE: Very good.MICHELE SCHNEIDER: Right. OK, so there we go. All right. So let's go with my economic modern family, right? Because that has always been my guide technically. So we can start with the Russell 2000, because I think that's key. A lot of people anticipated that we might see a little bit of softening in the tech and growth stocks in the NASDAQ and see some of that rotation to value.And, of course, that would be a better sign for the economy. And right now, that's not so terrible to think because IWM is actually doing pretty good. It is somewhat outperforming the spy. That's always a good thing. 193 was a key breakout on a two-year business cycle.The only thing right now is the momentum is declining, but there's no real divergence between what we're seeing in price and momentum. So right now, we could just say, yay, that's a good sign that we can notch up today's readiness as just a normal amount of correction that one would expect after so many green days.JARED BLIKRE: All right. A key part constituent of the Russell 2000 small caps is a financial sector. Regional banks, been under huge pressure this year. But we've seen them surge recently. I'm going to put up a chart of KRE, that's the SPDR S&P regional banking ETF. And what are what are we seeing here? We haven't quite made it back to that breakdown level from earlier in the year. In fact, we got quite a bit of space in there.MICHELE SCHNEIDER: Right. Actually, 52 would be a really good area to clear, to prove that we can actually get above all of that resistance that we had before. But right now-- again, this is actually also outperforming the S&P 500 right now. That's kind of an interesting sign that the banking is doing better.But on the momentum, once again, with this being read, we're seeing a slight possibility of a mean reversion here. So I'd say some kind of correction would not be crazy. It wouldn't necessarily mean tremendous weakness. But we're watching around that 44 level to really hold our 44-45. And if we can get through 52, that should be a nice rally, and a lot of these banks that were basically written off as dead.]
