Oil deficits are currently estimated at about 2 million barrels per day this quarter, according to Bloomberg data."Deepening OPEC+ supply cuts have collided with improved macroeconomic sentiment and all-time high world oil demand," read a recent report by the International Energy Agency."World oil demand is scaling record highs," said the report.Oil, miniatures of oil barrels and U.S. dollar banknote are seen in this illustration taken, June 6, 2023. REUTERS/Dado Ruvic/Illustration"Oil dropped dramatically from over $80 to as low as $67 when the regional banking crisis hit, based on fears that it would trigger a recession. Oil has recovered as it has become clear that there is no imminent recession," Jay Hatfield, CEO at Infrastructure Capital Management in New York, said in an email to Yahoo Finance.Goldman Sachs analysts recently reaffirmed their forecast of $93 per barrel for Brent crude and $86 per barrel for WTI by December, highlighting the market is less "pessimistic" about the global economy.Energy-related stocks have been on an upward trend in the last two months. The S&P 500's Energy Select ETF (XLE) is up more than 2% year to date. The sector had been negative earlier this year amid recession concerns and a lagging economic recovery in China post COVID lockdowns."Right now, the world is ignoring the economic collapse in China and focusing on the economic recovery in the West," Louis Navellier of Navellier Capital Investments said in a recent note to investors."Seasonal demand for crude oil is expected to peak around Labor Day, so I will be monitoring inventories very carefully. If crude oil inventories remain low, it will be safe to continue to hold many refineries and integrated oil companies," he added.Story continuesInes Ferre is a senior business reporter for Yahoo Finance. Follow her on Twitter at @ines_ferre.Click here for the latest stock market news and in-depth analysis, including events that move stocksRead the latest financial and business news from Yahoo Finance]

column4: Oil's seven-week rally ends amid China recovery concerns
column10: [Oil gains halt after a seven-week rally amid concerns regarding China's declining economic growth and a stronger U.S. dollar. Yahoo Finance Markets Reporter Ines Ferre takes a look at oil's stock movement.Video Transcript- Oil prices halted their seven-week rally amid major concerns about China's declining economy as well as a stronger dollar. Let's go now to Yahoo Finance's Ines Ferre to learn more about this. Hey, Ines.INES FERRE: Yeah, Rachelle. And those concerns about China and of course, that stronger dollar as oil is denominated in dollars. So when you see the dollar going up, you usually see the price of oil coming down. But I just want to take a look at WTI, which is trading above $82 per barrel. Also Brent Crude trading above $86 per barrel.But let me pull up a one-year chart so you can see the price action that we've seen. This really higher price action that we've seen from the end of June through July and just taking a look at that move that we've seen. So this has been significant when it comes to WTI, when it comes to Brent Crude as well. And the Russia and Saudi Arabia production cuts, they have really had an impact on supply, building up a deficit of about 2 million barrels per day this quarter. And at the same time, that anticipation of a soft landing or perhaps avoiding a recession here in the US is helping demand.Now, demand does peak around Labor Day, so it's important to keep a watchful eye on oil inventories. But coming into Labor Day, the International Energy Agency just recently said that world oil demand is reaching record highs, a strong summer travel. You have had the China reopening.And then just taking a look at where we're at with oil equities, oil-related equities. And I just want to point out a year to date chart of XLE up 2%. Earlier this year, you had XLE, which was the underperformer, it was down about 7 or 9% after. Those parabolic moves that we saw with oil-related stocks last year, they did see a pullback at the beginning of this year. But now, we are seeing that these energy stocks, they have been rallying.And one thing to also watch out for Rachelle is as we have seen oil prices going higher, this is a concern for inflation because a big component of inflation, of course, are energy costs, Rachelle.- Indeed. And we'd also been seeing gas prices that national average ticking up for five straight weeks as oil was rallying as well. So perhaps some relief at least a little bit at the gas pump coming up for some people as well. A big thank you there, our very own Ines Ferre.]

column4: China: 'Pessimism is enormous' on country's economic slowdown, strategist says
column10: [President Biden characterized China's economic situation as a "ticking time bomb" this week as the nation experiences a growth slowdown accompanied by deflation."It is the world's second-largest economy, and, on top of that, they've got some demographic headwinds: they have to grow rich before they grow old and they're growing old very quickly," Martin Schulz, Federated Hermes Head of International Equity Group, tells Yahoo Finance Live on the pressure Chinese officials are feeling to re-stimulate the economy.Schulz discusses how investors with exposure to China and Chinese stocks should feel about the country's economic outlook, while also eyeing emerging markets like Brazil, geopolitical headwinds surrounding energy prices, and U.S. recession risks.Video Transcript[MUSIC PLAYING]SEANA SMITH: Well, President Biden taking aim at China this week, warning that its economy is a ticking time bomb. The President pointed to recent challenges, including weak growth as evidence that the Chinese economy is in trouble.For more on what this means for investors, we want to bring in Martin Schulz, the Federated Hermes Head of International Equity Group. Martin, it's great to see you here.So it's no secret that China's recovery has been struggling to say the least. What does this mean, though, for investors? Is it way too early for investors to write off any investment opportunity within China?MARTIN SCHULZ: Well, Seana, thanks for having us. So at Federated Hermes here, we've actually been visiting China a lot the last few months. And you're absolutely correct that it's been a really tough road. In fact, I think the one takeaway that we had in our recent visits is that the pessimism is just enormous, whether it's the consumer, investors on the ground, private investors.Obviously, the market has been in a tough slide. Economically you've got property market, you have, again, lack of confidence, again, both on the consumption side, as well as on the investment side. And so it's been tough.Story continuesBut we think that as of about two or three weeks ago, the government started to really notice some of the issues that have been out there for us investors for quite some while, that indicate that they may actually be taking some steps right now to change their policy. And that's very, very important because at the end of the day, policy prescriptions in China have been very, very important to the property markets, which then in turn have led to a fairly strong economic situation.And for us, I think this contrarian view of being now thinking that China will actually outperform is probably one that we're behind.AKIKO FUJITA: Yep, Martin, with that said, I mean, how significant do you think some of these reforms are likely to be? Certainly a lot of focus on the real estate market right now, given where it's been. To what extent can any of these policies help stimulate the economy? And how big are they likely to be?MARTIN SCHULZ: Well, in the past, they've actually been very big. And I think for the last 10 years, the government has tried to kind of step back. And, Akiko, I think that's a very good question because at the end of the day, China is not growing nearly as fast as it once was as we all know. It is the world's second largest economy. And on top of that, they've got some demographic headwinds. They have to grow rich before they grow old. And they're growing old very quickly.So the government has a bunch of levers, a little less than what they used to. But on the monetary policy front, they've started to kind of just jiggle a little bit, but they've got the ability there to cut rates, much like some of the other emerging market banks such as Brazil and other places around the world. They've got that policy flexibility. And then on the property market, they really can they just moved some of the goalposts. They, for example, during COVID, you had to have an 80% cash down payment to get a mortgage. That's now down to 30% to 40%. So they do have levers to continue to knock that down.But, again, they are dealing with these demographic headwinds, but still remember that China is an economy and a nation that is still urbanizing. There are a lot of people still moving to the cities. And so you still have this job creation and this household formation situation that will continue to drive this economy forward.SEANA SMITH: Martin, what do you think is a realistic timeline from an investor's perspective when you're trying to identify investment opportunities over there, what looks most attractive? How do you view that recovery timeline and what this recovery phase is going to look like?MARTIN SCHULZ: Well, as you know, Seana, it's been very frustrating. We actually started to go even away to China last summer with the expectation that COVID restrictions would be lifted earlier. We also thought that some of the regulatory overhang would go away quicker. That's now starting to happen. But I think in the meantime obviously, we lost some confidence or investors have lost confidence, if you will.So we believe for the next two to three years and even from a technical perspective, China looks very, very interesting because it has been in such a funk for such a long time. So we think the next 6 to 12 months and therein lies, from our perspective, really a focus on internet commerce, consumption names that we like, the Alibabas of the world, if you will, the Tencents of the world-- companies that we think that will generate some really strong earnings going forward. And because the valuations are so low, the expectations are so low that we think they'll be able to outperform longer term.AKIKO FUJITA: Martin, outside of China, you've talked about other opportunities in emerging markets, particularly looking around central bank policy. I think you're the second or third guest this week to talk about Brazil as a potential opportunity when you consider monetary policy there. But talk about how you're viewing other central banks in this context and where the good investments are.MARTIN SCHULZ: Sure. So the emerging markets fronts, you're absolutely right, Brazil is one of the places that we've been overweight for quite some time. Our top down country allocation process, which we utilize is basically gets us to focus on those markets that are undervalued and have the least amount of risk. And Brazil fits in that category.And as they've been very-- using very conventional monetary policy. So they've been ahead of the game, ahead of the Fed, ahead of the ECB. And so they've been really a central bank and, you know, obviously political politics aside, a market that we think will continue to do well. And those companies that have the ability to leverage obviously declining rates are going to win the most.And so-- but on the other hand, there's been one central bank out there in Japan that is really trying to navigate the yield control, curve control situation. And so we think Japan is also a place, not obviously in the emerging markets, but one that we think will generate some decent upside returns for investors in the next few months and years.SEANA SMITH: Martin let's talk about what's going on with oil, with crude and not only here in the US, but really on a global scale because the International Energy Agency, the IEA out earlier today saying that OPEC plus supply cuts that they could potentially drive oil prices even higher. They went on to say that June was a record month here in terms of world oil demand.We've seen this steady rise in the price of crude, up now seven weeks in a row. How are you looking at this just in terms of a potential headwind to the economic recovery not only here in the US, but also when we talk about China and other areas of the world, the international picture as well?MARTIN SCHULZ: Yeah, Seana, that's a really great question. Because oil, at the end of the day, for both consumers as well as producers, there's obviously a tax if it goes up relative to it going down. So we do expect oil to stay stable and potentially rise. Part of that is because we think the global economy is bottoming and starting to grow.And in fact, China, thus far, has not been a big buyer of oil. I think the biggest issue is that, here in the US, we've been selling oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. And so there is this, if you will, a game being played between the oil producers and the US as it relates to oil price.But again, I think if we see the US not entering a recession, if the recession in Europe is fairly shallow as we expect, then we do expect that demand will increase. And as this ESG or environmental kind of focus on the green world continues, obviously, this transition period is going to be very long.Carbon, unfortunately, energy are going to continue to be a big part and a source of energy for the world's economy. And so we think that energy prices will be higher than expected. And what that's going to lead to is particularly, in the case of the Fed, that's going to lead to higher inflation rates.And we saw this in the PPI numbers today. We think that it will continue. And so I think investors, on the one hand, they're seeing inflation rates come down pretty quickly. And that's the good sign. But I think it's going to be a little stickier than people expect.And that's probably the one, if you will risk, that we see out there. And again, as oil prices remain high or at least these levels or higher, obviously, that, as I mentioned earlier, is a tax on the average consumer or producer. And so that's something we need to watch out for. And it may mean that rates around the world will remain higher than expected, because of that situation.AKIKO FUJITA: Yeah, that certainly adds to concerns about inflation reaccelerating. So when you're talking about where prices are likely to remain, I mean, the IEA says it could be-- it could go even higher in terms of demand this month. Is your base case here that they do remain elevated into year end?MARTIN SCHULZ: We do believe that they will remain elevated. Again, part of that has to do with the geopolitics and what happens with Saudi Arabia and Russia and some of the other swing producers right now. The problem is the US, for many years, was that swing producer.But right now, for several reasons, we are not that swing producer to the degree that we were once before in the last several 10-- some 10 years ago. And so for the near-term, we do expect that we will see elevated prices if these levels are higher.SEANA SMITH: Martin, when it comes to the US and the readings that we got on inflation this week, we got PPI, the producer price index, this morning coming in hotter than expected. And that contrasts to what we saw yesterday from CPI when, once again, we saw inflation pressures at least easing more than the Street had been looking for. What's your read on these two conflicting reports and what that tells us just about the Fed's long fight against inflation and the path forward?MARTIN SCHULZ: Yeah, you're basically highlighting a very interesting phenomena which is that interest rates are generally coming down much quicker than expected. But it's not a one-way direction, one-way street, so to speak. Obviously, post-COVID and the supply chain issues that we've had and some of the other machinations within the economy, we do think that inflation is coming down, but it will remain stickier than expected.And so in that vein, again, I think that the central banks-- I mean, you look at what's happening in the UK, the Bank of England either in Canada and in Australia, they're being much more careful about where they take interest rates based on some of these inflation numbers.So obviously, the risk is that higher rates will drive the global economy, or in this case, the US economy into a potential recession. But in the near-term, I think fighting inflation is going to be the number one task, and that's what they're focused on.AKIKO FUJITA: So in that debate, Martin, which camp are you in? Are you in the camp that expects a mild recession at least given how elevated rates are likely to remain?You know, at Federated Hermes, we were expecting a recession earlier in the year. And I think we've decided that because of where we are in the economic cycle and the monetary policy cycle and what we're seeing elsewhere, we do think that if we have a recession, it will be not-- it will be delayed until much later, probably late 2024. We'll see if that comes to fruition.But right now, the markets are telling us-- again, obviously at the end of the day, we are seeing some economic data that is very weak. But on the other hand, we're also seeing some other data, both economic as well as market-oriented, where we're seeing the market broadening out. And we're seeing a situation which we're getting so far away from this. And we could be in a very different situation.If you think about monetary policy in the past usually between 9 and 18 months, you saw some type of effect on the economy. It may be less pronounced now because of disintermediation. And it may be because the economy is just a post-COVID economy that is one that is growing, that is in a catch-up phase that will continue to move forward, unlike past cycles. And so we do expect that we'll see some slowdown next year, but probably not a recession at this point.SEANA SMITH: All right, optimistic tone here to end the conversation. Martin Schulz, always great to get your perspective, Federated Hermes, Head of International Equity Group, thanksMARTIN SCHULZ: Thank you.]

column4: Gas prices hit 2023 highs in California as Tropical Storm Hilary hammers state
column10: [Californians are seeing gas prices reach 2023 highs as Tropical Storm Hilary makes its way out of Southern California, leaving a trail of flooding, power outages, and other damage in its wake.The average price of gasoline rose $0.11 last week in the Golden State to $5.26 per gallon, the highest level of the year for the nation's most expensive state, according to AAA.Over the same period, prices rose $0.02 nationally to $3.87 per gallon, per AAA's data. According to the EIA, the price of a gallon of regular gas reached $3.96 nationally last week, the highest since October."We saw wholesale prices spike higher as sellers were unwilling to sell into a market that might see refiners threatened by power losses, or other issues," OPIS global head of energy analysis Tom Kloza told Yahoo Finance on Monday.California's gasoline is usually more expensive than the rest of the country because it is typically a special blend that is more expensive to produce. The state also imposes high taxes and fees associated with initiatives to reduce carbon emissions.The threat of power outages and flooding from Hilary's impact on the state also threatens California's refining and distribution systems, potentially pushing prices higher."If a refinery were to shut down in southern California due to flooding, I expect that wholesale prices would rise at least $0.20 per gallon and that would be passed on to the consumer in five to seven days," Andy Lipow of Lipow Oil Associates told Yahoo Finance."The news of a flooding event would also cause the consumer to drive into the nearest gas station and fill up, draining available supplies," he added.Gushing flood water and debris are seen during Tropical Storm Hilary, in Angeles National Forest, Calif., Aug. 20, 2023 in this screengrab from a handout video. (CALTRANS/Handout via REUTERS)Kloza is also on the lookout for a drop in demand as Hilary moves out of the area and the cleanup begins."All hurricanes destroy demand," he said. "Instinct tells me that what Californians pay this week may be the highest prices they pay in all of 2023 as demand is set to drop and there will be additional gasoline production in the last 75 days of the year."Story continuesNationally, prices are a bit harder to predict.Gas prices hit a 2023 high earlier this month, renewing concerns that US inflation will reverse its downward trend.The upward trend is largely due to the 15% jump in crude oil prices seen in July. West Texas Intermediate (CL=F) currently hovers above $81 per barrel."That $80 a barrel is really key area," Marketgauge.com chief strategist Michele Schneider recently told Yahoo Finance Live. "We have to continue really to watch what's happening with oil.""Where gasoline prices go over the next few weeks is going to depend more on the weather than anything else," said Lipow."By that I mean — will a hurricane come into the Gulf Coast and disrupt crude oil production and refinery operations? While gasoline prices have been steady the last few days, hurricane activity can spike prices $0.10 to $0.20," Lipow added.Ines Ferre is a senior business reporter for Yahoo Finance. Follow her on Twitter at @ines_ferre.Click here for the latest stock market news and in-depth analysis, including events that move stocksRead the latest financial and business news from Yahoo Finance]

column4: California gas prices rise above $5 a gallon
column10: [The average price for a gallon of gas in California rose to $5.26, up from $4.89 a month ago, but still lower than it was a year ago, according to AAA. Yahoo Finance Reporter Ines Ferre discusses the potential impact of Tropical Storm Hilary on gasoline prices in the state.Video TranscriptJULIE HYMAN: California gasoline prices are surging past $5 a gallon with no relief in sight. The average price per gallon now sits at $5.26, that's nearly $0.40 higher than a month ago. Yahoo Finance's Ines Ferre is here with the breakdown. So what's going on, Ines?INES FERRE: Yeah, Julie. And we know that Californians had for a while now been paying more for gas prices, compared to the national average. There's very high taxes and fees in California on gasoline. And also consumption of gasoline and diesel in California is pretty high as well.Just to give you an idea, one out of every 10 gallons of gasoline sold in the US is consumed in California. About one out of every 15 gallons of diesel sold in the US is consumed also in California. The concern, of course, is that with the tropical storm, once hurricane Hillary, that shows up in Southern California, that that could have a potential impact on local refining and distribution systems.Now, analysts don't expect that refineries in California would shut down because of the storm that passed throughout the weekend. But it could be impacted-- that there could be impacts by power outages and flooding conditions as well.So if a refinery were to shut down in Southern California because of, let's say, flooding, you'd see wholesale prices, according to Andy Lipow of Lipow Oil Associates, going up by about $0.20 per gallon. And the consumer would feel it in anywhere between five to seven days.On a national level, where gasoline prices go from here, well, that will a lot depend on the weather conditions. Of course, we are in the middle of hurricane season. And any activity that happens in the gulf and any refining capacity-- any refineries that are interrupted because of that hurricane activity can spike prices by anywhere between $0.10 and $0.20 a gallon, according to Lipow's estimates. By the way, Julie, right now, we're seeing, as you noted, the current national average for gasoline is at $3.87. It's only $0.03 away from what we saw around this time last year.JULIE HYMAN: Oh, interesting. Well, that's right. 390 versus 387 is not that big of a difference, but people have certain perceptions when it comes to gas prices for sure. Ines Ferre, thanks a lot. Appreciate it.]

column4: Oil prices to hit $91 by year-end, UBS says
column10: [Oil is poised to rally beyond $90 per barrel by the end of the year amid record demand and tightening supply, according to UBS strategists."We still see scope for global oil prices to rally,” said a recent UBS note to investors. “We now expect Brent to hit USD 95/bbl and the US WTI benchmark to rise to USD 91/bbl by end-December, up from the current USD 90/bbl and USD 85/bbl, respectively."Brent International (BZ=F) prices stand just below $85 per barrel, about 3% off year-to-date highs reached earlier in August. West Texas Intermediate (CL=F) is hovering above $80 per barrel.Concerns over China’s economy, the world’s second-largest consumer of crude, recently has put pressure on crude futures. Data released Tuesday by China's National Bureau of Statistics added to concerns of a sluggish recovery as Beijing unexpectedly cut policy rates and withheld information on youth unemployment."Some investors remain skeptical that China’s latest stimulus efforts—a 15- basis-point cut to its one-year medium-term lending facility (MLF) and a 10bps cut to the short-term 7-day reverse repo rate—will be sufficient to revive demand," the UBS note said. "China is the world’s largest oil importer, the second-largest consumer, and the seventh-largest producer."However, UBS strategists don’t expect the price slide to persist amid firming fundamentals. Those include declining inventories and tight supply as OPEC+ production nears a two year low.OPEC+ has been cutting production since October of last year. Saudi Arabia recently extended its one million barrel-per-day output reduction into September, while Russia announced it will slash oil exports.“We expect global oil demand to hit a record high in August,” the note said.A pump jack drills oil crude from the Yates Oilfield in West Texas’s Permian Basin, as a 1.5MW GE wind turbine from the Desert Sky Wind Farm is seen in the distance, near Iraan, Texas, U.S., March 17, 2023. (Bing Guan/REUTERS)Goldman Sachs analysts recently reaffirmed their forecast of $93 per barrel for Brent crude and $86 per barrel for WTI by December, highlighting the market is less "pessimistic" about the global economy.Story continuesInes Ferre is a senior business reporter for Yahoo Finance. Follow her on Twitter at @ines_ferre.Click here for the latest economic news and economic indicators to help you in your investing decisionsRead the latest financial and business news from Yahoo Finance]

column4: Oil prices: Three things to watch to find out where they may be headed next
column10: [Oil prices (CL=F, BZ=F) are starting to take a bit of a breather after a big run higher. AlphaSimplex Chief Research Strategist and Portfolio Manager Katy Kaminski tells Yahoo Finance Live that OPEC nations are trying to limit supply to prop up oil prices, but they are facing headwinds. Kaminski says there are three things to watch right now when it comes to oil prices. "Watch the consumer. Watch the strength of the dollar, because that's really going to be a headwind if it continues to recover, Kaminski said. Kaminski's third thing to watch is China and the weaker-than-expected data investors have been seeing.Video Transcript- Now to the commodities trade, which has definitely seen some inflows in recent weeks. Oil prices, chief among them. Though, they've seen a pullback of late now sitting around $80 a barrel after a seven week rally, the pressure comes amid that string of disappointing growth data in China. Katy Kaminski is still with us to do a deep dive on oil.You did mention a little bit about oil prices and we saw what had happened as a result. We saw this risk off trade with the latest China data. Is there now a question of demand destruction in play because of this?KATY KAMINSKI: So I would say that if you look at OPEC and the suppliers of oil, they're really focusing on trying to limit supply and get oil prices up for business. On the other hand, in recent period, you saw a stronger dollar, which was a headwind against their goal. And then now, you're seeing this data from China.And so if you looked at that graph of oil, what did you see? You saw a massive breakout, and then you saw it petering out a little bit. And so I think what we have to do is watch the consumer, watch the strength of the dollar because that's going to really be a headwind if it continues to recover, and third, if the China story continues its demand destruction going against the goal for having higher oil prices from suppliers.- So is was crude oil ripe for a breakout at this point?Story continuesKATY KAMINSKI: We had been really watching a positive trend. There had been a very strong technical signal on the upside for oil. You've seen a really massive recovery, and it looked like-- and most people were talking about, OK, it's the next leg up since 2022. And I was interested in this because oil is the first thing to watch when you think about inflation, because it's usually those raw materials that start the wave. And then after that starts, it kind of trickles into the rest of the economy.So that was a very interesting move for me. But then there was these headwinds with the dollar, and also just the China story that kind of murky the waters of whether or not we're really going to see that uptick.- Do you have concern about the elasticity of the consumer when it comes to oil?KATY KAMINSKI: Well, certainly. I mean, think about oil as such an important commodity for the US. I mean, it's something that is an input to so many different processes. It's a bottom line item for a lot of commuters. So it is really something if you're thinking about next wave of surprise and inflation. It's a good place to start looking.- And so additionally here, I mean, for the consumer that has looked across what they're paying for gas over the most recent years and known how much that's taken out of their pocket, it's been an additional kind of measure of the inflation that they feel in that pain at the pump as the administration had put it many times over. All that considered, does the consumer feel any better now as a result of oil or gas prices being lower at this point?KATY KAMINSKI: I would say, yes. I mean, anything that sort of alleviates some of the high costs that the consumer has taken on since last year, I think, is a pro. That's why we were concerned about oil prices going up because that could be sort of a catalyst into another wave. Because unfortunately, inflation doesn't just go away. It kind of goes in waves and it moves around. It's moving, and I was worried it was moving into oil.- Sure.- And speaking of catalysts, so one of the earlier predictions had been that demand from China would be a catalyst for crude. Is there still the potential for that demand to return or pick up from China?KATY KAMINSKI: Certainly. And I think if you look at oil prices earlier this year, they were pretty depressed and there was little movement. And I think a lot of that came from-- because you also had a weaker dollar, so you would have thought that would have helped, but came from that China demand, just not realizing.- And then just additionally here, Mizuho had been one of the upgrades that came through this morning on Chevron here. As we think about some of the oil and gas players that have been beneficiaries at least, over the course of 2022, and now, during 2023, still watching closely to see where there are additional inflows even after the year that was. You still have some firms that are saying that there's a benefit, even though oil mix has trended below long term 50% as talked about on their earnings call. What are some of the catalysts that could still move the oil and gas companies higher at this point?KATY KAMINSKI: Well, I mean, I think demand is obviously the first one. So we get demand back, particularly in China. If we continue to have a weaker dollar, that positions oil prices and our relative export prices competitively. So those are the first two things I would think about. And of course, how strong the consumer is in terms of general demand.- All right, Katy Kaminski, AlphaSimplex chief research strategist and portfolio manager. It's great to have you here with us in studio today.Thanks]

column4: China: U.S. economy an 'overpowering influence' on oil prices, analyst says
column10: [China's latest economic prints have pointed to slowing growth, especially in the nation's industrial sector. Could China's slowdown begin to hang over oil demand and prices?"The Chinese economy has been sputtering without doubt, we have had months of disappointing weak, macroeconomic data," Vanda Insights Founder Vandana Hari tells Yahoo Finance Live. "Something that has bucked the trend has been Chinese crude imports, the refining rates of the country, and ... end-user consumption, all of which has been quite healthy."Hari examines China's trade relationship with Russia over the latter's crude oil reserves, as well as the United States' energy outlook following OPEC+ production cuts and alternative commodity markets to invest in.Video TranscriptJULIE HYMAN: More weak data out of China weighing on oil markets as investors fear a slowing in demand. The world's second largest economy saw retail sales rise by a modest 2 and 1/2% compared to the prior year. Industrial production rose by just 3.7%, both of those prints coming in below economists' estimates.Ahead of these data releases, China's central bank cut a set of key interest rates in a bid to spur growth. Joining us now is Vandana Hari, who is Vanda Insights Founder. It is good to see you. So as we look at China and as it relates to oil here, how much of a headwind is the slow in growth there going to be for oil prices?VANDANA HARI: Good morning, Julie. So Chinese economy has been sputtering without doubt. We have had months of disappointing, weak macroeconomic data. Something that has bucked that trend has been Chinese crude imports, which-- and the refining rates of the country and consumption-- end-user consumption, all of which has been quite healthy.Mind you, it is-- it does come off a comparative low base of last year but relatively healthy. But if you look at everything else on the macroeconomic front, whether it be their exports, their industrial production, manufacturing activity, deflationary pressures, all of that is just big bad news in bold letters.Story continuesIt hasn't really weighed on crude prices as much as one would have expected because the major counterforce has been right there in your country. Since the start of July, we've seen quite an upturn in sentiment with regard to the US economy. And that has overpowered-- that's been an overpowering influence in crude. But looks like prices have hit the skids today. So it might be that the Chinese pessimism is coming home to roost, finally.BRAD SMITH: What are we still to extrapolate from the relationship that ensued post Russia invasion of Ukraine and the China-Russia relationship that had ensued there? Where does that stand right there? And how are investors best to continue evaluating that?VANDANA HARI: The entire scheme of things with regard to Russia, the Western sanctions, the embargoes on Russian oil has unleashed an unprecedented rewiring of trade globally. And, you know, in-- within that, again, we've seen China and India step up as major crude buyers of-- form Russia. And, of course, all of that crude has moved away from the European markets. So within that, you know, China and Russia were always-- were close-- geopolitically close and trade-wise as well. Of course, they share a major boundary between them.So there's not just by sea but pipeline imports of gas and crude from Russia as well. They do a fair amount of trade in their currencies as well, ruble and yuan, instead of the US dollar. So I guess it was just-- it was not surprising that the two countries have gotten even closer after the sanctions. And look, at the end of the day, for countries like China and India, if they're getting cheaper crude, especially in a high-price environment like we saw last year-- and even this year's prices are relatively high for these price-sensitive countries-- you know, they're just going to buy the Russian-- all the Russian crude and oil that they can get their hands on.JULIE HYMAN: So when we look at the trajectory of prices globally, do you think that we will-- you know, despite the pause that we're seeing today, do you think we'll continue to move higher given the US demand, given the Saudi production cuts, for example? Is the path still going to be upward?VANDANA HARI: So, Julie, there are definitely price-supportive factors. As I mentioned, as long as the optimism over a soft landing in the US survives or is alive, I think that is-- remains a major supporter factor for crude price sentiment after all, you know, the biggest economy and the biggest oil consumer as well, the US. And, of course, the OPEC+ cuts. I think those two are major supportive factors.However, I think in the last few weeks, as we've seen crude head towards, you know, seven-month highs for Brent, nine-month highs for WTI prices, I think they have heavily discounted not just the economic sluggishness in China, but the downturn in Europe as well. So I did not expect and I still do not expect crude to have much of an upside from current prices. At the same time, I don't see a very major downward pressure either, as long as-- well, OPEC+ cuts will remain.I think they are quite determined to make sure that they tighten the market, that they see inventories going down through the second half of the year. I think that the real tipping point here might be if we see anything happening that changes the sentiment, the level of sanguinity and optimism that we have in the markets right now with regard to the US. That could be a major downward pressure on crude. But all said, I don't see any reason for it to go much higher from here or much lower.BRAD SMITH: We've seen continued repricing of expectations to come out of China for this year, the latest one coming this morning from Goldman. And so for investors that are trying to best figure out where everything from crude prices to commodities that are impacted to even some of the equity market players that have the largest revenue base exposure within China are thinking about this, from your perspective, what, if any, pivot is apt to be able to be making right now in this environment?VANDANA HARI: Yeah, that's a big question, Brad. So in this part of the world, of course, Indian markets have been doing phenomenally well. I think the Indian economy is running full steam. And, you know, that's a good place to invest.China, unfortunately, I think, is going to take a long time to recover and, certainly, to regain the pre-COVID momentum that the economy had. A lot of the problems that we are seeing in China today-- of course, some of them have been exacerbated by the unprecedented nearly three years of strict no-- zero-COVID policy and lockdowns. But a lot of them pre-date COVID. The property market, for instance, is-- you know, these are very systemic, structural problems that are going to take a long time.You might see headlines, you know, analysts saying routinely that whatever little stimulus that is coming, fiscal or monetary, you know, in dribs and drabs is just not enough. And, you know, I subscribe to that as well. The government is being very careful not to overstimulate-- not to add more debt to the economy because that is already a problem. And that was already a problem in China, unfortunately, even before COVID. So it's going to be a very, very slow uphill climb for the Chinese market and the Chinese economy.JULIE HYMAN: Vandana Hari, it's always good to get your insights on these topics when it comes to the oil market. Really appreciate it, especially at-- after 10:00 PM in Singapore, I believe. Vanda Insights Founder. Thanks again. Really appreciate your time.]

column4: Oil prices slip as concerns about China's economic recovery grow
column10: [Oil prices (CL=F) are falling after seven weeks of gains, partly due to the China's slower-than-expected recovery from its pandemic shutdown. Blue Line Futures President Bill Baruch tells Yahoo Finance Live that China is continuing to import crude at near-record levels. "I think that if China picks up a bit, then this is some of the worst news being priced in," Baruch said.Video Transcript- Concern over China's economic recovery pressuring oil prices. Today we had crude pulling back after recording seven straight weeks of gains. Despite today's pressure, though, oil is still holding above 80 bucks a barrel and demand expected to remain at high levels for the rest of the year.So where are prices headed? We want to bring in Bill Baruch, President of Blue Line Futures. Bill, it's good to see you again. So here we are, just above 82 bucks a barrel. Lots of forecasts out there about rising demand. The fact that it's not going to stop anytime soon, at least for the next several months. What does that mean for crude prices?BILL BARUCH: You know, they're hanging up pretty good. I think the real underpinning right now is first Saudi Arabia and Russia, they've come through and cut production. They continue to at least do that for at least another month or two from this sort of secondary cut.Data at the end of last week also showed that Russia did cut another 50,000 barrels per day. And that got them in line with where they're supposed to be producing. There was a lot of fear that Russia was going to be overproducing. And although China's weakness is front and center, the Chinese Yuan weakening because of that, it's really weighing on the metals complex.It's weighing on energy too, but the thing is China continues to import crude at near-record levels. So they're-- despite the weakness, despite the slowing growth, they are there right now. I think the fear would be if we continue to see weaker and weaker growth, that would taper off. However, I'm on the other side of that trade and I think that China picks up a bit and this is some of the worst news being priced in.Story continues- Yeah. I mean, Bill, having said that, what do you make of the reaction to some of the news that we've gotten from China on the economic front? I mean, it was just last week, we heard from the IEA saying that China's demand has surprised to the upside, and yet there seems to be this constant concern that kind of percolates into the oil markets, about how strong that recovery looks like.BILL BARUCH: Yeah. I mean, that's why we had oil markets at near multi-month highs and setting near multi-month highs. 83 bucks was really an upside target for us, that now we're going to see the market consolidate a bit. And I think tonight's deluge of economic data is going to be crucial.We have fixed asset investment. What we need to see, though, is really some stimulus to help get them off the ground. And I think we could be close to hearing something. Obviously the hanging property fears, country garden, the news, again, from them was weighing on sentiment coming into the US hours.So there's a lot of things here that are boiling. But at the end of the day, the best and most simple way to look at it-- at what all this means is the Chinese Yuan and the CME group has a Chinese Yuan contract. It's the USD/CNH. So it shows the-- as it rises, it's melting higher right now. It means the dollar is strengthening against the Chinese Yuan or the renminbi.And it's back at levels-- going back into the early or late part of 2022, was it? Yeah. And that was-- that's basically them exporting deflation. If they're exporting deflation-- I mean, ultimately their currency purchases less commodities.And crude's been able to muscle through things because the US growth has remained steady. And the demand from China remains steady. But the metals complex has been pretty ugly because of it.- Bill, what's your outlook for US production? We just had Rick talking about that just a moment ago. We have certainly seen a recovery. Obviously, oil producers want to capitalize on the rise that we have seen in crude prices. But what do you think that future growth-- how much growth could we see within that?BILL BARUCH: Yeah. I think right now, we're starting to see the production pick back up. You got to think about it from the producer standpoint that multiple times in the last couple of decades, as we see production pick up-- you know, the prices go higher, production comes back online and it races back online.I think right now is a unique position where you have Saudi Arabia pulling back production. You have Russia in the situation that they're in and actually following through with some cuts, although there's more probably in the supply.But you know, right now, I think the fact that it is unique position where prices have come off, they've consolidated very well and I mean, maybe these energy companies could really, really hedge pretty well. But they're able to produce here at these levels and really not disrupt the price because of what OPEC's done and trying to be a bit under the price ultimately.So I think here you're getting-- the Permian has been producing quite a bit more, if you go through some of these earnings reports from these companies like Chevron is producing the Permian at their highest level. So I like to look at it as some opportunity for these companies and investing companies that have low-cost Permian assets or good margins in the Permian.Because that's where the production is going to come from. But also at the end of the day, the entire space has seen tremendous underinvestment. And that's what's going to be the longest driver-- steadfast driver in higher prices.Because there hasn't been much investment and your prior segment you're talking about, and the Biden administration not really being able to talk about the production coming back online because it's sort of against a lot of the narratives they've discussed.But really, the production because of those narratives is we've seen the underinvestment and that's what's going to underpin prices. And if we get steady flows from the Permian and other places here from these companies, I think it's not going to disrupt price. That's where I really like a lot of these energy stocks right now.- Bill, you know, that raises the concern what this all means for these energy companies, particularly big oil names for their trajectory moving forward. I mean, we're talking about where oil prices are. But as you said that the long-term trend is underinvestment.You know, ExxonMobil themselves have talked about sort of low carbon being a big driver in the future. I mean, how do you look at that side of the investment? It feels like that was more front and center last year in terms of conversation, but those investments are continuing in the back.BILL BARUCH: Well, last year was a reality shock. When Russia invaded Ukraine, it really was a reality shock that energy runs the world. It really does. If you look at every product from lip gloss to keychains, just different things that you see around. The plastics-- I mean, shoes, bottom-- you know, soles of your shoes, everything is coming from petroleum.So-- and I think that it became a big reminder in how important petroleum-- is not only in producing the products, but heating your home, going from place to place and fuel. I think that was a reality check. And the fact that how quickly those costs drove higher, everybody realized it's an inflation problem if there's this much underinvestment and the world is not ready to move away from it.So I think, again, that was a reality check where we came into this year or came from last year coming into this year. And now, you're starting to see production come back online. There's incentives for some production come back online. But again, coming back to a lot of these companies, if you look at a lot of these-- if you sift through the earnings reports, one of the themes was the revenues down.But these companies were beating earnings, though the revenues down because of the price of oil. Now if the price of oil goes higher, I mean, these companies-- the margins are going to increase. The free cash flow is there. It's going to increase. I think these companies have put themselves in a tremendous spot. And they're not just flooding the market with oil. They're bringing it back.And then that really brings me to the resource life of these assets that they're drilling. I mean, the resource life has basically been halved. You go back the last 10-15 years. So they're getting less oil. Ultimately, there's going to be less lifetime in these and they're going to have to find other ways to get it. So it just keeps the-- it's going to keep the entire landscape very tight for I think, for the foreseeable future.All right, Bill Baruch. We have to leave it there. President of Blue Line Futures. Thanks so much.]

column4: Gas prices: What rising fuel costs could mean for President Biden's inflation plan
column10: [The national average for U.S. gas prices has risen by $0.28 to $3.85 since the month of July. Yahoo Finance Senior Columnist Rick Newman breaks down what this could mean for President Biden's economic plans as U.S. oil production nears record highs while the Biden administration attempts to keep promises on energy consumption and clean energy adoption.Video Transcript[MUSIC PLAYING]AKIKO FUJITA: Crude oil prices have steadied today after rising for seven straight weeks, pushing gas prices higher. Much of that's been dictated by global demand, but those higher prices are putting pressure on the Biden administration at a time when inflation is starting to cool down. Yahoo Finance's Rick Newman has more. And Rick, there are questions about how this could all play out if things reaccelerate in inflation.RICK NEWMAN: I think the Biden administration has to get very nervous when they see gas prices approaching $4 a gallon. And I think gasoline prices punch above their weight in terms of consumer psyches. And I think it actually makes a lot of difference what that first number is on the price. If it's a 3, it's probably OK, even if it's in the high 3's, as it is now, around 385. If it's a 4, I think it's very bad, even if it's 401. And of course, it got all the way up to a little bit over $5 on average last summer.So the problem with Biden is that he's really struggling in terms of voters' attitudes toward his handling of the economy, and that probably is largely because of inflation. And among inflation, gasoline is the price that consumers-- it's more visible to consumers than anything else. So I think Biden has to be worried about this.There's a really interesting irony here, Akiko, which is that the Energy Information Administration, the EIA, said recently, they think US domestic crude oil production is going to hit a new record high by the end of this year or by sometime next year. And we are already at record levels of natural gas production. So the two biggest fossil fuels, oil and natural gas, the US is either at record high levels of production or perhaps about to get there.And the problem for Biden is, he can't really just come out and say this. He can't come out and brag and say, hey, we've had more drilling under me than even under President Trump. Because, of course, he's trying to appeal to environmentalists and he's pushing hard for the green energy shift, and he's got this huge jack or the one anniversary of this huge bill from last year that established all these green energy subsidies. So Biden has gotten the additional domestic oil that he was hoping for around this time last year. I just don't think he's going to get any credit for it.AKIKO FUJITA: It's a tricky message he's had to navigate, we should say, over the course of his presidency, trying to really-- seeing the both sides or at least seeing the positives on both ends, depending on which side you're trying to appeal to. Rick Newman, as always, thanks so much for that.]

column4: Oil takes breather after seven week rally
column10: [Crude prices dipped by less than 1% on Monday following a seven-week rally.Concerns over China’s lackluster economic growth and a rising dollar put pressure on oil. West Texas Intermediate (CL=F) futures settled at $82.51 per barrel while Brent International (BZ=F) closed at $86.21.The pullback is minor compared to oil’s recent moves. WTI and Brent futures are each up by about $15 per barrel since June 14.Output cuts by the world’s largest oil producers have kept a floor on prices as supplies tighten. Oil deficits are currently estimated at about 2 million barrels per day this quarter, according to Bloomberg data."Deepening OPEC+ supply cuts have collided with improved macroeconomic sentiment and all-time high world oil demand," read a recent report by the International Energy Agency."World oil demand is scaling record highs," said the report.Oil, miniatures of oil barrels and U.S. dollar banknote are seen in this illustration taken, June 6, 2023. REUTERS/Dado Ruvic/Illustration"Oil dropped dramatically from over $80 to as low as $67 when the regional banking crisis hit, based on fears that it would trigger a recession. Oil has recovered as it has become clear that there is no imminent recession," Jay Hatfield, CEO at Infrastructure Capital Management in New York, said in an email to Yahoo Finance.Goldman Sachs analysts recently reaffirmed their forecast of $93 per barrel for Brent crude and $86 per barrel for WTI by December, highlighting the market is less "pessimistic" about the global economy.Energy-related stocks have been on an upward trend in the last two months. The S&P 500's Energy Select ETF (XLE) is up more than 2% year to date. The sector had been negative earlier this year amid recession concerns and a lagging economic recovery in China post COVID lockdowns."Right now, the world is ignoring the economic collapse in China and focusing on the economic recovery in the West," Louis Navellier of Navellier Capital Investments said in a recent note to investors."Seasonal demand for crude oil is expected to peak around Labor Day, so I will be monitoring inventories very carefully. If crude oil inventories remain low, it will be safe to continue to hold many refineries and integrated oil companies," he added.Story continuesInes Ferre is a senior business reporter for Yahoo Finance. Follow her on Twitter at @ines_ferre.Click here for the latest stock market news and in-depth analysis, including events that move stocksRead the latest financial and business news from Yahoo Finance]

column4: Why oil prices need to shoot back above $100 per barrel
column10: [Oil prices have consistently ebbed and flowed above $80 a barrel in 2023. Smead Capital Management CEO Cole Smead believes it to be necessary for oil prices to rise above $100 for countries like the U.S. to fill the producer void left by China's economic troubles."We have to because this is a growing economy and barrels per day are growing, but as I pointed out... it is just not dominated by China like it was," Smead says. "The Western world's continued to grow despite all these difficulties in rates and the inflation headwinds and so on and so forth."Smead outlines American producers' potential to bring supply to the table as oil demand remains high.Video Transcript- A crude awakening. Oil prices ticking slightly lower this morning as supply concerns ease on hopes Iraqi supports will resume-- exports will resume. Excuse me. China's rocket recovery is still seen as the main driver of crude. Investors remain concerned over demand from the world's top importer.Cole Smead is still here with us. Cole, despite the possible easing of tighter oil supplies, you're optimistic on the oil outlook. Explain that to us. Walk us through your thesis there.COLE SMEAD: Yeah, so China used to be the tail that wags the dog. What China did sent marginal commodity prices higher or lower, including in oil. And what you're seeing is just the worst news out of China. And if you don't think it's bad, It's really bad, the news coming out of China.And yet, while this news is becoming greater and more precipitous and we're hearing about more defaults, delayed payments from financial institutions over there, you're watching oil stay tight or marginally climb over the last 60 days. So I think that really tells a different story.It's not about China's demand. It's about the tightness of supply. The tightness of supply being that if you look at the futures market right now, you'll find that the futures curve is terribly backwardated, which means that no new supply is going to grow in the next three, four years because no one gets compensated to go out and take that risk and hedge it in advance.Story continuesSo I think that's the continued trend we're seeing is just really tight supply. And therefore, as any demand goes on, prices have to edge up or stay firm because there's no one that can produce a new barrel or supply.- And Cole, in your estimation what is sort of the new threshold that oil would need to get to to make supply more attractive for the producers who have been cutting back to start producing more?COLE SMEAD: No one asks me that question or asks that. That's a great question. The answer is a minimum $100 a barrel. A minimum of $100.- And do you see it getting there any time soon?COLE SMEAD: We have to because this is a growing economy and barrels per day are growing. But as I pointed out a second ago, it's just not dominated by China like it was.So you look at the Western world. The Western world's continued to grow despite all these difficulties and rates and all these inflation headwinds and so on and so forth. So we really look at it as it's $100 a minimum, that you have to do that.And where you're going to get production first is from people who are already producing. Where they look and say, you know what, it's profitable to go out and poke that hole in that field that we were maybe waiting longer to do and now we're going to step up that investment.Now, where do you get a lot of big projects coming online at a later date, you're going to find those above $120 a barrel. But the rationality of the market-- people used to say that oil people will never get religion. They'll never come to know Jesus. They'll never quit drilling. Well, that's just not true.They quit drilling. And to watch an administration that loves renewables begging oil people to drill, it's just the oddest thing I've ever heard of. It's like stranger than fiction which means you know it's true. So I think those are the dynamics really at play in that market.And one other thing I'll add, it's got to come by Americans and Canadians because the Europeans, it's socially unacceptable to get oil and gas out of their ground even though they have those resources. So we're going to see this OPEC+, Canada, US, and parts of LATAM. That's the suppliers of oil globally.- Real quick before we let you go, Cole. How do you play this thesis on oil? Do you buy oil itself or do you buy oil producers or where in the stack do you do you buy?COLE SMEAD: We like the producers because they've just been really left for dead, and that's where the best money was made. The servicers weren't the better place to make money. So I would say, you're looking for what they call torque. You're looking for places where a $5 barrel increase of oil gives you a lot of operating leverage and really grows the free cash flow of the business.So you don't want to go by the majors, generally speaking, because they don't provide a lot of torque. Go look for names that have been more affected by things like gas. We own Ovintiv. They have a higher gas mix. Apache would be another name that I would throw out to people in that space.And if you go look in Canada, the MEG Energies of Canada and the Cenovuses that get WCS. A $5 increase in WTI directly affects Western Canada Select blend as well. So you'll see the Canadians will really punch their weight as we move forward here because they have more torque than a lot of the American players as well.- Cole, Thanks for spending some time with us this morning. If you go back to Seattle, you can get the fish seasoning for Brad, but I'll probably be there first so--- As long as somebody picks it up--COLE SMEAD: Thank you.- --for me, we're good.- Thanks, Cole.COLE SMEAD: I missed Top Pot Doughnuts. That's what I need is a Top Pot doughnut so--- I don't know that those will make it back with me. Cole Smead, Smead Capital Management CEO. Thank you so much. Appreciate it.]

column4: Gas prices hit 2023 highs in California as Tropical Storm Hilary hammers state
column10: [Californians are seeing gas prices reach 2023 highs as Tropical Storm Hilary makes its way out of Southern California, leaving a trail of flooding, power outages, and other damage in its wake.The average price of gasoline rose $0.11 last week in the Golden State to $5.26 per gallon, the highest level of the year for the nation's most expensive state, according to AAA.Over the same period, prices rose $0.02 nationally to $3.87 per gallon, per AAA's data. According to the EIA, the price of a gallon of regular gas reached $3.96 nationally last week, the highest since October."We saw wholesale prices spike higher as sellers were unwilling to sell into a market that might see refiners threatened by power losses, or other issues," OPIS global head of energy analysis Tom Kloza told Yahoo Finance on Monday.California's gasoline is usually more expensive than the rest of the country because it is typically a special blend that is more expensive to produce. The state also imposes high taxes and fees associated with initiatives to reduce carbon emissions.The threat of power outages and flooding from Hilary's impact on the state also threatens California's refining and distribution systems, potentially pushing prices higher."If a refinery were to shut down in southern California due to flooding, I expect that wholesale prices would rise at least $0.20 per gallon and that would be passed on to the consumer in five to seven days," Andy Lipow of Lipow Oil Associates told Yahoo Finance."The news of a flooding event would also cause the consumer to drive into the nearest gas station and fill up, draining available supplies," he added.Gushing flood water and debris are seen during Tropical Storm Hilary, in Angeles National Forest, Calif., Aug. 20, 2023 in this screengrab from a handout video. (CALTRANS/Handout via REUTERS)Kloza is also on the lookout for a drop in demand as Hilary moves out of the area and the cleanup begins."All hurricanes destroy demand," he said. "Instinct tells me that what Californians pay this week may be the highest prices they pay in all of 2023 as demand is set to drop and there will be additional gasoline production in the last 75 days of the year."Story continuesNationally, prices are a bit harder to predict.Gas prices hit a 2023 high earlier this month, renewing concerns that US inflation will reverse its downward trend.The upward trend is largely due to the 15% jump in crude oil prices seen in July. West Texas Intermediate (CL=F) currently hovers above $81 per barrel."That $80 a barrel is really key area," Marketgauge.com chief strategist Michele Schneider recently told Yahoo Finance Live. "We have to continue really to watch what's happening with oil.""Where gasoline prices go over the next few weeks is going to depend more on the weather than anything else," said Lipow."By that I mean — will a hurricane come into the Gulf Coast and disrupt crude oil production and refinery operations? While gasoline prices have been steady the last few days, hurricane activity can spike prices $0.10 to $0.20," Lipow added.Ines Ferre is a senior business reporter for Yahoo Finance. Follow her on Twitter at @ines_ferre.Click here for the latest stock market news and in-depth analysis, including events that move stocksRead the latest financial and business news from Yahoo Finance]

column4: California gas prices rise above $5 a gallon
column10: [The average price for a gallon of gas in California rose to $5.26, up from $4.89 a month ago, but still lower than it was a year ago, according to AAA. Yahoo Finance Reporter Ines Ferre discusses the potential impact of Tropical Storm Hilary on gasoline prices in the state.Video TranscriptJULIE HYMAN: California gasoline prices are surging past $5 a gallon with no relief in sight. The average price per gallon now sits at $5.26, that's nearly $0.40 higher than a month ago. Yahoo Finance's Ines Ferre is here with the breakdown. So what's going on, Ines?INES FERRE: Yeah, Julie. And we know that Californians had for a while now been paying more for gas prices, compared to the national average. There's very high taxes and fees in California on gasoline. And also consumption of gasoline and diesel in California is pretty high as well.Just to give you an idea, one out of every 10 gallons of gasoline sold in the US is consumed in California. About one out of every 15 gallons of diesel sold in the US is consumed also in California. The concern, of course, is that with the tropical storm, once hurricane Hillary, that shows up in Southern California, that that could have a potential impact on local refining and distribution systems.Now, analysts don't expect that refineries in California would shut down because of the storm that passed throughout the weekend. But it could be impacted-- that there could be impacts by power outages and flooding conditions as well.So if a refinery were to shut down in Southern California because of, let's say, flooding, you'd see wholesale prices, according to Andy Lipow of Lipow Oil Associates, going up by about $0.20 per gallon. And the consumer would feel it in anywhere between five to seven days.On a national level, where gasoline prices go from here, well, that will a lot depend on the weather conditions. Of course, we are in the middle of hurricane season. And any activity that happens in the gulf and any refining capacity-- any refineries that are interrupted because of that hurricane activity can spike prices by anywhere between $0.10 and $0.20 a gallon, according to Lipow's estimates. By the way, Julie, right now, we're seeing, as you noted, the current national average for gasoline is at $3.87. It's only $0.03 away from what we saw around this time last year.JULIE HYMAN: Oh, interesting. Well, that's right. 390 versus 387 is not that big of a difference, but people have certain perceptions when it comes to gas prices for sure. Ines Ferre, thanks a lot. Appreciate it.]

column4: Oil prices to hit $91 by year-end, UBS says
column10: [Oil is poised to rally beyond $90 per barrel by the end of the year amid record demand and tightening supply, according to UBS strategists."We still see scope for global oil prices to rally,” said a recent UBS note to investors. “We now expect Brent to hit USD 95/bbl and the US WTI benchmark to rise to USD 91/bbl by end-December, up from the current USD 90/bbl and USD 85/bbl, respectively."Brent International (BZ=F) prices stand just below $85 per barrel, about 3% off year-to-date highs reached earlier in August. West Texas Intermediate (CL=F) is hovering above $80 per barrel.Concerns over China’s economy, the world’s second-largest consumer of crude, recently has put pressure on crude futures. Data released Tuesday by China's National Bureau of Statistics added to concerns of a sluggish recovery as Beijing unexpectedly cut policy rates and withheld information on youth unemployment."Some investors remain skeptical that China’s latest stimulus efforts—a 15- basis-point cut to its one-year medium-term lending facility (MLF) and a 10bps cut to the short-term 7-day reverse repo rate—will be sufficient to revive demand," the UBS note said. "China is the world’s largest oil importer, the second-largest consumer, and the seventh-largest producer."However, UBS strategists don’t expect the price slide to persist amid firming fundamentals. Those include declining inventories and tight supply as OPEC+ production nears a two year low.OPEC+ has been cutting production since October of last year. Saudi Arabia recently extended its one million barrel-per-day output reduction into September, while Russia announced it will slash oil exports.“We expect global oil demand to hit a record high in August,” the note said.A pump jack drills oil crude from the Yates Oilfield in West Texas’s Permian Basin, as a 1.5MW GE wind turbine from the Desert Sky Wind Farm is seen in the distance, near Iraan, Texas, U.S., March 17, 2023. (Bing Guan/REUTERS)Goldman Sachs analysts recently reaffirmed their forecast of $93 per barrel for Brent crude and $86 per barrel for WTI by December, highlighting the market is less "pessimistic" about the global economy.Story continuesInes Ferre is a senior business reporter for Yahoo Finance. Follow her on Twitter at @ines_ferre.Click here for the latest economic news and economic indicators to help you in your investing decisionsRead the latest financial and business news from Yahoo Finance]

column4: Oil prices: Three things to watch to find out where they may be headed next
column10: [Oil prices (CL=F, BZ=F) are starting to take a bit of a breather after a big run higher. AlphaSimplex Chief Research Strategist and Portfolio Manager Katy Kaminski tells Yahoo Finance Live that OPEC nations are trying to limit supply to prop up oil prices, but they are facing headwinds. Kaminski says there are three things to watch right now when it comes to oil prices. "Watch the consumer. Watch the strength of the dollar, because that's really going to be a headwind if it continues to recover, Kaminski said. Kaminski's third thing to watch is China and the weaker-than-expected data investors have been seeing.Video Transcript- Now to the commodities trade, which has definitely seen some inflows in recent weeks. Oil prices, chief among them. Though, they've seen a pullback of late now sitting around $80 a barrel after a seven week rally, the pressure comes amid that string of disappointing growth data in China. Katy Kaminski is still with us to do a deep dive on oil.You did mention a little bit about oil prices and we saw what had happened as a result. We saw this risk off trade with the latest China data. Is there now a question of demand destruction in play because of this?KATY KAMINSKI: So I would say that if you look at OPEC and the suppliers of oil, they're really focusing on trying to limit supply and get oil prices up for business. On the other hand, in recent period, you saw a stronger dollar, which was a headwind against their goal. And then now, you're seeing this data from China.And so if you looked at that graph of oil, what did you see? You saw a massive breakout, and then you saw it petering out a little bit. And so I think what we have to do is watch the consumer, watch the strength of the dollar because that's going to really be a headwind if it continues to recover, and third, if the China story continues its demand destruction going against the goal for having higher oil prices from suppliers.- So is was crude oil ripe for a breakout at this point?Story continuesKATY KAMINSKI: We had been really watching a positive trend. There had been a very strong technical signal on the upside for oil. You've seen a really massive recovery, and it looked like-- and most people were talking about, OK, it's the next leg up since 2022. And I was interested in this because oil is the first thing to watch when you think about inflation, because it's usually those raw materials that start the wave. And then after that starts, it kind of trickles into the rest of the economy.So that was a very interesting move for me. But then there was these headwinds with the dollar, and also just the China story that kind of murky the waters of whether or not we're really going to see that uptick.- Do you have concern about the elasticity of the consumer when it comes to oil?KATY KAMINSKI: Well, certainly. I mean, think about oil as such an important commodity for the US. I mean, it's something that is an input to so many different processes. It's a bottom line item for a lot of commuters. So it is really something if you're thinking about next wave of surprise and inflation. It's a good place to start looking.- And so additionally here, I mean, for the consumer that has looked across what they're paying for gas over the most recent years and known how much that's taken out of their pocket, it's been an additional kind of measure of the inflation that they feel in that pain at the pump as the administration had put it many times over. All that considered, does the consumer feel any better now as a result of oil or gas prices being lower at this point?KATY KAMINSKI: I would say, yes. I mean, anything that sort of alleviates some of the high costs that the consumer has taken on since last year, I think, is a pro. That's why we were concerned about oil prices going up because that could be sort of a catalyst into another wave. Because unfortunately, inflation doesn't just go away. It kind of goes in waves and it moves around. It's moving, and I was worried it was moving into oil.- Sure.- And speaking of catalysts, so one of the earlier predictions had been that demand from China would be a catalyst for crude. Is there still the potential for that demand to return or pick up from China?KATY KAMINSKI: Certainly. And I think if you look at oil prices earlier this year, they were pretty depressed and there was little movement. And I think a lot of that came from-- because you also had a weaker dollar, so you would have thought that would have helped, but came from that China demand, just not realizing.- And then just additionally here, Mizuho had been one of the upgrades that came through this morning on Chevron here. As we think about some of the oil and gas players that have been beneficiaries at least, over the course of 2022, and now, during 2023, still watching closely to see where there are additional inflows even after the year that was. You still have some firms that are saying that there's a benefit, even though oil mix has trended below long term 50% as talked about on their earnings call. What are some of the catalysts that could still move the oil and gas companies higher at this point?KATY KAMINSKI: Well, I mean, I think demand is obviously the first one. So we get demand back, particularly in China. If we continue to have a weaker dollar, that positions oil prices and our relative export prices competitively. So those are the first two things I would think about. And of course, how strong the consumer is in terms of general demand.- All right, Katy Kaminski, AlphaSimplex chief research strategist and portfolio manager. It's great to have you here with us in studio today.Thanks]

column4: China: U.S. economy an 'overpowering influence' on oil prices, analyst says
column10: [China's latest economic prints have pointed to slowing growth, especially in the nation's industrial sector. Could China's slowdown begin to hang over oil demand and prices?"The Chinese economy has been sputtering without doubt, we have had months of disappointing weak, macroeconomic data," Vanda Insights Founder Vandana Hari tells Yahoo Finance Live. "Something that has bucked the trend has been Chinese crude imports, the refining rates of the country, and ... end-user consumption, all of which has been quite healthy."Hari examines China's trade relationship with Russia over the latter's crude oil reserves, as well as the United States' energy outlook following OPEC+ production cuts and alternative commodity markets to invest in.Video TranscriptJULIE HYMAN: More weak data out of China weighing on oil markets as investors fear a slowing in demand. The world's second largest economy saw retail sales rise by a modest 2 and 1/2% compared to the prior year. Industrial production rose by just 3.7%, both of those prints coming in below economists' estimates.Ahead of these data releases, China's central bank cut a set of key interest rates in a bid to spur growth. Joining us now is Vandana Hari, who is Vanda Insights Founder. It is good to see you. So as we look at China and as it relates to oil here, how much of a headwind is the slow in growth there going to be for oil prices?VANDANA HARI: Good morning, Julie. So Chinese economy has been sputtering without doubt. We have had months of disappointing, weak macroeconomic data. Something that has bucked that trend has been Chinese crude imports, which-- and the refining rates of the country and consumption-- end-user consumption, all of which has been quite healthy.Mind you, it is-- it does come off a comparative low base of last year but relatively healthy. But if you look at everything else on the macroeconomic front, whether it be their exports, their industrial production, manufacturing activity, deflationary pressures, all of that is just big bad news in bold letters.Story continuesIt hasn't really weighed on crude prices as much as one would have expected because the major counterforce has been right there in your country. Since the start of July, we've seen quite an upturn in sentiment with regard to the US economy. And that has overpowered-- that's been an overpowering influence in crude. But looks like prices have hit the skids today. So it might be that the Chinese pessimism is coming home to roost, finally.BRAD SMITH: What are we still to extrapolate from the relationship that ensued post Russia invasion of Ukraine and the China-Russia relationship that had ensued there? Where does that stand right there? And how are investors best to continue evaluating that?VANDANA HARI: The entire scheme of things with regard to Russia, the Western sanctions, the embargoes on Russian oil has unleashed an unprecedented rewiring of trade globally. And, you know, in-- within that, again, we've seen China and India step up as major crude buyers of-- form Russia. And, of course, all of that crude has moved away from the European markets. So within that, you know, China and Russia were always-- were close-- geopolitically close and trade-wise as well. Of course, they share a major boundary between them.So there's not just by sea but pipeline imports of gas and crude from Russia as well. They do a fair amount of trade in their currencies as well, ruble and yuan, instead of the US dollar. So I guess it was just-- it was not surprising that the two countries have gotten even closer after the sanctions. And look, at the end of the day, for countries like China and India, if they're getting cheaper crude, especially in a high-price environment like we saw last year-- and even this year's prices are relatively high for these price-sensitive countries-- you know, they're just going to buy the Russian-- all the Russian crude and oil that they can get their hands on.JULIE HYMAN: So when we look at the trajectory of prices globally, do you think that we will-- you know, despite the pause that we're seeing today, do you think we'll continue to move higher given the US demand, given the Saudi production cuts, for example? Is the path still going to be upward?VANDANA HARI: So, Julie, there are definitely price-supportive factors.
