column4: Why oil prices need to shoot back above $100 per barrel
column10: [Oil prices have consistently ebbed and flowed above $80 a barrel in 2023. Smead Capital Management CEO Cole Smead believes it to be necessary for oil prices to rise above $100 for countries like the U.S. to fill the producer void left by China's economic troubles."We have to because this is a growing economy and barrels per day are growing, but as I pointed out... it is just not dominated by China like it was," Smead says. "The Western world's continued to grow despite all these difficulties in rates and the inflation headwinds and so on and so forth."Smead outlines American producers' potential to bring supply to the table as oil demand remains high.Video Transcript- A crude awakening. Oil prices ticking slightly lower this morning as supply concerns ease on hopes Iraqi supports will resume-- exports will resume. Excuse me. China's rocket recovery is still seen as the main driver of crude. Investors remain concerned over demand from the world's top importer.Cole Smead is still here with us. Cole, despite the possible easing of tighter oil supplies, you're optimistic on the oil outlook. Explain that to us. Walk us through your thesis there.COLE SMEAD: Yeah, so China used to be the tail that wags the dog. What China did sent marginal commodity prices higher or lower, including in oil. And what you're seeing is just the worst news out of China. And if you don't think it's bad, It's really bad, the news coming out of China.And yet, while this news is becoming greater and more precipitous and we're hearing about more defaults, delayed payments from financial institutions over there, you're watching oil stay tight or marginally climb over the last 60 days. So I think that really tells a different story.It's not about China's demand. It's about the tightness of supply. The tightness of supply being that if you look at the futures market right now, you'll find that the futures curve is terribly backwardated, which means that no new supply is going to grow in the next three, four years because no one gets compensated to go out and take that risk and hedge it in advance.Story continuesSo I think that's the continued trend we're seeing is just really tight supply. And therefore, as any demand goes on, prices have to edge up or stay firm because there's no one that can produce a new barrel or supply.- And Cole, in your estimation what is sort of the new threshold that oil would need to get to to make supply more attractive for the producers who have been cutting back to start producing more?COLE SMEAD: No one asks me that question or asks that. That's a great question. The answer is a minimum $100 a barrel. A minimum of $100.- And do you see it getting there any time soon?COLE SMEAD: We have to because this is a growing economy and barrels per day are growing. But as I pointed out a second ago, it's just not dominated by China like it was.So you look at the Western world. The Western world's continued to grow despite all these difficulties and rates and all these inflation headwinds and so on and so forth. So we really look at it as it's $100 a minimum, that you have to do that.And where you're going to get production first is from people who are already producing. Where they look and say, you know what, it's profitable to go out and poke that hole in that field that we were maybe waiting longer to do and now we're going to step up that investment.Now, where do you get a lot of big projects coming online at a later date, you're going to find those above $120 a barrel. But the rationality of the market-- people used to say that oil people will never get religion. They'll never come to know Jesus. They'll never quit drilling. Well, that's just not true.They quit drilling. And to watch an administration that loves renewables begging oil people to drill, it's just the oddest thing I've ever heard of. It's like stranger than fiction which means you know it's true. So I think those are the dynamics really at play in that market.And one other thing I'll add, it's got to come by Americans and Canadians because the Europeans, it's socially unacceptable to get oil and gas out of their ground even though they have those resources. So we're going to see this OPEC+, Canada, US, and parts of LATAM. That's the suppliers of oil globally.- Real quick before we let you go, Cole. How do you play this thesis on oil? Do you buy oil itself or do you buy oil producers or where in the stack do you do you buy?COLE SMEAD: We like the producers because they've just been really left for dead, and that's where the best money was made. The servicers weren't the better place to make money. So I would say, you're looking for what they call torque. You're looking for places where a $5 barrel increase of oil gives you a lot of operating leverage and really grows the free cash flow of the business.So you don't want to go by the majors, generally speaking, because they don't provide a lot of torque. Go look for names that have been more affected by things like gas. We own Ovintiv. They have a higher gas mix. Apache would be another name that I would throw out to people in that space.And if you go look in Canada, the MEG Energies of Canada and the Cenovuses that get WCS. A $5 increase in WTI directly affects Western Canada Select blend as well. So you'll see the Canadians will really punch their weight as we move forward here because they have more torque than a lot of the American players as well.- Cole, Thanks for spending some time with us this morning. If you go back to Seattle, you can get the fish seasoning for Brad, but I'll probably be there first so--- As long as somebody picks it up--COLE SMEAD: Thank you.- --for me, we're good.- Thanks, Cole.COLE SMEAD: I missed Top Pot Doughnuts. That's what I need is a Top Pot doughnut so--- I don't know that those will make it back with me. Cole Smead, Smead Capital Management CEO. Thank you so much. Appreciate it.]

column4: Labor Day: Gas prices forcing drivers to scale back holiday travel
column10: [Gas prices continue to be a pain point for American travelers ahead of the Labor Day Weekend, sitting at a national average of $3.81 per gallon. AAA Northeast Senior Manager Robert Sinclair Jr. sits down with Yahoo Finance Live to discuss how inflation and gas prices are weathering on families' travel budgets."The concession that's being made is the distance that's being traveled," Sinclair Jr. says. "We did a local survey, and drivers told us their average trip is going to be 50 to 200 miles... I remember when it was 500 to 1,000 miles for a trip over a holiday weekend. So, they are cutting back in that regard."Sinclair Jr. outlines his outlook for gas prices amid OPEC's oil production cuts and the seasonal trends surrounding oil refining and the effects of hurricane season.Video TranscriptBRAD SMITH: Joining us now with what to expect from the holiday weekend, Robert Sinclair, Jr., AAA Northeast senior manager. Robert, always a pleasure to have you here in studio with us.ROBERT SINCLAIR: Thank you for having me.BRAD SMITH: All right, so set the scene for us. Labor Day weekend, what do we expect here?ROBERT SINCLAIR: It's going to be busy. Gasoline prices are lower than they were last year. But $3.81 per a gallon, That's still in the pain point for a lot of drivers. 40% of drivers told us in a survey in March of 2018 that $3 a gallon was the pain point. They'd have to cut back on driving, not eat out, put off making a major purchase like a big appliance in order to afford gasoline.But for a holiday, Americans get the fewest number of vacation days of any workers in the industrialized world. We get a freebie, we take advantage of it. I think the concession that's being made is the distance that's being traveled.We did a local survey, and drivers told us that the average trip is going to be 50 to 200 miles. I've been doing this job a long time. I remember when it was 500 to 1,000 miles for a trip over a holiday weekend. So they are cutting back in that regard.Story continuesAnd I think the scale of activities will be different for those that are going out. And I think also with inflation cutting into the family budget, that's why we're seeing lower demand for gasoline overall. Year to date, this year compared to last, we're 0.9% less demand compared to a year ago when gasoline was so much more expensive.SEANA SMITH: So what does that tell us then just where prices are headed if we're seeing lower demand? Are we then going to see lower prices?ROBERT SINCLAIR: Well, the OPEC+ instituted production cuts of 3.6 million barrels per day out of the 100 million per day that we're being produced, particularly Saudi Arabia and Russia. That started in July. And toward the end of the beginning-- middle or till the end of the month, we saw prices tick up. And that is going to remain the same.They're talking about continuing those production cuts into September, which starts tomorrow. So I think that's going to be one factor keeping prices higher. The factor that might keep them lower is the fact that we're at the end of the summer driving season after Labor Day. The kids are back in school and so there's a lot less demand.But also, we make the switch from summer blends to winter blends of gasoline effective September 15. Summer gasoline is much more expensive to refine and distribute. There are different blends used in different parts of the country. And you cannot share them. Different blends are used because of weather conditions.We use lower vapor pressure gasoline during the summer so you don't get the evaporative emissions because of the hot weather. And also, during the winter carbon monoxide is a bigger problem rather than volatile organic compounds like we see during the summer. So winter gas is very different from summer gas. You leave summer gas in your car in the middle of winter, try and start it, it probably won't run.That's how radically different the blends are. But they're much more expensive during the summer, so we might see a break. The problem is we're still vulnerable to hurricanes. A major hurricane hitting the Gulf Coast-- the oil-rich infrastructure of the Gulf Coast, which has about 45% of the drilling, refining, and distribution infrastructure-- could send prices skyrocketing overnight.BRAD SMITH: What type of economic impact are we anticipating from this hurricane season?ROBERT SINCLAIR: Probably not much. It did not do a lot of damage. It closed a lot of ports. And that particularly affects Florida. Florida gets 100% of their gasoline via maritime delivery-- barges or tankers.The only pipeline in Florida is from Tampa, the Port of Tampa, to Orlando. Now, there are other pipelines, particularly the Colonial Pipeline-- the biggest pipeline in the country, which runs from the Gulf Coast up the Eastern Seaboard with tributaries coming off it-- to feed of the most major cities up and down the Eastern Seaboard. That is susceptible to power outages. The pipeline will go down due to power outages.You might remember a couple of years ago, it was hacked. And that created a lot of problems. So it really remains to be seen what the effects of the hurricane will be going forward.I think so far, it's minimal. A lot of ports in Florida were closed as a result of the hurricane. And that would affect those deliveries. But it went through very quickly. We have to see what happens in North and South Carolina.]

column4: Why Hurricane Idalia won't move oil prices much
column10: [As Floridians prepare for Hurricane Idalia, Lipow Oil Associates President Andrew Lipow joins Yahoo Finance Live to discuss the impact of the hurricane on oil prices.Lipow says, “the impact of Hurricane Idalia on the energy infrastructure is actually very small. The majority of natural gas and oil production, if you will, is to the west of Mobile, Alabama.” Lipow explains what he is “really looking for is the supply disruptions coming from tanker deliveries of gasoline and diesel being delayed into the port of Tampa, as well as along the Florida panhandle from Pensacola over to Panama City.”“For the global oil market,” Lipow says, we’ve been focusing on “the production cuts that we’ve been seeing out of OPEC+, specifically Saudi Arabia, as they try to get the price back towards $90 a barrel for Brent crude oil. And we’ve seen Saudi Arabia impose voluntary production cuts,” that Lipow expects will “continue through October and perhaps through the end of the year.”Lipow notes that “the oil market has been… disappointed with the re-opening of the Chinese economy and the rate of growth that we’re seeing in oil demand.” Chinese oil demand in the second quarter was “very robust” at "16 million barrels a day… but we expect that demand is going to start to slack in the third and fourth quarter,” Lipow says.Video TranscriptAKIKO FUJITA: Andy, what's the immediate impact you're watching? And how significant is the disruption likely to be if we do, in fact, see this hurricane intensified to a category 3?ANDREW LIPOW: Well, thank you very much for having me. I think the impact of Hurricane Idalia on the energy infrastructure is actually very small. The majority of natural gas and oil production, if you will, is to the West of Mobile, Alabama. So if you would draw a North-South line through Alabama, the impacts are going to really be to the East side of that. Florida produces only 2,000 barrels a day of crude oil, while the nation is producing 12.8 million barrels a day.Story continuesWhat I'm really looking for is the supply disruptions coming from tanker deliveries of gasoline and diesel being delayed into the Port of Tampa as well as along the Florida panhandle from Pensacola over to Panama City.SEANA SMITH: And if we do see that, what could that potentially do then to prices?ANDREW LIPOW: Well, in the local Florida area, we would expect that prices go up. And the biggest concern is flooding and power outages of these terminals that are against the Gulf of Mexico. And should the storm surge come and impact them, then you can see a more difficult situation as gasoline supplies into the panhandle have to be trucked in.AKIKO FUJITA: Andy, as you look at this as one factor in oil prices and where they are moving right now, how significant is sort of looking-- when you look at the global factors right now-- I mean, how big of a mover is this likely to be in the grand scheme of things?ANDREW LIPOW: Well, the storm is actually going to be a very small impact on the overall oil market. For the global oil market, what we're really been focusing on is the production cuts that we've been seeing out of OPEC+ specifically Saudi Arabia as they try to get the price back towards $90 a barrel for Brent crude oil. And we've seen Saudi Arabia impose voluntary production cuts that I expect that are going to continue through October and perhaps through the end of the year.SEANA SMITH: Andy, how do you see the demand picture globally factoring in China, the slowing-- very slow recovery that we're seeing there, how that could potentially, I guess, keep oil prices in check? Because we kind of have this push-pull going on between demand out there, falling demand and then the supply picture and what that could look like.ANDREW LIPOW: Well, the oil market has been, frankly, disappointed with the reopening of the Chinese economy and the rate of growth that we're seeing in oil demand. In the second quarter, Chinese oil demand was still a very robust 16 million barrels a day, second only to the United States. But we expect that demand is going to start to slacken in the third and fourth quarter.And that is why we're seeing Saudi Arabia take these preemptive measures in order to get the oil market back in balance. I should also add that while OPEC+ has been trying to cut production, members of OPEC who are not subject to the quota like Libya, Iran, and Venezuela, they slowly but surely have been increasing their oil production. And that's really thrown a monkey wrench into Saudi Arabia's plans.AKIKO FUJITA: So when you consider that OPEC+ has cut roughly 5 million barrels a day since October of last year, you consider the softening demand out of China, what are those additional cuts you alluded to earlier? What does that look like?ANDREW LIPOW: Well, when we saw the OPEC+ production cuts, of course, that was from their quota levels, which were in excess of what they were actually producing. So in reality, the OPEC+ production cut of a headline of 5 million barrels per day only translated into about 2.7 million barrels a day, offset by what we saw come out of Iran and Venezuela and Libya.And that is really the difficulty that OPEC+ is having, that they haven't cut as much as they've announced. At the same time, the International Energy Agency is predicting a record oil demand this year, up 2.4 million barrels a day from last year, but a much slower growth going into 2024 of only 1 million barrels a day. And fortuitously, the US is supplying a significant amount of that increased oil demand through our increased production.]

column4: Rising diesel prices a 'hidden tax' on consumers as energy stokes inflation worries
column10: [Diesel prices have risen to their highest levels since March and are showing no immediate signs of easing their upward trend.The national price of diesel was at $4.38 per gallon as of Monday, $0.41 higher from a month ago, according to data from AAA. "As we go into the fall agricultural harvest season and the winter heating months, refinery outages can have a significant impact on diesel supplies and put upward pressure on prices, stoking inflation," Andy Lipow of Lipow Oil Associates told Yahoo Finance on Monday."The cost of diesel is a hidden tax on all the goods and services the consumer buys as higher prices are passed through."Part of the upward pressure is due to recent refinery disruptions.The latest interruption came last week after a fire at Marathon's Garyville, La., refinery caused a partial shutdown of the facility, the fourth largest in the country.A plume of smoke drifts from the Marathon Petroleum refinery in Garyville, La., toward the Southeast Louisiana War Veterans Home in nearby Reserve, La., Friday, Aug. 25, 2023. (AP Photo)"We could still see diesel prices really accelerating into the fall months, which could pose a challenge for retailers that are filling up their inventory ahead of the holidays. We do expect more pain at the pump for diesel," Patrick De Haan, GasBuddy head of petroleum analysis, told Yahoo Finance on Monday.Gas prices hit a 2023 high earlier this month, renewing concerns that US inflation would reverse its downward trend.The Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) index, the Fed's preferred inflation indicator, which will be released on Thursday morning, is expected to show prices rose 3.3% year-over-year in July, up from 3% in the prior month."As far as the PCE I think we probably would not be surprised to see some kind of a raise. After the last report we have seen gas prices and oil prices go up, and that's a big factor," Marketgauge.com chief strategist Michele Schneider told Yahoo Finance Live on Monday.Oil prices jumped 15% in the month of July.Tighter output levels from OPEC+ along with voluntary cuts from Saudi Arabia are contributing elevated crude prices. West Texas Intermediate (CL=F) closed fractionally higher at $80.10 per barrel on Monday, while Brent futures (BZ=F) settled at $84.42.Story continues"I think that Saudi Arabia is doing whatever it can to increase the price of Brent crude oil to $90 per barrel, and that will lead to them continuing with their voluntary production cut in October and perhaps beyond," added Lipow.Lipow also noted that Hurricane Idalia could impact tanker movements, pressuring near-term retail gas prices in the US.However, seasonality in gasoline demand could keep a lid on prices going into the fall months as hurricane threats wane, GasBuddy's De Haan said."Don't be surprised if gas prices do inch up here before Labor Day, but I think it should be a bit of a head fake. Once we get into September, especially mid-September, we should see gas prices easing," he said.Ines Ferre is a senior business reporter for Yahoo Finance. Follow her on Twitter at @ines_ferre.]

column4: Magellan Midstream-ONEOK merger creates 'more ways to win' in energy: CEO
column10: [Petroleum distributor Magellan Midstream Partners (MMP) is pushing forward with its $18.8 billion merger of natural gas operator ONEOK (OKE). Magellan Midstream CEO Aaron Milford joins Yahoo Finance to discuss."It will also add natural gas liquids and natural gas to that mix," Milford says on the company's investments in diversifying its natural gas assets. "As you look forward, we feel very, very good about how powerful this company can be as an infrastructure company... And from a regulatory perspective, we have cleared the regulatory hurdles that we need to."Milford also describes the opportunities and value that consolidation in the energy space offers amid the slow transition from traditional fossil fuel sources.Video Transcript[AUDIO LOGO]- Magellan Midstream is betting big on natural gas as it pushes its $18.8 billion merger with ONEOK. The combination would result in the fourth largest US midstream company worth about $60 billion and is up for approval on September 21st.For more on this, we're joined by Aaron Milford, Magellan Midstream CEO. Good to have you on the show here. So talk about the timing of this. And obviously, any time you talk mergers, you have to wonder, how likely is this to catch the eye of regulators?AARON MILFORD: Well, sure. You know, it takes a little time to put deals like this together, that's for sure. And as we had the opportunity to consider this opportunity with ONEOK, it was really about two things. It was about maximizing value for our unitholders and then also thinking about the future, what best sets up our company going forward.So we're a refined products and crude oil business today primarily. It's a very healthy business. But when you think about the merger that we're creating, it'll be a refined products business, crude oil business. And then as you mentioned, it'll also add natural gas liquids and natural gas to that mix. So as you look forward, we feel very, very good about how powerful this company can be as an infrastructure company as we look forward.Story continuesAnd from a regulatory perspective, we've cleared the regulatory hurdles that we need to. And the vote that we have outstanding on the 21st is our last major hurdle.- And so as a combined entity, how immediately do you believe that you're ready to go hit the ground running? And what type of fine-tuning from an organizational perspective do you still think needs to take place?AARON MILFORD: Well, what's great is our business is a little different than their business. Refined products and crude oil, it's additive. They're complementary businesses. But they're different.So from an integration standpoint, we expect it to go very, very well. We'll bring our business into the mix. They'll continue to run their business really well.And then as we put the two companies together, we expect there to be significant synergies. So we expect about $200 to $400 million a year of value that will create from putting these two companies together that frankly, neither one of us do by ourselves. So that'll be the focus-- integrating, running our business really, really well from day 1, but then focusing on generating that additional value for all our unitholders and shareholders.- And it's interesting because this is a relatively fragmented industry in the US. What does having this consolidation in this space do? How does it position you against the competition?AARON MILFORD: So when you look at our space, it's been consolidating for a while. You've had a lot of smaller companies coming together to make larger companies. So as you look forward, it's all about having more ways to win. When you have a strong refined products business, a strong crude oil transportation business, and you add to that a strong natural gas liquids and natural gas business, you simply have more ways to win. So you have more ways to create growth and value for our investors moving forward.So energy transition is uncertain. And the more ways you can adapt, the better off you're going to be as a company. And this merger allows us to do that.- When we think about where things stand right now in terms of transitioning and the broader energy transition that is taking place, is this tie-up, is this deal in this ultimate merger a means to make sure that both of these businesses can not only complement each other, but at the end of the day, in this shift of and towards clean energy and cleaner elements of energy as well, that there's more of an opportunity for growth? And how do you kind look at tapping into that as well?AARON MILFORD: So energy transition-- the world needs all the energy they can possibly get. From our perspective, that's energy of all forms. That's fossil fuel energy. It's renewable energy. It's all of the above. That's what the world needs to have a successful economy.So as a fossil fuel company, we expect to have a very bright future in providing those fossil fuels the world's going to need. So as you look at that continuing demand in the world, it's all about getting those fossil fuels, natural gas, natural gas liquids, refined products, crude oil into that world market, not just our domestic market here in the US, but also the world market. And as we're able to do that, it creates opportunity because again, it comes right back down to, we believe, at the end of the day, we need all of the energy in all of its forms in order to be successful.]

column4: Gas prices ahead of Labor Day: Where is demand hitting the hardest?
column10: [Experts are forecasting a resurgence in gas price volatility amid increasing oil demand, remarks by Republican candidates, and end-of-summer travel trends. Yahoo Finance Markets Reporter Ines Ferre examines U.S. gas prices ahead of the Labor Day weekend as officials negotiate with oil producers.Video TranscriptRACHELLE AKUFFO: Gas prices will be watched with an eagle eye ahead of the Labor Day weekend. And the price at the pump is as much a national issue now as it ever was. With that in mind, we're looking at last week's GOP presidential debate. The candidates slammed President Biden's clean energy policies and Bidenomics more widely as being part of the problem.So who do we blame this time, the current administration, OPEC, Russia? Well, Yahoo Finance's Ines Ferre has some insight. Ines, what are your thoughts?INES FERRE: Yeah, Rachelle. Well, first off, gasoline and diesel prices, those are expected to rise over the next week. Just taking a look at where we're at with the national average, what retail-- the price of retail gasoline is at. It's at 3.82. That's a national average. But market watchers are expecting it to increase $0.05 to $0.10 in the next week. You've got diesel prices that are at $4.38 on a national average. And that's up from a month ago. That was at $3.97.Why is this important? Well not only does this impact consumers. This also can have an impact, of course, on inflation going forward. Even Dollar Tree last week, had noted a rise in diesel prices. It wasn't just a sales mix and their sales mix and their shrinkage issue. They also had noted that diesel prices were rising. So we have seen this on the rise.Now we do have weather events that are impacting some of these prices as well. We had the hurricane or tropical storm in Southern California. We also have the Hurricane Idalia. That's expected to go into Florida. And that's not supposed to impact too much Florida, because it's bypassing the refineries. However, it could impact tanker traffic going into Florida.Story continuesThe big thing to talk about, of course, is oil supply because you've got OPEC Plus cuts. And the production numbers aren't as bad as the headline numbers are. So, for example, Russia was voluntarily going to reduce its production by 500,000 barrels a day in August, but only is doing so by 300,000. So no surprise there because you're seeing oil prices go higher, and Russia does need that money to fund its war.As far as the US administration and what it's trying to do for oil prices, well, the US wants to bring those oil prices down because, of course, we are going into an election year as well. There is some talk about talking with Venezuela to ease sanctions there, also negotiating a nuclear program with Iran. We have heard talks about this before.And you can see on our YFi Interactive, you've got WTI at $80 a barrel right now. Brent crude is at $85 a barrel Andy Lipow from Lipow Oil Associates thinks that Saudi Arabia is going to try everything possible to keep this around $90 a barrel, Brent crude at $90 a barrel.So you've got a lot of forces, different forces going on here as far as these oil prices are concerned. But the bottom line is that the higher the oil price is, the more impact this will have on energy costs, and this is not good for inflation.BRAD SMITH: Excellent break down there. Yahoo Finance's own Ines Ferre. Thanks so much, Ines.]

column4: Jobs report, China slowdown, oil demand: 3 Things
column10: [Stocks anticipate the reveal of Friday's jobs data report. China's economic situation worsens as investors pull trades from the country's stock market. Oil demand comes under pressure amid elevated interest rates and the threat of Tropical Storm Idalia as it is expected to intensify on its path through Florida.Yahoo Finance's Brad Smith highlights several of this morning's top stories in focus.Video TranscriptBRAD SMITH: Here are three things that you need to know to start off your day. Stocks limping to the finish in what's been a rocky August. The jobs report punctuates a busy week of data for investors, and now that Jay Powell has spoken, it's the next big catalyst. column4: Loews (NYSE:L) shareholders have earned a 19% CAGR over the last three years
column10: [By buying an index fund, investors can approximate the average market return. But if you choose individual stocks with prowess, you can make superior returns. Just take a look at Loews Corporation (NYSE:L), which is up 68%, over three years, soundly beating the market return of 19% (not including dividends). On the other hand, the returns haven't been quite so good recently, with shareholders up just 9.7% , including dividends .With that in mind, it's worth seeing if the company's underlying fundamentals have been the driver of long term performance, or if there are some discrepancies. View our latest analysis for Loews While markets are a powerful pricing mechanism, share prices reflect investor sentiment, not just underlying business performance. One imperfect but simple way to consider how the market perception of a company has shifted is to compare the change in the earnings per share (EPS) with the share price movement.During three years of share price growth, Loews moved from a loss to profitability. So we would expect a higher share price over the period.You can see how EPS has changed over time in the image below (click on the chart to see the exact values).earnings-per-share-growthIt's probably worth noting we've seen significant insider buying in the last quarter, which we consider a positive. On the other hand, we think the revenue and earnings trends are much more meaningful measures of the business. This free interactive report on Loews' earnings, revenue and cash flow is a great place to start, if you want to investigate the stock further.What About Dividends?It is important to consider the total shareholder return, as well as the share price return, for any given stock. Whereas the share price return only reflects the change in the share price, the TSR includes the value of dividends (assuming they were reinvested) and the benefit of any discounted capital raising or spin-off. Arguably, the TSR gives a more comprehensive picture of the return generated by a stock. As it happens, Loews' TSR for the last 3 years was 70%, which exceeds the share price return mentioned earlier. This is largely a result of its dividend payments!Story continuesA Different PerspectiveWe're pleased to report that Loews shareholders have received a total shareholder return of 9.7% over one year. Of course, that includes the dividend. That gain is better than the annual TSR over five years, which is 5%. Therefore it seems like sentiment around the company has been positive lately. Someone with an optimistic perspective could view the recent improvement in TSR as indicating that the business itself is getting better with time. It is all well and good that insiders have been buying shares, but we suggest you check here to see what price insiders were buying at.There are plenty of other companies that have insiders buying up shares. column4: Why oil prices need to shoot back above $100 per barrel
column10: [Oil prices have consistently ebbed and flowed above $80 a barrel in 2023. Smead Capital Management CEO Cole Smead believes it to be necessary for oil prices to rise above $100 for countries like the U.S. to fill the producer void left by China's economic troubles."We have to because this is a growing economy and barrels per day are growing, but as I pointed out... it is just not dominated by China like it was," Smead says. "The Western world's continued to grow despite all these difficulties in rates and the inflation headwinds and so on and so forth."Smead outlines American producers' potential to bring supply to the table as oil demand remains high.Video Transcript- A crude awakening. Oil prices ticking slightly lower this morning as supply concerns ease on hopes Iraqi supports will resume-- exports will resume. Excuse me. China's rocket recovery is still seen as the main driver of crude. Investors remain concerned over demand from the world's top importer.Cole Smead is still here with us. Cole, despite the possible easing of tighter oil supplies, you're optimistic on the oil outlook. Explain that to us. Walk us through your thesis there.COLE SMEAD: Yeah, so China used to be the tail that wags the dog. What China did sent marginal commodity prices higher or lower, including in oil. And what you're seeing is just the worst news out of China. And if you don't think it's bad, It's really bad, the news coming out of China.And yet, while this news is becoming greater and more precipitous and we're hearing about more defaults, delayed payments from financial institutions over there, you're watching oil stay tight or marginally climb over the last 60 days. So I think that really tells a different story.It's not about China's demand. It's about the tightness of supply. The tightness of supply being that if you look at the futures market right now, you'll find that the futures curve is terribly backwardated, which means that no new supply is going to grow in the next three, four years because no one gets compensated to go out and take that risk and hedge it in advance.Story continuesSo I think that's the continued trend we're seeing is just really tight supply. And therefore, as any demand goes on, prices have to edge up or stay firm because there's no one that can produce a new barrel or supply.- And Cole, in your estimation what is sort of the new threshold that oil would need to get to to make supply more attractive for the producers who have been cutting back to start producing more?COLE SMEAD: No one asks me that question or asks that. That's a great question. The answer is a minimum $100 a barrel. A minimum of $100.- And do you see it getting there any time soon?COLE SMEAD: We have to because this is a growing economy and barrels per day are growing. But as I pointed out a second ago, it's just not dominated by China like it was.So you look at the Western world. The Western world's continued to grow despite all these difficulties and rates and all these inflation headwinds and so on and so forth. So we really look at it as it's $100 a minimum, that you have to do that.And where you're going to get production first is from people who are already producing. Where they look and say, you know what, it's profitable to go out and poke that hole in that field that we were maybe waiting longer to do and now we're going to step up that investment.Now, where do you get a lot of big projects coming online at a later date, you're going to find those above $120 a barrel. But the rationality of the market-- people used to say that oil people will never get religion. They'll never come to know Jesus. They'll never quit drilling. Well, that's just not true.They quit drilling. And to watch an administration that loves renewables begging oil people to drill, it's just the oddest thing I've ever heard of. It's like stranger than fiction which means you know it's true. So I think those are the dynamics really at play in that market.And one other thing I'll add, it's got to come by Americans and Canadians because the Europeans, it's socially unacceptable to get oil and gas out of their ground even though they have those resources. So we're going to see this OPEC+, Canada, US, and parts of LATAM. That's the suppliers of oil globally.- Real quick before we let you go, Cole. How do you play this thesis on oil? Do you buy oil itself or do you buy oil producers or where in the stack do you do you buy?COLE SMEAD: We like the producers because they've just been really left for dead, and that's where the best money was made. The servicers weren't the better place to make money. So I would say, you're looking for what they call torque. You're looking for places where a $5 barrel increase of oil gives you a lot of operating leverage and really grows the free cash flow of the business.So you don't want to go by the majors, generally speaking, because they don't provide a lot of torque. Go look for names that have been more affected by things like gas. We own Ovintiv. They have a higher gas mix. Apache would be another name that I would throw out to people in that space.And if you go look in Canada, the MEG Energies of Canada and the Cenovuses that get WCS. A $5 increase in WTI directly affects Western Canada Select blend as well. So you'll see the Canadians will really punch their weight as we move forward here because they have more torque than a lot of the American players as well.- Cole, Thanks for spending some time with us this morning. If you go back to Seattle, you can get the fish seasoning for Brad, but I'll probably be there first so--- As long as somebody picks it up--COLE SMEAD: Thank you.- --for me, we're good.- Thanks, Cole.COLE SMEAD: I missed Top Pot Doughnuts. That's what I need is a Top Pot doughnut so--- I don't know that those will make it back with me. Cole Smead, Smead Capital Management CEO. Thank you so much. Appreciate it.]

column4: Oil prices up 25% since late June as supply cuts squeeze market
column10: [Oil jumped to 10 month highs on Tuesday after key OPEC+ players announced supply reductions intended to keep crude prices high.On Tuesday Brent International (BZ=F) closed at $90.04 per barrel for the first time since November and West Texas Intermediate (CL=F) futures settled at $86.69 per barrel after Saudi Arabia announced an extension of its unilateral production cuts until December.Russia also reduced its exports by 300,000 barrels per day through year-end. These cuts are in addition to OPEC+ reductions that started in November of last year.The market is feeling the upward pressure. Crude futures have rallied about 25% since late June despite a slower-than-expected recovery from China’s economy and increased production output by US producers.“Between now and next summer we will continue to see prices of crude oil continue to be where it is or go higher,” Ramanan Krishnamoorti, vice president for energy and innovation at the University of Houston, told Yahoo Finance.He sees no sign of abatement in OPEC+’s supply cut initiatives and Saudia Arabia’s need to fund ambitious internal projects.“They’re [Saudia Arabia] making money. They are starting to bolster their coffers,” said Krishnamoorti. He sees only one scenario that would create downward pressure on crude.“If you start to smell a recession coming along, you should anticipate that the price of crude will go down,” he said.Saudi Arabia's Minister of Energy Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman Al-Saud arrives for an OPEC meeting in Vienna, Austria, June 4, 2023. (Leonhard Foeger/REUTERS)“A return to recession for Europe and/or China and a surprise weakening in Japan's economic growth would likely be precursors to weaker prices from demand destruction,” Rob Haworth, senior investment strategist at U.S. Bank Wealth Management in Seattle, told Yahoo Finance.While China’s recovery has been lackluster, mobility demand post lockdowns has offset the country’s dampened demand for petrochemicals amid an ongoing property crisis. Industry watchers are paying close attention to the coming months.Tamar Essner, Vectis Energy Partners principal, told Yahoo Finance Live on Tuesday that the market is starting to appreciate that while Saudi Arabia is a "swing producer," China is "basically a swing buyer."Story continues"They have huge inventories, huge storage. They can buy as much as they want when prices are attractive to them as they definitely were earlier this year,” Essner said, adding that "I think their demand is good but it may start to cool off a little bit in the coming months because they have inventory to work off of."Her firm expects West Texas Intermediate to stay in the $75 to $90 range between now and the end of the year, barring any geopolitical developments.Ines Ferre is a senior business reporter for Yahoo Finance. Follow her on Twitter at @ines_ferre.Click here for the latest economic news and economic indicators to help you in your investing decisionsRead the latest financial and business news from Yahoo Finance]

column4: Labor Day: Gas prices forcing drivers to scale back holiday travel
column10: [Gas prices continue to be a pain point for American travelers ahead of the Labor Day Weekend, sitting at a national average of $3.81 per gallon. AAA Northeast Senior Manager Robert Sinclair Jr. sits down with Yahoo Finance Live to discuss how inflation and gas prices are weathering on families' travel budgets."The concession that's being made is the distance that's being traveled," Sinclair Jr. says. "We did a local survey, and drivers told us their average trip is going to be 50 to 200 miles... I remember when it was 500 to 1,000 miles for a trip over a holiday weekend. So, they are cutting back in that regard."Sinclair Jr. outlines his outlook for gas prices amid OPEC's oil production cuts and the seasonal trends surrounding oil refining and the effects of hurricane season.Video TranscriptBRAD SMITH: Joining us now with what to expect from the holiday weekend, Robert Sinclair, Jr., AAA Northeast senior manager. Robert, always a pleasure to have you here in studio with us.ROBERT SINCLAIR: Thank you for having me.BRAD SMITH: All right, so set the scene for us. Labor Day weekend, what do we expect here?ROBERT SINCLAIR: It's going to be busy. Gasoline prices are lower than they were last year. But $3.81 per a gallon, That's still in the pain point for a lot of drivers. 40% of drivers told us in a survey in March of 2018 that $3 a gallon was the pain point. They'd have to cut back on driving, not eat out, put off making a major purchase like a big appliance in order to afford gasoline.But for a holiday, Americans get the fewest number of vacation days of any workers in the industrialized world. We get a freebie, we take advantage of it. I think the concession that's being made is the distance that's being traveled.We did a local survey, and drivers told us that the average trip is going to be 50 to 200 miles. I've been doing this job a long time. I remember when it was 500 to 1,000 miles for a trip over a holiday weekend. So they are cutting back in that regard.Story continuesAnd I think the scale of activities will be different for those that are going out. And I think also with inflation cutting into the family budget, that's why we're seeing lower demand for gasoline overall. Year to date, this year compared to last, we're 0.9% less demand compared to a year ago when gasoline was so much more expensive.SEANA SMITH: So what does that tell us then just where prices are headed if we're seeing lower demand? Are we then going to see lower prices?ROBERT SINCLAIR: Well, the OPEC+ instituted production cuts of 3.6 million barrels per day out of the 100 million per day that we're being produced, particularly Saudi Arabia and Russia. That started in July. And toward the end of the beginning-- middle or till the end of the month, we saw prices tick up. And that is going to remain the same.They're talking about continuing those production cuts into September, which starts tomorrow. So I think that's going to be one factor keeping prices higher. The factor that might keep them lower is the fact that we're at the end of the summer driving season after Labor Day. The kids are back in school and so there's a lot less demand.But also, we make the switch from summer blends to winter blends of gasoline effective September 15. Summer gasoline is much more expensive to refine and distribute. There are different blends used in different parts of the country. And you cannot share them. Different blends are used because of weather conditions.We use lower vapor pressure gasoline during the summer so you don't get the evaporative emissions because of the hot weather. And also, during the winter carbon monoxide is a bigger problem rather than volatile organic compounds like we see during the summer. So winter gas is very different from summer gas. You leave summer gas in your car in the middle of winter, try and start it, it probably won't run.That's how radically different the blends are. But they're much more expensive during the summer, so we might see a break. The problem is we're still vulnerable to hurricanes. A major hurricane hitting the Gulf Coast-- the oil-rich infrastructure of the Gulf Coast, which has about 45% of the drilling, refining, and distribution infrastructure-- could send prices skyrocketing overnight.BRAD SMITH: What type of economic impact are we anticipating from this hurricane season?ROBERT SINCLAIR: Probably not much. It did not do a lot of damage. It closed a lot of ports. And that particularly affects Florida. Florida gets 100% of their gasoline via maritime delivery-- barges or tankers.The only pipeline in Florida is from Tampa, the Port of Tampa, to Orlando. Now, there are other pipelines, particularly the Colonial Pipeline-- the biggest pipeline in the country, which runs from the Gulf Coast up the Eastern Seaboard with tributaries coming off it-- to feed of the most major cities up and down the Eastern Seaboard. That is susceptible to power outages. The pipeline will go down due to power outages.You might remember a couple of years ago, it was hacked. And that created a lot of problems. So it really remains to be seen what the effects of the hurricane will be going forward.I think so far, it's minimal. A lot of ports in Florida were closed as a result of the hurricane. And that would affect those deliveries. But it went through very quickly. We have to see what happens in North and South Carolina.]

column4: Why Hurricane Idalia won't move oil prices much
column10: [As Floridians prepare for Hurricane Idalia, Lipow Oil Associates President Andrew Lipow joins Yahoo Finance Live to discuss the impact of the hurricane on oil prices.Lipow says, “the impact of Hurricane Idalia on the energy infrastructure is actually very small. The majority of natural gas and oil production, if you will, is to the west of Mobile, Alabama.” Lipow explains what he is “really looking for is the supply disruptions coming from tanker deliveries of gasoline and diesel being delayed into the port of Tampa, as well as along the Florida panhandle from Pensacola over to Panama City.”“For the global oil market,” Lipow says, we’ve been focusing on “the production cuts that we’ve been seeing out of OPEC+, specifically Saudi Arabia, as they try to get the price back towards $90 a barrel for Brent crude oil. And we’ve seen Saudi Arabia impose voluntary production cuts,” that Lipow expects will “continue through October and perhaps through the end of the year.”Lipow notes that “the oil market has been… disappointed with the re-opening of the Chinese economy and the rate of growth that we’re seeing in oil demand.” Chinese oil demand in the second quarter was “very robust” at "16 million barrels a day… but we expect that demand is going to start to slack in the third and fourth quarter,” Lipow says.Video TranscriptAKIKO FUJITA: Andy, what's the immediate impact you're watching? And how significant is the disruption likely to be if we do, in fact, see this hurricane intensified to a category 3?ANDREW LIPOW: Well, thank you very much for having me. I think the impact of Hurricane Idalia on the energy infrastructure is actually very small. The majority of natural gas and oil production, if you will, is to the West of Mobile, Alabama. So if you would draw a North-South line through Alabama, the impacts are going to really be to the East side of that. Florida produces only 2,000 barrels a day of crude oil, while the nation is producing 12.8 million barrels a day.Story continuesWhat I'm really looking for is the supply disruptions coming from tanker deliveries of gasoline and diesel being delayed into the Port of Tampa as well as along the Florida panhandle from Pensacola over to Panama City.SEANA SMITH: And if we do see that, what could that potentially do then to prices?ANDREW LIPOW: Well, in the local Florida area, we would expect that prices go up. And the biggest concern is flooding and power outages of these terminals that are against the Gulf of Mexico. And should the storm surge come and impact them, then you can see a more difficult situation as gasoline supplies into the panhandle have to be trucked in.AKIKO FUJITA: Andy, as you look at this as one factor in oil prices and where they are moving right now, how significant is sort of looking-- when you look at the global factors right now-- I mean, how big of a mover is this likely to be in the grand scheme of things?ANDREW LIPOW: Well, the storm is actually going to be a very small impact on the overall oil market. For the global oil market, what we're really been focusing on is the production cuts that we've been seeing out of OPEC+ specifically Saudi Arabia as they try to get the price back towards $90 a barrel for Brent crude oil. And we've seen Saudi Arabia impose voluntary production cuts that I expect that are going to continue through October and perhaps through the end of the year.SEANA SMITH: Andy, how do you see the demand picture globally factoring in China, the slowing-- very slow recovery that we're seeing there, how that could potentially, I guess, keep oil prices in check? Because we kind of have this push-pull going on between demand out there, falling demand and then the supply picture and what that could look like.ANDREW LIPOW: Well, the oil market has been, frankly, disappointed with the reopening of the Chinese economy and the rate of growth that we're seeing in oil demand. In the second quarter, Chinese oil demand was still a very robust 16 million barrels a day, second only to the United States. But we expect that demand is going to start to slacken in the third and fourth quarter.And that is why we're seeing Saudi Arabia take these preemptive measures in order to get the oil market back in balance. I should also add that while OPEC+ has been trying to cut production, members of OPEC who are not subject to the quota like Libya, Iran, and Venezuela, they slowly but surely have been increasing their oil production. And that's really thrown a monkey wrench into Saudi Arabia's plans.AKIKO FUJITA: So when you consider that OPEC+ has cut roughly 5 million barrels a day since October of last year, you consider the softening demand out of China, what are those additional cuts you alluded to earlier? What does that look like?ANDREW LIPOW: Well, when we saw the OPEC+ production cuts, of course, that was from their quota levels, which were in excess of what they were actually producing. So in reality, the OPEC+ production cut of a headline of 5 million barrels per day only translated into about 2.7 million barrels a day, offset by what we saw come out of Iran and Venezuela and Libya.And that is really the difficulty that OPEC+ is having, that they haven't cut as much as they've announced. At the same time, the International Energy Agency is predicting a record oil demand this year, up 2.4 million barrels a day from last year, but a much slower growth going into 2024 of only 1 million barrels a day. And fortuitously, the US is supplying a significant amount of that increased oil demand through our increased production.]

column4: Rising diesel prices a 'hidden tax' on consumers as energy stokes inflation worries
column10: [Diesel prices have risen to their highest levels since March and are showing no immediate signs of easing their upward trend.The national price of diesel was at $4.38 per gallon as of Monday, $0.41 higher from a month ago, according to data from AAA. "As we go into the fall agricultural harvest season and the winter heating months, refinery outages can have a significant impact on diesel supplies and put upward pressure on prices, stoking inflation," Andy Lipow of Lipow Oil Associates told Yahoo Finance on Monday."The cost of diesel is a hidden tax on all the goods and services the consumer buys as higher prices are passed through."Part of the upward pressure is due to recent refinery disruptions.The latest interruption came last week after a fire at Marathon's Garyville, La., refinery caused a partial shutdown of the facility, the fourth largest in the country.A plume of smoke drifts from the Marathon Petroleum refinery in Garyville, La., toward the Southeast Louisiana War Veterans Home in nearby Reserve, La., Friday, Aug. 25, 2023. (AP Photo)"We could still see diesel prices really accelerating into the fall months, which could pose a challenge for retailers that are filling up their inventory ahead of the holidays. We do expect more pain at the pump for diesel," Patrick De Haan, GasBuddy head of petroleum analysis, told Yahoo Finance on Monday.Gas prices hit a 2023 high earlier this month, renewing concerns that US inflation would reverse its downward trend.The Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) index, the Fed's preferred inflation indicator, which will be released on Thursday morning, is expected to show prices rose 3.3% year-over-year in July, up from 3% in the prior month."As far as the PCE I think we probably would not be surprised to see some kind of a raise. After the last report we have seen gas prices and oil prices go up, and that's a big factor," Marketgauge.com chief strategist Michele Schneider told Yahoo Finance Live on Monday.Oil prices jumped 15% in the month of July.Tighter output levels from OPEC+ along with voluntary cuts from Saudi Arabia are contributing elevated crude prices. West Texas Intermediate (CL=F) closed fractionally higher at $80.10 per barrel on Monday, while Brent futures (BZ=F) settled at $84.42.Story continues"I think that Saudi Arabia is doing whatever it can to increase the price of Brent crude oil to $90 per barrel, and that will lead to them continuing with their voluntary production cut in October and perhaps beyond," added Lipow.Lipow also noted that Hurricane Idalia could impact tanker movements, pressuring near-term retail gas prices in the US.However, seasonality in gasoline demand could keep a lid on prices going into the fall months as hurricane threats wane, GasBuddy's De Haan said."Don't be surprised if gas prices do inch up here before Labor Day, but I think it should be a bit of a head fake. Once we get into September, especially mid-September, we should see gas prices easing," he said.Ines Ferre is a senior business reporter for Yahoo Finance. Follow her on Twitter at @ines_ferre.]

column4: Magellan Midstream-ONEOK merger creates 'more ways to win' in energy: CEO
column10: [Petroleum distributor Magellan Midstream Partners (MMP) is pushing forward with its $18.8 billion merger of natural gas operator ONEOK (OKE). Magellan Midstream CEO Aaron Milford joins Yahoo Finance to discuss."It will also add natural gas liquids and natural gas to that mix," Milford says on the company's investments in diversifying its natural gas assets. "As you look forward, we feel very, very good about how powerful this company can be as an infrastructure company... And from a regulatory perspective, we have cleared the regulatory hurdles that we need to."Milford also describes the opportunities and value that consolidation in the energy space offers amid the slow transition from traditional fossil fuel sources.Video Transcript[AUDIO LOGO]- Magellan Midstream is betting big on natural gas as it pushes its $18.8 billion merger with ONEOK. The combination would result in the fourth largest US midstream company worth about $60 billion and is up for approval on September 21st.For more on this, we're joined by Aaron Milford, Magellan Midstream CEO. Good to have you on the show here. So talk about the timing of this. And obviously, any time you talk mergers, you have to wonder, how likely is this to catch the eye of regulators?AARON MILFORD: Well, sure. You know, it takes a little time to put deals like this together, that's for sure. And as we had the opportunity to consider this opportunity with ONEOK, it was really about two things. It was about maximizing value for our unitholders and then also thinking about the future, what best sets up our company going forward.So we're a refined products and crude oil business today primarily. It's a very healthy business. But when you think about the merger that we're creating, it'll be a refined products business, crude oil business. And then as you mentioned, it'll also add natural gas liquids and natural gas to that mix. So as you look forward, we feel very, very good about how powerful this company can be as an infrastructure company as we look forward.Story continuesAnd from a regulatory perspective, we've cleared the regulatory hurdles that we need to. And the vote that we have outstanding on the 21st is our last major hurdle.- And so as a combined entity, how immediately do you believe that you're ready to go hit the ground running? And what type of fine-tuning from an organizational perspective do you still think needs to take place?AARON MILFORD: Well, what's great is our business is a little different than their business. Refined products and crude oil, it's additive. They're complementary businesses. But they're different.So from an integration standpoint, we expect it to go very, very well. We'll bring our business into the mix. They'll continue to run their business really well.And then as we put the two companies together, we expect there to be significant synergies. So we expect about $200 to $400 million a year of value that will create from putting these two companies together that frankly, neither one of us do by ourselves. So that'll be the focus-- integrating, running our business really, really well from day 1, but then focusing on generating that additional value for all our unitholders and shareholders.- And it's interesting because this is a relatively fragmented industry in the US. What does having this consolidation in this space do? How does it position you against the competition?AARON MILFORD: So when you look at our space, it's been consolidating for a while. You've had a lot of smaller companies coming together to make larger companies. So as you look forward, it's all about having more ways to win. When you have a strong refined products business, a strong crude oil transportation business, and you add to that a strong natural gas liquids and natural gas business, you simply have more ways to win. So you have more ways to create growth and value for our investors moving forward.So energy transition is uncertain. And the more ways you can adapt, the better off you're going to be as a company. And this merger allows us to do that.- When we think about where things stand right now in terms of transitioning and the broader energy transition that is taking place, is this tie-up, is this deal in this ultimate merger a means to make sure that both of these businesses can not only complement each other, but at the end of the day, in this shift of and towards clean energy and cleaner elements of energy as well, that there's more of an opportunity for growth? And how do you kind look at tapping into that as well?AARON MILFORD: So energy transition-- the world needs all the energy they can possibly get. From our perspective, that's energy of all forms. That's fossil fuel energy. It's renewable energy. It's all of the above. That's what the world needs to have a successful economy.So as a fossil fuel company, we expect to have a very bright future in providing those fossil fuels the world's going to need. So as you look at that continuing demand in the world, it's all about getting those fossil fuels, natural gas, natural gas liquids, refined products, crude oil into that world market, not just our domestic market here in the US, but also the world market. And as we're able to do that, it creates opportunity because again, it comes right back down to, we believe, at the end of the day, we need all of the energy in all of its forms in order to be successful.]

column4: Gas prices ahead of Labor Day: Where is demand hitting the hardest?
column10: [Experts are forecasting a resurgence in gas price volatility amid increasing oil demand, remarks by Republican candidates, and end-of-summer travel trends. Yahoo Finance Markets Reporter Ines Ferre examines U.S. gas prices ahead of the Labor Day weekend as officials negotiate with oil producers.Video TranscriptRACHELLE AKUFFO: Gas prices will be watched with an eagle eye ahead of the Labor Day weekend. And the price at the pump is as much a national issue now as it ever was. With that in mind, we're looking at last week's GOP presidential debate. The candidates slammed President Biden's clean energy policies and Bidenomics more widely as being part of the problem.So who do we blame this time, the current administration, OPEC, Russia? Well, Yahoo Finance's Ines Ferre has some insight. Ines, what are your thoughts?INES FERRE: Yeah, Rachelle. Well, first off, gasoline and diesel prices, those are expected to rise over the next week. Just taking a look at where we're at with the national average, what retail-- the price of retail gasoline is at. It's at 3.82. That's a national average. But market watchers are expecting it to increase $0.05 to $0.10 in the next week. You've got diesel prices that are at $4.38 on a national average. And that's up from a month ago. That was at $3.97.Why is this important? Well not only does this impact consumers. This also can have an impact, of course, on inflation going forward. Even Dollar Tree last week, had noted a rise in diesel prices. It wasn't just a sales mix and their sales mix and their shrinkage issue. They also had noted that diesel prices were rising. So we have seen this on the rise.Now we do have weather events that are impacting some of these prices as well. We had the hurricane or tropical storm in Southern California. We also have the Hurricane Idalia. That's expected to go into Florida. And that's not supposed to impact too much Florida, because it's bypassing the refineries. However, it could impact tanker traffic going into Florida.Story continuesThe big thing to talk about, of course, is oil supply because you've got OPEC Plus cuts. And the production numbers aren't as bad as the headline numbers are. So, for example, Russia was voluntarily going to reduce its production by 500,000 barrels a day in August, but only is doing so by 300,000. So no surprise there because you're seeing oil prices go higher, and Russia does need that money to fund its war.As far as the US administration and what it's trying to do for oil prices, well, the US wants to bring those oil prices down because, of course, we are going into an election year as well. There is some talk about talking with Venezuela to ease sanctions there, also negotiating a nuclear program with Iran. We have heard talks about this before.And you can see on our YFi Interactive, you've got WTI at $80 a barrel right now. Brent crude is at $85 a barrel Andy Lipow from Lipow Oil Associates thinks that Saudi Arabia is going to try everything possible to keep this around $90 a barrel, Brent crude at $90 a barrel.So you've got a lot of forces, different forces going on here as far as these oil prices are concerned. But the bottom line is that the higher the oil price is, the more impact this will have on energy costs, and this is not good for inflation.BRAD SMITH: Excellent break down there. Yahoo Finance's own Ines Ferre. Thanks so much, Ines.]

column4: Loews (NYSE:L) shareholders have earned a 19% CAGR over the last three years
column10: [By buying an index fund, investors can approximate the average market return. But if you choose individual stocks with prowess, you can make superior returns. Just take a look at Loews Corporation (NYSE:L), which is up 68%, over three years, soundly beating the market return of 19% (not including dividends). On the other hand, the returns haven't been quite so good recently, with shareholders up just 9.7% , including dividends .With that in mind, it's worth seeing if the company's underlying fundamentals have been the driver of long term performance, or if there are some discrepancies. View our latest analysis for Loews While markets are a powerful pricing mechanism, share prices reflect investor sentiment, not just underlying business performance. One imperfect but simple way to consider how the market perception of a company has shifted is to compare the change in the earnings per share (EPS) with the share price movement.During three years of share price growth, Loews moved from a loss to profitability. So we would expect a higher share price over the period.You can see how EPS has changed over time in the image below (click on the chart to see the exact values).earnings-per-share-growthIt's probably worth noting we've seen significant insider buying in the last quarter, which we consider a positive. On the other hand, we think the revenue and earnings trends are much more meaningful measures of the business. This free interactive report on Loews' earnings, revenue and cash flow is a great place to start, if you want to investigate the stock further.What About Dividends?It is important to consider the total shareholder return, as well as the share price return, for any given stock. Whereas the share price return only reflects the change in the share price, the TSR includes the value of dividends (assuming they were reinvested) and the benefit of any discounted capital raising or spin-off. Arguably, the TSR gives a more comprehensive picture of the return generated by a stock. As it happens, Loews' TSR for the last 3 years was 70%, which exceeds the share price return mentioned earlier. Of course, that includes the dividend. That gain is better than the annual TSR over five years, which is 5%. Therefore it seems like sentiment around the company has been positive lately. Someone with an optimistic perspective could view the recent improvement in TSR as indicating that the business itself is getting better with time. column4: Rising gas prices: Impact on Biden re-election campaign
column10: [Gas prices are slowly creeping higher in the United States. How could this affect President Biden's re-election campaign? Yahoo Finance Senior Columnist Rick Newman joins the Live show to discuss the impact of rising gas prices on Biden's 2024 presidential campaign.Video Transcript- Gas prices are slowing and slowly creeping higher, I should say. Now sitting at $3.80 a gallon here in the US. And with a new "Wall Street Journal" poll showing just 37% approve of President Biden's handling of the economy, could this spell trouble for his upcoming re-election campaign? Yahoo Finance's Rick Newman joins us with the details. Hey, Rick.RICK NEWMAN: Hey, guys. I think President Biden has to be pretty worried about gasoline prices. One reason is that we are seeing oil prices go higher, and they seem likely to go higher still for reasons that President Biden can't really control.Saudi Arabia has done a big production cut. Russia also has cut production. And both of those countries have said they're going to continue those production cuts through the end of the year, suggesting, perhaps, they could continue them into 2024.So we're now seeing oil around 85 bucks a barrel, and I'm seeing some projections saying it could go to the mid 90s and even up to $100 per barrel. And that's just because of the global market dynamics for oil. The last time we had oil at $100 per barrel US gasoline prices were around $4.40.And I think for President Biden, any gasoline price that starts with a $4 is just bad news because that, as we all know, gas prices punch above their weight in term of-- in terms of consumer psyches. And when you start to see gasoline prices start with a $4, that just signals that something is wrong, and it bums people out. So this is something I think the White House is paying extremely close attention to.And there's not a lot that Biden will be able to do if gas prices get out of control again in 2024 when we're really in the thick of the next presidential election.Story continues- Rick, I was just out on the West Coast. Forget about $4, it's $5 out there. That was-- they do things differently out there for a variety of different reasons. But in any case, you talked about his lack of control.He has some control at the margins, right? When you're talking about things like the Petroleum Reserve, et cetera, like, are there sort of little things he can do? And how aggressively the closer to the election that we get do you think he's going to be?RICK NEWMAN: Well, Biden did tap the US Petroleum Reserve last year. He drew down 180 million barrels. And the US Reserve is now at the lowest level, I think, since 1983. That is supposed to be an emergency Reserve for things, like, if a hurricane comes through and knocks out refineries or something like that or if there's some geopolitical emergency that is not supposed to be just to lower gas prices and cut consumers a break.So, Biden, I guess, he could draw that down further, but I think that would generate a lot of criticism that he's, sort of, abusing the Strategic Reserve. Another thing that the Biden administration is doing pretty quietly is, kind of, making some tacit deals with unfriendly nations that happen to be oil suppliers. So, Venezuela, for example, last year, the Biden administration changed the sanctions regime on Venezuela a little bit so they can import more oil to the United States.There have also been some, kind of, behind the scenes negotiations with Iran with regard to their nuclear deal and the sanctions in there. And Iran has actually been producing more oil, putting it into the global market they're not necessarily selling it to the United States. But any additional oil that goes in-- goes into the global market will help keep prices down.And then, there's also this price cap on Russian oil and there have been some calls to lower that price cap to further punish Russia for its invasion of Ukraine. And it seems there's no chance that the Biden administration is going to try to lead the big nations known as the G7 to lower that price cap because that could mean less Russian oil. So there are things you're not seeing that the Biden administration is doing to try to keep oil supply going.And one last thing I'll mention, here in the United States, we are probably going to see a new high-- a record high in terms of US oil production, and that's not because of anything the government's doing, that's just private sector producers saying prices are high, so we want to pump more because we're going to make money off of it. But it remains an open question whether all of that will be enough to keep gasoline prices in the comfort zone here.- All right. Well, we'll see what happens. Rick, thank you so much. Appreciate and you can read more on this story on yahoofinance.com.]

column4: How global slowdown woes are hanging over the dollar and oil prices
column10: [Global economic growth could be hindered by headwinds tying back to interest rates and China's slower-than-expected recovery from the pandemic. So how are certain asset classes reacting to forecasts signaling a global slowdown?Yahoo Finance Live discusses how the U.S. dollar and oil prices are weathering calls for global economic slowdowns.Video TranscriptJULIE HYMAN: Well, global economic growth prospects are confronting a unique mix of headwinds from interest rate increases in hopes of containing inflation to lingering pandemic effects on China's recovery. But what could a slowdown mean for some asset classes? We are zeroing in on a couple of them this morning, in particular the US dollar, the strength behind that currency raising concerns for investors and sending Asian currencies to monthly lows. But the dollar continues to rise on signs that the US economy is improving here. Brian Sozzi spoke to Jan Hatzius, Goldman Sachs chief economist, on why he believes we'll most likely avoid a recession.JAN HATZIUS: I think there's increased evidence that we can see rebalancing of the economy, inflation coming under control, and it's not going to require a recession. So we've progressively reduced our recession probability. We had it in the 30%, 35% range around March when you had the financial turbulence and the banking turbulence. Always thought that it was less likely than 50%, but I've gotten incrementally more confident that recession can be avoided.JULIE HYMAN: Well, apparently he's not the only one, right?BRAD SMITH: Yeah.JULIE HYMAN: Because that's-- we have seen that sentiment really shift this year towards being more optimistic on the economy, and that is definitely one of the things that has helped support that strength in the US dollar.BRAD SMITH: Yeah, and one of the interesting things in the correlation between inflation, of course in relation to recession, but inflation also to the decline in dollar, there was the thinking earlier this year that US inflation, if it continued to at least abate here a little bit or decelerate, that it would further a decline in the dollar.Story continuesWe're continuing to watch more economic data that comes out that shows that inflation, even if we are continuing to see some type of cool, that the dollar for right now in the rise that we've seen most recently, the larger question being, where other assets and where perhaps in the riskier realm of some of those assets would there stand to be some type of benefit? And that was what many investors over the course of early this summer were paying close attention to-- a rise in some of the propensity for those risk assets given the weakness that we had seen in some of the dollar.But as of right now, I think for where we've seen the inflation picture continue to show itself at least in moving back towards a deceleration phase here, I think for a lot of consumers out there, they're are looking across what that means for a recession and just trying to figure out, OK, if this means soft landing, can I be confident in how much I'm going to spend or what some of the larger purchases that I can feel more confident in spending on right now is. Well, it's not a house and might not be a car as well here.JULIE HYMAN: Right.BRAD SMITH: But that all in relation to how strong or weak the dollar has been moving even over the past two months.JULIE HYMAN: Yeah, so the dollar-- I mean, forget about consumers for a minute.BRAD SMITH: Sure.JULIE HYMAN: The dollar has important implications as well for other countries and for companies. If I'm a company and the dollar is strengthening, that means that there are implications for me bringing my overseas revenue back to the US, right? And the value of that not being as strong if the dollar is stronger than those local currencies.And there are also implications for other nations because if the dollar is strengthening, conversely, their currencies are weakening. Japan in particular seems alarmed about that. An official-- top currency official there saying that Japan is ready to take action amid some of the speculative moves that we've seen in the market. The PBOC in China as well, the central bank there, also talking about that issue and issuing some stronger guidance for its reference rate for the yuan. So a lot of different implications here when it comes to what's going on with the currencies globally.BRAD SMITH: Yeah, and another asset that we are watching this morning is oil. We're watching this closely as a clear driver for inflation globally. Oil jumped to 10-month highs on Tuesday after Russia and Saudi Arabia announced supply reductions intended to keep crude prices high.One of the huge kind of parts of this as well-- the price of Russia's flagship, we've been watching that here, and that has continued to be above some of the G7 price caps. That particularly has been of note, especially as Russia is continuing to kind of move forward and monitor or say at least that they're looking to stabilize prices. But price stabilization for them is something that's a little bit more detrimental for the rest of the world.JULIE HYMAN: Yeah, the dynamics in the oil market recently have been really interesting. We were just talking about the strength in the dollar, which traditionally has not meant strength for commodities and oil prices in particular. But the oil has been strengthening lately, and WTI in particular is up more than 20% this quarter thus far-- on track for its best performance since the first quarter of 2022. So we've seen that strength. Now a little bit of a pullback.There are some potential indications that oil is getting a little stretched or a little overbought. If you look at momentum indicators, Brent that we just saw-- so we were showing Brent and WTI-- Brent below $90 for the first time since last November. So after this climb that we have seen, a little bit of a pullback occurring today, even as some of the analysts who watch oil that we've talked to say they don't expect oil necessarily to fall much further, even with some of the global growth concerns surrounding China.BRAD SMITH: Yeah, and for China, the oil demand has not been held up as strongly as many would have anticipated with the growth projections that were set forth at the beginning of this year. So that also having an impact because China not purchasing as much from some of the other counterparts or global and specifically Russia purchase agreements that they had set forth or at least discussed last year amid the ongoing invasion of Ukraine and then this relationship that furthered itself between Russia and China as well.]
