Amazon could be hit by an FTC antitrust lawsuit later this month, with the action expected to target its most popular marketplace. Now the Wall Street Journal report says that the online retail giant hasn't offered concessions, in what looks like they could be the last discussions before a filing.]

column4: Oil prices up 25% since late June as supply cuts squeeze market
column10: [Oil jumped to 10 month highs on Tuesday after key OPEC+ players announced supply reductions intended to keep crude prices high.On Tuesday Brent International (BZ=F) closed at $90.04 per barrel for the first time since November and West Texas Intermediate (CL=F) futures settled at $86.69 per barrel after Saudi Arabia announced an extension of its unilateral production cuts until December.Russia also reduced its exports by 300,000 barrels per day through year-end. These cuts are in addition to OPEC+ reductions that started in November of last year.The market is feeling the upward pressure. Crude futures have rallied about 25% since late June despite a slower-than-expected recovery from China’s economy and increased production output by US producers.“Between now and next summer we will continue to see prices of crude oil continue to be where it is or go higher,” Ramanan Krishnamoorti, vice president for energy and innovation at the University of Houston, told Yahoo Finance.He sees no sign of abatement in OPEC+’s supply cut initiatives and Saudia Arabia’s need to fund ambitious internal projects.“They’re [Saudia Arabia] making money. They are starting to bolster their coffers,” said Krishnamoorti. He sees only one scenario that would create downward pressure on crude.“If you start to smell a recession coming along, you should anticipate that the price of crude will go down,” he said.Saudi Arabia's Minister of Energy Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman Al-Saud arrives for an OPEC meeting in Vienna, Austria, June 4, 2023. (Leonhard Foeger/REUTERS)“A return to recession for Europe and/or China and a surprise weakening in Japan's economic growth would likely be precursors to weaker prices from demand destruction,” Rob Haworth, senior investment strategist at U.S. Bank Wealth Management in Seattle, told Yahoo Finance.While China’s recovery has been lackluster, mobility demand post lockdowns has offset the country’s dampened demand for petrochemicals amid an ongoing property crisis. Industry watchers are paying close attention to the coming months.Tamar Essner, Vectis Energy Partners principal, told Yahoo Finance Live on Tuesday that the market is starting to appreciate that while Saudi Arabia is a "swing producer," China is "basically a swing buyer."Story continues"They have huge inventories, huge storage. They can buy as much as they want when prices are attractive to them as they definitely were earlier this year,” Essner said, adding that "I think their demand is good but it may start to cool off a little bit in the coming months because they have inventory to work off of."Her firm expects West Texas Intermediate to stay in the $75 to $90 range between now and the end of the year, barring any geopolitical developments.Ines Ferre is a senior business reporter for Yahoo Finance. Follow her on Twitter at @ines_ferre.Click here for the latest economic news and economic indicators to help you in your investing decisionsRead the latest financial and business news from Yahoo Finance]

column4: Inflation, IPOs, iPhones: What investors are paying attention to
column10: [Investors' hands are full this week as Apple (AAPL) kicks off its annual event revealing the iPhone 15 on Tuesday, ahead of the August CPI print and the Arm (ARM) and Instacart's IPOs.Yahoo Finance Markets Reporter Ines Ferre breaks down this week's top stories to come, also analyzing how impactful energy costs and oil prices will be on the latest inflation data.Video TranscriptRACHELLE AKUFFO: Consumer price index will be released on Wednesday. Arm's IPO is set to begin trading this week. And of course, Apple's newest iPhone will release this year. Now, Yahoo Finance reporter Ines Ferre is here to tell us more about this big week ahead. Hey, Ines.INES FERRE: Hey, Rachelle, a lot to watch this week. Well, let's start out with that inflation print, which this Wednesday we are expected to be getting the August consumer price index. The CPI is expected to increase by 0.6% from the prior month, an acceleration from July's 0.2%. Now, year over year, inflation is expected to jump to 3.6% versus 3.2% in July. Core CPI, which strips out food and energy, is expected to stay unchanged month over month. But of course, you could see a surprise to the upside, and that's due to energy prices.Oil, we have seen skyrocketing over the last couple of months up about 25% since late June. So we are watching for that CPI print to come in a little bit hotter because of those oil prices. We're also taking a look at the IPO market this week. As we are awaiting Arm's public debut, the British chip designer has a price range of $47 to $51 per share, valuing the company at up to $52 billion. And this is expected to be the biggest IPO of 2023.Meanwhile, also Instacart submitted an updated filing, setting an offering price of between $26 and $28 per share. At the higher end of the range, Instacart is valued at $7.7 billion, and the online grocery delivery company will be raising about $616 million in its public offering. Look, these debuts are going to be really testing the IPO market after it essentially froze after 2020, 2021. We saw a peak during the pandemic of IPOs, of SPACs. And with that tighter monetary policy that we have seen over the last year, we've seen the IPO market basically freeze. So we will see how the reception is for Arm this week. Also, we're-- Rachelle?Story continuesRACHELLE AKUFFO: Well, Ines, just to hop in here, we're coming up on one of the most exciting times of the year, of course, for Apple, its new product unveiling. What can we expect from them?INES FERRE: Yeah, the iPhone 15, that lineup is expected, including the iPhone 15 pro and Pro Max. So if you're an Apple buff, you will want to pay attention to this. Apple will reportedly have a new display technology, also new titanium casings that could reduce the weight. Also, Apple is reportedly doing away with the physical ringer button that's on the left hand side of the phone for the 15 pro line. Instead, it will have a programmable button, which is going to be able to handle a number of tasks, including launching the camera.But the biggest change is a switch to USB-C charging ports. And that's, according to Bloomberg, European tech regulations call for companies to use USB-C Chargers that way, that's across the board, in order to reduce E-waste. So Apple already uses USB-C for its iPad Pros and the Mac lines of products. So this will be a change, a pretty significant change when it comes to the iPhone 15. Rachelle.RACHELLE AKUFFO: Indeed. That's the same charge that we use for Samsung. So as an Android person, I might be doing a little bit of hate watching on this Apple announcement. But we'll see, I'm sure I'll be a little bit jealous. A big thank you for that update, Ines Ferre, there for us.]

column4: 'Nothing worse than higher oil prices' as Fed fights inflation
column10: [Oil's upward price movement is making the Federal Reserve’s path toward a 2% inflation target more difficult.The crude market's rise is likely to have lifted overall inflation last month. And while core inflation — which strips out food and energy costs — has been on a downward trend, economists worry that higher energy prices could increase input costs for goods and services, leading companies to raise prices on everything from airfares to furniture."I’d say the rise in oil prices since late June/early July has clearly put upward pressure on gasoline prices and will lead to a large boost in the August headline CPI [Consumer Price Index]," Omair Sharif, president of Inflation Insights, tells Yahoo Finance.He added, “You may see higher fuel surcharges seep into higher prices for food, for food services, and a variety of goods that are moved by truck — for example furniture, appliances. You can also see higher jet fuel costs make their way into higher airfares."August's Consumer Price Index report, slated for release Wednesday, is expected to show prices increased 0.5% from the prior month, an acceleration from July's 0.2%. Year-over-year inflation is expected to jump 3.6% versus 3.2% in July.Core CPI is expected to stay unchanged but could surprise to the upside because of the higher transportation fuel costs Sharif referenced.Earlier this week, United Airlines, Southwest, and Alaska Air all warned of higher fuel costs in the third quarter.Since mid-July, "jet fuel prices have climbed over 20%,” noted United Airlines in an 8-K filing on Wednesday.Why oil prices are risingWest Texas Intermediate (CL=F) and Brent crude futures (BZ=F) have rallied more than 25% since late June. Output cuts are putting a squeeze on the oil market, despite China’s slower-than-expected economic recovery and increased production output by US producers.Earlier this week Saudi Arabia announced an extension of its unilateral production cuts for the next three months. Russia also reduced its exports by 300,000 barrels per day through year-end. These cuts are in addition to OPEC+ reductions that started at the end of last year.Story continuesWall Street analysts are starting to talk about $100 oil if momentum in the oil market continues.In July, the Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the 11th time since March 2022, in what officials hinted could be the first of two rate hikes considered for the rest of the year.US Federal Reserve Board Chairman Jerome Powell speaks during a news conference following a closed two-day meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee on interest rate policy in Washington, U.S., July 26, 2023. (Elizabeth Frantz/REUTERS)The Fed is expected to hold rates steady when it meets on Sept. 19 and 20 as it continues to watch inflation data and make sure it's still cooling.Wall Street analysts have walked back their calls for a recession, with Goldman Sachs bringing down the probability to 15% in the next year. A relatively strong, though slowing, labor market is prompting speculation that the Fed may be able to pull off a 'soft landing'."Everything is consistent with a soft landing, but you throw in the mix higher oil prices — if they keep going higher and stay higher, that could be a problem," Mark Zandi, Moody's Analytics chief economist, told Yahoo Finance Live this week."There's nothing worse than higher oil prices," said Zandi. "There's nothing more deleterious to the economy than higher oil, gasoline prices that slows growth. It sucks purchasing power of consumers. And it adds to inflation expectations."The economy's trajectory is looking less optimistic the longer consumers and companies are forced to deal with elevated energy costs."The more sustainable [the increase] becomes, the more of an impact it could have on corporate profits going into the next several quarters. And of course it can complicate this soft landing situation that the market has been baking in," Amy Kong, partner at Corient, told Yahoo Finance this week. "We wouldn’t be surprised to see inflation potentially picking up a little bit, or just not slowing down as much. That obviously will throw a wrench into the Fed story of potentially pausing for the time being," she added.Ines Ferre is a senior business reporter for Yahoo Finance. Follow her on Twitter at @ines_ferre.Click here for the latest economic news and economic indicators to help you in your investing decisionsRead the latest financial and business news from Yahoo Finance]

column4: Oil prices creating difficulties for Fed's inflation goal
column10: [Rising oil prices could prove to be one of the biggest challenges to the Fed's inflation rate target. Yahoo Finance Markets Reporter Ines Ferre takes a look at crude oil prices as experts worry about energy costs seeping into core inflation, keeping it elevated for longer.Video Transcript[VIDEO LOGO]RACHELLE AKUFFO: In July, the Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the 11th time since March of 2022. The Fed is expected to hold steady, while watching inflation data, hoping for it to go down to 2%. But with oil prices increasing, hitting those inflation targets might be more difficult than predicted. To talk more about this is "Yahoo Finance's" reporter Ines Ferre. Ines, what are you watching?INES FERRE: Well, Rachelle, next week, we'll be getting the inflation print for August. Year-over-year inflation is expected to jump to an annualized rate of 3.6% in August versus 3.2% in July. Meanwhile, economists forecast core inflation, which strips out food and energy costs. That will stay unchanged.Now, the Fed tends to watch core CPI, and that's been on a downward trend. But higher oil costs can still seep into the core. That's through higher diesel, higher gasoline costs, jet fuel prices, all derivatives of crude.Omair Sharif of Inflation Insights tells "Yahoo Finance," we may see higher restaurant prices and any goods that is moved by trucks, such as furniture and appliances. Even airfares could see a bump this week. United Airlines said that in July, since mid-July, jet fuel prices have climbed over 20%.Now, the Fed is expected to hold rates steady when it meets later this month. It's still watching that data to make sure that inflation continues to fall. And Wall Street analysts have walked back the possibility of recession, prompting some speculation that the Fed could actually pull off a soft landing.But economists say, if you throw in the mix the higher oil prices that could pose a problem, there's nothing worse than higher oil prices. It will slow growth, it sucks purchasing power, and it adds to inflation expectations, Rachelle.Story continuesRACHELLE AKUFFO: And as you mentioned, they're really seeping into a bit of everything in terms of how we pay for airfare and put gas in our cars as well. So then, what are oil market analysts saying about where prices will go from here?INES FERRE: Well, let's take a look at where they're at right now. Because we are watching WTI crude that's at $87.61. Brent Crude up above $90 per barrel. I'm going to pull up a year-to-date chart because you can see here, from the end of June into right now, we are seeing this that's up about 25% for both WTI and for crude oil. So an increase of 25% in these prices.A lot of this has to do with the production cuts that have been announced by OPEC+, Saudi Arabia's unilateral production cuts. And Saudi Arabia analysts are telling me, they want oil prices to be above $80 per barrel. And they will do everything possible to maintain it that way.So I spoke to one analyst that said to me, look, between now and next summer, you can expect to see these prices elevated. The only thing that would bring down oil prices, though, is if we do see a recession.RACHELLE AKUFFO: And certainly, seeing that perhaps telegraphed perhaps for 2024. So we'll have to wait and see. Ines Ferre, I appreciate you breaking all that down for us. Thanks so much.]

column4: Global economy: Saudi Arabia's crude partnerships could be 'biggest unknown'
column10: [While economies around the world deal with a barrage of uncertainty, Saudi Arabia has been extended an invitation to join the BRICS bloc of nations, currently comprised of Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa. Walser Wealth Management President Rebecca Walser joins Yahoo Finance Live to discuss the global impacts these trade partnerships could have and how investors can position their portfolios on economic prints.Turning her attention to the U.S. economic growth outlook, Walser states "there's a lot of things we can take away with the U.S. being resilient, but... all things will eventually get to us and we will have to have that reckoning here as well."Video Transcript- Well, looking at the global economy, inflation remains sticky, central banks are tightening, and consumers' confidence, low. Joining us now, we've got Rebecca Walser, President of Walser Wealth Management. Rebecca, great to have you here in studio with us.REBECCA WALSER: Great to be here. Thank you, [? Brantley, ?] for having me.- Absolutely. Bringing some of that Florida energy here for us. Where are the biggest risks in the global economy, though, right now? Well, I think the biggest unknown right now is this announcement that we got out of Johannesburg, obviously, of Saudi Arabia and the UAE joining the BRICS bloc.And really focusing on that conference on a lot of bilateral trade and domestic currencies, which we know we saw in March the first amount of currency transactions in China for the first time in Chinese Yuan outside of US dollar. So that was already alarming. The number of US dollar denominated bank reserves retrenching is alarming. The M2 money supply coming down, alarming. All of these things are macroeconomically globally alarming.But I think that what was really interesting [? telling ?] [? Brad ?] was when they said that Saudi Arabia and UAE aren't joining until January. It kind of gave them a time-- a framework of time to develop a framework with which the ultimate, which is really what I worry about, them announcing that they will start selling crude outside of US dollar for the first time since 1974. That happens, and we have potentially catastrophic dollar effects.Story continues- There doesn't seem to be an imminent sign that is happening, to your point. And in the meantime, the US economic data, as we've been discussing, has been pretty resilient. If you look at the Citi economic surprise index, the rate at which our reports have been beating, and you compare that with the likes of the eurozone say or the likes of China-- although you can argue all day about Chinese economic data. But the point is our data has been doing really well versus expectations.REBECCA WALSER: Yes.- So how do you look at that data and read the change in economic sentiment that we've seen in the US this year?REBECCA WALSER: Well, I think, Julia, the United States is always the last. All of these impacts-- we look at Asia and we look at Europe specifically because they're leading indicators for what will eventually come to America. And that's simply a product of the fact that we are the largest GDP. We do have the most-- we are it.We're obviously controlling the global Reserve currency, as well, so that obviously has given us a tremendous amount of benefits since 1944 Bretton Woods agreement. So I think that I look at those things and America being so resilient kind of as a bifurcation of our economy. There's still a lot of haves, but there's also very much a lot of have-nots.And that's why people are so disjointed and hearing the good economic data and saying, but that's not me. I'm still feeling it in my pocket. To your point earlier about the student loans resuming next month, that's $5 billion a month of spending that can't go to service and can't go to goods.We have Gen Z-ers that graduated in 2019, 2020 that have worked for 3 and 1/2 years and never even made a student loan payment. Have they budgeted for that? Did they plan on it? Because they expected this administration potentially forgive some of that student loan debt, so maybe they didn't budget it or expect it to be less.So there's a lot of things that we can take away with the US being resilient, but eventually, Julia, all things will eventually get to us, and we will have to have that reckoning here, as well.- So with all of these factors on the table, what are your clients asking you right now? Where are you kind of positioning portfolios?REBECCA WALSER: I think people are confused because they're seeing bad data, good data, bad data, good data. They're seeing Powell saying we have to raise, raise, raise, hawkish comments in Jackson Hole. But yet weakening and softening labor, and we're starting to see those things but then also this week coming back and unemployment claims going down.So there's such bifurcated data that people get confused. I think the thing to understand is there is an economic situation that has to come. We have to deal with the fact that we printed so much money and it has implicated inflation, obviously. But Powell has done the best he can.He's been able to really be aggressive because he's had labor as a stalwart. When we start to see labor softening, that's when we start to think that Powell has got to change his tune. So people are just wanting to-- if it's not going to be a soft landing, is it going to be a soft landing?Can we just get through and can we get back to some level of normalcy? I think people are just-- we're just all tired of it being so chaotic, right? And it has been, I think, since 2022, really. 2020 probably.]

column4: U.S. economy, oil inflation, China vs. Apple: Top 3 takeaways of the week
column10: [The U.S. economy is showing signs of resiliency as jobless claims hit their lowest levels since February and consumers have shown they are willing to spend more money on travel and experiences in the post-COVID era.Yahoo Finance Live examines the economic challenges consumers are bracing for amid the resumption of student loan payments, Saudi Arabia and Russia’s extensive oil production cuts, and Apple’s stock sell-off inspired by the Chinese government’s iPhone ban.Video TranscriptJULIE HYMAN: But top takeaways from this week, Brad and I have three of them. And we start with the US economy being resilient out of this week, showing the services sector in the US gained strength in August, jobless claims unexpectedly fell the prior week. That indicates a tighter than anticipated job market that is continuing here.And what's interesting is, yes, we had two reads on the services economy. The one from ISM did show surprising strength. The one from S&P which is one could argue a more comprehensive look includes more sizes of companies, was not as strong. Nonetheless, broadly here, when you look at the economic data we've been getting over the past several months, it has indeed been surprising to the upside. And that's really been the story for much of the year as well but we just kind of keep getting little reminders of it.BRAD SMITH: Yeah, and as we think about the shift in spending that's taking place here from goods to services for so many consumers out there and thinking about this kind of consumer resiliency that we've heard about over the course of this earnings season from a myriad of different companies, how does that showing up? Well, one area that I would look at that's not necessarily the economic data but is a piece of broader data that we can string together is how much people are spending on the experiences economy and traveling particularly here.And I was looking at some TSA passenger throughput numbers, really looking through the summer months here. So essentially, from Memorial Day weekend all the way through Labor Day weekend, now that we have the data and can layer that year over year, we are running at 102% of pre-pandemic levels on the TSA checkpoint travel numbers as of right now. So running that this morning, and so the travel spending continuing to remain strong at this point.Story continuesBut this resiliency is going to come with some tests. We should note, too. The student loans and that coming once again back on the table for repayment, that's going to be a test, October 1 there is when that recommences. And then additionally, you've seen excess savings start to be depleted a little bit more among households. So that shift in how households are spending, that certainly of note here in some of the tests for that consumer resiliency that we're going to be watching closely for.JULIE HYMAN: It's also important just quickly how all of this is playing through in asset classes, right? Because we have this US economic strength that has meant a stronger dollar, which we've been talking a lot about this week as well. And the implications for US companies and for international economies and currencies. So the dollar strength part of the story.And what also we have been seeing in terms of yields in the treasury market is also obviously part of the story. What are the implications for the Federal Reserve? And whether it's going to have to, if not keep raising rates, keep them higher for longer as the conversation keeps going. We've got 10-year yields that are sort of hovering near their highest that they have been in more than a year. So that's something we continue to watch as well.BRAD SMITH: Yeah, absolutely. One other thing that we're watching here, the second big thing that Julie and I have our eye on or learned from this week, oil. Maybe the deflation spoiler. On Tuesday Saudi Arabia and Russia agreed to extend their oil production cuts through the year's end. Both Brent and West Texas crude rose to their highest levels since November, fueling fears that elevated oil prices could stop moderating inflation here.And particularly, we had a soundbite or at least one of the comments on this from Mark Zandi, chief economist over at Moody's, who had said that $90 a barrel oil for any length of time would be problematic. Oil higher for longer in this instance essentially would be a problem for the Fed's fight against inflation.JULIE HYMAN: Yeah, and most of the oil analysts that we've spoken to have also said they don't expect it to, if it does fall, it's not going to fall by much. It seems to kind of be the consensus view here. We even have some estimates out from Goldman Sachs for it to be going significantly higher as well.Now, we know that the Fed doesn't specifically watch energy prices on their own because they do tend to be volatile but the question is the feed through to other stuff. There are also implications for gasoline prices at the pump, which we're showing here now, and what that's going to mean politically, which is sort of a down the line story but something that our Rick Newman has been talking about and has been watching very closely.And then sort of on a related note when we talk about politics, we could talk about geopolitics. And the third takeaway from the week is the latest victim of the trade war and tensions between the US and China taking a bite out of Apple. Shares of the tech giant falling this week on reports that China's iPhone ban is broadening across government, not just government agencies but government-sponsored enterprises.China, one of the tech giant's biggest markets, it accounts for just under 19% of overall revenue. And Beijing has already limited government officials from using iPhones again reportedly. This new report would significantly broaden that ban signal a bigger crackdown. And for a company that has traditionally had more of a favorable relationship with the Chinese government, this perhaps signals a new front or a new move in the tensions between the two countries sort of ensnaring Apple within it as we talked about big drop in those shares. But again, it raises these bigger questions about geopolitical maneuvering on the part of different nations.BRAD SMITH: And where companies have found themselves in the throes of that, I mean, when we think back to in kind of the chronological order that all of this has taken place within and ranging over administrations at this point, because China has a far further out view of how they want to play this. And I think for right now, the companies that have found themselves in the midst of this, sure, it's been TikTok and ByteDance.But then additionally, you've also found some of the chip companies finding themselves squarely within the throes of a tit for tat on intellectual property and where chips can be purchased or where they can be sold to. And now, even more so, it's coming into the consumer technology companies and Apple finding themselves in the throes of that this week, and that coming to light especially with the ban on government officials being able to use their devices.Now, the next question is-- and investors would be smart to think about-- where else might this overflow into? Well, there's an interesting call out this morning and particularly looking at other auto players within China that could be maintaining or at least gaining some more favorability here that could impact companies like Tesla, that could impact companies like Ford, who are all trying to release some of the most popular US models that they've had on the mass market scale into China as well, and produce there, and have better favoritism there among consumers on price at least. And so in that battling for price, that's one area that investors would be smart or apt to just think about where else this could permeate out into as well.]

column4: Rising gas prices: Impact on Biden re-election campaign
column10: [Gas prices are slowly creeping higher in the United States. How could this affect President Biden's re-election campaign? Yahoo Finance Senior Columnist Rick Newman joins the Live show to discuss the impact of rising gas prices on Biden's 2024 presidential campaign.Video Transcript- Gas prices are slowing and slowly creeping higher, I should say. Now sitting at $3.80 a gallon here in the US. And with a new "Wall Street Journal" poll showing just 37% approve of President Biden's handling of the economy, could this spell trouble for his upcoming re-election campaign? Yahoo Finance's Rick Newman joins us with the details. Hey, Rick.RICK NEWMAN: Hey, guys. I think President Biden has to be pretty worried about gasoline prices. One reason is that we are seeing oil prices go higher, and they seem likely to go higher still for reasons that President Biden can't really control.Saudi Arabia has done a big production cut. Russia also has cut production. And both of those countries have said they're going to continue those production cuts through the end of the year, suggesting, perhaps, they could continue them into 2024.So we're now seeing oil around 85 bucks a barrel, and I'm seeing some projections saying it could go to the mid 90s and even up to $100 per barrel. And that's just because of the global market dynamics for oil. The last time we had oil at $100 per barrel US gasoline prices were around $4.40.And I think for President Biden, any gasoline price that starts with a $4 is just bad news because that, as we all know, gas prices punch above their weight in term of-- in terms of consumer psyches. And when you start to see gasoline prices start with a $4, that just signals that something is wrong, and it bums people out. So this is something I think the White House is paying extremely close attention to.And there's not a lot that Biden will be able to do if gas prices get out of control again in 2024 when we're really in the thick of the next presidential election.Story continues- Rick, I was just out on the West Coast. Forget about $4, it's $5 out there. That was-- they do things differently out there for a variety of different reasons. But in any case, you talked about his lack of control.He has some control at the margins, right? When you're talking about things like the Petroleum Reserve, et cetera, like, are there sort of little things he can do? And how aggressively the closer to the election that we get do you think he's going to be?RICK NEWMAN: Well, Biden did tap the US Petroleum Reserve last year. He drew down 180 million barrels. And the US Reserve is now at the lowest level, I think, since 1983. That is supposed to be an emergency Reserve for things, like, if a hurricane comes through and knocks out refineries or something like that or if there's some geopolitical emergency that is not supposed to be just to lower gas prices and cut consumers a break.So, Biden, I guess, he could draw that down further, but I think that would generate a lot of criticism that he's, sort of, abusing the Strategic Reserve. Another thing that the Biden administration is doing pretty quietly is, kind of, making some tacit deals with unfriendly nations that happen to be oil suppliers. So, Venezuela, for example, last year, the Biden administration changed the sanctions regime on Venezuela a little bit so they can import more oil to the United States.There have also been some, kind of, behind the scenes negotiations with Iran with regard to their nuclear deal and the sanctions in there. And Iran has actually been producing more oil, putting it into the global market they're not necessarily selling it to the United States. But any additional oil that goes in-- goes into the global market will help keep prices down.And then, there's also this price cap on Russian oil and there have been some calls to lower that price cap to further punish Russia for its invasion of Ukraine. And it seems there's no chance that the Biden administration is going to try to lead the big nations known as the G7 to lower that price cap because that could mean less Russian oil. So there are things you're not seeing that the Biden administration is doing to try to keep oil supply going.And one last thing I'll mention, here in the United States, we are probably going to see a new high-- a record high in terms of US oil production, and that's not because of anything the government's doing, that's just private sector producers saying prices are high, so we want to pump more because we're going to make money off of it. But it remains an open question whether all of that will be enough to keep gasoline prices in the comfort zone here.- All right. Well, we'll see what happens. Rick, thank you so much. Appreciate and you can read more on this story on yahoofinance.com.]

column4: How global slowdown woes are hanging over the dollar and oil prices
column10: [Global economic growth could be hindered by headwinds tying back to interest rates and China's slower-than-expected recovery from the pandemic. So how are certain asset classes reacting to forecasts signaling a global slowdown?Yahoo Finance Live discusses how the U.S. dollar and oil prices are weathering calls for global economic slowdowns.Video TranscriptJULIE HYMAN: Well, global economic growth prospects are confronting a unique mix of headwinds from interest rate increases in hopes of containing inflation to lingering pandemic effects on China's recovery. But what could a slowdown mean for some asset classes? We are zeroing in on a couple of them this morning, in particular the US dollar, the strength behind that currency raising concerns for investors and sending Asian currencies to monthly lows. But the dollar continues to rise on signs that the US economy is improving here. Brian Sozzi spoke to Jan Hatzius, Goldman Sachs chief economist, on why he believes we'll most likely avoid a recession.JAN HATZIUS: I think there's increased evidence that we can see rebalancing of the economy, inflation coming under control, and it's not going to require a recession. So we've progressively reduced our recession probability. We had it in the 30%, 35% range around March when you had the financial turbulence and the banking turbulence. Always thought that it was less likely than 50%, but I've gotten incrementally more confident that recession can be avoided.JULIE HYMAN: Well, apparently he's not the only one, right?BRAD SMITH: Yeah.JULIE HYMAN: Because that's-- we have seen that sentiment really shift this year towards being more optimistic on the economy, and that is definitely one of the things that has helped support that strength in the US dollar.BRAD SMITH: Yeah, and one of the interesting things in the correlation between inflation, of course in relation to recession, but inflation also to the decline in dollar, there was the thinking earlier this year that US inflation, if it continued to at least abate here a little bit or decelerate, that it would further a decline in the dollar.Story continuesWe're continuing to watch more economic data that comes out that shows that inflation, even if we are continuing to see some type of cool, that the dollar for right now in the rise that we've seen most recently, the larger question being, where other assets and where perhaps in the riskier realm of some of those assets would there stand to be some type of benefit? And that was what many investors over the course of early this summer were paying close attention to-- a rise in some of the propensity for those risk assets given the weakness that we had seen in some of the dollar.But as of right now, I think for where we've seen the inflation picture continue to show itself at least in moving back towards a deceleration phase here, I think for a lot of consumers out there, they're are looking across what that means for a recession and just trying to figure out, OK, if this means soft landing, can I be confident in how much I'm going to spend or what some of the larger purchases that I can feel more confident in spending on right now is. Well, it's not a house and might not be a car as well here.JULIE HYMAN: Right.BRAD SMITH: But that all in relation to how strong or weak the dollar has been moving even over the past two months.JULIE HYMAN: Yeah, so the dollar-- I mean, forget about consumers for a minute.BRAD SMITH: Sure.JULIE HYMAN: The dollar has important implications as well for other countries and for companies. If I'm a company and the dollar is strengthening, that means that there are implications for me bringing my overseas revenue back to the US, right? And the value of that not being as strong if the dollar is stronger than those local currencies.And there are also implications for other nations because if the dollar is strengthening, conversely, their currencies are weakening. Japan in particular seems alarmed about that. An official-- top currency official there saying that Japan is ready to take action amid some of the speculative moves that we've seen in the market. The PBOC in China as well, the central bank there, also talking about that issue and issuing some stronger guidance for its reference rate for the yuan. So a lot of different implications here when it comes to what's going on with the currencies globally.BRAD SMITH: Yeah, and another asset that we are watching this morning is oil. We're watching this closely as a clear driver for inflation globally. Oil jumped to 10-month highs on Tuesday after Russia and Saudi Arabia announced supply reductions intended to keep crude prices high.One of the huge kind of parts of this as well-- the price of Russia's flagship, we've been watching that here, and that has continued to be above some of the G7 price caps. That particularly has been of note, especially as Russia is continuing to kind of move forward and monitor or say at least that they're looking to stabilize prices. But price stabilization for them is something that's a little bit more detrimental for the rest of the world.JULIE HYMAN: Yeah, the dynamics in the oil market recently have been really interesting. We were just talking about the strength in the dollar, which traditionally has not meant strength for commodities and oil prices in particular. But the oil has been strengthening lately, and WTI in particular is up more than 20% this quarter thus far-- on track for its best performance since the first quarter of 2022. So we've seen that strength. Now a little bit of a pullback.There are some potential indications that oil is getting a little stretched or a little overbought. If you look at momentum indicators, Brent that we just saw-- so we were showing Brent and WTI-- Brent below $90 for the first time since last November. So after this climb that we have seen, a little bit of a pullback occurring today, even as some of the analysts who watch oil that we've talked to say they don't expect oil necessarily to fall much further, even with some of the global growth concerns surrounding China.BRAD SMITH: Yeah, and for China, the oil demand has not been held up as strongly as many would have anticipated with the growth projections that were set forth at the beginning of this year. So that also having an impact because China not purchasing as much from some of the other counterparts or global and specifically Russia purchase agreements that they had set forth or at least discussed last year amid the ongoing invasion of Ukraine and then this relationship that furthered itself between Russia and China as well.]

column4: Oil trades at 10-month high: What it could mean for the Fed
column10: [Oil (CL=F) is trading at a fresh 10-month high. Yahoo Finance Markets Reporter Jared Blikre breaks down the charts and explains why higher oil prices could complicate things for the Federal Reserve.Video Transcript- Well, oil prices jumping to their highest level this year. Jared Blikre is here with a closer look.JARED BLIKRE: Hey, there. Well, let's take a look at crude oil, what it's doing over the last three months. In fact, all the tickers here on the top line here representing commodities are up more than 15%. That begins with heating oil, but we want to talk about crude oil today.Here's what it's done. Up 32%. And you might say, is it done? Has it gone too far too fast? And I say the answer is no because this is a look at what's happened over the last year. We just broke above a resistance level. But basically, we've been trading sideways. Should we break above $90? Let me show you what could be in store. We could be heading to these highs around $120 per barrel.By the way, yesterday, JP Morgan CEO Jamie Dimon was saying we could see $120, $130 crude oil. Probably talking Brent, but WTI would be close behind here. What could be the catalyst? Well, we also have, from the Biden administration, they are rebuilding the SPR. That is a strategic petroleum reserve. They just started that relatively recently around here. And decidedly not down by those $66 per barrel prices. So this is just going to be another marginal consumer of crude oil which could raise prices.And all of this is against the backdrop of slightly rising energy prices. So far, RBOB Gasoline futures here, those have been trading sideways over the last three months. Arguably the last year as well. And if we go to a two-year chart, you can see the resistance level. You start chopping above $3 per whatever their-- per unit, you're probably going to see to at least $4, and we could even get far beyond that.Here's a five-year look at what's happening. So with next year being an election year, RBOB Gasoline futures ticking up. Also we have CPI tomorrow. I think some of this latest energy data is going to be included in there. That's why we're seeing a handle of 3.6% on that headline CPI print. If all that comes to pass, this just shows that goods inflation, the price of commodities is finally affecting that place of the market where the Fed hasn't been concentrated because the Fed has been concentrated on the services side.Story continuesIt's great that rent inflation is coming down, but if we see energy prices ticking up and if we see crude oil shoot above $90 a barrel, if we see RBOB Gasoline futures go to $3, we're going to have a mini crisis on our hands again.- Maybe.JARED BLIKRE: Maybe.- We'll see.- Mini. It's all relative.JARED BLIKRE: It's all relative, I guess. I don't know. This rate of inflation still has slowed way down. But if it re-accelerates.- Yeah. Q1 next year.JARED BLIKRE: All right. We'll keep an eye on it. Thanks so much, Jared. Appreciate it.]

column4: Inflation, IPOs, iPhones: What investors are paying attention to

Arm's IPO is set to begin trading this week. And of course, Apple's newest iPhone will release this year. Now, Yahoo Finance reporter Ines Ferre is here to tell us more about this big week ahead. Hey, Ines.INES FERRE: Hey, Rachelle, a lot to watch this week. Well, let's start out with that inflation print, which this Wednesday we are expected to be getting the August consumer price index. The CPI is expected to increase by 0.6% from the prior month, an acceleration from July's 0.2%. Now, year over year, inflation is expected to jump to 3.6% versus 3.2% in July. Core CPI, which strips out food and energy, is expected to stay unchanged month over month. But of course, you could see a surprise to the upside, and that's due to energy prices.Oil, we have seen skyrocketing over the last couple of months up about 25% since late June. So we are watching for that CPI print to come in a little bit hotter because of those oil prices. We're also taking a look at the IPO market this week. As we are awaiting Arm's public debut, the British chip designer has a price range of $47 to $51 per share, valuing the company at up to $52 billion. And this is expected to be the biggest IPO of 2023.Meanwhile, also Instacart submitted an updated filing, setting an offering price of between $26 and $28 per share. At the higher end of the range, Instacart is valued at $7.7 billion, and the online grocery delivery company will be raising about $616 million in its public offering. And with that tighter monetary policy that we have seen over the last year, we've seen the IPO market basically freeze. So we will see how the reception is for Arm this week. Also, we're-- Rachelle?Story continuesRACHELLE AKUFFO: Well, Ines, just to hop in here, we're coming up on one of the most exciting times of the year, of course, for Apple, its new product unveiling. What can we expect from them?INES FERRE: Yeah, the iPhone 15, that lineup is expected, including the iPhone 15 pro and Pro Max. So if you're an Apple buff, you will want to pay attention to this. Apple will reportedly have a new display technology, also new titanium casings that could reduce the weight. Also, Apple is reportedly doing away with the physical ringer button that's on the left hand side of the phone for the 15 pro line. So Apple already uses USB-C for its iPad Pros and the Mac lines of products. So this will be a change, a pretty significant change when it comes to the iPhone 15. Rachelle.RACHELLE AKUFFO: Indeed. column4: 'Nothing worse than higher oil prices' as Fed fights inflation
column10: [Oil's upward price movement is making the Federal Reserve’s path toward a 2% inflation target more difficult.The crude market's rise is likely to have lifted overall inflation last month. And while core inflation — which strips out food and energy costs — has been on a downward trend, economists worry that higher energy prices could increase input costs for goods and services, leading companies to raise prices on everything from airfares to furniture."I’d say the rise in oil prices since late June/early July has clearly put upward pressure on gasoline prices and will lead to a large boost in the August headline CPI [Consumer Price Index]," Omair Sharif, president of Inflation Insights, tells Yahoo Finance.He added, “You may see higher fuel surcharges seep into higher prices for food, for food services, and a variety of goods that are moved by truck — for example furniture, appliances. You can also see higher jet fuel costs make their way into higher airfares."August's Consumer Price Index report, slated for release Wednesday, is expected to show prices increased 0.5% from the prior month, an acceleration from July's 0.2%. Year-over-year inflation is expected to jump 3.6% versus 3.2% in July.Core CPI is expected to stay unchanged but could surprise to the upside because of the higher transportation fuel costs Sharif referenced.Earlier this week, United Airlines, Southwest, and Alaska Air all warned of higher fuel costs in the third quarter.Since mid-July, "jet fuel prices have climbed over 20%,” noted United Airlines in an 8-K filing on Wednesday.Why oil prices are risingWest Texas Intermediate (CL=F) and Brent crude futures (BZ=F) have rallied more than 25% since late June. Output cuts are putting a squeeze on the oil market, despite China’s slower-than-expected economic recovery and increased production output by US producers.Earlier this week Saudi Arabia announced an extension of its unilateral production cuts for the next three months. Russia also reduced its exports by 300,000 barrels per day through year-end. These cuts are in addition to OPEC+ reductions that started at the end of last year.Story continuesWall Street analysts are starting to talk about $100 oil if momentum in the oil market continues.In July, the Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the 11th time since March 2022, in what officials hinted could be the first of two rate hikes considered for the rest of the year.US Federal Reserve Board Chairman Jerome Powell speaks during a news conference following a closed two-day meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee on interest rate policy in Washington, U.S., July 26, 2023. (Elizabeth Frantz/REUTERS)The Fed is expected to hold rates steady when it meets on Sept. 19 and 20 as it continues to watch inflation data and make sure it's still cooling.Wall Street analysts have walked back their calls for a recession, with Goldman Sachs bringing down the probability to 15% in the next year. A relatively strong, though slowing, labor market is prompting speculation that the Fed may be able to pull off a 'soft landing'."Everything is consistent with a soft landing, but you throw in the mix higher oil prices — if they keep going higher and stay higher, that could be a problem," Mark Zandi, Moody's Analytics chief economist, told Yahoo Finance Live this week."There's nothing worse than higher oil prices," said Zandi. "There's nothing more deleterious to the economy than higher oil, gasoline prices that slows growth. It sucks purchasing power of consumers. And it adds to inflation expectations."The economy's trajectory is looking less optimistic the longer consumers and companies are forced to deal with elevated energy costs."The more sustainable [the increase] becomes, the more of an impact it could have on corporate profits going into the next several quarters. And of course it can complicate this soft landing situation that the market has been baking in," Amy Kong, partner at Corient, told Yahoo Finance this week. "We wouldn’t be surprised to see inflation potentially picking up a little bit, or just not slowing down as much. That obviously will throw a wrench into the Fed story of potentially pausing for the time being," she added.Ines Ferre is a senior business reporter for Yahoo Finance. Follow her on Twitter at @ines_ferre.Click here for the latest economic news and economic indicators to help you in your investing decisionsRead the latest financial and business news from Yahoo Finance]

column4: Oil prices creating difficulties for Fed's inflation goal
column10: [Rising oil prices could prove to be one of the biggest challenges to the Fed's inflation rate target. Yahoo Finance Markets Reporter Ines Ferre takes a look at crude oil prices as experts worry about energy costs seeping into core inflation, keeping it elevated for longer.Video Transcript[VIDEO LOGO]RACHELLE AKUFFO: In July, the Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the 11th time since March of 2022. The Fed is expected to hold steady, while watching inflation data, hoping for it to go down to 2%. But with oil prices increasing, hitting those inflation targets might be more difficult than predicted. To talk more about this is "Yahoo Finance's" reporter Ines Ferre. Ines, what are you watching?INES FERRE: Well, Rachelle, next week, we'll be getting the inflation print for August. Year-over-year inflation is expected to jump to an annualized rate of 3.6% in August versus 3.2% in July. Meanwhile, economists forecast core inflation, which strips out food and energy costs. That will stay unchanged.Now, the Fed tends to watch core CPI, and that's been on a downward trend. But higher oil costs can still seep into the core. That's through higher diesel, higher gasoline costs, jet fuel prices, all derivatives of crude.Omair Sharif of Inflation Insights tells "Yahoo Finance," we may see higher restaurant prices and any goods that is moved by trucks, such as furniture and appliances. Even airfares could see a bump this week. United Airlines said that in July, since mid-July, jet fuel prices have climbed over 20%.Now, the Fed is expected to hold rates steady when it meets later this month. It's still watching that data to make sure that inflation continues to fall. And Wall Street analysts have walked back the possibility of recession, prompting some speculation that the Fed could actually pull off a soft landing.But economists say, if you throw in the mix the higher oil prices that could pose a problem, there's nothing worse than higher oil prices. It will slow growth, it sucks purchasing power, and it adds to inflation expectations, Rachelle.Story continuesRACHELLE AKUFFO: And as you mentioned, they're really seeping into a bit of everything in terms of how we pay for airfare and put gas in our cars as well. So then, what are oil market analysts saying about where prices will go from here?INES FERRE: Well, let's take a look at where they're at right now. Because we are watching WTI crude that's at $87.61. Brent Crude up above $90 per barrel. I'm going to pull up a year-to-date chart because you can see here, from the end of June into right now, we are seeing this that's up about 25% for both WTI and for crude oil. So an increase of 25% in these prices.A lot of this has to do with the production cuts that have been announced by OPEC+, Saudi Arabia's unilateral production cuts. And Saudi Arabia analysts are telling me, they want oil prices to be above $80 per barrel. And they will do everything possible to maintain it that way.So I spoke to one analyst that said to me, look, between now and next summer, you can expect to see these prices elevated. The only thing that would bring down oil prices, though, is if we do see a recession.RACHELLE AKUFFO: And certainly, seeing that perhaps telegraphed perhaps for 2024. So we'll have to wait and see. Ines Ferre, I appreciate you breaking all that down for us. Thanks so much.]

column4: Global economy: Saudi Arabia's crude partnerships could be 'biggest unknown'
column10: [While economies around the world deal with a barrage of uncertainty, Saudi Arabia has been extended an invitation to join the BRICS bloc of nations, currently comprised of Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa. Walser Wealth Management President Rebecca Walser joins Yahoo Finance Live to discuss the global impacts these trade partnerships could have and how investors can position their portfolios on economic prints.Turning her attention to the U.S. economic growth outlook, Walser states "there's a lot of things we can take away with the U.S. being resilient, but... all things will eventually get to us and we will have to have that reckoning here as well."Video Transcript- Well, looking at the global economy, inflation remains sticky, central banks are tightening, and consumers' confidence, low. Joining us now, we've got Rebecca Walser, President of Walser Wealth Management. Rebecca, great to have you here in studio with us.REBECCA WALSER: Great to be here. Thank you, [? Brantley, ?] for having me.- Absolutely. Bringing some of that Florida energy here for us. Where are the biggest risks in the global economy, though, right now? Well, I think the biggest unknown right now is this announcement that we got out of Johannesburg, obviously, of Saudi Arabia and the UAE joining the BRICS bloc.And really focusing on that conference on a lot of bilateral trade and domestic currencies, which we know we saw in March the first amount of currency transactions in China for the first time in Chinese Yuan outside of US dollar. So that was already alarming. The number of US dollar denominated bank reserves retrenching is alarming. The M2 money supply coming down, alarming. All of these things are macroeconomically globally alarming.But I think that what was really interesting [? telling ?] [? Brad ?] was when they said that Saudi Arabia and UAE aren't joining until January. It kind of gave them a time-- a framework of time to develop a framework with which the ultimate, which is really what I worry about, them announcing that they will start selling crude outside of US dollar for the first time since 1974. That happens, and we have potentially catastrophic dollar effects.Story continues- There doesn't seem to be an imminent sign that is happening, to your point. And in the meantime, the US economic data, as we've been discussing, has been pretty resilient. If you look at the Citi economic surprise index, the rate at which our reports have been beating, and you compare that with the likes of the eurozone say or the likes of China-- although you can argue all day about Chinese economic data. But the point is our data has been doing really well versus expectations.REBECCA WALSER: Yes.- So how do you look at that data and read the change in economic sentiment that we've seen in the US this year?REBECCA WALSER: Well, I think, Julia, the United States is always the last. All of these impacts-- we look at Asia and we look at Europe specifically because they're leading indicators for what will eventually come to America. And that's simply a product of the fact that we are the largest GDP. We do have the most-- we are it.We're obviously controlling the global Reserve currency, as well, so that obviously has given us a tremendous amount of benefits since 1944 Bretton Woods agreement. So I think that I look at those things and America being so resilient kind of as a bifurcation of our economy. There's still a lot of haves, but there's also very much a lot of have-nots.And that's why people are so disjointed and hearing the good economic data and saying, but that's not me. I'm still feeling it in my pocket. To your point earlier about the student loans resuming next month, that's $5 billion a month of spending that can't go to service and can't go to goods.We have Gen Z-ers that graduated in 2019, 2020 that have worked for 3 and 1/2 years and never even made a student loan payment. Have they budgeted for that? Did they plan on it? Because they expected this administration potentially forgive some of that student loan debt, so maybe they didn't budget it or expect it to be less.So there's a lot of things that we can take away with the US being resilient, but eventually, Julia, all things will eventually get to us, and we will have to have that reckoning here, as well.- So with all of these factors on the table, what are your clients asking you right now? Where are you kind of positioning portfolios?REBECCA WALSER: I think people are confused because they're seeing bad data, good data, bad data, good data. They're seeing Powell saying we have to raise, raise, raise, hawkish comments in Jackson Hole. But yet weakening and softening labor, and we're starting to see those things but then also this week coming back and unemployment claims going down.So there's such bifurcated data that people get confused. I think the thing to understand is there is an economic situation that has to come. We have to deal with the fact that we printed so much money and it has implicated inflation, obviously. But Powell has done the best he can.He's been able to really be aggressive because he's had labor as a stalwart. When we start to see labor softening, that's when we start to think that Powell has got to change his tune. So people are just wanting to-- if it's not going to be a soft landing, is it going to be a soft landing?Can we just get through and can we get back to some level of normalcy? I think people are just-- we're just all tired of it being so chaotic, right? And it has been, I think, since 2022, really. 2020 probably.]

column4: Investors are ignoring surging energy inflation at their own peril: Morning Brief
column10: [This is The Takeaway from today's Morning Brief, which you can sign up to receive in your inbox every morning along with:The chart of the dayWhat we're watchingWhat we're readingEconomic data releases and earningsInvestors were treated with an uncomfortable surprise on Wednesday: The Consumer Price Index came in higher than expected, jumping 0.3 percentage points in August and ratcheting up the year-over-year comparison to 3.7% — the highest since May.As anyone with a (non-EV) car knows, surging energy prices accounted for much of the increase, with the gasoline subcomponent soaring 10.6% in August alone — the third-largest monthly rise since the Global Financial Crisis.But stocks barely batted an eyelash, and the Nasdaq (^IXIC) and S&P 500 (^GSPC) finished the day in the green. The Dow ended down fractionally.Investors thinking ahead to next week's Federal Reserve meeting might be forgiven for looking through the headline print to the core number, which the Fed prefers. Core inflation excludes volatile food and energy and just dropped to 4.3% — the lowest since September 2021. And with good news out of core inflation, why should investors think the Fed should react to high gas prices, which, if anything, suppress spending on non-gasoline items?But those higher gasoline prices come as WTI crude oil (CL=F) has rallied 28% over the last three months, with technicals pointing to huge potential upside. In early September, WTI broke to new highs on the year, and now $90 per barrel is only minor potential resistance on the path to last year's highs around $120.To those who would laugh at $120 crude, we point to the recent words of JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon. Only days ago — and to little fanfare — he raised the possibility of an eyewatering $150 handle.Speaking at a Barclays conference, Dimon said his general bearishness last year is based on "huge, semi-tectonic shifts" that he's seeing in the economy — signs that point to potentially higher prices across the board one year from now.Story continuesDimon said he wouldn't be surprised to see the US 10-year Treasury note (^TNX) yielding 5.5% (over 100 basis points higher than the current 4.3% rate) and crude oil landing between $120 and $150."These things are tectonic differences from what you've experienced since 1945," he added. When the chairman of the world's biggest bank says we haven't seen the likes of this environment since the end of World War II, investors might well listen.Looking at the historical reaction of stocks on CPI release dates reveals a tight correlation to the overall direction of the market.While the correlation isn't perfect, the big drops in the orange line (shown above) reflect just how sudden and dramatic changes in critical data can lead to a major repricing of risk.Should headline CPI continue to accelerate to the upside, it will eventually force a reckoning with the bullish pricing of stocks. For those looking to time an exit to the substantial bull market rally off last year's October lows, this event could well be that catalyst.If Jamie Dimon is correct, then the time frame is sometime in the next year.morning brief imageClick here for the latest stock market news and in-depth analysis, including events that move stocksRead the latest financial and business news from Yahoo Finance]

column4: CPI report: Rising gas prices a 'big deal for families'
column10: [August's CPI report illustrates prices rising 0.6% month-over-month alongside inflation gains of 3.7% year-over-year. Rising gas prices and energy costs have been cited as key drivers in inflation bearing down on consumers. KPMG Senior Economist Yelena Maleyev and Sahm Consulting Founder Claudia Sahm — who is also a former Federal Reserve Board economist — join Yahoo Finance Live to break down August's data and analyze what is behind the trends in energy prices."This should be a reminder to all of us that the Fed is not in charge of inflation. These are geopolitical events that are driving energy prices and this is a good reminder that today, it is not all about the Fed in terms of policy responses," Sahm states.Maleyev referred to peaks in energy prices in June 2022 as the "lowest-hanging fruit" for inflation relief that has already been picked: "We have been seeing an overall deceleration, just a few months of increased gas or energy prices does not a trend yet make."Video TranscriptJULIE HYMAN: Let's talk more about the implications of these numbers, how to read them, what it could mean for the Federal Reserve, as well. We're joined by Claudia Sahm, consulting founder. And Yelena Maleyev, KPMG economist. Thanks to you both for being here.Claudia, let's start with you. Just give us first of all your broad read on this number. Directionally, it still feels right. But then you've got this oil issue. And I don't know how much of an issue it is going to be going forward and feeding through to the core number.CLAUDIA SAHM: The oil issue, the higher gas prices, this should be a reminder to all of us that the Fed is not in charge of inflation. These are geopolitical events that are driving energy prices. And so I think it's just a good reminder of today is not all about the Fed in terms of policy responses.It is a big deal. It's a big deal for families. It is a necessity good. So that's very disconcerting. And yet, we do see over the past months some real relief in terms of inflation coming down in a steady way across other categories.Story continuesBRAD SMITH: And Yelena, would love to get your perspective on this as well. So if it is more geopolitically driven, then when can or should we expect any of the, at least, gasoline or energy-related inflation puts that are within this report and continuing to show up in the numbers? When should we expect that to abate?YELENA MALEYEV: Well, we've actually already started to see some of those relief from inflation numbers coming in over the last few months. Remember, energy prices peaked in June of last year. So the lowest hanging fruit on that inflation relief have already been picked. So we have been seeing an overall deceleration. Just a few months of increase gas or energy prices does not a trend yet make.And I agree with Claudia. This is not up to the Fed to influence, especially food and energy prices. The question is going forward, whether or not those prices are going to be bled through, embedded through to other categories. That's what is the concern here. And that's what we didn't see in the 2010s when energy prices were increasing.So that's what officials will be paying attention to going forward in future months to see if those costs are going into other costs as well.JULIE HYMAN: How do we know if they will, Claudia? What does history tell us about the speed with which some of these energy costs feed through to other types of prices? And what do we watch to see whether it's going to happen again this time?CLAUDIA SAHM: Yelena is absolutely correct. This relationship has not been a stable one over time. As with many things of inflation, we just watch. When you see these big reactions in energy intensive sectors, like the airlines, transportation, it makes sense that we see it there. There are other places where it could be. But, in general, the thought is that quote, unquote, "pass through" how much energy prices affect other prices is relatively small.And, again, we are past the really big increases in these prices, which we saw last year. And frankly, there wasn't that much evidence of big effects outside of energy then.BRAD SMITH: Looking at some of the areas where we did see, at least, some decreases, at least, in certain index. Lodging away from home, used cars and trucks, recreation among some of the indexes that did decrease over the month. If you're a consumer looking at this data that's come out this morning, Yelena, what should your broader read be on it?YELENA MALEYEV: Well, most consumers are really impacted by things like food and energy prices. So those are the things they're going to be looking at, first and foremost. But then that will potentially impact their decision on spending on other things. So whether they think about taking vacations, taking airfares, buying airfares versus taking their car when they're traveling.And so these are the kinds of decisions that households have to make when inflation is still really high. Remember, we're talking about inflation, which is the change in prices. The actual level of prices is still increasing. Those price levels are still higher than a year ago and higher than two years ago. And that's really squeezing consumer wallets.And when we've only recently seen wages actually coming up higher in terms of growth rates, higher than inflation only recently in the last few months, households have been getting squeezed for a while. So this silver lining, really, is that might temper some spending on other goods and other services, which would help bring down the underlying inflation pressures. But the food and energy definitely help drive the consumer decisions, especially when prices are still high.]

column4: Gas prices surged in August amid oil's supply crunch
column10: [Energy prices, specifically gasoline, were the biggest culprit of August's hotter than expected inflation print. The Bureau of Labor Statistic's Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 3.7% on year-over-year basis in August, topping economist expectations of 3.6%."The index for gasoline was the largest contributor to the monthly all-items increase, accounting for over half of the increase," read the CPI release.The energy index rose 5.6% in August from the prior month, a sharp re-acceleration from a 0.1% increase in July, as oil prices rallied and prices at the pump hit 2023 highs. The gasoline index saw the biggest price increase among the energy components, with a 10.6% rise in August on a monthly basis, following a 0.2% increase in July.Across the board all the energy components saw a month-over-month increase in prices. Electricity rose 0.2% in August after decreasing 0.7% in July. Natural gas jumped 0.1% over the month, following a 2% increase in July. Fuel oil also rose by 9.1% in the last month.Despite the month-over-month rise, the energy index is down 3.6% when compared to 12 months ago. All of the components within the sector, except for electricity, are down on a year-over-year basis.Oil's is on a three-month rally, up around 30% since late June amid a tight supply squeeze following OPEC+ production cuts and unilateral output reductions extended by Saudi Arabia and Russia.Gas prices climbed in August, pushing up the inflation rate. REUTERS/Bing Guan"The math is simple — declining supply and rising demand equal higher prices," Adam Turnquist, chief technical strategist for LPL Financial, recently wrote in a note to investors.West Texas Intermediate (CL=F) crossed $89 per barrel on Wednesday. column4: Oil prices hit 2023 highs as market faces supply squeeze
column10: [Oil prices hit new 2023 highs on Tuesday amid a supply crunch resulting from output reductions by Saudi Arabia and Russia.West Texas Intermediate (CL=F) hovered just below $89 per barrel in midday trading. Brent crude futures (BZ=F) sat above $91 per barrel. column4: Inflation: Could higher gas prices be good?
column10: [Could higher gas prices actually be a beneficial factor in the Federal Reserve's fight against inflation? Gas prices are largely behind that jump, with prices spiking nearly 11%.Let's bring in Yahoo Finance's Josh Schafer to discuss more. And so that's normally what we focus on. But I've been sort of struck by the gas price increase and what that means for headlines. So what I'm sitting next to you right now is that headline inflation number-- the overall CPI number, where you can see we had our nice little uptick over the last two months, coming up to 3.7% over the last month.And then when you take a look at gas prices, you can see-- oil prices rather, and how that translates to gas prices, you can see a similar uptick in what that means. And so what we've been looking at is what gas prices actually mean for the fight against inflation and what economists have to say about that.So Morgan Stanley said this could actually be a positive overall in the fight against inflation, specifically for the Fed and here's why. So if you take a look at how gas prices pass through core CPI versus overall CPI, the purple lines we have here is headline CPI. column4: Investors are ignoring surging energy inflation at their own peril: Morning Brief

column4: CPI report: Rising gas prices a 'big deal for families'
column10: [August's CPI report illustrates prices rising 0.6% month-over-month alongside inflation gains of 3.7% year-over-year. Rising gas prices and energy costs have been cited as key drivers in inflation bearing down on consumers. KPMG Senior Economist Yelena Maleyev and Sahm Consulting Founder Claudia Sahm — who is also a former Federal Reserve Board economist — join Yahoo Finance Live to break down August's data and analyze what is behind the trends in energy prices."This should be a reminder to all of us that the Fed is not in charge of inflation. These are geopolitical events that are driving energy prices and this is a good reminder that today, it is not all about the Fed in terms of policy responses," Sahm states.Maleyev referred to peaks in energy prices in June 2022 as the "lowest-hanging fruit" for inflation relief that has already been picked: "We have been seeing an overall deceleration, just a few months of increased gas or energy prices does not a trend yet make."Video TranscriptJULIE HYMAN: Let's talk more about the implications of these numbers, how to read them, what it could mean for the Federal Reserve, as well. We're joined by Claudia Sahm, consulting founder. And Yelena Maleyev, KPMG economist. Thanks to you both for being here.Claudia, let's start with you. Just give us first of all your broad read on this number. Directionally, it still feels right. But then you've got this oil issue. And I don't know how much of an issue it is going to be going forward and feeding through to the core number.CLAUDIA SAHM: The oil issue, the higher gas prices, this should be a reminder to all of us that the Fed is not in charge of inflation. These are geopolitical events that are driving energy prices. And so I think it's just a good reminder of today is not all about the Fed in terms of policy responses.It is a big deal. It's a big deal for families. It is a necessity good. So that's very disconcerting. And yet, we do see over the past months some real relief in terms of inflation coming down in a steady way across other categories.Story continuesBRAD SMITH: And Yelena, would love to get your perspective on this as well. So if it is more geopolitically driven, then when can or should we expect any of the, at least, gasoline or energy-related inflation puts that are within this report and continuing to show up in the numbers? When should we expect that to abate?YELENA MALEYEV: Well, we've actually already started to see some of those relief from inflation numbers coming in over the last few months. Remember, energy prices peaked in June of last year. So the lowest hanging fruit on that inflation relief have already been picked. So we have been seeing an overall deceleration. Just a few months of increase gas or energy prices does not a trend yet make.And I agree with Claudia. This is not up to the Fed to influence, especially food and energy prices. The question is going forward, whether or not those prices are going to be bled through, embedded through to other categories. That's what is the concern here. And that's what we didn't see in the 2010s when energy prices were increasing.So that's what officials will be paying attention to going forward in future months to see if those costs are going into other costs as well.JULIE HYMAN: How do we know if they will, Claudia? What does history tell us about the speed with which some of these energy costs feed through to other types of prices? And what do we watch to see whether it's going to happen again this time?CLAUDIA SAHM: Yelena is absolutely correct. This relationship has not been a stable one over time. As with many things of inflation, we just watch. When you see these big reactions in energy intensive sectors, like the airlines, transportation, it makes sense that we see it there. There are other places where it could be. But, in general, the thought is that quote, unquote, "pass through" how much energy prices affect other prices is relatively small.And, again, we are past the really big increases in these prices, which we saw last year. And frankly, there wasn't that much evidence of big effects outside of energy then.BRAD SMITH: Looking at some of the areas where we did see, at least, some decreases, at least, in certain index. Lodging away from home, used cars and trucks, recreation among some of the indexes that did decrease over the month. If you're a consumer looking at this data that's come out this morning, Yelena, what should your broader read be on it?YELENA MALEYEV: Well, most consumers are really impacted by things like food and energy prices. So those are the things they're going to be looking at, first and foremost. But then that will potentially impact their decision on spending on other things. So whether they think about taking vacations, taking airfares, buying airfares versus taking their car when they're traveling.And so these are the kinds of decisions that households have to make when inflation is still really high. Remember, we're talking about inflation, which is the change in prices. The actual level of prices is still increasing. Those price levels are still higher than a year ago and higher than two years ago. And that's really squeezing consumer wallets.And when we've only recently seen wages actually coming up higher in terms of growth rates, higher than inflation only recently in the last few months, households have been getting squeezed for a while. So this silver lining, really, is that might temper some spending on other goods and other services, which would help bring down the underlying inflation pressures. But the food and energy definitely help drive the consumer decisions, especially when prices are still high.]

column4: Gas prices surged in August amid oil's supply crunch
column10: [Energy prices, specifically gasoline, were the biggest culprit of August's hotter than expected inflation print. The Bureau of Labor Statistic's Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 3.7% on year-over-year basis in August, topping economist expectations of 3.6%."The index for gasoline was the largest contributor to the monthly all-items increase, accounting for over half of the increase," read the CPI release.The energy index rose 5.6% in August from the prior month, a sharp re-acceleration from a 0.1% increase in July, as oil prices rallied and prices at the pump hit 2023 highs. The gasoline index saw the biggest price increase among the energy components, with a 10.6% rise in August on a monthly basis, following a 0.2% increase in July.Across the board all the energy components saw a month-over-month increase in prices. Electricity rose 0.2% in August after decreasing 0.7% in July. Natural gas jumped 0.1% over the month, following a 2% increase in July. Fuel oil also rose by 9.1% in the last month.Despite the month-over-month rise, the energy index is down 3.6% when compared to 12 months ago. All of the components within the sector, except for electricity, are down on a year-over-year basis.Oil's is on a three-month rally, up around 30% since late June amid a tight supply squeeze following OPEC+ production cuts and unilateral output reductions extended by Saudi Arabia and Russia.Gas prices climbed in August, pushing up the inflation rate. column10: [Energy prices, specifically gasoline, were the biggest culprit of August's hotter than expected inflation print.
